dt-69k.spoken: After the knight goes to c2, the rook is boxed in and can't find active play. The bishops cooperate: one guards the pawn while the other controls the squares in front of it, so White struggles to make headway.

dt-69p.spoken: White's b5 lets Black's king slip into d4, cracking the fortress. Black follows with knight d6 and bishop e3, threatening to take on d2 and then step the king to c3.

dt-69e.spoken: Black plays g5 to force a decision from the bishop. If it drops back to g3, it abandons the vital f4 square, the one that keeps the d4 pawn in check. If the bishop grabs c7, it walks off the f4 diagonal entirely.

dt-68z.spoken: White plays the Carlsen game: one move at a time, each move creating problems, survive another move, and wait for time pressure to force an error.

dt-692.spoken: Black's bishop can jump to d5, attacking the knight and forcing b3. That shows Black's pieces are getting active and creating threats.

dt-691.spoken: Pushing f5 now is a mistake — White answers f3, robbing Black’s bishop of its squares and leaving Black’s pawns fragile.

dt-69z.spoken: Black’s e6 is coming, and then g5 hits hard. It offers a knight trade and reshapes the pawns, while the e5-pawn locks down f6 and d6, those key squares for Black.

dt-6a3.spoken: When the opponent is thinking, build general plans and positional understanding instead of calculating variations. This is the Russian School method — calculate on your own time, and on theirs focus on typical ideas and motifs.

dt-695.spoken: Bishop to e3 opens the king's route to safety and sets up threats like the knight landing on e3 with check to win the rook.

dt-6a1.spoken: The rook goes to d8 instead of the bishop to b7. That leaves a7 weak for the long run — the knight can hop to a3 and then b5, hitting a7 and eyeing d6.

dt-68t.spoken: After g6, the knight ends up awkward on the rim. Black moves the king to g7, dodging a fork on f7 and staying connected to that knight.

dt-69q.spoken: The fortress is a defensive structure that cannot be broken into, blocking all progress. Here, Black's fortress collapses the moment White's king lands on d4, stopping the opponent from regrouping.

dt-68y.spoken: White eyes the fianchetto to b7, aiming for tactics down the long diagonal, while a queen trade into the endgame favors White's passer and active pieces, making it no easy task for Black.

dt-69h.spoken: The bishop on b4 is the better piece, not the knight, because it controls d2 right in front of the pawn and stops White from advancing it. The knight on b4 only guards the pawn, not the square ahead.

dt-69d.spoken: Black gives up the pawn on c7 to throw everything at the d4 passed pawn, and that pawn is Black's main counterplay. White's pieces stay tied down blockading it, so Black's activity makes up for the missing material.

dt-6a0.spoken: After the knights come off and Black's bishop settles on b7, queen g4 packs a punch—it eyes h6 once Black castles, hammering the weak f6 square. Black can't answer with bishop f6, because the pawn on e5 controls that spot.

dt-69x.spoken: Black's b6 threatens setup with e6 and Be7, consolidating. White must strike now with d4, opening the center — this may be the last opportunity.

dt-69i.spoken: Black's king on e6 stops White from playing Bd6, which would trade bishops and then rooks, leaving Black with fewer pieces and a worse endgame.

dt-69v.spoken: Hold Rc1 in reserve—with the queen on e6, Black's kingside development is already cramped. Playing Rc1 now just pushes the queen back to d7, which solves Black's problem. Keep the queenside pressure going with a5.

dt-69t.spoken: White aims to trade that bishop on e6 and gain tempi, forcing Black's queen to move and delaying his kingside development.

cb-a.spoken: The early pawn thrusts leave the knight stranded without defense.

dt-6ae.spoken: White's pawn grip cramps Black's development, and the key is to stop Black from castling while targeting the weak b5 square.

cb-3.spoken: With a full piece extra, every trade helps. Fewer enemy pieces mean less counterplay, and converting the material becomes simpler.

cb-m.spoken: The rook enters the game after the trade, and the bishop comes alive. The advanced pawn holds vital squares and feeds the attack.

dt-6a7.spoken: White’s pieces cover the queenside, center, and kingside, squeezing Black from every direction. That kind of dominance usually decides the game unless a blunder slips in.

cb-i.spoken: The exposed king turns every pin into a weapon. Once the queen finishes its job, redeploy it to a central or active square where it joins the attack and creates fresh threats.

cb-k.spoken: The pin turns the enemy piece into a wall. Push the wall forward, and the back rank mate appears on the other side.

cb-l.spoken: Control of the key central square is the whole fight. Cover it with your pieces, and the opponent never gets to stand there.

dt-6a8.spoken: Black's king is exposed, so that's where the focus moves. A quick check on h5 fails to g6, and the piece falls.

cb-g.spoken: Trading a bishop for a knight pays off when it cracks the position open and wakes up the queen and rook. Losing the bishop is worth it when the open files and diagonals fuel a real attack.

cb-1.spoken: A pawn push invites the knight to grab bait. When it takes, lines open and waiting pieces swarm in, making the attack unstoppable.

cb-8.spoken: The backward pawn on the open file urges the central break, but the real plan points the other way. Playing on the queenside, not the center, is the correct response.

dt-6ah.spoken: Trading queens favors White because the a7 pawn is weak and Black's kingside pieces are still at home. The knight heads for the b5 outpost to hammer a7; if Black stops that, it goes to c4, eyeing Ne5+.

cb-2.spoken: The knight develops to the second rank first, blocking a knight jump that would hit the bishop. That is prophylaxis — stop the threat before it starts.

cb-b.spoken: The winning side comes out ahead in development with the enemy king still in the center. The queen threatens mate and targets soft pawns, while the bishop cuts off castling.

cb-4.spoken: The pawn thrust attacks the knight directly, and the knight must flee or be taken. That single push starts the attack rolling without any need to soften the target first.

dt-6a4.spoken: Once Black retreats the bishop, it signals full retreat. White eyes Rd1, pinning the queen and threatening c4 — but caution is needed. If Black answers with Nf6, capturing the knight leaves the rooks exposed. The position brims with tactical chances.

cb-6.spoken: The knight jumps into that central square, and you must judge it at once, especially with your king castled. It tempts you to capture, but the trade is welcome; the f-pawn recaptures and your position improves.

dt-6ai.spoken: After Black plays e6, White can try Nb5, a key idea. That knight hits a7 and hands White a small but lasting edge.

cb-n.spoken: The bishop stands too far off to arrive in time, so the focus turns to swinging the rook to the third rank for the assault. The pawn on the fifth file locks down vital squares and anchors the whole plan.

cb-h.spoken: The bishop stays home in the Stonewall, not venturing out as in the London. So any bishop sortie is off-system and threatens nothing.

cb-5.spoken: In the Stonewall, the quiet pawn push often matters more than developing the knight, because it keeps the enemy knight off the annoying square.

cb-c.spoken: The pawn push is a mistake; trading the light-squared bishop was the better plan. The knight is already a problem, and the pawn thrust forces it back, stopping the knight from coming out and the pawn from advancing.

cb-9.spoken: When the opponent pushes the kingside pawn early in the Stonewall, that weakens the king's shelter. It invites a quick thrust with your own kingside pawn, and that opens lines for tactics—pinning the knight and threatening the queen on the rim.

cb-0.spoken: In the Stonewall, Black's worst position comes when their own pieces block both central pawn breaks. With no way to advance, they sit passively while White's flank push targets their king.

dt-6ab.spoken: White’s a-pawn is already on the seventh rank, effectively a passed pawn and a decisive edge. Black’s pieces are scattered, and the rook on b7 pins Black down. The plan is to bring the rook into play and push that pawn home.

cb-e.spoken: The pawn is the backbone of the Stonewall, keeping the central square out of enemy hands and propping up the knight. Letting it advance would surrender that grip; leave it in place and find play elsewhere.

cb-o.spoken: The pinned piece holds the line, so a pawn push toward the edge creates a real threat. Taking on the open file with rook and bishop backfires, because a single check down that line turns the tables. Advance the pawn instead.

cb-10.spoken: Pawns that can't advance turn into weaknesses or block your own pieces, so they need support or a trade.

cb-z.spoken: The king stepping into the fight is the right defensive idea, and it keeps the opponent in the game.

cb-w.spoken: The rook is boxed in on the back rank, and the opponent's reply is forced — after that, a full piece falls.

cb-x.spoken: The king joins the fight, which is right, but the pawns are stuck. Trading pieces is the way to turn the advantage into a win.

cb-1k.spoken: Up a piece, the win still isn't certain because the rook hasn't entered the game. The opponent may still hand us more mistakes.

cb-1y.spoken: The knight on that central outpost is the anchor. The bishop behind it gives support, and the pawn push becomes the lever to reinforce or build threats.

cb-15.spoken: Black often answers c3 with Nc6, and White can try Bb5 or other moves, keeping the pawn chain and developing naturally.

cb-1m.spoken: The bishop holds a critical square, so the tactic that works without a defender fails here. The queen threatens capture, forcing the knight to respond, and then the pawn advance traps the bishop.

cb-1t.spoken: Waiting moves gift the opponent time to reorganize. When a bishop slides to its ideal square, the position turns in their favor.

cb-1i.spoken: The king steps forward and the knight hangs, but the knight slips to safety, and the trade leaves you a piece up.

cb-13.spoken: Promoting several pawns to bishops and lining them up to deliver mate is a rare trick, impractical but a fine show of imagination.

cb-1n.spoken: The pawn wall cramps the bishop's activity. The f-pawn push is a double-edged moment—it becomes a weakness or a strength purely by how the opponent answers.

cb-1v.spoken: The h-pawn push creates kingside space and attacking potential. Even if the opponent seeks trades, the advance keeps its value.

cb-1e.spoken: The knight jumps to the central outpost, creating a mate threat. The opponent must answer with the pawn push, which leaves the d-pawn backward and weak.

cb-1u.spoken: When both sides pick the same opening, the game slips into symmetrical structures where tiny differences decide. One small deviation — a pawn to the fifth instead of the usual move — leaves dark-square weaknesses behind.

cb-1l.spoken: In the King's Gambit, accepting the pawn is the standard reply. Against rare lines, general principles beat memorized preparation.

cb-16.spoken: A knight landing on that outpost square faces a pawn thrust that chases it off. If the knight has no escape, the pawn wins it outright.

cb-1q.spoken: The doubled pawns share the bishop’s color, and that advantage decides the game. The long maneuver finally nets a pawn, then the grind continues with careful moves to sidestep stalemate.

cb-17.spoken: The king steps to the corner, shielding the pawn while dodging back-rank threats. The queen stays free to work the kingside.

cb-1o.spoken: A wall of pawns seals the diagonal and strangles the bishop's range, freeing the knight to reroute through the center.

cb-18.spoken: The bishops work as a pair in the endgame, controlling every square in their path. When the opponent has no counterplay, their coordination tightens into a net that forces threats the defense cannot answer.

cb-1z.spoken: The bishop is gone, and the position has no rhythm. With the king exposed and several moves to choose from, none of them fixes the real problem — the missing piece leaves the defense hollow.

cb-11.spoken: The center is unresolved, so decide: capture or develop. But before committing, check the counterstrike in the center.

cb-1s.spoken: The player salvages a draw with the only move that holds. Taking the pawn with check looks natural but loses. Any other try, like the bishop or rook stepping in, hands the win to the opponent.

cb-q.spoken: The early queen probe is met not with a pawn thrust that invites a central counterstrike, but with a quiet support move. When the center pawns are exchanged symmetrically, the position simplifies, and White keeps the cleaner path to center and kingside play.

cb-6j.spoken: The extra piece and pawn is the whole game. Trade pieces freely, liquidate into a winning endgame, and chase the knight with pawns until it has to trade on your terms.

cb-66.spoken: The bishop settles on the long diagonal in the London, rare but playable. White either pushes the c-pawn or lets the bishop come out and trades. Pushing is the sharper choice, leaving Black with a cramped structure, like a worse French.

cb-84.spoken: Overconfidence sees just enough to miscalculate.

cb-82.spoken: The endgame may hold a forced win, but the clock makes it untouchable.

cb-7i.spoken: The bishop hides at the edge to dodge harassment, settle into the ideal setup, and clear the path for castling.

cb-7f.spoken: In time pressure, use your clock when several moves make sense, not when only one is legal. Keep the saved seconds for a real decision, not a forced sequence.

cb-7u.spoken: The exposed king leaves little room for loose pawn pushes. Seize the bishop pair, then turn on the queenside with a pawn advance that creates threats.

cb-83.spoken: Respect every opponent, regardless of rating. A surprising move can come from anyone, so never assume.

cb-7s.spoken: The dark-squared bishop is trapped behind its own pawns. Tuck it away on a safe diagonal, and if the enemy pawn advances, the light-squared bishop is ready to trade.

cb-7v.spoken: The exposed king invites a tempting capture, but the safe route reaches the same goal without the risk.

cb-7w.spoken: The gambit pawn comes with a check, so take it first, then reinforce the e-file against the coming attack.

cb-89.spoken: When every arrow points at their king and none at yours, the position favors you.

cb-7l.spoken: The attack doesn't stop after winning a piece. Bring the queen, push the pawn, and lift the rook to add more firepower. The opponent must respect the mate threat on the back rank.

cb-85.spoken: A pawn to the side gains space and invites the queen to exchange. If she takes, the resulting structure favors you.

cb-87.spoken: Tenacious defense is an instinct, not a plan. Holding on delays the loss, but it never changes the verdict.

cb-7r.spoken: The bishop pins and attacks, but the queen steps out with counterplay against the knight. Retreating the bishop along the diagonal keeps everything safe—the pawn is already won, and the extra material stays secure.

cb-7k.spoken: A weak knight sits on the rim, and pushing the pawn beside it attacks it directly. If the opponent defends with a pawn push, the bishop captures that pawn, and the pawn push still wins the knight.

cb-8k.spoken: The pawn recapture keeps the center sound. Grabbing back with the knight breaks opening principles and demands precise play through the complications.

cb-7y.spoken: The material edge turns into a slow squeeze. Each false hope costs the opponent another mistake, and the relay keeps stretching until the win is unavoidable.

cb-7e.spoken: The bishop pins the knight to the queen, so the defender cannot move the knight without losing the queen. This gives the attacker a free tempo to strengthen the center.

cb-8j.spoken: In the endgame, activate the rook and take no unnecessary risks. A won pawn is worthless if the king stays exposed to mate.

cb-88.spoken: A quiet pawn move in this opening is low-energy and apologetic. It dodges the theory but hands over the tempo.

cb-7q.spoken: The knight's early arrival leaves the d-pawn exposed, since that square is no longer available to support it. Pushing the c-pawn challenges the center and targets that weakness directly.

cb-7h.spoken: The pawn advance prevents the queenside pawn break that gives Black counterplay. Even without that threat, it is a sound prophylactic move, especially alongside the c-pawn, to restrict Black's space on that flank.

cb-8p.spoken: The extra piece only pays if it joins the fight. Bring the bishop out to an active square, where it creates threats and pressure.

cb-86.spoken: A bare king gets no rest. Drive it forward with checks and forcing moves until the net closes, and the mating attack lands.

cb-7n.spoken: A king shuffle in a lost endgame can look brilliant to the engine, since every move may be the best in the position. That inflates your accuracy score without real skill.

cb-81.spoken: The eye skips what the queen protects and what the bishop's long diagonal covers. That hanging pawn is still hanging — the board just hides it.

cb-8i.spoken: When the knight threatens a strong square, clumsy defensive moves leave you passive. Find a proactive move that also blocks that outpost.

cb-7x.spoken: The knight hops in to trap the queen, and the opponent misses it. A quiet move to guard the key square is tempting, but the safe route keeps control. When the opponent rushes, the pressure cracks them open, and the attack wins.

cb-7z.spoken: The knight-and-pawn formation is a pleasing prize, but it costs material. Chasing the trophy while your opponent hunts your king concedes the initiative and leaves you exposed.

cb-8l.spoken: The king stuck in the center with the kingside undeveloped is a target. The queen steps out, the rook lifts, a pawn break strikes — each move creates an immediate threat.

cb-8n.spoken: The bishop stays home while the knights come out, because Black's grip on the pawn is annoying to fight early. The bishop waits and later steps to its natural square.

cb-8b.spoken: The queen drifts to the edge on unrelated errands while the center goes unclaimed. The pawn that was meant to anchor the center now leaves it exposed, and a simple capture wins material.

cb-8o.spoken: The bishop comes out to pin, then the pawn kicks it. When the knight chases it once more, the bishop has nowhere safe to land, and the knight wins it outright. The real point: that light-squared bishop was never going to develop easily.

cb-7g.spoken: The stall wastes time, but the best reply is to stay calm and use the pause for deeper analysis. Do not enter the psychological fight.

cb-8d.spoken: In the endgame, when ahead on material with a healthier pawn chain, plain moves that cover every weakness and then advance a pawn to create a passer are enough.

cb-80.spoken: The knight on the seventh looks like the same idea as the knight fork, but the timing shifts with the opponent's reply, and the later square often proves the better one.

cb-7p.spoken: The bishop steps out early, but it does not pressure the center, so the pawn advance comes at once. The knight lunge looks scary, yet the weak point is easy to defend, and the threat fades.

cb-8a.spoken: Supporting the center pawn with the bishop first is the key idea. Once the bishop is developed and the pawn exchange happens, another pawn step guards the center and keeps it from falling.

cb-8c.spoken: The pawn grab leaves doubled pawns as wreckage. Post the bishop where it eyes the knight’s outposts, then push the f-pawn to challenge that knight, and swing the bishop to its best diagonal.

cb-7j.spoken: When the opponent lags in development, prying open the center punishes them. Plant the rook on the open file, and the knight finds its perfect outpost.

cb-8h.spoken: The trade of light-squared bishop for knight keeps material equal but damages the pawn chain. The doubled isolated pawns left behind become a lasting structural weakness.

cb-7t.spoken: The early pawn push invites the bishop trade, and White takes it. Removing that defender strips the kingside and leaves the dark squares weak.

cb-7o.spoken: The bishop is the target of an early knight raid. Pushing the h-pawn denies the knight its strong squares, or you may simply accept the trade. If the opponent later pushes the f-pawn, the knight's retreat is gone and the raid proves costly.

cb-8q.spoken: The bishop slides forward along the diagonal, and once it lands, good things tend to happen—often including a sacrifice.

cb-8x.spoken: The trapped queen gets chased off, then traded, and the endgame simplifies to a winning extra piece.

cb-9i.spoken: Material up, trade pieces. Queens especially — less counterplay, simpler conversion.

cb-9g.spoken: The isolated, unsupported piece is a target. Develop an attack against it instead of rushing to capture.

cb-9x.spoken: A protected passed pawn, backed by its pawn chain, is a decisive asset that often wins the game on its own.

cb-a0.spoken: A bishop with no safe squares is a prize. Trap it, and the material falls into your hands.

cb-9n.spoken: When the enemy king is exposed, improve your pieces and open lines to build mating threats — no need to calculate every variation.

cb-9j.spoken: An open g-file points at the castled king. Pressure builds down that line, so reposition pieces or castle to safety before the attack lands.

cb-98.spoken: Doubling the pawns with a bishop capture is almost always worth it — the structure weakens, and the position becomes easy to play.

cb-9k.spoken: The game is not over when you lose. A loss leaves points on the board that are yours to reclaim, and that is the stronger position.

cb-9v.spoken: The queen trade costs a pawn, so sidestep it. If the opponent grabs in a certain way, a staircase checkmate is on the board.

cb-8u.spoken: The win is secured, but the work is not done. Shore up the pawns, watch the open file, and give the king his square before it becomes a problem.

cb-9m.spoken: When you're ahead, the win doesn't need fireworks. Develop to natural squares, control the center, and let the material advantage convert itself.

cb-9w.spoken: Up a piece, trade pieces. Each exchange simplifies the board, strips away counterplay, and eases the conversion.

cb-9y.spoken: The rook smells the exposed king. If it can reach the key square, the net closes and mate follows.

cb-9t.spoken: The knight looks stranded, but there is no hurry to take it. Keep the bishop active and retreat it to guard the critical squares instead.

cb-8v.spoken: The bishop takes its natural square outside the pawn chain, and the queen's quick sortie hits two weak points at once, forcing a defense that cannot cover both.

cb-8s.spoken: The pawn is won, but the game is not. Trading queens and waking the bishop only consolidates the gain; the bishop finds its long diagonal and the position firms up.

cb-99.spoken: The knight that jumps forward too soon lands without support, and the attack turns into a target.

cb-9d.spoken: Up material, trade pieces. Simplify the position, deny the opponent any counterplay, and conversion stays winning even against solid defense.

cb-9r.spoken: The rook finds an open file and presses on the weak pawns. The queen joins in, and the knight on its outpost anchors the attack.

cb-94.spoken: The pawn stays loose on purpose. Development and the center come first; the pawn gets defended only after the kingside pressure is answered.

cb-92.spoken: The knight grabs the pawn, and both sides end up with hanging pawns. When the bishop comes out, the knight strikes again, attacking it and winning a pawn.

cb-9s.spoken: The bishop is safe on its square, so White chases the queen with pawns and gains ground. A later edge pawn stops the pin, and Black's knight sits stranded on the rim.

cb-95.spoken: The center is secured, and the long diagonal has done its work. Now the bishop redeploys to develop, while the queen steps out to attack the weak pawn on the far flank.

cb-93.spoken: The endgame pawn race belongs to the faster king or the faster pawns. Break through with strong maneuvering, and spend time wisely—it decides the win.

cb-9q.spoken: The d-pawn advance stakes out space in the center. Against a passive setup, the plan is straightforward: develop the bishop, castle, and land a knight on the e-file to pressure the pawn.

cb-9e.spoken: The king is exposed, and the extra pawn means the endgame favors the stronger side. Checks push the enemy king forward, while rook maneuvers sidestep knight forks and create mating threats that win material.

cb-8r.spoken: The pawn push at the edge creates a nasty bind. If Black responds on the same wing, the knight leaps and the pawn advances to fork pieces and win material. The quiet capture that rescues the bishop is the right move, but it is easy to miss.

cb-9c.spoken: The flank pawn lunge strikes at the center pawn immediately and also denies the bishop its aggressive square. That setup sidesteps the early checkmate threats while pressing on Black's center.

cb-9z.spoken: A development lead turns into attack when you open a file.

cb-9l.spoken: The early h-pawn push stops the pin before it starts, a quiet prophylactic that saves the bishop from being traded off.

cb-9f.spoken: The opponent may blunder pieces, but a solid player rarely does. Even with a winning position, one mistake can let the advantage slip away, so convert carefully.

cb-8y.spoken: Fix the target pawn, take it, then advance your passed pawn while slicing the enemy king off from the defense, and the extra piece turns the endgame into a simple mate.

cb-9u.spoken: The plan is to push the pawn and gain space, but that push must be prepared. Once the pawn advances, the pawn behind it can become weak, so the bishop needs to land on the square that protects it.

cb-97.spoken: The opening's whole point is to target a pawn attacked twice and defended once. The defender tries to hold it and fails, or drops a piece along the way.

cb-8z.spoken: The center pawn advances boldly into enemy territory. Chasing a Queen's Gambit from this opening misfires and lands in inferior positions.

cb-8t.spoken: The knight is the key target, and the goal is to stop it from settling. Pushing the pawn to kick it works, but the capture that clears the diagonal invites the knight to that square instead.

cb-9a.spoken: The king sits exposed in the center while the bishop pair promises long-term strength. Prying open the position with the f- and e-pawns strikes at the unsafe king and the enemy's clumsy piece coordination.

cb-96.spoken: The extra pawn sits idle while the center and pressure do the work. Doubling rooks and pressing the light squares sets up a pin that wins the rook—and the pawn behind it hangs as well.

cb-a1.spoken: The knight on the natural developing square blocks the bishop's line. That lets the opponent strike at the king's wing or hit the queen, and the bishop stays undefended.

cb-9h.spoken: The king's second-rank pawn is exposed before castling, and enemy pieces aim at it from the diagonal and the file.

cb-9b.spoken: The trades simplify the position in your favor. You keep the extra rook and pawns, while your opponent's pieces keep running out of squares.

cb-8w.spoken: When Black pushes a pawn to challenge the center early, the Queen's Gambit is off the table. Push your own pawn forward instead and take a solid position, no need to pretend.

cb-b1.spoken: The knight escapes the pin and jumps forward, forcing a capture that opens the file and exposes the enemy king.

cb-a9.spoken: The pawn move creates a lasting weakness: it denies the knight its natural square and leaves the kingside exposed.

cb-aj.spoken: The knight retreats to a passive square, a clear sign of development trouble. We seize the initiative and turn the pressure onto the kingside.

cb-b5.spoken: Playing e3 here is a trap: if Black captures the knight on f3, White answers with Bb5, pinning the queen and threatening to win material. But it’s only a surprise weapon, not the strongest move.

cb-ab.spoken: In a symmetrical Stonewall, Black equalizes easily — White's attacking ideas run dry, and the extra move grants no real advantage.

cb-au.spoken: The pawn wants the checkmate itself, but the king slips to safety, and the dream dies.

cb-ae.spoken: When both pieces come under attack, saving the rook costs the bishop. The law of exchange rules: lose three, not five.

cb-bb.spoken: The wing pawn buys a central pawn, and the knight lands with tempo.

cb-ag.spoken: The knight's departure strips the bishop of its defender. When the bishop is taken, the recapture falls to a heavier piece, and that can get awkward.

cb-am.spoken: The rook hangs, and a bishop on the long diagonal threatens mate. Capturing into the center opens the f-file and leaves the king exposed.

cb-ac.spoken: The queen and knight attack runs out of steam when the defender responds accurately. Bring up more pieces or the attack fizzles.

cb-aq.spoken: After Black plays d5, White can't immediately go g5, and Black can't play g4 either. That locks down Black's pawn breaks, so counterplay is tough to create.

cb-b0.spoken: The knight on the outpost is immune to the dark-squared bishop, so it sits stable and dominates the board.

cb-ap.spoken: The knight lands on the rim, where a pawn push traps it. The opponent must retreat it or lose the piece outright.

cb-b7.spoken: The rook drifts into a poor square, and the opponent pays for it. Each attack on that rook gains time, and the pressure eventually wins material.

cb-an.spoken: The opponent trades their dark-squared bishop to remove the knight, but that gift leaves the dark squares exposed and the position weak.

cb-ad.spoken: The Stonewall only bites when pawn chains clash. If Black mirrors your structure, symmetry cancels your extra move and the opening's sting is gone.

cb-b4.spoken: In the English, if Black answers c4 e5 g3 with d5, White takes at once with cxd5. Waiting hands Black time to equalize or stir up counterplay.

cb-ah.spoken: The knight belongs on the active square, not the passive one. The pawn on the third rank opens the path, and from there the knight supports the center; the other square leaves it idle.

cb-ai.spoken: The knight sits in the center and locks out the enemy knight's best square. Forced back to its home corner, the opposing piece is out of play, and that grip makes the position hard to crack.

cb-a4.spoken: The knight is attacked but not taken. Sliding the queen to the edge threatens mate and exploits the broken kingside. Sometimes leaving that knight behind and sacrificing it turns into a sharp tactic.

cb-av.spoken: The queen on the back rank guards a key flight square, which lets the knight occupy the strong central outpost without material cost. That cover also frees a pawn push, unpins the knight, and feeds central play.

cb-ax.spoken: The pawn’s position decides whether the tactic works. With the pawn one square advanced, the queen and bishop can hit the knight at once and the win follows. With the pawn back a square, the same idea loses its immediate punch.

cb-aw.spoken: The pawn steps back instead of forward, an odd but sound choice. It leaves the center pawn able to advance later while keeping the Stonewall formation intact, with the bishop's diagonal opened and castling still on the table.

cb-b6.spoken: The knight sits as an overextended target, and the method is slow pressure, not a rush. Pawn attacks that come too early open the center to counterplay, so the patient build-up traps the piece without weakening the position.

cb-ba.spoken: The king is stalemated, so mate must be forced with pieces. Advance the pawns, coordinate the rook and bishop to tighten the net, but keep Black’s pawn and rook in mind — they prevent stalemate, so play with care.

cb-al.spoken: The dark-squared bishop is gone, a common gap in the Stonewall. That leaves the dark squares around the king exposed.

cb-b2.spoken: The knight sits as a magnet: Black must take it, which opens the f-file and lets the f-pawn push forward, hitting queen and bishop at once.

cb-b3.spoken: The knight on a dark square is immune to the bishop's attacks, and the extra material turns that safety into a winning position.

cb-a8.spoken: The bishop finds its strongest square, controlling the board from the center. If it lands with a threat of mate or material gain, it can be decisive—when the rook defends, the queen delivers mate on the spot.

cb-ay.spoken: The Stonewall player still aims for the push, whether the pawn goes forward or gets taken. The outpost on that square remains the key goal.

cb-aa.spoken: In the Stonewall setup, early knight development prevents the enemy knight from jumping to an annoying square. Once that knight lands, exchanges follow and White's attacking potential shrinks.

cb-a2.spoken: The pawn push is a distraction. Taking it opens your king's file and loosens the center. Decline the bait, keep the pawn guarding the knight's outpost, and proceed with the plan.

cb-a7.spoken: The knight is attacked. First ask if leaving it to die buys an attack. If not, retreat. Either way, the pawn push has left a hole behind it — a square that invites your own pawn forward.

cb-af.spoken: Starting with the quiet move first solidifies the center and prepares the pawn advance, which blocks the opponent's freeing break.

cb-a3.spoken: Recapture with the f-pawn to open the file for the rook and hold the center. Taking back with the c-pawn instead hands the opponent a strong central presence.

cb-a5.spoken: The f-pawn advance is the backbone of the Stonewall: it claims the central square and can shut out the enemy bishop or queen. But pushing it early is a risk — it invites the queen to a sharp attack or strands the bishop on its diagonal.

cb-b9.spoken: Trade pieces when ahead. After winning material, simplify by trading queens, then push the pawns to chase the knights, and threaten the bishop trade to win more.

cb-cn.spoken: The extra rook is real, but tangled pieces delay the payoff. Untangle and coordinate first, and only then does the material advantage start to bite.

cb-co.spoken: Offering the queen trade against an early queen sortie costs nothing. If the opponent declines, their threat evaporates and their development falls behind.

cb-c2.spoken: If your opponent plays c5, keep your pawn chain intact by playing e3. If their pawn goes to b5, challenge it with a4, opening lines for your pieces.

cb-bq.spoken: The queen recapture looks like the simpler way back to familiar ground, but it pulls the queen into the center and settles for the wrong opening shape.

cb-ce.spoken: The knight check drives the rook into a trap, and the queen sacrifice pays off. Black sheds major pieces, and White converts to a winning material edge.

cb-c5.spoken: The bishop owns the long diagonal and dictates the attack. Sacrificing the queen is justified when that bishop’s power outweighs the material.

cb-cc.spoken: The bishop pair is the prize when the opponent hands over the center. Use a quiet pawn push to force the trade, then the center pawns gain tempo and pressure.

cb-bo.spoken: The rook slides behind the d-pawn to support it, and that support lets the knight leap forward to the outpost.

cb-bs.spoken: The connected passed pawns advance together, while the opponent's passers are split. A pawn hangs, but no real threat exists, so the capture waits.

cb-bw.spoken: The bishop retreats with a purpose: it shifts to a stronger diagonal or attacks weaknesses. The position is so strong that it feels like everything must break through.

cb-bk.spoken: The knight jumps forward, but you don't have to take it right away. Step around and claim the squares it abandoned, keeping the pressure on.

cb-bz.spoken: The pawn push weakens the king's shelter. White's knight gains threats on both wings, and if the king steps to the corner, the attack lands at once.

cb-ca.spoken: White's pieces stand better and the center is his. With the opponent's forces misplaced, active play keeps the pressure on.

cb-cf.spoken: The central pawns advance, opening lines the opponent can use. With the bishop pair gone and development lagging, the position cracks under tactical pressure.

cb-cj.spoken: The pawn thrust traps the rook, leaving it no safe escape square, while the looming queen strike hits both queen and knight. White takes the rook and comes out ahead in material.

cb-cd.spoken: The bishop trades down for a knight, but the exchange favors White—the bishop is the far more active piece. That leaves the diagonal open, and White attacks the weak squares, pinning pieces and piling on threats.

cb-bp.spoken: The center pawns stake out space, and the plan is to hold them there. A quiet king move and a flank pawn push prepare the advance that keeps the space and locks the opponent out.

cb-br.spoken: The knight heads for an outpost square, but before trading bishop for rook, check the queen’s path — once the bishop leaves, that diagonal opens and the queen can strike.

cb-c8.spoken: The bishop gives itself up on the king's doorstep to punish a monarch still in the center and pieces left undefended, and the follow-up queen check forces a fatal choice.

cb-c7.spoken: When the opponent's king sits in the center and you hold more space, a pawn storm on the wing gains real force. A quiet pawn move can block a knight from jumping in and prepares the break you want to launch.

cb-ck.spoken: The extra rook does not end the job—the king still needs a safe square before the pieces can untangle. Moving the king to the safer edge avoids the queen's forking threats, and once a pawn falls, the queen relocates to clear the path for the rook.

cb-bi.spoken: The early pawn thrust invites White to take the center with both pawns. The forward pawn eyes the key square, so Black cannot challenge the center. The structure stays solid, and Black's queen wanders, losing time.

cb-bm.spoken: The seventh rank turns into a decisive weakness. A rook parked there pins down the enemy king and collects material.

cb-bx.spoken: The position has no dark-square bishop, and the knight on that outpost is holding everything together — the attack expected a full collapse and found none.

cb-cg.spoken: Black locks the center, castles, and builds a kingside attack. Opening the center instead costs a bishop, leaves development behind, and exposes the king to tactics.

cb-bg.spoken: The pawn looks loose, but taking it leaves the bishop hanging. Blocking with the pawn gains the knight squares, yet the move is better saved — castling first keeps every option open.

cb-bt.spoken: A knight with no retreat and no pawn breaks is already a problem: the position will not open itself.

cb-bh.spoken: The pawn advances to block the bishop and deny the knight its squares. Well-defended, it shrugs off attack; the knight slides behind it to guard.

cb-c0.spoken: The winning move order matters: capture first, then attack. The queen takes the pawn, and the follow-up check forces the pawn to step forward, trapping the piece.

cb-bu.spoken: The knight must answer that pawn thrust at once, or Black seizes full control. Strike back immediately, and if Black still sets up, White is in serious trouble.

cb-c9.spoken: The bishop and knight are out early, but the enemy blocks a quick expansion. Push the f-pawn to force the center open, then the dark-squared bishop comes alive. Meanwhile, the enemy knight sits on the rim, while your whole army is ready.

cb-bl.spoken: When the enemy king is exposed, every attacker counts more than any pawn. Bring another piece to the open file—the king's safety outweighs all material.

cb-by.spoken: The bishop points at the corner, tempting the capture. But opening the file lets Black's pieces swarm down it.

cb-cp.spoken: The bishops pin the enemy knights, and a protected passed pawn caps the position. Now look for any capture or threat that presses the pinned pieces harder.

cb-c3.spoken: The outside passed pawn is decisive here. The extra pawn and active bishops let the king escort it forward while enemy pieces stay tied down.

cb-ch.spoken: The knight hop looks tempting, but Black has natural ways to blunt it. White instead pushes both center pawns and seizes the center before castling.

cb-c4.spoken: The setup requires tracking three threats: a knight jumping to the center, a pawn advance there, and a knight invading on the other flank. If the pawn push is not urgent, hold back the bishop and answer the other two with quiet pawn moves.

cb-cq.spoken: Once the win is in hand, pre-moving and trading down locks it in, especially when the clock is tight.

cb-dz.spoken: Three connected pawns rolling forward, the rook backing them, the king safe behind — that formation is powerful and often unstoppable.

cb-d2.spoken: In a rook endgame, the extra pawn means fight with the rook, not the pawns. Avoid needless pawn moves and activate the rook to cut off the enemy king.

cb-db.spoken: The bishop on the third rank cuts through to the corner, pinning the king in place and threatening mate.

cb-e0.spoken: When the opponent gives up a rook for a single pawn, the trade is only good if your extra passed pawns can march home and win the king and pawn endgame.

cb-ds.spoken: The queen's retreat gives you the green light. Push the wing pawn to choke the opponent's pieces, then keep pressing the attack.

cb-d8.spoken: That queen sortie looks strange, but it is not a trap. The queen has escape squares and aggressive ideas behind it. Black simply declines the bait.

cb-dj.spoken: The missing b-pawn opens an early path for the queen. That unusual setup creates tactical chances that would not exist otherwise.

cb-cz.spoken: The knight and queen team up to press the kingside, but if the opponent's queen enters early, Black's setup becomes uncomfortable.

cb-dt.spoken: The pawns roll forward with no way to halt them, and the game is decided. The defense collapses once a forced mate lands on the king's doorstep.

cb-d9.spoken: A queen sacrifice is a fair try when it trades a queen for a knight to avoid a losing deficit, even if it is not the objectively strongest move.

cb-dn.spoken: The knight sits on an outpost while the extra pawn and uncastled enemy king give White the edge. Trading pieces simplifies down to a winning pawn endgame.

cb-cr.spoken: The bishop setup on the long diagonal targets the center, while a flank pawn push prepares to undermine the opponent's structure. The battle hinges on who seizes the central squares first.

cb-dr.spoken: The opponent's pawn move cracks the shield around their king, and the weaknesses outlive any pawn they grab later. Their safety ends the moment that pawn steps forward.

cb-d0.spoken: The knight comes under attack, and the choice is retreat or trade. Moving it to protect a pawn may hold the material, but it often boxes the army in and leaves a cramped position.

cb-do.spoken: The pawn thrust is not a real threat. Meeting it with the kingside pawn move wastes a tempo, and normal development gives White a lead in development.

cb-d1.spoken: The knight and pawn form a shield in front of the king. A sacrifice on either nearby square opens lines, and the knight that lands there becomes a powerful piece, carrying mate threats.

cb-dh.spoken: The unclaimed pawn is pure profit. When Black feels forced to push a center pawn to challenge it, that advance can create permanent weaknesses.

cb-cs.spoken: The knight on the rim and the bishop at home still cover both flanks, while the white knight sits passively and needs a better square to connect the pieces.

cb-d5.spoken: The queen stands safely there, no immediate attack threatens her. The pin on the pawn, plus the chance to push a pawn and drive the bishop away, leaves the knight hanging and makes tactics.

cb-dl.spoken: The opponent's play is loose at this level, and the rook falls to a simple blunder. The speaker skirts a checkmate threat, then spots it just in time.

cb-dx.spoken: The king belongs in the center in the endgame. Black challenges the rook with the rook on the open file, and if the rook is trapped, trading rooks leaves a winning pawn endgame. The bishop can threaten a check that forces queen trades.

cb-cy.spoken: The central pawn push is the key here. It clears the way for a later advance that gains space and cramps the opponent. Settling for a quiet flank move instead lets that initiative slip away.

cb-cx.spoken: A bishop that bites from the corner controls every dark square, yet the fight belongs on light squares. Trade the rooks and queens to simplify, and the conversion grows easier, especially when the clock is short.

cb-d3.spoken: The queen steps into the attack on the king's weak square. When the opponent tucks the pawn to guard it, the bishop retreats and the pawn push prevents the pin.

cb-da.spoken: The knight lands on a square that weakens Black's coordination, handing White a slight edge.

cb-dy.spoken: The stranded bishop sits far from the battle, and that absence gives the attacker real tactical chances.

cb-d7.spoken: The trades simplify to a rook endgame with the bishop, and the position favors us. The opponent plays far stronger than their rating suggests.

cb-d6.spoken: The long-diagonal bishop runs the game if it stays put. Pawn moves on that wing keep it anchored to the diagonal.

cb-dq.spoken: The dark-square pawn chain boxes in the bishop and turns it into a poor piece. When the opponent trades off the light-squared bishops, you are stuck with the weaker one.

cb-dk.spoken: The bishop strikes the knight, and the queen stands in the path of a mating net. If she slips, the rook joins the attack and the threat lands.

cb-cu.spoken: The pure English setup is sound but plays for less than immediate central control. Black's flexible structure invites White to develop with options open.

cb-d4.spoken: The h-file is open and the queen already eyes the enemy king. A sacrifice on the g-pawn rips open lines. If the bishop is captured, the knight hangs loose, and a pawn push wins a piece.

cb-dv.spoken: The bishop is a target on the diagonal; Black can chase it with pawns or trade it off. Once White commits both pawns forward, the bishop sits exposed. Black's queen slides in to block the escape square, and the king steps aside to safety.

cb-di.spoken: The material is won, but the game is not over. Trade pieces down and the bishop pair plus active pieces convert the endgame.

cb-df.spoken: The b-pawn offer trades itself for a center pawn. If Black takes, White recaptures and then supports with the c-pawn. When the knight grabs the pawn instead, it walks into a trap.

cb-cv.spoken: The knight and pawn work together to eye the center square. When the opponent readies that advance with a pawn, the knight steps in—refusing the pawn break and preserving the English pawn structure.

cb-dg.spoken: A material lead lets you play flexibly. Trading queen for rook and piece stays winning, or you just outplay them with extra pieces. The long bishop and the central knight together dominate the board.

cb-el.spoken: The knight grabs the pawn instead of the pawn recapturing, leaving it hanging and inviting the pawn push. That line favors Black.

cb-eo.spoken: The knight's best squares get taken away when Black pushes pawns to claim space and shrink its options.

cb-e9.spoken: The early pawn advance transposes into a reversed opening with a spare tempo, handing White a comfortable edge.

cb-ee.spoken: A knight on the f-file becomes a real threat when it backs a pawn push that opens the king's flank, and the pressure builds on the castled position.

cb-ec.spoken: A clean extra pawn is easiest to convert by steering into a pawn structure that favors you, like doubling the opponent's pawns.

cb-ez.spoken: The rook takes the only open file, a key positional asset. Pawns guard the sole weakness, and the rook stays off the seventh rank to avoid stale-mate ideas later.

cb-ew.spoken: The player has all pieces out, castled, and the queen active. The opponent has two pieces moved and no castling in sight. That development gap decides the game.

cb-em.spoken: The fork threat demands an immediate response. There is no time for a quiet move or a retreat, because the attack comes at once. The knight must take the pawn and answer the threat directly.

cb-eb.spoken: A loose bishop ties the knight to its defense, freezing it in place. That leaves squares the knight would guard unguarded, and those squares become tactical targets.

cb-ej.spoken: The knight waits, coiled, for the kingside to weaken with that pawn push. When it finally comes, the knight jumps in and the attack lands.

cb-f2.spoken: The opponent's early pawn move is a common error—it lets you push your center pawn two squares, striking a piece with tempo. That wins time and space.

cb-e7.spoken: Trading down in the endgame costs nothing, because the king steps to the center and takes charge of the file. Giving up that file stops mattering once rooks come off and the position simplifies to a win.

cb-e2.spoken: The queen trade looks like a free pawn, but it actually walks into a lost endgame. White's active pieces and cleaner pawn structure take over, and the king marches in to collect more pawns.

cb-f8.spoken: The knight is a fighter worth a full piece, so trades end the game. When Black refuses them, shore up the knight with a pawn and build a blockade that chokes every counter.

cb-e6.spoken: The rook joins the attack on the open file, and the second rook follows behind to double. The threats pile up until the defense cracks and mate lands.

cb-f0.spoken: The queen steps in to hit the knight and block its advance. When the opponent pushes the other queen to force a trade, the bishop comes out and drives her off, completing the exchange while a rook ahead.

cb-eu.spoken: The enemy passed up the sharper h-pawn push or the knight to the fourth rank. Instead, they grabbed on the flank, which is not wrong but hands you time to consolidate.

cb-et.spoken: The bishop guards the pawn, stops the annoying h-pawn push, and shields itself from pins—so the position feels safe.

cb-ef.spoken: A developing move that carries a threat gains a tempo and can snowball into a major development lead if the opponent mishandles the opening.

cb-f6.spoken: The queen offers a draw by repetition, but you decline it. Take the pawn, then swing the rook over to keep the attack alive.

cb-ev.spoken: The opponent skips the theoretical pawn thrust, and the battle leaves the book lines. White sidesteps the main struggle and the game drifts into uncharted territory.

cb-er.spoken: The opponent sidesteps the gambit and pushes the c-pawn instead. Play solidly, skip the h-pawn rush, and develop slowly while tying down the enemy knight.

cb-ei.spoken: A missing dark-squared bishop leaves its squares unguarded. A knight settled there cannot be chased by a bishop, and it backs up more queenside gains.

cb-f7.spoken: The queen steps out early and lands on a square where she's exposed. The stronger player skips the obvious recapture, because grabbing it turns the queen into a target — yet even his alternative lets White seize a decisive edge.

cb-e8.spoken: The central file is the highway, and whoever controls it restricts the enemy rook and lets the king march safely into the middle of the board.

cb-ed.spoken: The king stands safer on the opposite color when enemy bishops patrol that square, dodging the line of fire and cutting down check chances.

cb-eq.spoken: The enemy has poured everything into the queenside, so strike back with mate on the kingside. The buildup can be slow—boot the knight, creep the queen forward—as long as the assault finally breaks through.

cb-f4.spoken: The knight develops and the king castles as natural moves, but the real threat comes from the pawn advance. Attack the pawn before it strikes.

cb-f3.spoken: The misplaced bishop keeps getting chased, and each retreat costs tempo. A pawn push from the side finally traps it, and that lost tempo turns into two pieces lost.

cb-ep.spoken: The knight has no good squares—every outpost is covered. That positional edge quietly caps the opponent's activity.

cb-e3.spoken: Behind the passed pawn, the rook stands at full strength. If rooks come off, the pawn endgame turns winning on the active king and healthier pawns.

cb-es.spoken: The pawn takes back, and the next push restricts the knight further. The bishop already covers the only annoying pawn break, so the position is secure.

cb-en.spoken: Black can target White's castling rights by leaving the bishop on its long diagonal, undefended, after the capture on that square. That becomes a long-term strategic aim.

cb-eh.spoken: If Black sends the knight to g6, White plays h6 to stop Ng5. That keeps f7 safe and sends the knight back, no real cost — White still develops the bishop and pushes d6.

cb-e5.spoken: The g-pawn advance blocks the knight's best square and keeps it out of the game. Without that move, the knight slips in and becomes a constant nuisance.

cb-f1.spoken: The knight attacks the key square, and the opponent has no good reply. Simply advancing a quiet pawn keeps the material edge; grabbing the rook is not even required.

cb-e4.spoken: The pawn cramps the knight’s route to its best square. Capturing it works, but refusing keeps the plan simple and the position clear.

cb-fd.spoken: Black’s early pawn push weakens the queenside. White answers by trading on that square to open the file for the rook.

cb-f5.spoken: A dominant knight anchors the whole plan. Push the pawn to open the file beside it, then bring the rook down that file while the knight keeps its grip.

cb-ea.spoken: The bishop sits loose, so the knight's pin is empty. The queen can capture the pawn safely and win material.

cb-fa.spoken: After Black's c5, White could have pushed c4 but rejected it, since d4 would shut in the bishop on b2. Instead, taking on c5 keeps the position open and lets White play c4 later.

cb-fr.spoken: The knight recaptures on the same square and threatens mate. White must answer the threat, and Black keeps pressing the weakened light squares.

cb-gk.spoken: The light-squared bishop is traded away, and that trade is a mistake — it was the piece holding the key squares together.

cb-g7.spoken: The fianchettoed bishop guards the kingside squares, so a rook lift there gets nowhere. Aim the attack at a different side of the board.

cb-g0.spoken: The knight retreats to a passive square, and every white piece points at the king. White attacks for mate, or wins the exchange.

cb-ff.spoken: The knight and bishop aim at the king's shelter, and the open lines invite the queen to finish the job.

cb-gl.spoken: The king marches up the board after the trades, and with the queens gone it is safe—and it joins the fight to win material.

cb-ft.spoken: The queen feels natural here, but Black has the answer. White keeps the extra material, though the advantage stays modest.

cb-fp.spoken: The queen on the open file attacks the rook and threatens checkmate at the same time. The opponent must choose which threat to answer, and the other one lands.

cb-ge.spoken: The pawn thrust puts pressure on the bishop and attacks the square where the opponent's piece sits, forcing it into a cramped spot.

cb-fg.spoken: A rook slides to the second rank, but the bishop steps onto the long diagonal and traps it. The rook is pinned to the king, and the pin wins the piece.

cb-fi.spoken: The early bishop to the opponent's queenside is a basic error. Develop your bishop first, then follow with the pawn — not the pawn first.

cb-fu.spoken: Trade with the endgame in mind: ask which pieces you want left on the board, then exchange the ones that favor your opponent's chances.

cb-fh.spoken: The position is already winning. Simplify by trading queens or taking pawns, and avoid any unnecessary risk.

cb-gb.spoken: A long pause often signals doubt. Strike with a threat that forces the error.

cb-fx.spoken: The fianchettoed bishop turns the king's shelter into a liability. Pushing the g-pawn and f-pawn weakens the castled position and opens diagonals, making the bishop far more dangerous.

cb-gi.spoken: The knight's advance into the center is premature. Pushing the flank pawns forward punishes it, leaving the attacker's pieces tangled with no useful squares.

cb-fv.spoken: Trade your weak piece for their strong one. Swapping the bishop for theirs takes out a key defender.

cb-fl.spoken: The bishop and knight come out early to control the center from the side. When the opponent attacks the advanced pawn, the reply strikes at their pawn chain and gains space.

cb-go.spoken: The bishop takes the pawn, then the knight settles on its strong square. That sequence is a known plan—easy to recall and it creates clear targets.

cb-g1.spoken: The pawn push anticipates the knight trade that would challenge the strong outpost. After the king steps aside and the rook supports the pawn, that advance gains real force.

cb-g9.spoken: A bad bishop is a long-term weakness, a piece trapped behind its own pawns. Spotting one is the first step to planning around it.

cb-gj.spoken: White's whole army is active and aimed at the king, while black's pieces sit stranded on the far side of the board. That imbalance makes the position winning.

cb-g4.spoken: Multiple black pieces bear down on the same square, and White cannot match the pressure. The attack was launched before any preparation was done.

cb-ga.spoken: Doubled pawns are a tool, not a verdict. Here they are accepted willingly, because the resulting structure or attacking chances outweigh the weakness.

cb-gh.spoken: The knight sits on a bad square, and the position turns jumbled as pieces run out of good squares. That mistake leads to a cramped game.

cb-fy.spoken: The bishop slides to the long diagonal, reinforcing the center. If the opponent loosens their kingside, that bishop turns into a major threat.

cb-fe.spoken: The bishop on the long diagonal supports a quick advance, and the pressure shifts toward the king's flank. The enemy bishop stands awkwardly, so the knight jumps to the center, hitting it and gaining tempo.

cb-fk.spoken: With extra pawns and the enemy pieces out of sync, the win is a matter of choice: sweep up the pawns or chase the mate.

cb-fj.spoken: The knight heads for the center outpost, improving its activity as the position simplifies. The opponent's weak pawns and tied-down pieces leave them without good counterplay.

cb-gd.spoken: The opponent's advance is a bid to free their bishop. Meet it with a pawn push that blocks the center break and keeps their piece locked in.

cb-fz.spoken: The knight heads for e5, and the queen sits on e2 to stay flexible. Black's g6 opens the door for a kingside push with h4-h5, so castling kingside suits the plan.

cb-fm.spoken: The center push gains space, but the opponent keeps counterplay. The rook backs a timely pawn break to open lines, while the knight sits on a strong outpost. Still, watch for tactics—a bishop can strike from the flank.

cb-gf.spoken: With the king exposed, keeping pieces on gives the opponent more ways to go wrong. The rook lifts to the open file, and the knight leaps in with tactical threats to complicate the game.

cb-gc.spoken: Against a fianchetto setup, the classic kingside raid with a rook lift and a knight planted in the center is dead. The plan turns to the c-pawn, striking at the heart of the pawn chain.

cb-g2.spoken: The bishop is out of the game and must be rerouted, while the queen stays in play to fuel the attack. The queenside plan is handled by quiet moves that keep the initiative without trading off the attacker.

cb-g5.spoken: An early bishop to that central square denies White the usual bishop post. Without it, the position remains good but loses much of its punch.

cb-g8.spoken: When the opponent has only shuffling moves left, the game is practically won even without a forced line. Cutting off their options is the strategic aim.

cb-fo.spoken: The pawn at the center is attacked, and White’s planned push leaves it undefended, so the knight strikes it and wins material.

cb-gg.spoken: The early pawn push can backfire: once the knight is pinned, the enemy posts pieces on that square and development stalls. A safer order develops the other knight and the c-pawn first.

cb-fq.spoken: The center stays tense, so the pawn steps forward to lock it. That keeps the lines closed and leaves the opponent's pieces without targets.

cb-fs.spoken: The knight goes to its natural square, the bishop to the long diagonal, and the c-pawn steps in front of the knight. White skips the other setup with bishop to the third rank and knight to the second.

cb-fw.spoken: A knight retreat can be purposeful, not wasted. Stepping back now lets the piece leap out again to a stronger post.

cb-gn.spoken: Close the center first, regardless of which pawn Black advances. After the capture, push the f-pawn forward to stop Black from doing the same.

cb-ha.spoken: Delaying castling keeps the king flexible and denies the opponent a target or an option to exploit.

cb-hf.spoken: The queen invasion lands first, and the knight is trapped anyway, so the faster knockout wins the race.

cb-gs.spoken: The knight challenges the bishop on its outpost, forcing an exchange that usually favors White.

cb-h1.spoken: Doubling rooks on a file sets up either a sacrifice or relentless pressure on a weak point.

cb-h0.spoken: A reliable system against the King's Indian gives a clear plan through the entire middle game without improvisation.

cb-gy.spoken: A clean piece ahead, trades shorten the game. Doubling rooks on an open file locks the win, even when a sacrifice tempts.

cb-gt.spoken: The trades leave White up material because Black never fixed the hanging rook or gave the queen safe squares.

cb-gx.spoken: An early central push in the Semi-Slav catches the unprepared opponent off guard and hands you the initiative.

cb-he.spoken: The bishop is a thorn, but there is a better prize than the queen. Take the bishop first, and the queen falls next.

cb-h8.spoken: Playing c3 when Black hits with c5 is a solid response. No need to fear c4, since the e-pawn always recaptures. The plan is the classic Stonewall break with e4.

cb-ho.spoken: The pawn advance keeps the position sealed and blocks the open file. The threat on the seventh rank is severe, so the opponent has no choice but to answer it.

cb-hb.spoken: Castling first keeps the option open; pushing the pawn early only creates a weakness the opponent can target.

cb-gr.spoken: Preventing the knight from leaping into the center is critical. Once blocked, the bishop and pawn advance together, claiming central space and seizing the initiative.

cb-h5.spoken: The flashy capture grabs attention, but doubling rooks on the open file is the solid path. The spectacular move is not the strongest.

cb-gw.spoken: When pawns block one bishop's diagonals, it turns into a spectator while the other bishop runs the whole board.

cb-h2.spoken: In a Stonewall, both sides mirror each other's plans. The edge goes to the player who finds the small structural improvement first.

cb-gu.spoken: The pawn storm widens the attack. Push the center pawn, then the queenside pawns, then bring the knight to a central outpost to choke the position.

cb-h7.spoken: The good bishop was traded for the opponent's bad one. Your bishop stays active, waiting on the knight to move, so it remains the better piece.

cb-hu.spoken: Against a queenside pawn thrust, the solid reply keeps the pawn chain intact and halts the opponent’s space gain.

cb-hm.spoken: The capture is tempting, but opening the file invites trouble. Development first, and if the bishop stands badly, reroute it to a useful square.

cb-h4.spoken: The protected passed pawn locks the kingside pawns onto light squares, and that strangles the enemy bishop. The rook on the second rank is misplaced and does nothing.

cb-h3.spoken: A knight planted deep in enemy territory is a powerful outpost, especially once the opponent's healthy bishop is traded off. The long journey that piece makes to reach that square shows the value of rerouting.

cb-hx.spoken: The h-pawn advance is tempting, but it hands Black an open file. Pushing the e-pawn instead threatens material and narrows Black's choices, keeping the position under control.

cb-hs.spoken: Your rook owns the only open file, a genuine advantage. With the enemy king still stranded in the center, piece pressure against it creates threats that keep castling out of reach.

cb-hl.spoken: The Stonewall wall of pawns locks the center and chokes counterplay. Improve piece by piece, pushing the side pawn to chase the queen, then tuck the king and bring the rook out.

cb-hz.spoken: The king hides on the color square the enemy bishop cannot attack. The rook climbs to the third rank and the queen joins beside it, and the enemy king, still stuck in the center or far away, faces immediate mating threats.

cb-hy.spoken: The knight is stranded on the edge, out of play. A check clears the path to a better square. If the opponent blocks one route, that defense weakens a key central square.

cb-hw.spoken: The c-pawn push is weak while that pawn still holds the center—the defender is covered. Once the queen steps to the side and guards it from afar, only then does the push carry real force.

cb-hd.spoken: A piece lands on the knight's doorstep and the queen rushes in, a second piece joins her, and the attack ends the game. The opponent's central queen reply is a surprise, yet the forcing sequence still wins.

cb-hg.spoken: In the Stonewall, an early edge pawn move weakens the adjacent square, so a knight on that outpost becomes much harder to evict.

cb-h9.spoken: The bishop check forces a weakness. Playing it to that square is awful because it undermines the dark squares around the king.

cb-gq.spoken: The pawn on the rim denies the knight its central square, so the bishop and pawn advance without fear.

cb-gz.spoken: Before sacrificing on that square, castle first. Castling brings the rook into play for a lift and keeps your king safe from checks.

cb-hh.spoken: The candidate move looks tempting, but the line runs through captures on the same square and a knight fork. Calculate the full sequence before committing.

cb-hk.spoken: Bishop to d2 is the setup to prepare Rfe1.

cb-h6.spoken: The pawn push leaves a protected passer, and every pawn sits on light squares. That strands the enemy dark-squared bishop, and the rook on the open file turns active and menacing.

cb-hn.spoken: Two plans compete: the calm capture that trades down into two pieces for a rook, or the immediate pawn thrust that starts a messy race. The capture first secures the stable advantage.

cb-hc.spoken: The queen presses forward, but the knight steps in to shield the bishop and silence the threat. That central push gains strength because after any capture, the knight leaps to a deep outpost.

cb-hv.spoken: The Stonewall setup leaves the king vulnerable. The a-pawn stops one bishop check, but the g-pawn and the knight push open lines against an uncastled king.

cb-gv.spoken: The Queen's Gambit often leaves Black short on active plans, and the resulting passive position lets White pile on the pressure.

cb-hi.spoken: The h-pawn advance is a useful prophylactic, weakening the square in front of the fianchettoed bishop. Even if it looks safe now, once a knight lands on the adjacent outpost and the pawn in front is kicked, that weakened square becomes a target.

cb-hj.spoken: The pawn recapture opens lines for the bishop, and once the light squares around the enemy king turn weak, the bishop grows into a dominant piece.

cb-ih.spoken: The extra pawns decide the endgame once the position simplifies and the opponent's pieces are trapped.

cb-il.spoken: In the Stonewall, White's early knight move is strong because it clears the way for their own f4, a central idea in this structure.

cb-j4.spoken: A piece is handed over for nothing, with no visible compensation. That move is simply a blunder.

cb-i9.spoken: The queen and knight line up against the king's corner, threatening mate. When the opponent blocks that path, the mate simply moves to the other corner.

cb-jb.spoken: The knight and queen combine to threaten both checkmate and the queen itself. The defender faces two threats at once and cannot neutralize both.

cb-io.spoken: The kingside pawn majority turns the endgame into a forced win. Advancing the h-pawn creates passed pawns, and that march decides the game.

cb-ik.spoken: The early knight move frees the queen from its starting square, leaving the bishop beside it undefended. That bishop must move before it is captured.

cb-ii.spoken: The center pawn is under attack, and losing it would wreck the pawn structure. A quiet pawn push shores up the middle and sets up a future home for the knight.

cb-jd.spoken: The knight steps back to its starting square, a known maneuver that sidesteps tactical trouble and keeps the position solid, setting up a recapture on the center pawn with the knight if needed.

cb-j8.spoken: The knights sit without pawn support, so neither one is a real outpost. The enemy pawn advance drives them off, and the knights have no safe square to retreat to.

cb-iu.spoken: The bishop owns the open diagonals and fuels the attack. Breaking the pin to take the queen is the key call, but the two queen moves are so close in value that neither deserves a brilliancy.

cb-in.spoken: Letting the rook sit on the open file is safe if it cannot break in. Black turns to the center, advances the c-pawn, and later swings the queen at the weak b-pawn.

cb-i4.spoken: After the win, keep the king trapped in the center. Checks from the side deny escape, and the queen steps forward to seal off the flight squares.

cb-ic.spoken: When the opponent pins your knight with a bishop, sidestep the bishop first, then chase the knight off with a pawn, and later reroute the bishop.

cb-j0.spoken: The knight lurks to jump into the center square the pawn would vacate. Cover that square first with a piece, or play the pawn anyway if you can answer the jump.

cb-j6.spoken: The bishop move is easy to miss because the queen move looks more natural, yet the bishop is the stronger choice.

cb-j5.spoken: The exchanges clear the board of immediate threats. Recognize the calm and do not invent dangers that are not there.

cb-ir.spoken: The knight wants that outpost, but when the opponent blocks it, that square next door goes unguarded. Push the pawn there as a central break; holding it back until development is complete works just as well.

cb-ix.spoken: The knight is boxed in on the rim, and the king covers its only escape square. Move the king to the square that denies that escape, and the knight stays trapped while the pawns roll forward.

cb-j7.spoken: The knight sits oddly on that square, and opponents misjudge it. Later it jumps to a central outpost where it blocks the key pawn breaks and locks down the position.

cb-i3.spoken: The king's flank is the target, and direct queen checks force clumsy blocks or retreats. A well-timed piece sacrifice on the kingside can be calculated to gain material or strip the king's shielding pawns.

cb-ib.spoken: The knight lands in the center and offers a capture. Take it back with the knight, not the bishop — the bishop stays on its strong diagonal, while the other capture leaves that diagonal weak and hands the opponent the edge.

cb-ip.spoken: The knight sits on its outpost, and the opponent's pawn push weakens their own kingside. That pawn advance becomes the attacking lever, and even after the pieces come off, the pawn structure still favors the attacker.

cb-j2.spoken: All pieces coordinate on the enemy king, and that pressure makes a tactical strike nearly inevitable.

cb-it.spoken: The bishop retreat is often the cleanest path. With no good replies, the opponent crumbles.

cb-im.spoken: Choose the recapture that holds the key squares for good. Taking with the bishop leaves a bishop against a knight—a favorable trade—and opens the g-file for the rook.

cb-j9.spoken: The knight quietly guards the critical squares, including the one that protects the king, and its reach blocks both freeing pawn breaks.

cb-i2.spoken: The Stonewall setup tempts an early pawn break, but pushing it releases the central pressure and can cost the dark-squared bishop or worse.

cb-ja.spoken: The bishop presses down the long diagonal, and after the trades it stays active. White wins a pawn and keeps the pressure on.

cb-iy.spoken: Pawns belong on the squares your bishop does not command, so your bishop covers the rest. Dark pawns let the enemy king camp on light squares and stop them.

cb-jc.spoken: The bishop retreats to the long diagonal while the pawns launch forward, hammering the fianchetto setup before it can breathe.

cb-i8.spoken: The f-pawn and bishop aim squarely at the enemy's f-pawn, and the g-pawn push seeks to open lines. If the capture is accepted, the queen recaptures on the f-pawn square with devastating effect.

cb-ia.spoken: Stopping Black's knight from reaching e4 is key in the Stonewall. If it lands there and Black follows with f5, the position becomes a symmetrical Stonewall that's tough to crack.

cb-is.spoken: The enemy king is exposed, and the pawns are crushing the position. Once the opponent locked in with d5 and f5, the pawn storm became unstoppable. Many moves work, but the clearest path wins.

cb-i7.spoken: The queen unpins the knight, which captures with a threat. She then slides to a square that keeps the pressure alive, and the f-pawn recapture remains the key. The bishop becomes active from behind its own pawns, and the attack on the f-square is strong.

cb-iq.spoken: The enemy bishop on the long diagonal is a nuisance—it pins a pawn and rules the key diagonals. You can break the pin or tuck the queen to guard the king, but that bishop still stands as the board's strongest piece.

cb-if.spoken: The pawn grab is tempting, but the rook sacrifice wins two pawns outright — and both ideas stay on the board.

cb-ie.spoken: That pawn on the fourth rank opens lines for rook and bishop. If it captures inward, the recapture with the bishop gives it a clear diagonal and real power.

cb-ij.spoken: The enemy bishop steps out and leaves the back door open. Queen to the edge threatens mate on the king's home square — the rook behind is blocked by its own piece, the pawn is pinned, and nothing can interpose.

cb-ig.spoken: The Stonewall pawn chain, capped by the early e-pawn push and the f-file capture, secures a lasting edge. The central structure alone generates active play, so the heavy pieces never have to leave home.

cb-iv.spoken: The Stonewall pawn chain answers an enemy c-pawn push with a solid c-pawn step, keeping the chain intact. The plan then is to push the e-pawn and open the center, while the bishop develops actively and the knight lands on a strong outpost.

cb-kf.spoken: The knight jumps forward with tempo, striking the queen while also aiming at the pawn it defends.

cb-km.spoken: Doubled isolated pawns are a permanent weakness. With the enemy king exposed, two knights and a queen can build a mating net.

cb-js.spoken: The fast win is not there. The opponent defends well and trades pieces, so the position refuses to cooperate.

cb-ju.spoken: The king is trapped on the back rank, blocked in by its own pieces. The attackers are already aligned, so the mate lands without an escape.

cb-jx.spoken: Repeating a strong move is a habit, not a plan. The knight and queen each find one good square, and the repetition turns each into a liability.

cb-kj.spoken: The bishop already pressures the center pawn, so Black's early queen sorties gain nothing. White develops with tempo, and any checkmate idea is no real threat.

cb-k0.spoken: The queen can take with check, fall back, or push the pawn. If the opponent answers with the flank pawn, the push is still welcome.

cb-kn.spoken: The pawn push prepares a fianchetto that bears down on the center. When Black hits the pawn with the center pawn, White ignores the threat and strikes back in the center instead.

cb-kh.spoken: The early queen sortie is no threat. A knight jumps to the center, hits queen and pawn at once, and gains a tempo while winning material.

cb-ke.spoken: The pawn is defended from the rear, so winning it outright is not on the table. The position stays level, but Black's pieces come out with less grace.

cb-jh.spoken: The queen’s move opens a tactic like the knight taking on the h-file pawn. If the bishop also takes there, and the opponent steps the bishop back, the knight jumps forward in reply.

cb-k2.spoken: In the London System, when White advances e4 and Black takes with the pawn, White recaptures with the knight and gains active play. The engine prefers Black slightly after h4-h5, but knowing the ideas lets you outplay anyone even in an equal position.

cb-jm.spoken: The knight comes under attack after the pawn push. Instead of capturing back, the knight leaps to the rim, mirroring the Fried Liver. When the pawn advances, that knight takes the defender, keeping the pawn structure intact.

cb-jp.spoken: The pin attempt looks tempting, but the queen slips away to a square that threatens mate. Black gains time by forcing White to answer the threat instead of completing development.

cb-ji.spoken: The knight steps to its new post, and Black answers by fianchettoing the bishop to cover two key squares. The knight sits well, and Black probes the queenside with pawn breaks to pry the position open.

cb-jk.spoken: The bishop develops with a threat, but the reply that prepares the pawn break must watch for a flanking pawn move. Tucking the king to safety sidesteps the pin and keeps the plan rolling.

cb-k7.spoken: The knight leaps into the center, eyeing the bishop's escape square. While the rook supports from behind, the queen finds safety, and the knight's threat alone forces concessions. Even when the opponent dodges, the pressure yields early tactics.

cb-jw.spoken: The d-pawn advance meets the c-pawn opening head-on, striking at the heart of a system that is already shaky for Black.

cb-k4.spoken: The recapture tempts you into a pawn grab, but the real target is the other pawn. Skip the capture, keep the pressure, and the weakness stays under attack.

cb-jf.spoken: The knight is under attack, but the real danger is the pawn. Retreating keeps the structure intact and stops the opponent from creating a protected passed pawn.

cb-ko.spoken: The pawn push attacks the knight, and wherever it runs, White gains. If it steps forward, a pawn advance traps it. If it retreats elsewhere, the center pawn falls.

cb-jj.spoken: The center pawn falls, and Black's knight steps forward to claim space. The capture leaves Black comfortable and roomy, with easy equality — solid, even if not decisive.

cb-k6.spoken: The pawn looks free, but the bishop’s angle turns that into a trap. If the opponent pushes the pawn forward, they drop one with check—so they must tread carefully.

cb-jn.spoken: The pawn push is the signal. If it doesn't threaten the knight's route, ignore it. If it attacks the pawn, capture at once, and when the knight comes, your own knight answers the threat.
