cb-kl.spoken: The extra material means a win, but a lone king endgame is not the fastest path. Keep the queens and use the exposed king as a target—her checks become constant threats that turn the advantage into a direct attack.

cb-ka.spoken: The b-pawn and fianchettoed bishop create a pin on the f-file. If the pawn is captured, the trade favors White, giving up the edge pawn for a center pawn. Advancing the d-pawn gains nothing. White develops the bishop and plays the c- and e-pawns to gain tempi.

cb-jv.spoken: Long castling is safer: the rook lands where it is protected, and if the bishop takes the knight, that check gives the king an escape square.

cb-kg.spoken: The pawn storms forward to attack the knight on its natural square. If the knight hops forward in reply, it lands trapped, and White collects the piece.

cb-k1.spoken: The bishop probe looks active but modern theory neutralizes it easily, and Black equalizes or even comes out better. That is why the line has fallen out of fashion.

cb-jt.spoken: The pawn thrust kicks the knight back, where a knight move would let it capture and wreck the pawn structure.

cb-kk.spoken: In the Sokolsky, the bishop on b2 stands behind the c4 and b4 pawns, and the knight usually lands on c3. The goal is to hit e5 early, sometimes grabbing a pawn by move three if Black slips up.

cb-kc.spoken: The queen gets hounded before she ever reaches her target, because that early pawn move shuts the mate square down.

cb-jg.spoken: The c-pawn holds the knight off that square, so the enemy knight landing there is no threat. The h-pawn gives the queen an escape from future attacks.

cb-k5.spoken: The rook retreats to the back rank, and the player wonders if a different square would have been the smarter choice—one that defends and consolidates.

cb-jz.spoken: In the London, when Black pushes the c-pawn, finish the queenside development first. Leave the kingside knight and bishop on their starting squares.

cb-je.spoken: The prophylactic pawn move stops the knight from landing on the outpost square, shutting down the tactics that target the queen.

cb-lj.spoken: The king is out of immediate danger, and the trade has surrendered the dark squares. Your threats now outweigh theirs.

cb-l7.spoken: The knight is trapped, and every escape attempt fails. The opponent sees through the tricks, so the rescue is hopeless.

cb-lr.spoken: The player who slides the queen behind their own rook on the shared open file seizes control of it before the opponent can.

cb-lz.spoken: The pawn push weakens the light squares, exactly the ones the opponent’s bishop controls, and the structure suffers for it.

cb-l4.spoken: Develop fast, don't push pawns. Each pawn move spends a tempo; developing pieces and castling restricts the opponent and opens lines for attack.

cb-kz.spoken: The center pawn is worth more than the wing pawn. Give up the b-pawn, push the center pawn to open lines, and the attack flows through.

cb-l8.spoken: The queen trade offer works as a threat, not a promise. If the opponent refuses, the offer still forces them to respond, and that concession improves your position while steering toward a favorable endgame.

cb-li.spoken: The knight steps out to a different square than usual. White's bishop attack looks sharp but is no real threat—Black welcomes the capture and gains full control of the dark squares.

cb-ku.spoken: The enemy pawn sits on a key target. Push your own pawns to challenge it directly. If they take, you recapture with the pawn and open lines for your pieces.

cb-lk.spoken: The queen looks tempting for the rook lift, but that square walks into a mating net. The double attack is no threat—the defender has a resource that answers it.

cb-kq.spoken: Up a big chunk of material, trades beat pawn grabs. Simplifying the board cuts the opponent's counterplay.

cb-kw.spoken: The queenside pawn push opens a line for the queen to leap to the kingside with real threats. The bishops already aim that way, and the opponent's many pawn moves have left the king exposed.

cb-l2.spoken: The queen comes out early to a vulnerable square. A pawn push denies the bishop its pin, then a knight leap attacks the queen, and the net closes.

cb-lo.spoken: The pin looks deadly, but the fianchetto bishop is the real target. Pawn pushes chase it back or win it outright, and the pinned knight never mattered.

cb-lu.spoken: Both queens guard the trade square, so neither rook can capture without letting the enemy queen slip behind it. That standstill forces both sides to improve elsewhere instead of forcing the exchange.

cb-lw.spoken: The rook takes the open file, but only one square is safe. The queen attacks the other, so the rook must settle for the weaker file.

cb-l6.spoken: The Sokolsky opening baits opponents into unfamiliar lines, and the early queen sally is a common overreaction that invites punishment.

cb-lq.spoken: The pawn majority on the queenside can force a passed pawn by pushing pawns and avoiding trades. If the opponent cannot exchange rooks, they cannot stop that pawn.

cb-l0.spoken: The rook and bishop combine for a classic mate: the rook captures on the seventh, the king steps aside, the rook returns to deliver check, then slides along the back rank for checkmate.

cb-lt.spoken: The rook steps forward to open the file for the queen behind it, when the enemy queen cannot cover the trade square. That gains the file outright, where a quiet rook move only holds it.

cb-ld.spoken: The queen takes the pawn, and the king steps in to cover the escape square, forcing mate. So the capture is safe. White can even sacrifice both rooks for the queen just to dodge the mate.

cb-lv.spoken: The rook steps onto the open line and attacks the enemy rook. With the queen not guarding that square, the opponent must trade into a favorable exchange or retreat and hand over the file.

cb-l9.spoken: The knight jumps forward into enemy territory, offering a pawn. If the opponent takes it, the queen recaptures and the position is fine, but keeping the piece there complicates matters for the opponent.

cb-m1.spoken: The opening's power swings with the rating. Weak players fall to it early, solid players hold it, and strong players mishandle the main lines and get crushed.

cb-lf.spoken: The pawn advance looks scary, but Black has a central square to step into. The endgame that follows favors Black: the bishop stands strong, and after pushing the f-pawn and trading bishops, the g-file opens with the king sheltered behind a pawn wall.

cb-kt.spoken: The opponent's many pawn pushes have left their center fragile. Your pawns on b5 and c4, with the bishop on b2, clamp down on the position. From h5 the queen joins the attack, aiming at the kingside.

cb-m0.spoken: When you are up material but stuck with a bad bishop, opening the position with pawn breaks still works—it shatters pins and wakes your pieces, especially if you own the squares left behind.

cb-lx.spoken: The king's fianchetto is the bait. The early pawn moves tempt a quick h-pawn push that stops a pin, but the bishop slides out to that same square anyway and takes the knight.

cb-l3.spoken: The dark squares have been a weakness all game. The long diagonal bishop strikes the final blow and wins material.

cb-la.spoken: In the Sicilian, Black develops easily on the queenside and keeps pieces on the board with natural moves, complicating the game for the opponent.

cb-ly.spoken: Pawns belong on the color your bishop does not cover. That dulls the enemy bishop’s range and undercuts the power of their bishop pair.

cb-ll.spoken: The early castle is a familiar home, but not always the safest one. When the pawn advances to the central square, the queen gains a clear path to the edge for active play.

cb-kx.spoken: The queen steps away, and taking the rook becomes the best practical shot. The bishop that came out early sweeps the whole board, and its long-range support for the king's corner is what makes the capture work.

cb-lb.spoken: The pawn push guards the kingside against instant threats while the long-diagonal bishop stays dominant. When the opponent's flank pawn advances, the pressure is not fully restored, so there is no fear.

cb-kv.spoken: The center is weak when the opponent pushes too many pawns. A soft spot like this invites central pawns to advance and chip away at the structure.

cb-l1.spoken: The pawn push cracks open the kingside and unmasks the queen’s diagonal. When a bishop backs the queen’s advance, the attack lands before the king can breathe.

cb-ks.spoken: The pawn is defended, so the capture is off the table. The bishop still threatens the other pawn, and that threat must be answered.

cb-l5.spoken: After a3 stops the threat, the knight heads to d4 instead of c3 — d4 is the safer square, and if Black plays Nc6, it can set a trap for the queen.

cb-lm.spoken: Dark-square control and a material lead. Open the position with the central pawn push to turn that development and activity advantage into an attack on the exposed king.

cb-lc.spoken: The bishop to that far square is often overrated—not the threat it appears. After the knight develops, a capture on the pawn is the real worry; that bishop move itself rarely impresses.

cb-lg.spoken: The bishop on the long diagonal is the heart of this opening. It bears down on the center and joins the attack on the king. When the opponent blocks it with a pawn, that pawn becomes a permanent weakness, because it chokes off the attacker's own pawn advances.

cb-n9.spoken: The knight steps back and the pin stays on. Black loses the center pawn and the pressure never lets go.

cb-mu.spoken: A knight landing on that square creates a temporary crack in the pawn chain. The opponent wants to force that capture, but cannot always make it happen.

cb-mv.spoken: Advancing the pawns can lock the opponent's queenside pawns in place, especially when they sit on light squares. The light-squared bishop guards the whole chain from behind.

cb-mn.spoken: The king often stays in the center because castling invites a quick attack with queen and bishop. The pawn chain is solid enough to keep him safe.

cb-my.spoken: Castle first, then walk the king to the other wing. The bishop drops back one square to become a light-square piece, and that placement can prove useful.

cb-mj.spoken: The king is stranded mid-board with no safe castling. Strike with the central pawn break, even sacrificing a pawn, to blast the position open and bring every piece to life.

cb-nc.spoken: After the knight lands, a pawn push chases it off, or a different pawn advance closes the bishop's diagonal and supports its counterpart.

cb-md.spoken: White's h-pawn is on the wrong square, so the planned Nd7 is no longer possible. The position has become uncomfortable.

cb-n0.spoken: A rook move that looks active can turn sour when the rook gets chased. If it comes under attack, pull it back to safety rather than invite chaos.

cb-mt.spoken: A loose pawn becomes a target and can do real damage. The key is to have answers ready for counterplay, like checks or tactics.

cb-na.spoken: The knight exploits the pin to grab both central pawns, then retreats to force another trade. When Black refuses the queen exchange, White converts that refusal into more material, and the extra pawn eventually promotes for checkmate.

cb-mp.spoken: Pushing the pawns up the kingside puts pressure on the dark squares and forces the opponent to answer real threats, shutting down their easy pre-moves.

cb-m5.spoken: The knight fork loses its sting when the queen sits outside its reach. Better to post the knight where it pressures the center, ready to leap forward the moment the pawn advances.

cb-ms.spoken: The rook abandons the e-file, and the f-pawn advance turns safer. The bishop already on that long diagonal points at the kingside, backing any attack that follows.

cb-n1.spoken: A sacrifice demands exact calculation. The knight may strike hard, but when your options narrow, the defender must find the one precise sequence.

cb-mx.spoken: The king shepherds the h-pawn while the f- and g-pawns trade, clearing the path. Once the passers form, the king steps in front to escort it home.

cb-n2.spoken: A move can look aggressive and still threaten nothing. Spot the harmless gesture and stay on your plan.

cb-mf.spoken: Pawns roll up the kingside while the enemy king is boxed in. The march forces a mating net, and the calculation turns the trap into a finish.

cb-n4.spoken: Doubling rooks on an open file, then after a capture goes unanswered, one rook breaks free and takes control.

cb-ml.spoken: The extra piece is the clearer asset, not the two rooks for the queen. A clean piece up simplifies the win; the imbalance leaves the outcome clouded.

cb-mk.spoken: The knight jumps to a square where it attacks the bishop again. If the bishop takes, the queen recaptures and hits the rook in the corner. That creates tactical pressure and a chance to win material.

cb-n5.spoken: The pawn push fixes the enemy pawns on their current squares, planting a permanent weakness to target later. The sequence matters: first force the commitment, then lock the structure in place.

cb-me.spoken: That move lands where it hurts most — the plans fall apart even with material in hand. It works because it creates threats and preys on the player's clock.

cb-mz.spoken: When the opponent attacks your bishop, retreat is not the only option — the queen or rook can come to its defense. But check that the defender is truly enough, or a knight fork may punish the line.

cb-ma.spoken: The pawn push invites a pawn break, but the tactics after it favor White. The safer path is to pull the knight back and let the opponent's pawn chain overextend.

cb-m8.spoken: Black's setup flows naturally into solid endgames, where the extra activity often tells. With the knight, bishop, and king safety handled, Black keeps pieces on the board and plays for the long game.

cb-m9.spoken: The pawn break is tempting, but trading into an endgame is the smooth road. Even a wild exchange sacrifice works here because Black's pieces coordinate well and White's doubled pawns stay weak.

cb-mb.spoken: The pawn push drives the knight off its post, and the follow-up knight jump turns into a decisive threat. The defender’s only legal reply lets the queen capture cleanly, and the position collapses.

cb-m7.spoken: In the Taimanov, Black welcomes the endgame. Even a forced queen trade leaves Black's structure and activity at least equal, often more.

cb-nb.spoken: The bishop controls squares the knight can never touch, so keep it active and let the light pawns guard the dark ones.

cb-mq.spoken: The pawn on that square is the weak link. If it falls, the structure cracks and the pieces around it lose their footing.

cb-mg.spoken: Black answers the push on the queenside with the same push, halting the advance. If White pushes past instead, the knight jumps into the outpost.

cb-mh.spoken: The knight may win a pawn with a fork, but only if the opponent gets no compensation for it.

cb-mw.spoken: When the opponent can meet your queenside pawn push with their own pawn break, look for a central alternative, especially if the supporting square is covered. A central push may close the position, which is not always what you want.

cb-mm.spoken: Dark-squared bishops need opposite-colored pawns: put your pawns on dark squares, your king on light squares, and the enemy bishop runs out of targets.

cb-nd.spoken: A quiet pawn move that keeps every option open, especially when the foe may post the bishop early. If that happens, the center push gains a tempo and strikes at once.

cb-n3.spoken: A knight planted in the center can aim for the square that attacks the weak pawn in front of the enemy king. If that pawn is fragile, it becomes the target.

cb-mi.spoken: The choice on the recapture depends on the target: the central pawn or the wing pawn. Keep the tension in the middle, or grab the flank and unbalance the position.

cb-mo.spoken: The plan stops the enemy pawn push with a flank pawn, then advances your own flank pawn, and may reroute the knight to the outpost in front of it. That squeezes the opponent's pawn and targets the dark squares.

cb-n8.spoken: The knight must wait for a clear path. Pushing that pawn leaves the knight without a useful square, so White develops and lets Black commit first.

cb-od.spoken: Black trades the bishop, blocks the knight, and leaves development aimless. White then squeezes the position at leisure.

cb-o6.spoken: The rook and pawn combine to trap the king away from safety, but the defending king can still get back in time to hold the position.

cb-og.spoken: The knight leaps to the edge to attack the bishop. When it retreats, the pawns advance to trap it and win the piece.

cb-o1.spoken: The king is trapped on the edge, and every check along the rank shrinks his escape squares. The rook keeps hammering until the king has nowhere left to run.

cb-o0.spoken: The king gets trapped on that square, and the knight and rook close in to weave a checkmating net.

cb-o2.spoken: The knight deflects the check and uncovers a mating threat. If the rook accepts, the king steps forward with check and the attack rolls on.

cb-nv.spoken: Two knights outplay a lone bishop, and the centralized knight is the key: it dominates the center and is nearly impossible to challenge.

cb-oo.spoken: The opponent reaches move twenty with no development, the king exposed, pieces still on the back rank, down material, and the queen trapping its own pawns.

cb-nl.spoken: When ahead in material, every trade works in your favor—simplifying the position and stripping away the opponent's counterplay.

cb-oe.spoken: The knight settles on the outpost, the pawns roll forward, and the queen centralizes behind them. That grip on the center turns into lasting pressure.

cb-nm.spoken: The rook slides onto the file to cut off the queen's escape, and the trap is set.

cb-ok.spoken: In the Slav Defense, Black usually wants the light-squared bishop out to f5 or g4 before e6, since e6 locks it in. White's whole plan is to hit that bishop right away.

cb-ne.spoken: Dark-square pawns and a light-squared bishop leave the dark squares weak for the opponent, and those squares become targets for pawn pushes and queen maneuvers.

cb-no.spoken: The pawn push gains space and tempo by striking the knight. The early queen sortie only hands the opponent a free tempo.

cb-nn.spoken: The knight challenges the b-pawn's advance, but the pawn pushes on anyway, gaining space and either winning the pawn or forcing a trade that favors White.

cb-o8.spoken: The tricky plan is to step the king forward and slide the rook across, cutting the enemy king off from one side. But a precise defense still holds the draw.

cb-np.spoken: The extra pawn and lead in development leave the knight badly placed. Opening the center targets that bishop, and recapturing with the pawn keeps the structure sound and castling possible.

cb-ng.spoken: Up material, offer trades to simplify and drain counterplay. A king left in the center is safe when the position stays closed or pieces keep coming off.

cb-nt.spoken: Two knights outwork a lone bishop here, and the outpost knight is hard to dislodge. The bishop stays cramped, while White's center holds firm but offers no easy break.

cb-om.spoken: The pawn is held by a supporting pawn on the wing. Attacking that supporter forces the opponent to either push forward or defend passively—either way, the initiative shifts.

cb-on.spoken: The opponent feeds pawns onto dark squares while the light-square bishop sits at home. Those pawns guard nothing the bishop can use, so the piece stays dead and the squares stay weak.

cb-ob.spoken: The dark-squared bishop traded early leaves Black with a bad bishop and pawns on light squares. White's bishop seizes the strong diagonal and dominates the dark squares, while Black's misplaced knight blocks development.

cb-o4.spoken: The king trapped on the edge faces mate threats. The rook must stay active, cutting off the enemy king to build winning chances.

cb-oj.spoken: The bishop on the kingside becomes a target. Pushing the h-pawn forces a choice: capture and the queen recaptures, gaining time, or retreat and White gains space while developing.

cb-o7.spoken: The king's file matters more than the pawn's push. Blocked from the pawn's path, the attacking king cannot help it advance, while the defender's king arrives in time to stop promotion.

cb-ny.spoken: The knight sits central and active, reaching everywhere. The rook joins it while the opponent's rooks stumble over each other, and the back rank stays soft — every king move carries that threat.

cb-o3.spoken: The knight checks and chases the king onto a worse square. Then the rook joins the attack, while moving the rook first only invites endless checks against your own king.

cb-ns.spoken: The opening's early pawn push gains queenside space and secures control of the light squares, whether Black answers with a central pawn or a knight to that same central square.

cb-nq.spoken: The knight sits out of play, and a pawn push drives it back. The bishop stands strong, the rook is active, and every option wins — capture on the seventh or double the pawns.

cb-oc.spoken: The e-pawn advances first, then the queen slides out to join it, landing on the central square where she dominates. From there she radiates threats, and the bishop or more pawn pushes follow to keep the center growing.

cb-op.spoken: Pushing the center pawn gains space and opens lines.

cb-nh.spoken: One well-placed piece can dominate the board and win material. Tempting shots may look unsound, but when they work, they end the game fast.

cb-nu.spoken: Two knights against a bishop can favor the side that traded the exchange for them, especially when a knight sits on an outpost.

cb-nj.spoken: When the enemy king sits exposed, a queen check or a knight fork lands with real force. Even when not decisive on the spot, these threats are brutal to answer.

cb-oi.spoken: The misplaced knight gets chased away, leaving the weak pawn behind. White keeps pressure on both the queenside and center, while the enemy king remains stuck in the middle.

cb-ni.spoken: Playing b4 often leaves Black's d-pawn loose, so Bf7 looks tempting, but trading the light-squared bishop is usually a bad deal. If Black answers with d5, the bishop gets trapped, so White should not take it.

cb-of.spoken: The queen's bishop is ready to push the center pawn two squares when Black fianchettoes. The game takes on a Queen's Gambit shape — not identical, but close enough to play by familiar rules.

cb-nr.spoken: The endgame favors White decisively. Black accepts the queen trade, and every move leads toward a near-stalemate — only one legal move remains, and it cannot save the game.

cb-oa.spoken: The knight steps out early, and White answers by pushing the pawn with tempo — the center falls under White's control, and development comes with gain of time.

cb-nx.spoken: The rook drops back to a rank, baiting a capture. If taken, the rook slides across with check, and the follow-up threatens mate, so the capture fails. The knight is dominant, and a pawn is already won.

cb-nw.spoken: The speaker eyes the queen move as bait, hoping White grabs the pawn and strands it isolated, with another pawn already dangling.

cb-nz.spoken: Up a whole piece, the win is not automatic. Active pieces and the enemy rooks tripping over each other give real compensation.

cb-o5.spoken: An edge pawn changes the math. If the defender's king reaches the e-file, proximity earns the draw. The d-file loses; the e-file holds.

cb-o9.spoken: The king steps to the side, and the pawn's path to promotion opens because the defender's checks dry up. The king weaves to dodge the perpetual, and if needed, the rook goes as sacrifice to clear the way.

cb-px.spoken: The knight and pawn push are both strong options. The pawn push comes first because it opens lines and creates new threats.

cb-pu.spoken: The attacker forgets their own back rank while the bishop sits idle far away. Strike the weakness and the game flips.

cb-pj.spoken: Against passive play, just finish development and build a big center. If Black cannot pin the knight, skip the prophylactic pawn move.

cb-pt.spoken: The reckless sacrifice hands you material with no compensation. A hanging knight is a fatal oversight, so consolidate your position and counterattack.

cb-pc.spoken: A development lead fuels a direct attack, even at the cost of material to open lines. With the king exposed, checkmate threats force concessions.

cb-p8.spoken: The knight develops awkwardly on that side of the board. The long plan is to reroute it across, but that maneuver turns dangerous once the position sharpens.

cb-pp.spoken: Playing Bc5 in the Italian is a common 1300-level error. It hands White the initiative and lets them build a real advantage.

cb-q1.spoken: Two bishops against one: put your pawns on the color the enemy bishop walks on. That bishop goes passive, and your remaining bishop owns the other color.

cb-pk.spoken: Pawn moves and an early queen outing leave the knights passive and the bishops at home. By move ten castling is still impossible, which is the clearest sign of an opening gone wrong.

cb-pd.spoken: The opponent's sharp pawn thrust demands a steady reply. Shelter the king first, then challenge the center for space. The goal is to survive the opening with a sound structure.

cb-p0.spoken: The dark-squared bishop is gone and development lags, so the dark squares are exposed. The knight sits deep in enemy territory, the bishop aims down the long diagonal, and the queen waits to join the assault.

cb-ov.spoken: The outpost knight dominates the board, and the pawn push threatens to win material. The queen cannot dislodge it while the other knight stands guard. Dropping the rook to the seventh rank forces the king out and opens the door to more gains.

cb-ps.spoken: The opening is blocked before your system can form. When the first move stops your setup, abandon the plan and switch strategies.

cb-p2.spoken: The queen and bishop line up on the diagonal while the rook slides in—every piece coordinates against the king, and the checkmate threat is decisive.

cb-pb.spoken: Accepting the gambit invites a trap. Cover the king with a pawn push, then support the center and the threats dissolve.

cb-p9.spoken: Trading a bishop for a knight leaves the dark squares soft, especially when the enemy bishop stays walled in by pawns. In a closed game, bishops lose power, so the fight shifts to those weak squares.

cb-os.spoken: Material advantage means nothing if the pieces cannot work together. A lone knight can get trapped, and the extra pawns vanish into an unclear fight.

cb-pn.spoken: The pin is a trap the opponent walks into. Wait for the piece to move into the line, then the win falls into your hands.

cb-ox.spoken: The center pawn is a trap: if Black ignores it, it falls. If Black takes, the push forward gives White real compensation. The mirrored pawn advance on the flank poses no threat.

cb-py.spoken: The knight leaps forward, and the bishop offers itself on the pawn. If the pawn takes it, the king is caught — either mate comes or the queen falls. The natural defense is the losing one.

cb-ot.spoken: The knight leaps into the heart of the kingside and strikes the pawn. If the pawn takes, the king is forced out, and the queen and rook hang helpless in the open.

cb-pm.spoken: The bishop pair plus an extra pawn is a steady edge after the queen trade. The enemy knight sits passive, while White castles and develops the bishop to a strong square for a comfortable advantage.

cb-pf.spoken: The pawns matter more than the exchange here. First the pawn push blocks counterplay, then the knight chases the queen and opens the rook's file, forcing the enemy knight to retreat. Three passed pawns outweigh the exchange, so take the pawns.

cb-p7.spoken: The knight starts off awkward and needs a route into the game. Long-term, it can slide across to the queenside and find a strong square. But in sharp positions, leaving it on the kingside is the better call for the attack.

cb-pl.spoken: The opponent's early pawn thrusts and quick bishop development leave their position already tilting your way. Their follow-up moves wander without purpose, a clear sign they are flailing.

cb-pg.spoken: The king joins the attack while the three passed pawns do the heavy lifting. The exchange is a fair price, but the pawns are worth more. When the bishop pins by landing on that central square, the king walks up and chases it off instead of trading.

cb-oq.spoken: The knight on the rim is crushing: it dominates the center, threatens tactical blows, and leaves the opponent's pieces passive.

cb-q0.spoken: The c-pawn advance loosens the grip on the central square. Keeping the d-pawn back preserves that control and holds the structure together.

cb-or.spoken: The queen strikes two weaknesses at once, and the opponent can capture neither way without losing material.

cb-pz.spoken: After gaining material, secure the king with a pawn move that opens an escape square, then double rooks on the open file and push a distantly passed pawn.

cb-p3.spoken: When you lead in development and the opponent’s pieces sit passive, stack your pieces on one target. Queen, bishop, and rook combine for mate.

cb-pq.spoken: The bishop chooses the passive square, and that single step forfeits the pressure that holds back the pawn break.

cb-pr.spoken: The sniper bishop on the long diagonal keeps a pawn pinned in its sights, and Black keeps dropping it anyway.

cb-ou.spoken: When the opponent's queen attacks the b-pawn, defend by pushing the pawn or by moving the bishop back, or else bring a knight over to guard it indirectly.

cb-pi.spoken: The knight lands on a square where Black can't meet it with a tempo-gaining recapture. That makes the outpost easier to chase away, and if it's taken, White gains no tempo from the attack.

cb-ph.spoken: The c-pawn push is judged by Black's own c-pawn. If Black has already advanced it, the push weakens the center and invites targets. If Black hasn't, the push gains space and control.

cb-oz.spoken: The pawns sit on the third rank to keep the king's bishop's diagonal open, avoiding the wall that would trap it. Development follows, and the rook later lifts to the third rank.

cb-pe.spoken: The pawns are messier, so the structure favors you. The bishop steps out to a slightly weaker but defended square, the rook heads to an active file, and the queen checks from afar, forcing the king to shuffle.

cb-po.spoken: The knight is pinned, so it cannot move without being captured. After the exchange, the pawn endgame is winning.

cb-pa.spoken: Sacrificing the knight to crack open the king’s shelter wins a pawn and hits rook and bishop at the same time. Every pawn counts when the endgame arrives.

cb-oy.spoken: Break the symmetry when they copy you — strike at their unready pieces. But often the stronger choice is to hold control and let them make the first mistake.

cb-r5.spoken: Doubled pawns are a lasting weakness. Even without a clear tactic, that structural edge guarantees a good game.

cb-qv.spoken: A space advantage turns brittle if pawns sit on light squares. Push them to dark squares instead, and the opponent's pieces stay cramped.

cb-qw.spoken: The pawn advance blocks the knight's infiltration route and keeps control of the central squares.

cb-q6.spoken: Opening the d-file invites the rook to contest it. Guard the e-file first, so the enemy rook has no rank to exploit.

cb-qr.spoken: The pawn push is a mistake. White should take it, or the chance fades and the advantage slips away.

cb-q9.spoken: The knight heads to a square that avoids the trade and lands where the opponent least wants it. From that outpost it hits like a truck.

cb-r0.spoken: The queen move is tempting, but it walks into a pin. When the bishop pins the knight, the central pawn push hangs the pinned piece, and the attack stalls.

cb-qs.spoken: Pushing the a-pawn stops the freeing break on that wing, but the pawn itself can become a permanent target.

cb-qu.spoken: The extra pawn is a lead, not a license. The plan is to break through and convert, but careless defense can hand the advantage back.

cb-rc.spoken: Multiple targets across the board and two pawns hanging while the opponent is severely underdeveloped create an overwhelming position — they cannot defend everything at once.

cb-q7.spoken: A queen sally that looks terrifying can be worth a pawn, because the complications it creates often outweigh the material cost.

cb-r9.spoken: If Black plays a6 in the Benoni, White answers at once with a4, stopping b5 and setting up a5. Should Black ever try Ne5, White takes with the pawn and gets the better structure.

cb-ql.spoken: The e-pawn advances and the queen and rook generate threats that force checkmate or win material. Even after a slip, the position stays dominant.

cb-r2.spoken: A move forced by the threat of a decisive space gain matters for its necessity, not its fine evaluation. The point is the threat, not the numbers.

cb-r1.spoken: The bishop weighs two plans: doubling Black's pawns or developing and castling. When Black pins the knight with the bishop, sidestep the knight instead of accepting the pin.

cb-qy.spoken: White's pawn pushes shut down Black's plan to trade bishops and fortify on dark squares, while another advance grabs space. Black's knights end up dominated.

cb-rb.spoken: One side has several weaknesses at once — loose pawns, pieces still at home. The opponent attacks them all, and one target must fall.

cb-r8.spoken: Up a pawn, the king and pieces need to coordinate before the win is real. Activating the king and centralizing the rook consolidates the advantage and builds threats at the same time.

cb-qk.spoken: The knight sits stranded on the rim while White owns the center and the active pieces. The rook and bishop combine to threaten the pawn, and the knight steps forward to pile on more pressure.

cb-qq.spoken: The c-pawn is already advanced in this line, so the knight development is the natural follow-up. Playing the knight first is slightly better than forcing the pawn forward.

cb-ra.spoken: The bishop steps out early, and the knight chases it off. That harassment is a standard idea in this opening, gaining time while forcing the bishop to commit or retreat.

cb-q2.spoken: The opponent aims to trade bishops on the diagonal, which would expose the dark squares. A prophylactic pawn advance keeps that square covered and preserves the bishop's guard.

cb-q5.spoken: The knight advances to meet the pawn push, though it looks odd. If no tactic appears, retreat or find a better square; suspicion is fine when nothing sharper exists.

cb-qx.spoken: White dominates the center and bears down on the knight, so Black cannot free the position with a flank pawn push. White's pieces roam, while Black's minor pieces have no safe landing spots.

cb-qj.spoken: The bishop lands on a poor square here, sitting passively while White takes the center. A check instead, then castling and trading the bishop, keeps Black sound — but few find it.

cb-r4.spoken: The bishop pair gives White space to push the pawn on the queenside, squeezing Black's pieces. Pushing the other pawn first works too, but only if the center pawn's advance is already answered.

cb-qd.spoken: The knight sits on a deep outpost, well past enemy lines. The rival knight is stranded on the rim, out of play, and the defender's pieces hold the greater activity. The flank pawn supports the outpost and keeps a key central square under guard.

cb-r7.spoken: When the isolated queen's pawn stands exposed, the defender picks between two plans: clamp down on the square in front of it, or trade pieces off and attack the pawns that remain. Here, the choice is to take the pawn and then hunt the isolated weaknesses.

cb-qa.spoken: A quiet pawn push can look harmless at first, yet later it opens the line for a killing strike. The move that seemed loose becomes the key.

cb-q4.spoken: The knight routes toward active squares, and the queen sits on the same file to back those jumps. The other knight stays put unless a concrete need arises, because stepping forward would block the pawn in front of it.

cb-qt.spoken: The bishop slides to oppose the fianchettoed bishop, and that single trade secures the key positional goal.

cb-q3.spoken: Accepting the gambit pawn is reasonable, but the sharp reply that opens lines and creates threats brings complications you must be ready for.

cb-rd.spoken: White's d4 and e3 pawns build a sturdy center, but the c1 bishop is locked in. The priority is controlling e5 and developing smoothly, without letting Black break the pawn chain.

cb-qz.spoken: The pawn push looks tempting, but it opens the door to a knight landing in the center. That knight becomes a strong piece staring straight at the bishop.

cb-qm.spoken: The center pawn advances and the position opens in your favor. If the opponent wastes time with piece shuffles, the advance gives you a dominant setup.

cb-qg.spoken: Black's early knight to the queenside square is unusual. Natural development, like castling, works fine, but the immediate pawn push to the center is an interesting challenge.

cb-qn.spoken: The queen steps out first, keeping the bishop at home. That bishop stays flexible, ready to head to either central square or wait for the pawn push to open a better line.

cb-q8.spoken: The opponent’s move breaks Taimanov convention, but the surprise is no cause for alarm. Flip the colors and the position becomes a reversed Sicilian, a structure that rewards steady play.

cb-qf.spoken: The rook sits idle, cut off from the action, while the pawn threatens to promote. The enemy pieces stand badly, and the bishop strikes the rook while sealing off the critical squares.

cb-r6.spoken: The choice is between taking the pawn at once or forcing the bishop to commit first. If it retreats, the same capture works even better. If it takes, the two bishops and central control give a slower, more comfortable game.

cb-qh.spoken: The queen recaptures and the enemy king sits exposed. Avoid trades to keep the pressure on. The knight jump looks tempting, but it lets the pawn advance and create chaos. A bishop move is safer, keeping the king central and ready to castle.

cb-qo.spoken: Those Black pawn moves are weak, so welcome them and pick a different opening instead of forcing the Queen's Gambit.

cb-qp.spoken: The bishop slides out against that early pawn move, pinning the knight and preparing to strike the pawn behind it. If the pawn falls, the next one goes too.

cb-sd.spoken: The London System rewards fast development. Getting every piece out quickly builds the pressure.

cb-s1.spoken: When the king is checked, stepping toward the center is a sound defensive rule. That move activates the king and sidesteps mating threats.

cb-sn.spoken: Resignation is correct when the advantage is decisive and the game is hopeless.

cb-rq.spoken: The doubled rooks on the f-file deliver mate, with the bishop supporting from the diagonal. The king is boxed in by its own pawns and has no escape.

cb-ry.spoken: The knight is the engine of the Stonewall. If the opponent shuts it out before it lands, the whole attack sputters and they often collapse.

cb-s6.spoken: The king is tucked away and the rook lifts onto an open line of attack. Even when the opponent castles on the same side, that pawn storm still crashes through.

cb-so.spoken: Even in time trouble, a simple win can slip away. Ignoring the clock or losing focus invites mistakes and a loss on time.

cb-rh.spoken: The Stonewall ignores the queenside entirely; all play funnels through the center and kingside. The light-squared bishop is the main weapon, and keeping its diagonal open is everything.

cb-sb.spoken: The opponent dodges mate with defensive rook moves that shut down the queen sacrifice. The moves are not best, but they stop the forced checkmate.

cb-sf.spoken: The knight sits trapped on the rim, with no useful squares left, and becomes a permanent liability.

cb-rr.spoken: The knight develops first so the f-pawn can follow. This move order blocks White's central break and outpost, letting Black build the Stonewall wall unchallenged.

cb-rv.spoken: The knight's natural jump is blocked, so the file in front of the king lies exposed. The pawn on that file pushes forward to open lines at once.

cb-s3.spoken: The pawn push looks natural, but it gives the knight a jump to the center with tempo. The capture is off the table, so the knight lands and forces a response.

cb-sk.spoken: The position is winning, but the win is long. The opponent defends stubbornly, so no quick mate exists—patience and small gains are the path.

cb-s0.spoken: The knight lands on a protected square with two pawns holding it. If the opponent grabs it, they trade a piece for a mere pawn and hand over the outpost for free.

cb-rm.spoken: Black holds off on the Stonewall pawn push, playing the other central pawns first. That keeps White guessing about the real pawn structure and forces them to commit early.

cb-sg.spoken: The rook pins the queen down, but pawn breaks may offer an escape. Keep the pressure on until a clean attacking line opens up.

cb-sp.spoken: Play the solid line, not the flashy one. Steady play converts an edge without the risk of a quick attack gone wrong.

cb-sm.spoken: Resigning when clearly lost shows respect for the game. Stronger opponents tend to do it earlier, and knowing when to resign is itself good sportsmanship.

cb-si.spoken: The queen is won, but the mate is missed. One square delivers mate on the spot, yet the focus on a different defensive reply hides it.

cb-sl.spoken: Several moves here look winning, not just one. Pick any sound plan, but keep the queen safe — a single blunder can throw the whole game away.

cb-rf.spoken: The pawn push opens the bishop's line, but it invites tactics that demand precise calculation. Safer preparatory moves first give the king luft and bring the rook onto the third rank before forcing the break.

cb-s4.spoken: The Stonewall structure is so solid that even accurate defense rarely holds. Attackers profit most when the opponent grabs the outpost knight.

cb-rn.spoken: The knight sits on an outpost, backed by a pawn and controlling vital squares. The enemy knight wanders without purpose and poses little threat.

cb-sc.spoken: The pawn chain props up the knight, and the central break follows naturally. The structure steers every piece and attack plan almost on its own.

cb-s2.spoken: The pawn blocks one mate, but the bishop steps in with a new one. The enemy king stays boxed in while the attacker keeps the pressure on.

cb-rp.spoken: The knight sacrifice looks tempting, but Black can simply decline it. The mate threat on the king's square is answered by a quiet defensive move, and Black would rather let White castle first before striking at the king.

cb-sh.spoken: The rook lift tempts a sacrifice, but the rook itself hangs. The pawn capture, king step, and knight block leave the attack unclear — the sacrifice only works if the threat survives the reply.

cb-s9.spoken: When the queen steps to that square, she can get trapped. The knight holds the escape route open and sets up a bishop pin that creates threats.

cb-s8.spoken: The knight on the outpost dominates the position, eyeing the king's weak point and freeing the bishop to join the attack. Moving it to a quieter square costs that pressure and threatens far less.

cb-ru.spoken: The Stonewall setup frustrates London players by blocking their usual plans and forcing them into awkward kingside defense. Even a slightly worse position for Black brings real practical value through the discomfort it imposes on White.

cb-rx.spoken: The knight check is too obvious—cheap and easily parried. First, the bishop forces a trade that strands the rook. Then the knight shields it, and the queen joins in with a decisive attack.

cb-rt.spoken: The knight grabs the free pawn on offer, and suddenly that outpost defends the kingside while the queen lines up behind it. The bishop joins in from the long diagonal, and the pawn chain supports a push that keeps the pressure rolling.

cb-s5.spoken: The e-pawn supports the center pawn, so when the center is captured, the e-pawn recaptures and the center stays solid.

cb-sj.spoken: Black’s typical breaks here are c5 or e6, but this time e5 is the move, and White cannot stop it. The Bf4 and e3 setup is solid, yet it lets Black push in the center.

cb-ro.spoken: The pawn chain locks the center and cramps the opponent's pieces. The bishops sweep open diagonals, and the rook takes the open file.

cb-se.spoken: The f-pawn advances, and the bishop fianchettoes to cover the center and threaten a pawn push. The threat is too strong—the opponent must answer it and drops a pawn.

cb-sa.spoken: Even with the king exposed, sacrificing any piece to that critical square forces a concession or runs straight into mate. The piece itself doesn't matter — the threat does.

cb-rg.spoken: The queen check forces the king to react, and the follow-up capture opens lines for the center pawn, bringing the bishop to life and eyeing the knight. Later, the bishop slides over to pressure the kingside.

cb-rs.spoken: The bishop is idle on the kingside attack, so trading it off or leaving it passive costs nothing. The rook climbs to the sixth rank, then swings to the h- or g-file — a classic Stonewall attacking pattern.

cb-rw.spoken: The knight on the enemy side eyes the key square, so your knight cannot jump there. Push the pawn alongside to open lines instead—the slower pawn would waste the chance, but this one strikes at once.

cb-ri.spoken: The e-pawn recaptures on that square to keep the pawn chain whole. Developing the knight to that other square blocks the enemy knight's jump, while the natural development leaves that jump open and invites a harmful pawn push.

cb-s7.spoken: Castling first is the solid choice—striking immediately lets the rival push back and soften your light squares.

cb-rk.spoken: The Stonewall is a weapon with a condition, not a universal answer. It works best when the opponent’s early pawn move blocks their light-squared bishop. If that bishop gets out to an active square, the Stonewall loses its bite.

cb-rl.spoken: The queen uses the c-file to eye the central outpost, and that pressure alone keeps the enemy knight off the square. Move her one file over, and the knight lands there safely — no capture, no challenge, a permanent strongpoint.

cb-re.spoken: The knight is a threat, but White challenges it with a move that attacks it three times. Forced to move, the knight loses its outpost, while White also prevents a knight intrusion and secures a strong square of his own.

cb-tt.spoken: The knight sits on a poor square with no good moves. Declining the trade strands the opponent with a piece that has no future.

cb-tn.spoken: The pawn push hits the knight directly. If the knight is taken, Black's pawns double and White keeps the edge. The alternative knight move is just as strong, aiming at the key squares.

cb-t9.spoken: A bishop on that diagonal is a killer move, restricting development and creating threats. The stronger player takes away the opponent's key squares.

cb-tf.spoken: The center is locked and their army is still at home. Crack it open with the pawn levers, and their slow development becomes a fatal lag.

cb-t5.spoken: The bishop strikes the pawn and forces a passive defense. Once the pawn falls and the bishop retreats, the opponent is left with a shattered structure.

cb-t4.spoken: The pawn chain is frozen, with no breaks to loosen it. Black cannot stir up counterplay while White banks a lasting structural edge.

cb-th.spoken: The bishops dominate the board. The center pawn is worth more than the wing pawn, so take it. Once captured, the rook slides to the file and hits the weak pawn, creating a double attack.

cb-te.spoken: The knight finds a permanent outpost in the open position, and both sides suddenly have attractive ideas: pushing the pawn forward or placing the rook on the open file without the queen's pressure.

cb-tp.spoken: Two pawns up, Black welcomes any queen trade — the broken pawns mean the extra material decides a rook endgame.

cb-tq.spoken: The rook forces the trade by checking along the file, and once the rooks come off, the extra pawns decide the king and pawn endgame.

cb-t1.spoken: The bishop is trapped against its own color, your pawns sit safe on the opposite shade. Once the rooks come off, the endgame plays itself.

cb-t3.spoken: Two pieces against a rook with even pawns should win. The enemy king stayed home and the bishop sits passively, so the plan is to turn the extra piece activity into a decisive attack.

cb-su.spoken: The choice is between capturing and pushing past. Pushing is the aggressive route, opening the file for the rook. Trading bishops also removes a key defender.

cb-tr.spoken: The opponent has no pieces developed and is trying strange moves like a6, g5, g4. That lack of coordination makes d4 safe, so the knight captures and keeps the bishops on.

cb-sx.spoken: The king steps forward to back the pawns and take hold of the critical squares. Pressure down the file looks strong, but surrendering it costs nothing when the opponent cannot use it.

cb-ta.spoken: Covering every escape square makes the mate unstoppable. Even a pawn can join the net, and once all flight squares are sealed, the king has no way out.

cb-sv.spoken: The dark-squared bishop trade for the knight shifts the fight to the files. When Black tries the break, White captures, and the rooks take over the open line for lasting pressure.

cb-t7.spoken: The queen sits idle while the army waits at home, and Black's pieces pull in different directions. White owns the center and every active square.

cb-ss.spoken: The pawn advantage is fragile, and the instinct to push forward is tempting. But the priority is denying the enemy knight a strong square.

cb-tb.spoken: Black’s early g5 is provocative — it threatens little, yet hands White a read on Black’s plans. White eyes queen to d3, targeting the light squares and setting up d5, e4, and knight to e3.

cb-td.spoken: The pawn chain starts with two center pawns facing off. Do not let the opponent lock the chain so it cramps your pieces for space.

cb-tv.spoken: The opponent's development lags, so aggression with the pawns is justified — even a pawn sacrifice works, because the opponent cannot punish it quickly.

cb-tc.spoken: When the opponent pushes pawns and ignores piece development, they hand you a free head start. Every pawn move is time you can spend building a stronger position.

cb-sq.spoken: The clock is low, and there are two ways out: the sound, safe win, or the creative risk. Choosing the flashier road trades certainty for a chance to make something beautiful.

cb-u1.spoken: The queen steps into the center, forcing the pawn forward to push her back. That pawn move weakens the dark squares and opens the door for more pressure—a serious positional threat.

cb-sr.spoken: The check forces the opponent into a self-pin, but they escape with a strong defensive move. The queen move looked good but fails to save the piece because a discovered attack or deflection refutes it.

cb-tw.spoken: The knight sits on a strong outpost but needs an escort. When it comes under attack, the pawn steps forward to hold the line, and then the center can keep pushing.

cb-u0.spoken: The extra pawn is banked, but the opponent's bishop can strike at your light squares near the king. Retreat and consolidate the gain instead of hunting for more.

cb-tx.spoken: The g-pawn advance strips away the knight's escape square, forcing it into a bad spot. Then trading pieces simplifies the position into a won endgame.

cb-t6.spoken: The pawns are frozen — no active breaks anywhere. The blocked pawn chain leaves one side stuck, and every attempt to push only makes the immobility worse. That long-term burden is yours to exploit.

cb-ty.spoken: The center is settled, your pieces are developed, and the bishop stands well on an open board. Pushing the pawn two squares challenges the center, and when the opponent advances past it, the knight hops out to win the hanging pawn.

cb-tk.spoken: The knight chooses between central outpost or immediate gain. One square controls key points, the other wins a pawn. Pick based on whether position or material matters more.

cb-st.spoken: The knight steps out before the bishop commits, then the pawn chain advances in the center. The queen slides to the side, keeping the bishop's diagonal open and the king safe, and only then does the central break come.

cb-tj.spoken: The loose knight sits on the rim, eyeing a central pawn it can attack next move. That same pawn covers the other knight, making it fragile. The choice is to plant the knight forward where it rules key squares, or grab the hanging piece at once.

cb-tz.spoken: White's bishop on b2 and the knight heading to d5 secure a clear edge. The open center suits the bishop pair.

cb-sz.spoken: The bishop setup and the c-pawn push are the signal. If the opponent’s pawn blocks their own bishop, that is a good sign. Keep the center closed and never open lines for them.

cb-t8.spoken: The Greek Gift needs four conditions: a pawn fixed on the king's file, no knight defending the kingside, the bishop and queen lined up on the diagonal, and control of the blocking square.

cb-tm.spoken: The setup recalls the Dragon, but White owns extra tempi. Control of the center squares is the whole game, and giving up the bishop there is the standard way to seize the light squares.

cb-sw.spoken: White weighs whether to hold the open file or abandon it, knowing the opponent cannot truly use it because the pawns guard every entry square. That freedom turns attention to other plans, like pushing the h-pawn.

cb-tl.spoken: Doubling rooks on the open file and nudging the pawn to chase the bishop keeps options open while improving the position. When the opponent answers with a knight hop or rook slide, build pressure first.

cb-ts.spoken: The rook stands exposed, so mass the pieces on the pawn file and threaten the capture. If the bishop steps away and leaves the knight, the pawn falls.

cb-tg.spoken: When Black plays his pawn to c6, the center looks tempting with e4 and d4, but against the Sicilian-style setup, playing d3 keeps more flexibility.

cb-v2.spoken: The knight on the key outpost works perfectly with the attack on the king's side.

cb-v8.spoken: The knight and the king each have a square that matters more than any deep calculation.

cb-u9.spoken: Center the knights and look for pawn breaks to crack the position. Quiet moves that control key squares are slow but useful.

cb-v9.spoken: Deep analysis pays off in adjournments: the player who finds the right idea under pressure wins.

cb-uz.spoken: After winning a piece, push the center pawn, open the center, and swing every piece to the kingside. The rook lift is secondary—the pawn push activates more pieces.

cb-us.spoken: The pawn thrust attacks the enemy knight and gains space. It chases the piece back and opens lines for the attack.

cb-v5.spoken: The champion never tires of winning. The appetite for victory stays sharp at the top, just as it does for any elite athlete.

cb-ul.spoken: The knight on the outpost is anchored by pawns on both sides. When the opponent declines to capture it, that piece stays planted and cramps their whole position.

cb-va.spoken: The study of chess is a mental workout, not a memory test. The work is thinking through positions and plans, not memorizing moves.

cb-v1.spoken: The copied wall has a hidden crack. Push the undermining pawns to pry it open, and the lines toward the king unravel.

cb-v4.spoken: Winning once never satisfies the drive. The top player keeps chasing victory because the hunger to win never fades.

cb-up.spoken: The knight sits on an outpost in the Stonewall, radiating threats that force the opponent to respond, which often opens the door to tactics or a mating net.

cb-ua.spoken: The move itself is sound, but the follow-up is what decides. A correct first move means little if the next one goes wrong.

cb-uk.spoken: The knight jumps too early, and the opponent’s pawn strikes at your center. With no knight ready to block, the recapture falls apart, because your other knight hangs unprotected.

cb-uq.spoken: If Black plays e4, then e6 and d5, followed by f5 after dxe5, that forms the Stonewall. Playing c6 shields the d5 pawn, so if White takes it, the queen recaptures and avoids the pin.

cb-v6.spoken: Winning ten straight after any loss or draw is the bet. One slip ends the streak, so every game must be won with no margin for error.

cb-vb.spoken: Keeping the threat alive outranks carrying it out — the risk of what may come forces the opponent to answer shadows, and the uncertainty itself becomes the advantage.

cb-vc.spoken: Overprotection and prophylaxis come straight from "My System" — reinforce the key squares and pieces before the opponent strikes, and you keep control without ever defending reactively.

cb-ui.spoken: A protected passed pawn is the prize, and it buys Black a lasting edge. The enemy bishop strikes the pawn while also eyeing the rook, so the rook slides to a safer square, still lined up with the queen.

cb-u6.spoken: Up a piece, keep it simple. A plain capture leaves you ahead with threats still on the board — far easier to convert than a messy tactical tangle.

cb-v0.spoken: The king is caged in the endgame. When the pawn push comes, you meet it with your own, and if they capture, checks force the king onward until mate follows.

cb-uc.spoken: The queen steps out to challenge the pin, defending the pawn she just attacked. That same square keeps the earlier threat alive, and it is more active than tucking the king away.

cb-un.spoken: The knight joins the queen’s attack on the weak squares around the king. A queen check forces the king forward, then the knight checks from the side and drives him into a mating net.

cb-ut.spoken: The bishop slides to the corner, then the queen joins it on the diagonal. The enemy king, exposed, faces mate or major loss, and no defense holds.

cb-uj.spoken: The knight setup blocks the opponent's key square and stops their knight from reaching its best post. Mirroring the pawn structure means you cannot stop the same idea on the other side.

cb-v3.spoken: Accept the gift without flinching. Their sacrifice costs them material, and the initiative stays yours — the desperation simply doesn't hold.

cb-u7.spoken: A sharp counter in this opening can catch opponents off guard. It is not necessarily best, but a personal preference for Black.

cb-uw.spoken: The bishop covers the square the opponent wants. Placing it there both guards the rook and shuts down the pawn push that would otherwise be strong.

cb-uv.spoken: The pawn advances to open the diagonal and free the bishop. The enemy knight becomes a target, and the move creates threats while opening lines.

cb-u3.spoken: The knight takes the pawn when it is defended, and the capture sets up a fork or another winning tactic.

cb-uy.spoken: An early knight to the second rank stops the opponent from planting a knight on that outpost. If they try a flanking knight move instead, the queen steps to safety and chases it back.

cb-u5.spoken: When exchanges strip the pawn cover, the knight owns the center square as an outpost. If the defender steps back, pins or captures join in to tighten the grip.

cb-ue.spoken: In the Stonewall, the bishop belongs on the strong diagonal before the f-pawn advances, because it blocks the opponent's key defensive resources and feeds the attack. Moving the queen to the other side misreads the opening's king-side aggression.

cb-ub.spoken: The bishop pins the knight, but the queen retreats along the same file to unpin. That move also watches the key central square and sets up a slide to the edge for attack. The other queen move fails because it drifts away from the kingside plan.

cb-uh.spoken: The c-pawn recaptures, and in doing so hands Black a protected passed pawn. That pawn is secure and cramps White's pieces — a lasting positional edge.

cb-uo.spoken: The e-pawn capture opens the file and exposes the bishop. The f-pawn capture keeps the wall intact and is the safer choice.

cb-u8.spoken: The knight heads for a square where the enemy bishop cannot pin it, so the pin never gets a chance to start.

cb-ux.spoken: The bishop pins the structure together, forbidding the pawn thrust that would strike the knight and unsettle the whole setup.

cb-uu.spoken: The knight lands on the central outpost and takes over. From that square it dominates the board and turns the game winning.

cb-uf.spoken: The knight seeks that central outpost as a home. If the opponent blocks the direct path with a pawn, chase that pawn away or find another route — the square is still reachable.

cb-vd.spoken: The early pawn push does not fight for the center nor develop a piece, so it spends a tempo for nothing. White then builds the stonewall, advances the f-pawn, and reroutes the knight to the outpost square.

cb-um.spoken: The Stonewall's biggest break: push the pawn that sits in front of the backward pawn. That erases the weakness and frees the bishop. Capturing toward the center can win a pawn, and a bishop check from the diagonal exposes the king.

cb-wh.spoken: The queen is a decoy, not the prize. Leave her standing while the attack on the king rolls on.

cb-vw.spoken: A pawn recaptures into the center, and if the opponent grabs it, the push opens the bishop and frees the knight.

cb-wj.spoken: The queen is bait. Refusing to take it keeps the attack flowing and turns the win into mate.

cb-wc.spoken: The knight is pinned by the bishop, and the key defender is removed from the fight.

cb-vu.spoken: Trade down to a won endgame: the extra pawn and the active king decide it. Safe exchanges beat risky complications.

cb-vh.spoken: When you're up a full piece, the win is mostly a formality. Trade pieces, push pawns, but stay alert for counterplay. A pawn move like that can fix the opponent's structure and create passed pawns.

cb-wn.spoken: The queen and knight work together, controlling key squares and threatening the weak pawn to win a piece. A discovered attack is possible but not needed.

cb-vj.spoken: Pushing the pawn to attack the knight is not a real threat. The queen slides over to cover the key squares, hits the attacking queen, and the pawn advance leaves the king's flank weak.

cb-w3.spoken: Three minor pieces working together can outplay a lone queen, and that coordination turns the material deficit into a winning advantage.

cb-w6.spoken: The knight on the seventh rank is stuck. Your queen attacks it, and every escape square is closed — the opponent has no good answer.

cb-w0.spoken: The d-pawn strikes the center first, then the knights develop to natural squares. If the queen comes out early, the queen and knight regroup behind it, ready to challenge the center.

cb-w7.spoken: The king's fianchetto bishop stares down the rook down an open diagonal, which is not the usual pattern from this setup.

cb-vo.spoken: The king is exposed, so the second knight joins the assault. Sacrificing the bishop is tempting, but the quieter continuation wins faster.

cb-vs.spoken: The two bishops and the advanced pawn give a lasting edge. The rook lifts and the pawn push adds pressure, while the king stays safe and grows stronger as the endgame nears.

cb-vq.spoken: White is pushing toward a kingside attack with g4, Ng5, and f5. The opponent has several replies, but some are clearly stronger. White can safely ignore play on the queenside and focus only on the center and the kingside.

cb-we.spoken: The hardest part is dragging the king to the edge. Once there, the mate executes fast—knight and bishop finish the job in seconds.

cb-vk.spoken: The bishop and knight quietly prepare the center break. Once the pawn advances, White gains space and the bishop comes alive, while the knight supports the push from behind.

cb-wp.spoken: The knight attacks the weak pawns while the king joins the action. With opposite-colored bishops, those pawns stay vulnerable, and the active king gives the knight side the edge.

cb-wi.spoken: Opening the rook’s line through a quiet king-pawn push, then sliding the rook behind the pawn, clears the file and sharpens the attack on the enemy king.

cb-vp.spoken: The knight lands on the outpost square, and when the opponent cannot challenge it, the win comes almost by itself — the easiest victories in the Stonewall.

cb-vn.spoken: The choice favors the queen move over the pawn push because it stays flexible. The knight cannot land on the key square, since the bishop covers it.

cb-vr.spoken: The knight darts forward as bait. If the opponent takes it, the recapture with the pawn opens the rook's file. But that pawn recapture leaves the knight hanging, so the opponent is forced to capture, and the resulting pawn structure favors you.

cb-vl.spoken: The knight should leap forward to control the key central square, stopping the enemy knight from landing there. Defending the pawn passively wastes the chance to gain that control.

cb-wa.spoken: The knight is chased from its best squares, so it reroutes to a central outpost instead. The rook already stands ready on the open file, and when the pawn lunges to drive the knight off, it nearly gets trapped but finds a way out.

cb-vy.spoken: The knight's post decides the timing. Black holds back the pawn break until White commits the knight forward, because if that knight is still at home, a flank push only chases it into a safer square.

cb-wl.spoken: Castle kingside, and Black's plan is set: develop the whole queenside and prepare a strike on the opposite wing. The knight sits securely on its outpost because the queen guards it, while the enemy queen stands offside, doing nothing useful.

cb-w1.spoken: When the bishop takes the knight and sits on that square, recapturing at once is not forced. Leaving the bishop there and carrying on with a bigger idea often beats letting the opponent take back with a piece.

cb-wg.spoken: One pawn can dominate the whole position, forcing awkward replies while your rooks stay active.

cb-vv.spoken: Control of the central square is critical in this setup, so the queen steps in before the knight to keep the opponent from occupying it.

cb-vx.spoken: In the Stonewall, the key is denying the opponent the central break. Post a knight on that square or keep it covered with pawns.

cb-wb.spoken: Trading queens suits Black—it simplifies into a rook endgame where the rook sits active on the open file while the opponent's rook stays passive on the edge.

cb-vt.spoken: Controlling the central square early is the point, sometimes before developing the knight. The queen steps in to keep the opponent from occupying that square, and later pawn and knight moves reinforce it.

cb-vi.spoken: The rook attacks a pawn and threatens mate on the back rank behind a pinned bishop. The pin cripples the defense, so the opponent cannot meet both threats.

cb-vg.spoken: When the opponent pushes the kingside pawn to gain escape squares, they threaten to jump the knight in and hit your queen, winning a piece. Play a quiet preparatory move that keeps that square covered before you advance the g-pawn.

cb-wk.spoken: The Sicilian setup gives Black a flexible, solid formation with the knight, queen, and pawn on the queenside. White's two central pawn pushes each cost a tempo, and Black outdevelops White.

cb-wf.spoken: The pawn thrust looks tempting, but pulling the knight back is the error. The king move and rook shuffles miss the real shot — the knight takes the pawn. So the queen slides over and prays for the long castle.

cb-w5.spoken: The bishop pair aims down the long diagonal, while the rooks double on the open file to exploit weak light squares—White's pawn on the third rank blocks the diagonal and stifles those plans.

cb-vf.spoken: The Stonewall is a London on steroids — its light-squared bishop sits safely behind the pawn chain, untouchable by the knight's harassment, and the whole setup presses harder.

cb-vm.spoken: A knight planted on that outpost is nearly untouchable: the enemy knight can’t challenge it, and their bishop’s diagonal is blocked. That square becomes a launchpad for attack.

cb-w2.spoken: Flatten the pawn before it advances. The first setup invites a push that proves annoying, so the second avoids that weakness entirely.

cb-xg.spoken: The knight should not recapture here—it surrenders the center and abandons its ideal square.

cb-xr.spoken: The bishop threatens mate, but the knight guards the escape square. Development plus control of the key squares keeps the attack alive.

cb-xq.spoken: The knight grab exposes the king. Checks and trades keep the pressure on, and forcing the queens off leads straight to mate.

cb-xl.spoken: The king marches up to gather pawns and nothing can halt him. The bishop and king work together to close the mate.

cb-xw.spoken: Capturing on that square leaves Black with an isolated pawn no matter how he retakes—a lasting weakness to target.

cb-x2.spoken: The passed pawn marches, and the mere threat of promotion forces the opponent to react and answer.

cb-xf.spoken: The queen slides in with a mate threat, but a pawn push from either side kicks her away.

cb-xa.spoken: The enemy bishop is more threat than strength — it targets your position, but the real danger is the plan that follows once it settles in.

cb-xd.spoken: The fianchettoed rook sits on an open file with no pawns to shield it, and that exposure is a weakness the opponent must answer for.

cb-x1.spoken: The pawn is weak because the rook alone guards it. Pressing it with the queen and another pawn strains the whole queenside.

cb-xx.spoken: The queen lands on a square that hits the rook, the pawn, and the bishop all at once. Meanwhile, the pin down the file keeps both rooks stuck defending the pawn.

cb-xc.spoken: Castling and the rook on the open file coax the knight into action. When the captures end, the rook hangs, and that is exactly the gain.

cb-ww.spoken: When the opponent moves their king repeatedly, that signals weakness. First make a threat that forces them to play knight to e5, and only then push e5.

cb-xz.spoken: The piece attacks the rook and the pawn, but the defender stands protected. Without the pawn shield, a capture would land there, yet no discovered threat exists right now.

cb-xk.spoken: The king marches up once queens are off, gathering pawns while the bishop sets the mating net. Active king, bishop checkmate — that is the endgame plan.

cb-ws.spoken: Winning the exchange is only the start. Simplify with quiet trades instead of flashy moves, then push the center forward and aim at the weak pawns.

cb-xv.spoken: An early pawn move on the edge does nothing for the center and simply spends a tempo. Since White already owns the first-move advantage, this gesture costs nothing.

cb-wx.spoken: The queen and knight coordinate to hit weak targets, while the enemy king stands exposed. A check from the queen forces the defense to bend, and the loose pieces fall next.

cb-xp.spoken: The opening targets the central square and backs a pawn storm on the kingside. The knight steps in front of the bishop to vacate the file, and the advance becomes automatic.

cb-x6.spoken: The early pawn thrust takes away the usual outpost, so the knight cannot settle there. The standard plan must be reshaped around that missing square.

cb-x8.spoken: The bishop pair finds open diagonals when no central pawns block them, so the setup rolls forward unopposed and claims the center for free.

cb-x9.spoken: The pawn push that blocks the bishop is met with a calm reply. If the center pawn advances instead, that move is welcome because it opens the center.

cb-x0.spoken: The rook advantage means even a simple trade keeps the win. Black's backward pawns struggle to coordinate, and that weakness never goes away.

cb-wv.spoken: The early h-pawn creates a haven for the bishop and blunts the e-pawn's strike. The bishop avoids that square because the advance would drive it back.

cb-x5.spoken: The pawn capture not only takes material but also strengthens the center and gives the king's pawn extra protection. Although the rook to the open file is not the strongest choice, White still keeps a slight edge.

cb-xu.spoken: The premove is a habit at this level, not a plan. When the opponent rushes the same response without reading the position, the counter is yours to take.

cb-wu.spoken: The knight escapes the pin by moving, and when the enemy fails to capture, the same move turns the tables—the knight attacks the piece that pinned it, and that counterattack is almost always strong.

cb-xh.spoken: The center is not a gift. Letting a pawn that guards the middle squares go costs control, and the bishop stands ready to back a knight that lands on the key square.

cb-xb.spoken: The knight eyes the bishop, and the capture would hurt. Pushing the pawn to chase the knight off is a real option, even if it's not the prettiest move.

cb-xi.spoken: The bishop and knight combine against the king's fortress. The central pawn advances to open a line for the bishop, the knight leaps to strike the weak point, and the rook lifts to the seventh rank to build a mating net.

cb-xo.spoken: The kingside attack starts with the pawns advancing together, and the knight in front supports their march. The queen hovers to create threats, and the doubled rooks stack on the same file to pile on pressure. Every piece stays active and working as one.

cb-xs.spoken: The knight's retreat answers both threats at once. The pawn advance shields against the knight's pressure, then the bishop steps out with a double menace: a check on the diagonal and a strike at the enemy king's doorstep.

cb-y0.spoken: The pawn advance keeps the enemy bishop boxed in. White shores up the center and weighs three tries: trading bishop for rook, sending the queen out to grab a pawn, or a check from the bishop. The enemy queen parked in the middle of the board looks exposed.

cb-y1.spoken: The pawn cannot recapture after the trade — the bishop hangs. So the bishop steps out first, then the pawn takes. The knight heads to a strong square, and Black must watch for the bishop landing on a diagonal that hits the king side or the queen.

cb-xj.spoken: The three threats to stop are the center push, the knight jumping to the middle, and the knight hopping to the edge. Blocking the center push matters most.

cb-wt.spoken: The enemy bishop stays at home, so queen-to-b6 ideas are harmless — no threat there.

cb-xe.spoken: The bishop on the long diagonal goes unnoticed, and the knight hops to a strong central square to attack.

cb-xm.spoken: Take the pawn. Trying to force your usual setup against this response is a waste of effort.

cb-x7.spoken: After the center opens, the attack targets the weak pawn and the exposed king. Pushing the pawn, bringing the bishop out, and jumping the knight in create threats and win material.

cb-wy.spoken: The opponent's clock is ticking and the position is won. Trading queens simplifies into an easy endgame, but keeping queens on board keeps the pressure and invites mistakes.

cb-x4.spoken: The enemy queen sits on a common square. Do not fear it. Push the center pawns and reposition your queen behind them; the flank pawn push that follows is no real threat.

cb-wz.spoken: Early development invites a space grab. Central pawn advances and a queen sortie put pressure on both weak pawns at once.

cb-wq.spoken: The knight belongs on c3 instead of the usual c3, to aim for b5 and press on c7.

cb-y5.spoken: The bishop pull-back to the third rank sidesteps the tension, keeps the structure clean, and avoids doubled pawns.

cb-yj.spoken: The opponent must meet a condition, not just win — that pressure is theirs. Ignore the clock and read the board.

cb-yx.spoken: A pawn storm against an exposed king opens lines and turns the attack into mating threats.

cb-z4.spoken: The bishop strikes the target, and the ensuing exchanges clear the board. The rook then seizes the open file and carries the win into the endgame.

cb-z3.spoken: The pawn is a trap, not a prize. Grabbing it leaves you up material but stuck defending, so leave it and keep the pressure instead.

cb-y3.spoken: The queen's early arrival hits the bishop but threatens nothing. The same forward move costs time, and her exposed position invites a trap that ruins coordination.

cb-y7.spoken: The London pawn chain asks for a choice. Against the c-pawn push, the c-pawn steps up to lock the center. If the knight comes out instead, the other c-pawn advances for space.

cb-z2.spoken: The pawn storm and knight maneuvers carve the light squares. The enemy knight is dominated, so the rook or knight breaks through.

cb-zd.spoken: Black advances the pawn to attack the bishop, which also stops the opponent's queenside push. Delaying that advance lets the opponent consolidate the extra pawn.

cb-yh.spoken: The knight takes, the pawn recaptures, the bishop takes, then the bishop takes the queen. But the defender can block with a piece, so the sequence is a trap, not a winning line.

cb-z7.spoken: The Stonewall keeps paying off no matter the rating. Past 2200, you can't reliably steer speedruns into your preferred openings, but this one holds up at every level.

cb-ys.spoken: The rook and queen combine against a king stripped of its pawn shield. Together they force mate threats the defender cannot meet.

cb-ye.spoken: In a closed position, the attacker prepares pawn storms on the kingside and brings the king toward the center to connect the rooks. The plan is to pry open lines with a pawn push and strike at the weak squares left behind.

cb-z0.spoken: The open file points at the bishop, and the tempting capture wins two pieces for a rook—but that trade only pays if the opponent has no counterplay to punish it.

cb-yn.spoken: In a Maroczy-style bind, the c-pawn advance fixes Black's structure. Then knights and pawn thrusts on the queenside pile on the weakness and squeeze Black's position.

cb-yd.spoken: White sets up with Qb3, provoking Qb6, then strikes with c4 and b4 to pile pressure on the queenside. This line hands White a very strong position.

cb-yt.spoken: The knight to the central outpost was the missed opportunity. The light-square plan felt forced and artificial.

cb-ya.spoken: When the king is exposed, coordinated pieces hunt it down. Capturing toward the king keeps it trapped in the center, where it cannot escape.

cb-yg.spoken: Keeping queens on preserves the attacking pressure. Trading them off blunts the attack and makes it far harder to create winning chances.

cb-yy.spoken: With extra material, trade down toward an endgame where the bishop pair keeps its edge—that converts the advantage into a win.

cb-yz.spoken: A pawn push like this keeps the tension and dodges the exchange, holding the position sharp when complexity is what you want.

cb-y9.spoken: When Black stretches too far on the kingside, active play punishes it. Natural moves tempt, but capturing toward the center stays simpler and stronger than chasing fancy tactics.
