cb-2ct.spoken: White locks the center and pushes the kingside pawns, f3 followed by h4-h5. That builds the attack against the Hedgehog.

cb-2dt.spoken: White's pawns march to g4 and h4, opening the h-file for attack. The knight on f6 is Black's key defender; remove it and checkmate threats appear.

cb-2dh.spoken: After Bxh7+ forces the king to flee, the key is cutting off its escape. First play Qh5+, then finish with the queen and bishop.

cb-2d2.spoken: White has won material, so this position is winning. Simple, solid moves are best—just consolidate and avoid blunders.

cb-2cw.spoken: If Black plays d4, e5, and then takes back with f6, White should not grab that pawn right away. Push e4 instead to open the position and target Black's loosened kingside.

cb-2d9.spoken: White’s twin pawns in the center give him a space edge. Black’s knight on d5 sits nicely, but White can challenge it. This is a Taimanov Sicilian with an early c3, pointing at a solid build.

cb-2dz.spoken: When you're ahead in material, trade pieces while keeping your threats alive. A check that wins material or forks is ideal. And a pin only matters if it actually costs you something — with a big material edge, you can ignore it.

cb-2dl.spoken: Bf5 threatens devastation here. Even a player who spots it has no adequate defense and often drops material.

cb-2d4.spoken: White's extra rook and Black's stranded king decide the outcome. The rook on the seventh rank with passed pawns turns this into a winning endgame.

cb-2du.spoken: Black's plan is a kingside attack, pushing pawns and bringing pieces up to open lines against White's king, all without giving up material.

cb-2cy.spoken: Black has moved that same knight three times while White’s pieces come out. White gains a lead in development and holds the center.

cb-2db.spoken: After the fork lands, White wins a rook either way—picking between them is just taste. Both are strong.

cb-2dp.spoken: White has two extra pawns and a powerful knight outpost on c6 once the dark-squared bishops are traded, while Black’s queen sits passively on e8.

cb-2cx.spoken: In the Dutch Defense, White plays c4 to keep the classical setup. The knight goes to f3, and e4 follows as standard preparation.

cb-2da.spoken: Opening the center with d5 is the idea here, especially while the enemy king sits in the center. If Black captures, White gets a fork or a check and takes the initiative.

cb-2cq.spoken: White's pawns on d5 and e4 give a strong center, and his pieces stand actively. Black's knights have no good squares.

cb-2cz.spoken: White’s center pawns can push to d5 or e4, gaining space and squeezing Black’s pieces, whose knight on d5 has shuffled too many times and now lands on a weak square like b4 or c6.

cb-2e0.spoken: The d4 pawn is attacked, and the e5 pawn is threatened too. The center hangs in the balance, and White must answer Black’s threat to take the e5 pawn.

cb-2cs.spoken: White controls the key squares and dominates the board. Black's pieces sit poorly, and White threatens invasion on several fronts. Grabbing material now is not always the best choice; positional pressure carries greater value.

cb-2d1.spoken: White has developed many pieces while Black has moved the same knight twice and pushed the queen and king out early. That gives White a big development lead, so a direct attack is possible — long castling with a pawn storm, or even a piece sacrifice.

cb-2eo.spoken: If White aims for e4, Black must place a knight on e4 right away, before castling.

cb-2en.spoken: Both f5 and e4 are interesting pawn breaks here. Playing f5 right away opens lines, and if Black takes it, White gets a strong attack.

cb-2eu.spoken: White considered Qf4 after Black's f6, targeting that pawn while keeping the queen active for kingside pressure.

cb-2f2.spoken: Black’s early a6 stops White from playing Bg5 and denies the e2 square to White’s knight, keeping setups like Ng3 out of reach.

cb-2f4.spoken: Against the pawn trio d4, c4 and e3, the fianchetto is a passive move that never fights for the center.

cb-2fa.spoken: Knight e4 grabs the center and threatens real tactics. If bishop takes, queen h7 or h8 follows, and White's attack wins.

cb-2fd.spoken: Against the King's Indian, White builds a system with Bg5 and f4, then follows with g4 to stop Black's usual f5 break.

cb-2ep.spoken: Black has the extra pawn and a strong center, but White’s threat of knight to g5 forces Black to play h6 and stop the tactics.

cb-2f7.spoken: A passed pawn is a prize, but advancing it carelessly here lets Black take one pawn, then swing back to grab the other.

cb-2f1.spoken: If White wastes a tempo to stop Nb4 with a3, Black can strike with e5, leaving White with an isolated pawn. That's only slightly better, not the aggressive game White is after.

cb-2e4.spoken: Black's knight lands on c6, but White has already taken the d4 pawn. That knight is misplaced, and b4 can target it. White should castle and develop first — grabbing the piece could cost the center.

cb-2eh.spoken: The knight on e5 is a strong outpost, and White wants to play f4 to reinforce it. This break keeps Black from copying your setup and hands White a clear space edge.

cb-2ez.spoken: Black threatens e5, which frees their pieces and challenges White's center. White must stop e5 first, even before handling threats like Nb4.

cb-2f9.spoken: Play bishop to d2, defending the rook on a1. The rook looks exposed, but it's safe thanks to tactical resources.

cb-2es.spoken: White's g4 pushes the knight on f6, a key defender. Once it moves, Bxh7+ opens the way for Qh5 with mate threats.

cb-2et.spoken: White’s b4 clears b2 to fianchetto the bishop, producing opposite-colored bishops that favor the attacker. Black’s odd bishop move hands White free space on the queenside.

cb-2ec.spoken: Black plays b5, an aggressive grab of queenside space. It shows energy, but it can backfire if White answers correctly. White should look at pushing the b-pawn to undermine Black's structure.

cb-2em.spoken: White's position is strong now that Black's ideas are stopped. The next step is bringing the knight to life, ready to push f4 or e4 and open the game.

cb-2ey.spoken: White feared Black's e5 would free the position, so a3 or castling were options to keep control.

cb-2ea.spoken: Sacrificing material, like a knight, can sometimes simplify the position and dodge heavy calculation, especially when things get murky.

cb-2ej.spoken: White's dark-squared bishop is a key attacker, and trading it off makes no sense. Keep it and aim it at Black's kingside.

cb-2ev.spoken: Black's early Bb4 is weak. White answers with c3 and gains a tempo, while that bishop has no real role in Black's position.

cb-2ew.spoken: White’s extra pawn is clean, and the attack is already well formed. The bishop on d3 locks in Black’s king, and White’s pawns keep rolling forward. Hold the pressure and avoid messy complications.

cb-2eb.spoken: White’s e-pawn sits on the fifth rank, while Black’s d4-pawn cramps the position and claims central control. Sharp play follows.

cb-2fb.spoken: White's f-pawn targets Black's knight on f6, and the position stays sharp with tactics for both sides.

cb-2f6.spoken: Two hanging pieces can't protect each other, and no checks exist — this is a critical tactical moment.

cb-2el.spoken: Trading dark-squared bishops here gives White a light-squared bishop stuck behind light-squared pawns, usually a bad deal. Better to dodge the exchange, even if the bishop drops back to c1.

cb-2fv.spoken: Black's plan to castle comes at the cost of a rook, but White must refuse the bait. Stopping castling leaves the black king exposed and keeps the attack rolling.

cb-2fg.spoken: White missed a check that wins a piece on the spot, but the pawn structure is still winning. This position is nearly impossible to lose.

cb-2g6.spoken: The bishop on e2 is solid, but not yet a deciding factor. Develop naturally and get ready to fight for the center.

cb-2fr.spoken: The knight on f3 stands well in this setup. If Black tries e5, the knight jumps to d4. If Black instead plays d5, White captures and then pushes d3, squeezing Black's pieces.

cb-2fm.spoken: Black's d5 is a mistake. It surrenders the center and hands White free developing tempi. White keeps two center pawns, can easily chase the queen, and roll the pawns forward.

cb-2gd.spoken: White's extra piece outweighs the queen trade, and opening lines toward the king pays off. The queen can take b6, but Black should sacrifice material and allow the capture, setting up mate in two.

cb-2g5.spoken: A pawn on f5 lets Black block White's pawns and tie down the king. Advancing the king puts White in zugzwang, forcing checkmate or a decisive material win.

cb-2fw.spoken: With the knight misplaced on f3, White should reroute it to b3 and then c5, where it pressures Black's center and queenside.

cb-2fq.spoken: Black's queen on e7 is a roadblock in front of the f8-bishop, and that awkward setup gives White a target. Strike at the center now, before Black untangles and frees the position.

cb-2fh.spoken: Black often answers with Ne7 and d5. A pawn push to h4 invites counterplay in the center, so White must develop pieces first before advancing.

cb-2ff.spoken: Black's a6 move threatens nothing, so White can focus on g4 and Qg3, hitting the weak g7 pawn and the rook on a8. The knight can head to d6 to trade pieces, but that is not the urgent plan.

cb-2gj.spoken: If Black meets the e4 push with c5, White shouldn't take on c5 or advance d5. Play Nf3 instead, developing and waiting.

cb-2gh.spoken: White grabs the center with e4, and Black usually develops the bishop to f5 or g4 before committing to e6.

cb-2fp.spoken: When Black answers with d5 and the queen steps out, that’s a good sign for White—it usually lands White a tempo ahead.

cb-2fi.spoken: Black’s plan of pushing d5 and c5 after e5, once the bishop develops, works remarkably well against White’s h4-h5 pawn storm. That attack can backfire if Black strikes the center.

cb-2hg.spoken: If White tries Bg5, Black answers with f6 and wins a piece — the bishop is attacked and has no adequate defense.

cb-2h6.spoken: The knight on c3 is defended by the queen and bishop, but a clumsy queen maneuver like Qe2 or Qd2 removes those defenders. Attack the knight now and White loses material.

hp-b.spoken: The bishop develops toward the center, then the pawn thrusts forward, and the knight steps back. Black keeps the tension by refusing trades, preserving pieces to keep any edge small.

cb-2h4.spoken: White's d3 instead of d4 hands Black a free tempo in the Taimanov setup.

hp-r.spoken: The pawns roll forward in sequence, each step gaining space. Break open the position with the long pawn advance, and the initiative belongs to you.

hp-o.spoken: A pawn sacrificed to wake up the pieces earns attacking chances. Black, a pawn up, tries to consolidate but lets White seize too much activity, and the position turns difficult.

hp-1t.spoken: The bishop steps out to trade queens, and the extra pawn decides the game. White's initiative vanishes, and Black's advantage is decisive.

hp-2s.spoken: The queen steps to the wrong square, and the winning edge remains — but only with the most precise follow-up, or the pressure slips away.

hp-4z.spoken: The queen move invites a pawn thrust that locks the center in White's favor. The defender had to break up that pawn mass before it grows into a cage.

hp-4s.spoken: The exchange is given up to lock down the key central square and pile on pressure. The weak pawn is the real target, but pushing too soon walks into a tactic and loses the point.

hp-5j.spoken: When Black advances the center pawn, meet it with the quieter reply to keep the center solid. If Black holds back, White pushes forward and opens the game on favorable terms.

hp-4x.spoken: The knight retreats to regroup, and the queen drops back to control the key squares. When the knight shifts again and the queen advances to press the kingside, one careless pawn move there cracks the defense wide open.

hp-5b.spoken: The recapture choice decides the whole endgame. If Black takes back with the knight, White pushes the pawn again and creates a protected passed pawn that is nearly winning. So Black must take back with the queen or advance the pawn first.

hp-51.spoken: The pawn wedges deep in enemy territory, the rook pressure builds down the file, and the light-square bishop dominates. Black is cramped and has no comfortable defense.

hp-50.spoken: The knight stands poorly after the pawn advance. Heading to the central square lets White trade it off and win the pawn. Retreating to the back rank leaves the piece permanently out of play.

hp-4k.spoken: The knight step invites the bishop out to pin, and Black reaches easy equality — a tame result, not a challenge.

hp-5n.spoken: The knight retreats so the pawn can advance, then the knight returns to pressure the king's wing. This maneuver speeds the attack, even if it abandons the central square.

hp-4n.spoken: The knight stays on the home file so the bishop can develop to its active square unblocked, shielding the king's corner and lessening the pressure there.

hp-5i.spoken: The knight develops to a square that blocks the immediate pawn push to the center. White then chooses between a sharper or a quieter setup, and either keeps a slight edge when played correctly.

hp-5q.spoken: The queen falls, but before grabbing it back, Black slips in a check with the bishop. White must answer, and after the recapture, material is level, the doubled pawn is healed, and that bishop stands as possibly the strongest piece on the board.

hp-4o.spoken: Supporting the f-pawn keeps control of the key square, stopping the knight from landing there. Pressuring the h-pawn instead forces a weakening pawn move first.

hp-4v.spoken: The bishop develops to an active square, and Black can simply trade it off for equality. Several moves work, with the pawn advance a solid choice—it readies a strike at the center, and the passed pawn there is no real worry.

hp-5p.spoken: The bishop comes out to pin or pressure, and the queen lifts into the attack rather than grabbing the pawn. Taking the pawn lets the opponent check with the bishop, recapture, and keep a better bishop and clean pawns.

hp-59.spoken:
The knight move
offers Black several paths. Pushing the pawn instead signals a separate
gambit, not the usual defense. White answers with a pin, and once the
center resolves, the game shifts to a different character.

hp-4q.spoken: Castling longside sidesteps the typical short-castle setup. White gains space on the queenside and prepares a pawn break, while rerouting the bishop or queen to a strong diagonal keeps Black uncomfortable.

hp-5e.spoken: The knight reaches out from its outpost, hits the key square, and threatens to break through if the defender ignores it.

hp-4w.spoken: The main move is tested, but sidelines exist too. Early bishop or knight play stops Black's pawn push or shifts the fight to other imbalances.

hp-4m.spoken: The knight retreats to cover the king's pawn, the bishop slides to the center, and castling long would expose the king to a ruinous pawn storm.

hp-5u.spoken: The knight should defend the pawn instead of the pawn move. Then black pins with the bishop, and white must answer by capturing the knight. After the recapture, the pawn move becomes safe—fewer targets to grab, no attackers left.

hp-62.spoken: The knight posts on the edge, a tested line with theory and model games behind it.

hp-6c.spoken: The center is broad but brittle; Black strikes it with the wing pawn, steering into a Benoni or Sicilian shape, a sound practical weapon.

hp-6r.spoken: The h-pawn push is a bluff, not a threat. With the bishop free to develop, Black answers in the center and claims the proper setup without fear.

hp-5v.spoken: The flexible setup keeps several options open: pawn expansion, different bishop squares, or a central break. This adaptability is the theme—it keeps the opponent guessing.

hp-6d.spoken: The pawn break forces the issue. Once the knight lands on the outpost, the recapture with the pawn anchors it, and the square becomes a permanent thorn.

hp-76.spoken: The bishop recaptures, then the queen steps out to hit the weak pawn and make the center pawn immune — the position is perfectly sound.

hp-6l.spoken: The bishop pins the knight, but the center break outweighs a flank pawn. Playing the knight out and preparing the advance is safe, since the pawn capture is less important.

hp-6n.spoken: The bishop sits active on the long diagonal, and Black can hope to crack the center open with a later pawn break.

hp-6k.spoken: The queen drifts to the edge, making threats, while the bishop sits misplaced and takes no part in the defense.

hp-5z.spoken: This opening demands mastery of its own pawn skeletons and recurring patterns. Classical clarity is traded away, so intuition alone will not guide you.

hp-61.spoken: The standard King's Indian setup still works against these sidelines. Aim for the usual pieces and pawns, and the position stays roughly equal without deep theory.

hp-6g.spoken: The dark-squared bishop trades itself for the knight to contest the key central square. When the opponent dodges with the knight, the bishop takes it anyway and piles pressure on the center pawn.

hp-6q.spoken: The bishop's placement on that diagonal is a liability. Once the pawn is captured, the knight slides into the outpost and attacks both pawns at once.

hp-64.spoken: The King's Indian trades solid pawns for piece activity and tactical chances — that's the compensation. Fighters like Fischer and Kasparov built their reputations on exactly this trade-off.

hp-72.spoken: The knight is stranded on its starting square, so defending the pawn is awkward. Pushing the pawn forward invites punishment, so the knight must step out. Then the pawn thrust gains more than equality.

hp-63.spoken: The king's Indian gives Black a solid setup, but passivity later turns it into a losing liability. Keep the position dynamic and preserve counterplay or the initiative slips away.

hp-6v.spoken: The bishop recaptures and threatens the f-pawn with check. White blocks, but the rook joins the attack, and the pressure becomes triple. The pawn falls.

hp-6a.spoken: If White delays the central push, Black takes the pawn and then locks the center with the pawn advance, reaching the Maroczy bind — a structure that suits Black just like the Dragon setup.

hp-73.spoken: The pin on the knight invites Black to strike at the b-pawn, pulling the defender away. The fight turns rich: Black owns a hole, White owns a hole, and both armies have targets.

hp-6z.spoken: The knight retreats, and Black brings the knight to the rim. If the center pawn advances, the queen steps out again. A pawn push to chase her back gets captured, and Black gives up material in exchange for open lines, pawns, and a dangerous attack.

hp-6b.spoken: The knight lands on its outpost, but the attack that usually follows never comes. White's kingside chances stay thin, and the position drifts.

hp-6s.spoken: The bishop steps into a trap. Once the pawn captures it, the knight travels to the outpost and hits both weak pawns at once. The attacked pawn forces a defensive move, and the pressure stays on.

hp-5w.spoken: The knight stays on its original square to keep the pawn's advance open, aiming for the bind. If the knight develops early, the opponent's central pawn break comes easier, so the knight goes wide instead, forcing a passive pawn move and a Hedgehog structure.

hp-60.spoken: The King's Indian asks for activity at a price: a weaker pawn chain or a looser king. That trade is the plan, not a flaw.

hp-75.spoken: Black posts the knight, then strikes the c-pawn with the pawn. White blocks with the knight, but Black's next pawn move is stronger than the other option — it prepares development while keeping the pressure on.

hp-5y.spoken: The engine favors White in the King's Indian, but that is not a verdict. The opening trades a small static edge for Black's dynamic chances, and the game stays fully playable.

hp-66.spoken: The bishop lands between two targets—the queen and the knight—and hits both at once. The queen is forced to step across and shield the knight, and then the rook slides in behind her. That skewer wins material.

hp-6p.spoken: The knight retreats to the edge under attack, but it is a trap — it must not be captured. White prepares a pawn push on the queenside, yet Black's own pawn advance in the center gives the stronger counterplay.

hp-70.spoken: White pushes the kingside pawns to storm the castle, the usual Dragon pattern. Black answers with the c-pawn to mirror that structure, and if the pawn is taken, the queen, knight, and d-pawn all join the fight for the center.

hp-65.spoken: The engine may call this clearly better for White, but the King's Indian never runs out of practical chances. Tactical resources keep Black in the fight, especially against a human.

hp-6f.spoken: The king belongs on the other wing. If Black castles short, White's pawn storm loses its bite, so keep the king away and develop, then strike at the center.

hp-6e.spoken: The race is set: White pushes to break in the center and create a passed pawn, Black strikes on the flank to counter. Whoever lands their break first usually takes a decisive edge.

hp-6u.spoken: The queen steps out, the pawn falls, and after the recapture the rook slides to the fourth rank. It cannot be captured — the queen would be lost to the knight — and it suffocates the kingside while eyeing the f-pawn.

hp-6y.spoken: The knight steps out to its natural square. When the queen probes, the h-pawn move is too slow — Black develops the bishop, and if White advances the d-pawn, Black trades it off, leaving equal pawns but a lively bishop against a passive one.

hp-7z.spoken: Experience beats memorization. Practice games teach more than theory ever will — every mistake is a lesson.

hp-7i.spoken: The queen move leaves the knight hanging. Black must fix that before anything else, or the bishop move simply drops the piece.

hp-83.spoken: Losing the d-pawn costs the game. Defend it properly before the position collapses.

hp-81.spoken: The knight move is non-committal: it leaves the queen's path clear, keeps the g-pawn flexible, and preserves options. It performs well and trails the mainline only slightly.

hp-7w.spoken: The bishop hangs loose, and the queen strikes at it and the g-pawn at the same time. Black must answer both threats or drop material.

hp-77.spoken: The pawn looks free, but taking it leaves another one hanging, so the offer is a trap. The queen's pressure creates threats no one can ignore.

hp-7s.spoken: Forcing moves first: checks and captures narrow the opponent’s replies. Calculate every one, since a hanging piece or a check can turn confusion into a decisive trap.

hp-7g.spoken: The knight leaps to the edge and the queen attacks it, so the pawn often must step up to defend. Pushing that pawn further is sometimes possible later, but only if the opponent's moves allow it in that exact position.

hp-8f.spoken: The bishop gets blocked in, not traded away. If White plays a quiet move first, Black slides the bishop to the open diagonal and develops easily, while the Catalan bishop loses its bite.

hp-7m.spoken: The bishop retreats to a quieter square, yet Black's plan does not change: hit the knight and keep developing. The quieter bishop does help against a nuisance knight, but it sits passively, and an unprepared opponent rarely plays it.

hp-8g.spoken: The knight jumps to a central outpost and controls the square the bishop needs. If the bishop tries to reach it, the knight takes it. If the bishop stays home, it remains passive on its starting square.

hp-7j.spoken: The bishop develops to the open diagonal, and the knight answers by developing toward the center. That one move does double duty: it adds pressure on the enemy position, and in some lines it can step in front of checks along the open file.

hp-82.spoken: A knight sitting on strong central squares is doing real work. Pulling it back to a worse square is a blunder unless the retreat lands it somewhere useful without costing a tempo.

hp-7f.spoken: The main line is what White expects and prepares for, leading into sharp gambit play. The defensive reply sidesteps that and steers into a different game, where the attack is less direct.

hp-7c.spoken: The bishop pins the knight to the king, and the knight cannot simply be taken — the recapture opens lines that hurt the attacker. Let the pin stand and meet the threat instead.

hp-8i.spoken: Black keeps the extra pawn and gains activity, so the queen sortie is not the line to choose. After the recapture, prefer castling, the main line, over the deviations.

hp-8b.spoken: The knight stepping out before the bishop does changes White's plan. The usual push chases the bishop and then widens the attack, but when the pawn already supports the bishop, White can strike in the center instead, keeping the kingside solid.

hp-7v.spoken: The knight on the kingside is a target, not a fortress. Black skips the preparatory pawn move and pushes the g-pawn straight into it, gaining space and chasing the piece away.

hp-7y.spoken: Play the opening to learn it. Practical games teach more than memorizing long theoretical lines.

hp-7x.spoken: The knight retreats to an active square, not a passive one. Developing toward the center keeps the piece in the fight and contests the key square.

hp-7e.spoken: The knight steps back to the rim, yet it is not misplaced — it guards the f-pawn and stands as prophylaxis, blocking the bishop's easy development and stifling the attack down the f-file.

hp-79.spoken: The pawn on the seventh pulls the defender into a recapture. That recapture opens the a-file, where the rook is given up to clear the queen's path, and the knight holds the critical square so the queen arrives unopposed.

hp-7u.spoken: The queen steps out early, and Black strikes the center at once. That pawn break challenges White before the d-pawn can advance and consolidate the setup.

hp-8a.spoken: The early bishop steps out before the knight has come to its natural square. That leaves the center pawn push unopposed, so White advances the pawn and gains space — a better outcome than if the knight had already been developed to prevent it.

hp-78.spoken: The knight sits on the active square, not the rim, so the queen or rook can slide behind it and fire the strike. Parked on the rim square, the knight blocks that path.

hp-80.spoken: The bishop gambit tempts a queen check, but the knight chases it and gains time. A quiet developing move works better.

hp-7t.spoken: An unusual but sound move can catch an opponent off guard, especially online or at club level. Even if the engine prefers something else, the surprise itself earns a practical edge.

hp-8d.spoken: The pawn recapture on that square is harmless and equalizes. Pushing the rook pawn is the real test, sharp and double-edged, giving White attacking chances.

hp-8c.spoken: The knight leap exploits the unprotected pawn. When the pawn advances to challenge the center, the knight jumps forward, and if the bishop retreats, the pawn push traps it and wins the pawn.

hp-7a.spoken: The knight heads for the central outpost, and if it lands, capturing invites a recapture that drops the pawn and opens the door to queen checks and grabs on the queenside.

hp-7n.spoken: The knight defending the pawn becomes a target once the pawn falls. After the recapture, the queen lands active, and the rook lift threatens. But traps lurk — a bishop may strike to cage the queen, so calculate before committing.

hp-7d.spoken: The knight develops and hits the pawn in the center, questioning White's foothold.

hp-7q.spoken: Deep plans often start with a quiet bishop move. The piece sits back, yet it supports a later pawn push or maneuver, and its purpose only appears many moves later.

hp-8e.spoken: The light-squared bishop is trouble in this setup — the e-pawn walls it in. Sliding it out to prepare a challenge to the fianchettoed bishop is the natural fix.

hp-84.spoken: Black’s knight to the edge of the center waits without commitment. It keeps the queen’s road clear for a later strike, holds key central squares, and lets Black adapt to White’s setup.

hp-85.spoken: The knight steps forward, inviting either pawn push. If the pawn advances, the knight leaps to attack the bishop and seizes the initiative. If the other pawn advances, the knight lands centrally, menacing both weaknesses and backing the queen's coming attack.

hp-7l.spoken: The rook overshoots its post when the file shuts, stranded from the pawn it meant to pressure. Black's bishop and queen finish development into a comfortable setup.

hp-9f.spoken: The rook must hold the file to keep the king out. If it grabs the pawn instead, the king breaks through and the defense collapses.

hp-9a.spoken: The pawn break is too slow while Black's pieces hold the bind. Black waits, keeps the pressure, and zugzwang forces White to weaken further.

hp-9g.spoken: The rook cuts the king off from the center, barring the path through. The task is to break that blockade and bring the king into play.

hp-94.spoken: The knight must reroute to target the weak pawns, or sacrifice if the king strays. Pushing the pawns forward can also create a passed pawn.

hp-8n.spoken: The statistics for the rook move say the score is decent, but it demands serious preparation. Strong players have used it, yet without the theory it is risky.

hp-9d.spoken: The pawn push does double duty: it rescues the pawn and fixes the enemy pawns on their current squares, making them permanent targets.

hp-9k.spoken: Black owns the only open file, and that edge is real. Meeting the rook head-on risks a draw or worse, so White must find another plan.

hp-96.spoken: Passive waiting lets Black carry out the plan without resistance. Even in an objectively equal position, that hands Black practical chances and psychological edge.

hp-9o.spoken: The point is to know what you aim for and see the real issue: Black's rook outranks White's, but that pawn push flips the comparison.

hp-8u.spoken: The gambit is unsound on paper, but it buys sharp chaos where Black trades material for active pieces and attacking chances. White's job is to pick a reply that sidesteps the complications entirely.

hp-8r.spoken: The knight heads for a strong square to accelerate the attack. If the opponent posts a knight centrally, the trade simplifies and the bishop and rook join in faster.

hp-9i.spoken: The king and knight outweigh equal material here. With the pawn advanced, the active pieces force the win.

hp-8y.spoken: Choose the sound, patient setup over the sharpest line. It keeps the edge without handing Black a spark, and shuts down their active pieces before they stir.

hp-9n.spoken: The file-busting move flips the game in your favor, handing White a growing edge with best play. It exploits the closed files and plants a target on the queenside.

hp-8w.spoken: The queen check forces either a weakening or a queen trade. When the knight blocks the check, the pawn push targets the advanced pawn and keeps the trade offer alive.

hp-99.spoken: In a pawn race, count every runner. Once the minor pieces are gone, each side's pawns keep advancing, but the one whose king stands closer to the action wins the race.

hp-8p.spoken: The knight retreats to blockade the isolated pawn, and that setup favors White. Black must strike with the e-pawn to create counterplay, or the position sours before the IQP structure even appears.

hp-9l.spoken: The pawn break opens the a-file, waking the rook to full activity. If the opponent slams the door with a pawn advance, the follow-up crack forces them to guard the seventh rank.

hp-98.spoken: The bishop's long road ends on the same diagonal that pins the knight down. That tie lets the king walk in. If the minor pieces come off, the king and pawns stand better and the endgame is won.

hp-9u.spoken: The pawn chains point in opposite directions, and each side must attack where its chain aims. Black pushes on the kingside with f-pawn advances, while White strikes on the queenside with b-pawn and c-pawn pushes.

hp-9b.spoken: The pawns race, but Black's king decides it. Even if White blocks the break, the king slips in, and White's pawns are too slow to queen first — so pushing them early just loses.

hp-9c.spoken: The position is dead equal, but the plan is what matters. One side has a clear pawn break to aim for, and that makes the game easier to play. The other side must defend precisely and find counterplay to turn the tables.

hp-97.spoken: The bishop slides all the way in, and White's position turns critical. The knight is pinned to its duty defending key squares; if it steps away, the opposing king walks straight through the gap. The bishop's diagonals seal the rest.

hp-91.spoken: The pawn push forces the rook to the corner to hold the balance. That square lets Black meet the capture by trading rooks, driving the knight offside, and resetting the endgame. White keeps the better pawns from future breaks, but Black can neutralize.

hp-9e.spoken: Black's aim is to trade pieces and stir up kingside counterplay, while the white knight sits firmly on its central outpost, shielding the weak point and keeping the position solid.

hp-9m.spoken: The rook endgame turns on activity: White’s rook patrols the open file while Black’s rook sits idle, cut off from the king’s side. The kingside pawn majority loses its punch because the active rook and king cancel it out.

hp-9r.spoken: Black castles into the King's Indian, keeping both pawn breaks open. White's knight develops, and Black waits to see whether the center advances.

hp-9s.spoken: The h-pawn advance looks quiet but sets up the pawn storm. Black answers in the center; that pawn is no gift, since capturing it hands Black exactly the kind of position he wants.

hp-8q.spoken: The queen's trip out is too slow. Black gives the pawn back, then the pawn thrust creates real counterplay — Black is at least equal, maybe better.

hp-8t.spoken: The knight leap refutes the idea of developing the bishop for free, which is why that line fell out of favor. Black can castle queenside, accepting White's edge with accurate play, but gaining counterplay. Or Black chooses the rook move for a safer setup.

hp-8o.spoken: If Black dodges the sharp pawn break and develops instead, the engine hands White a clear edge. Capturing on the diagonal doubles Black's pawns, then a knight hop blockades them. The break is Black's only path to counterplay, though it demands theory.

hp-8k.spoken: The center is won when the knight retreats to the edge. Push the pawn, and when the knight falls back, develop the bishop and bring the knight out to claim the middle. The misplaced knight lets you storm the center with the pawn.

hp-8z.spoken: Complex endgames reward plans over single moves, since there is time to adapt and carry out a sound idea. Precise calculation matters only in forcing races, such as pawn races where both sides promote.

hp-93.spoken: The pawn thrust buys space and sets up the king's path forward. White answers by centralizing, while Black shuffles pieces and prepares a pawn break, all against White's quiet prophylaxis.

hp-9p.spoken: The bishop on the long diagonal eyeing the queenside weakens White's grip on the central light squares. With the bishop posted there instead, White’s advance in the center stays under pressure, and the key square remains contested.

hp-90.spoken: The e-pawn advance is the hinge. Until White achieves it, the position is roughly equal. Once played, White stands better, especially with Black's doubled pawns and little play on the queenside.

hp-8l.spoken: The bishop’s retreat gives White two replies, one simple, one aggressive. Take the simple path. The knight reroutes to its natural square, and if the pawn tries to advance to defend itself, a bishop check stops it cold, so the knight re-takes what is owed.

hp-9z.spoken: In a sharp kingside attack, closing the position is a mistake when the attacker has already committed pieces there. Once the h-pawn advances, lines open and the weakened pawns become targets.

hp-an.spoken: A lead in development is a danger, not a comfort. Falling behind in it puts the game at immediate risk.

hp-9v.spoken: The pawn advance is a prophylactic move, stopping the opponent's typical queenside expansion before it starts and cutting off their counterplay.

hp-ae.spoken: Neglect of development is the real collapse. Even with no blunder, pieces left at home let the opponent pile on pressure until the position resigns itself.

hp-am.spoken: The knight steps in, defending the pawn and attacking both bishops at once. The capture comes first, then the bishop retreats to grab another pawn, leaving two pawns ahead.

hp-aq.spoken: When the bishop pins the knight, several replies work. Some block the pin, others accept it — group them that way.

hp-a0.spoken: The defender's pieces sit badly and the queen is boxed in behind pawns. With no counterplay and a pawn in hand, the attacker's edge is decisive.

hp-b6.spoken: The knight jumps out to attack the pawn, but this is a sideline. The opponent can punish it.

hp-aj.spoken: The early bishop move invites a central pawn push or a knight hop into the center, and the engine calls the position clearly better for the opponent.

hp-av.spoken: The pawn push opens a heavily analyzed, sharp theoretical line where the position is so non-standard that the outcome stays unclear and draws are unlikely.

hp-al.spoken: The bishop slides back to defend, keeping the advantage intact. The best reply sacrifices material to rescue the rook from the skewer.

hp-a5.spoken: The bishop pins the knight to the queen, so capturing it forces recapture with the pawn. That doubled pawn ruins the structure. The knight must stay put.

hp-a3.spoken: The position is winning, yet the game ends drawn. Even strong players let frustration or doubt talk them out of a win.

hp-ac.spoken: The central pawn thrust challenges the center directly. If the opponent answers with their own pawn push, a flank pawn move harasses the bishop and drives it to an awkward square. That frees the key central square for piece activity.

hp-ak.spoken: The knight leaps in to land the decisive blow, but only after the bishop gives it cover. Play the quiet threat first, and the winning invasion follows.

hp-af.spoken: A knight sitting on an outpost square is not a threat until it can retreat. If the trap is set, the piece becomes overextended and the real gain comes from winning material elsewhere.

hp-ax.spoken: Black's pawn move stops the bishop from landing on the attacking square, but it costs tempo and hands White the initiative. White picks either a quiet setup or the aggressive central push, and the sharp line leaves Black facing the threat of losing a piece.

hp-au.spoken: The queen check pulls the pawn forward, and after the exchanges White's central pawn mass takes shape. The theory runs deep and the verdict is unclear, but the imbalance points to a decisive game.

hp-ah.spoken: The retreating bishop keeps its diagonal, covering both the rook's escape square and a vulnerable pawn. By denying the rook its freeing move and maintaining the attack, any knight move drops material.

hp-ap.spoken: The bishop trades for the knight, and how Black recaptures decides the cost. Taking back with the e-pawn gives White two central pawns against one, a lasting structural edge. Taking back with the g-pawn weakens the kingside and dents castling prospects.

hp-b5.spoken: The d-pawn leaves Black cramped and reactive. Taking the knight forces the e-pawn to recapture, mirroring the fianchetto structure. White keeps the bishop on the long diagonal with a flexible knight, and the position stays comfortable.

hp-a6.spoken: The knight offer to trade queens looks tempting, but declining it with the knight blocks the bishop's path. Meanwhile, the white knight jumps to a square that pressures Black, and if Black fianchettoes the bishop, that jump gains even more strength.

hp-at.spoken: Against the bishop's early posting, Black picks between a solid central push or an aggressive wing strike. When Black goes aggressive, White can steer into a quiet setup or a sharp one — the sharp choice chases complex play and quick development.

hp-a9.spoken: The rook steps into the open file and Black has solid choices: contest that file with the rook, reroute the knight to support a central pawn break, or push the center pawn to fight for space. The game stays level, but passive play would let the advantage slip.

hp-a1.spoken: Precision decides. The queen move hits the rook directly. Instead, the bishop lets the defender trade off an attacker. Removing a defender is fine only when the initiative stays yours.

hp-9w.spoken: The pawn thrust challenges Black's kingside setup directly; the slower piece move lets Black's plan go unanswered. Pushing both pawns on that flank builds counterplay against the coming break.

hp-a8.spoken: The pawn move shuts down the knight's jump to that annoying square. Skip it, and the knight leaps in to hit both weak points at once, creating real threats.

hp-b0.spoken: The d-pawn push is a psychological concession — it enters a structure many knight players dislike. White sidesteps the main lines and transposes elsewhere, using the move order to unsettle Black.

hp-aw.spoken: The opening is only half the lesson. The real test is the middlegame structures it leads to.

hp-ao.spoken: The bishop steps out before the knights and before castling, which looks strange but has a clear point. It threatens to trade itself for the knight and double the f-pawns, creating an imbalance in the position.

hp-aa.spoken: The pawn thrust challenges the center and sets up a later attack on the bishop with a flank pawn. It avoids weakening the diagonal early, unlike the other pawn move.

hp-ay.spoken: The king is safer on the queenside, where he avoids the pawn storm on the other wing. The structure stays balanced, but White holds more space, and piece activity plus king safety decide the game—Black's king is usually in trouble first.

hp-ad.spoken: Bishop moves outside the pawn chain, but the reply attacks it and also menaces the rook. If the rook gets defended, the pawn structure gets ruined; if Black counters, White keeps tactical chances.

hp-a2.spoken: Black wins on the strength of a pawn advantage, a bishop that soon occupies the long diagonal’s center, and relentless pressure on the weak f-pawn. White’s pieces sit passive, and the bishop faces no rival.

hp-b4.spoken: The bishop trades itself for the knight, forcing the pawn to recapture and doubling Black's pawns. That leaves a Caro-Kann-like structure with White's position simpler to play. Watch for the pawn push that attacks the fianchetto wing.

hp-a7.spoken: The bishop on the long diagonal looks active but gets in the way, and the knight can leap to a more aggressive square because the position is otherwise mirror-symmetric except White has one extra tempo from developing that bishop early.

hp-9y.spoken: The pawn push is a rash decision — it lets White shut down the kingside. Better to capture toward the attack and keep it alive. Once the pawn advances, White recaptures and lines the queen up against the h-pawn, and Black is in trouble.

hp-bd.spoken: The king steps to the corner as a prophylactic move after the knight develops. The engine favors Black slightly, and the attack has real chances.

hp-c5.spoken: A passed-pawn threat prods the opponent into pushing pawns, and every advance becomes a fresh target for your bishop.

hp-c4.spoken: Place pawns on your bishop’s color to box in the enemy knight, and those squares become permanent weaknesses the knight can never safely touch.

hp-ci.spoken: Both defenders are frozen — the rook and bishop stay or give up material, and no pawn can change it. A rare, instructive zugzwang.

hp-bt.spoken: The bishop looks active but guards nothing that matters. It lets the king stroll to the key square, and once there, Black's position collapses.

hp-cb.spoken: The king is safer and the bishop owns the long diagonal, while the knight and bishop sit stranded on the queenside. Material is equal, but the pieces prove the difference.

hp-bs.spoken: The king's activity decides rook-and-bishop endgames. A cut-off king cannot stop the enemy king from penetrating to the sixth rank, so the defender must fight to prevent that invasion.

hp-cc.spoken: The pawn moves forced by threats become permanent targets. Each one is a weakness the king and pieces can strike at later.

hp-ce.spoken: The pawn is left to fall, and the bishop steps onto an open diagonal with the king still active. Pressure outlasts protection.

hp-cf.spoken: The rook slides to the back rank instead of marching the king. That keeps the rook active, stops black’s pieces from entering, and sidesteps light squares the bishop could target.

hp-c8.spoken: The pawn is bait, and the hole it leaves is the real prize. That hole gives your bishop a permanent outpost while denying the enemy knight any safe square near it.

hp-bv.spoken: The active rook and better king decide rook endgames on equal material. One side's rook dominates, the opponent's pawns are weak, and their own are sound — that imbalance is the whole game.

hp-bx.spoken: Material is level, but all three weaknesses sit on black's side. Grabbing the pawn kicks off a forced sequence that ends in a draw, so the position asks for something quieter.

hp-ca.spoken: The bishop outshines the knight in the endgame, and the passed pawns call the shots. The bishop holds the key squares and clears the road for the pawns to march.

hp-bi.spoken: The knight jumps to challenge the bishop, and Black must spend a move to stop it landing on that strong square. Then Black develops normally, while White burns tempi just to capture the bishop.

hp-c2.spoken: The protected passed pawn ends the fight. The enemy rook is chained to blocking it, so your king walks up to escort it home. The kingside pawns no longer matter — that pawn decides the game.

hp-bp.spoken: The knight retreats to create a battering ram. When the pawn advances to strike the rival knight, the bishop slides back, and the pawn push forces a choice that clears the way to trade off the bishops.

hp-b7.spoken: The bishop sits exposed on its diagonal, and the pawn thrust forces a choice. Advancing to meet it looks natural but plants a fixed weakness that stays for good.

hp-by.spoken: The prophylactic pawn advance creates a critical moment. If the rook grabs the a-pawn, the king slides in and collects both queenside pawns, yet with precise defense Black still holds. The position is improved for White, not decisive.

hp-be.spoken: The rook lifts to the third rank, the other rook comes to the open file, and the queen drops back to the second. Black begins the queenside push with the pawn advance — that is the usual trigger for the attack.

hp-bq.spoken: The bishop and queen line up on the same diagonal, and that battery demands an answer. From there, either pawns chase the knight off and open lines toward the king, or the king tucks away on the opposite side while pawns storm forward to break through.

hp-bk.spoken: The bishop steps out, and the knight maneuvers to strike the g-pawn. Black must answer that threat, but the pawn push that freed the knight has left a hole — that pawn now hangs as a permanent weakness.

hp-cd.spoken: The rook offer is a trap, not a threat. Ignore the trade, slide the rook deep into black's camp, and the pressure on the uncastled pieces stays on. If the bishop flinches, the rook gains a tempo and the pawn falls.

hp-b9.spoken: The h-pawn’s second push is premature when the bishop is still undefended; first, the quiet step gives the bishop a retreat square, and only after the knight develops and the other piece joins does the advance become sound.

hp-c9.spoken: The extra pawn is real, but the cost of keeping it may be the initiative. If the knight's activity comes at the price of a pawn, the material is only compensation when the position stops being passive — and the pawn-up side must keep counterplay closed.

hp-c6.spoken: The opponent's pieces are pinned down guarding weaknesses. Improve your own pieces and build double threats.

hp-c3.spoken: One passed pawn can force the enemy rook to sacrifice for it, yet converting demands exact timing and dodging every trap.

hp-bf.spoken: Black pushes the a-pawn to open queenside lines and start play against White's structure. The position stays balanced, with chances for both sides.

hp-bu.spoken: The king march is the real threat. Counterplay must come from actual pressure, not slow pawn moves that only hand the opponent time to step deeper into your position.

hp-br.spoken: The knight has better prospects on the other square, where it eyes the central outpost. The alternative square lets White plant a piece in the center and pressure the key point.

hp-bl.spoken: Against the knight slipping to the edge, Black trades the light-squared bishop to push the g-pawn, forcing the horse back. That puts pawns on light squares and leaves dark squares soft, yet it stops White from nursing a lasting initiative.

hp-bg.spoken: The bishop posts where it cannot be punished, and the pawn stays home, keeping the king’s shelter intact. Yet Black’s chances stay good, and a quick pawn push opens the rook’s file at once.

hp-bb.spoken: The knight retreats for one purpose only: to guard the key square. If the enemy knight captures anyway, the queen recaptures, and the cost is castling rights—leaving the attacker worse off.

hp-bw.spoken: The natural capture looks tempting, but it wakes the enemy rook. Letting it into the active rank trades your winning chances for a draw. Find the precise move that keeps the pressure.

hp-bm.spoken: The knight's move to the active square lets Black push the pawn and post the bishop to challenge the defender. Capturing with the rook is wrong since the bishop isn't on that diagonal; instead, the h-pawn takes to open lines at once.

hp-cg.spoken: The king belongs on the dark squares here. Light squares invite the enemy bishop’s harassment, even when no immediate threat appears.

hp-c0.spoken: A rook lift to the third rank defends the weak pawn and, more importantly, blocks the enemy king's escape route. The defending rook is left passive, unable to cover the weak pawns efficiently.

hp-bh.spoken: The pawn offer tempts a grab, but pushing the b-pawn instead gains space and opens lines. If White accepts the gift, the rook slides to the back rank, captures on the seventh, and play stays equal but murky.

hp-bj.spoken: The pawn advance to solidify the bishop lets the queen pressure the knight twice, forcing the capture. The flank pawn push allows the bishop take that gains a tempo, but the reply recaptures and leaves the pawn exposed to attack.

hp-bc.spoken: The bishop pins the knight, so Black develops with a tempo on the queen. Each check or threat gains tempi, and the queen retreats, leaving White's pawn a permanent weakness.

hp-dc.spoken: Some books teach the ideas clearly, others just list moves, and online tools let you build the repertoire around your own games.

hp-d1.spoken: The knight outshines the bishop in this endgame, so White trades into it before the pieces come off.

hp-cz.spoken: The knight trade for the bishop hands White the advantage. Once the rooks come off, the endgame is winning.

hp-cv.spoken: White holds a space edge on the queenside and better pieces. Black's bishop and knight sit passive, far from the fight.

hp-co.spoken: Two fixed weaknesses in the enemy camp are enough to win, as long as they survive the piece trades. If they do, the endgame is worth entering.

hp-dt.spoken: Playing against a human-like opponent that gives feedback and wanders off the main lines beats reading books or watching videos.

hp-cn.spoken: Two fixed flaws in the enemy pawns, like doubled or isolated ones that last into the endgame, are often enough to win.

hp-d9.spoken: The c-pawn trades for Black's central pawn, and White is left with the central majority. That is the Sicilian theme, working in reverse.

hp-cu.spoken: The pawn majority looks stuck, but tactics unlock it. Break through with a timely push, using pins and tactical motifs to force the way.

hp-cp.spoken: A queenside pawn majority outvalues a kingside one: the enemy king sits farther away, so your passed pawns run faster than his can be caught, while his own are easier to stop.

hp-d4.spoken: The pawn at the center is the load-bearing piece of the structure. When it comes under attack, the supporting pawn steps up to reinforce it, and the chain holds firm.

hp-d6.spoken: The opening move grabs control of the center square and discourages the opponent from claiming it. White stays flexible, with no pawn structure or piece placement committed yet.

hp-cs.spoken: A queenside pawn majority pays off late. Trading pieces makes it stronger, so head for exchanges that leave those pawns on the board.

hp-cm.spoken: The endgame after the trades favors White. The activity of the remaining pieces outweighs the material count.

hp-cw.spoken: The exchange of rooks and queens leaves White's bishops roaming free while Black's pieces sit passive, so material is equal but the edge is nearly winning.

hp-cj.spoken: The rook's last move attacks a pawn and locks the bishop out of the game. Save the pawn, and the bishop stays passive; abandon it, and the pawn drops.

hp-ck.spoken: The middlegame decision hinges on the endgame. Look ahead and ask whether your position stays favorable once the pieces come off.

hp-da.spoken: The c-pawn advances twice in three moves to strike the overextended center pawn. If White captures, Black gambits the pawn for activity.

hp-d5.spoken: Black's choice here sets the whole middlegame. Taking the pawn or developing the knight changes nothing about the central question — pushing the pawn opens the center, while the other push keeps it closed.

hp-cr.spoken: A queenside pawn majority and the superior bishop make the endgame worth chasing. Trading down into it is the plan, even when a loose pawn tempts you to grab it instead.

hp-di.spoken: The French Defense shelters Black in a familiar pawn chain, anchored by a bishop that has no good squares. The four weapons exist to drag Black into structures they have not studied, breaking the comfort of their usual plans.

hp-dh.spoken: The French player's comfort is a locked pawn chain — solid, cramped, and with a bad light-squared bishop. Each side line fights the structure itself, forcing a change in the pawns or the pieces.

hp-df.spoken: The queen move provocatively stops the opponent from advancing the center pawn, because capturing it would expose a pinned pawn that cannot recapture. That forces a different setup, and the queen’s unusual post remains awkward but workable.

hp-dg.spoken: The f-pawn thrust is provocative but nearly sound, with Black holding only a whisper of an edge. Answer it in the center with the d-pawn to punish the early advance — the same remedy as in the two Sicilian setups.

hp-dq.spoken: The knight's counterattack is the sharpest test, eyeing the center pawn. If White tries to defend with the f-pawn, the queen and knight combine for a crushing finish. So White must push the pawn forward, but that concedes the blocked structure Black wanted.

hp-d0.spoken: The bishop watches from the sideline while Black's king finds no way in. The knight creeps forward, guards the weak points, and conjures threats one by one.

hp-cl.spoken: Black keeps both bishops and pressure on the pawn, but the doubled c-pawns poison the queenside majority. White’s kingside majority is sound, so the endgame favors White.

hp-cy.spoken: The plan is to shed both rooks and queens, steering into an endgame that favors you — not to chase gain.

hp-dp.spoken: The bishop on D7 blocks the queen from checking on E2. When Black answers with bishop E7, the F6 bishop becomes pinned. White captures on F6, then the knight on C3 attacks the hanging D5 pawn. Black's king sits awkwardly, and the position collapses.

hp-de.spoken: The Horwitz Attack delays the center, develops the bishop to the long diagonal, and fights for the dark squares. Black either accepts the temporary pawn sacrifice or builds a solid French-style center.

hp-db.spoken: The advanced pawn chain invites an early challenge from the c-pawn. That break is a known, tested path, and it stands as a solid alternative to the more common bishop development.

hp-dm.spoken: Develop the knight to the rim piece's square, then to the bishop's square. Once Black develops the queenside bishop, capture the central pawn and post the knight there, readying a kingside pawn storm.

hp-ds.spoken: The Horwitz Attack gives White lasting attacking chances. If Black castles, the attack flows. If not, the king stays central and White opens lines with a pawn storm. The bad bishop improves by rerouting once the king's destination is known.

hp-ct.spoken: The queenside majority is already advanced, while the opponent's still sits on the second rank. That gap decides the endgame, so trading rooks plays into the stronger side.

hp-cq.spoken: A knight thrives against a bishop when no pawns can be attacked, hopping freely to hit weak points. The king gains entry squares, while the opponent must create pawn weaknesses just to break in.

hp-dd.spoken: The French Defense is a hard opening for White to crack. Black’s solid pawn chain and bad light-squared bishop blunt the attack, and French players are ready for every common line.

hp-du.spoken: The queen move stops the d-pawn from advancing. If Black pushes anyway, White recaptures, then develops the knight with tempo, reaching a Scandinavian-style setup where Black's bishop stays trapped on its home square behind the e-pawn.

hp-dj.spoken: The bishop on the long diagonal pressures the center while the kingside pawn advances to undermine the knight's outpost. If the pawn is captured, the square left behind becomes a permanent weakness that grants lasting compensation.

hp-d8.spoken: After kingside pawn moves produce a reversed Sicilian, White holds an extra tempo. That tempo buys the choice between a fianchetto setup and an early central break.

hp-ex.spoken: In the Lipnitsky Attack, White chooses between pushing the f-pawn to press the attack or consolidating with the queen. Castling is a mistake when it hands Black time to organize counterplay.

hp-f5.spoken: The engine's line is sharp but sound, yet most players score better with the queen supporting the center, keeping the push and the flanking idea alive.

hp-e6.spoken: White delays the center push, first supporting it and rerouting the knight, so the d-pawn advance comes with full preparation. The light-squared bishop sits elsewhere than in the similar variation, which slightly changes the setup.

hp-f0.spoken: The main choice in the Lipnitsky hangs on black's b-pawn. Playing it early shuts down white's f-pawn advance. Delaying it invites that advance instead.

hp-ez.spoken: The flank pawn thrust stops the queenside expansion cold. With that break denied, White develops at leisure and keeps the kingside attack waiting.

hp-e5.spoken: The isolated queen pawn side wants to attack fast, while the defender blocks. The knight on the blockading square is hard to dislodge without adjacent pawns to chase it off.

hp-ea.spoken: White must only keep the pressure on; the attacking plan runs itself. Even with perfect defense, the position stays near equal, but White's side is far simpler to handle.

hp-e0.spoken: The knight reroutes to the outpost when the pawns advance. With the bishop’s diagonal blocked, White can skip the usual pawn breaks and lean on the knight instead.

hp-el.spoken: The knight grabs the pawn, and the rook pins the line to create triple pressure on the weak pawn. Black's usual push still loses, as the bishop piles on the knight and the breakthrough wins material.

hp-e3.spoken: The queen recapture hands White a free tempo with the knight. Recapture with the knight instead. Against the bishop pin, answer with the other knight, not the c-pawn, even while that pawn remains available.

hp-en.spoken: The pawn thrust opens a target. When the queen comes out to hit the kingside, castling into the attack fails — the central pawn advance forks rook and knight, and material falls.

hp-eu.spoken: White's forces dominate the center and kingside. Black's defense is stretched thin, and the slightest slip such as an awkward rook or passive queen lets White break through with tactical blows.

hp-e4.spoken: The bishop pins the knight, and if Black blocks with the pawn, White lines up pieces against it and pressures the pinned defender. The proper answer is to develop the other knight instead, like in the accelerated Panov.

hp-eb.spoken: The knight develops to its natural square, and Black still has solid options. Pushing the rook pawn instead is a sideline: White's pawn advance forces the bishop trade, then White's bishop slides out to pin the knight and backs the center push.

hp-ew.spoken: The knight stands as the attacker's spearhead, and the defender trades it off to blunt the offensive. That exchange steers the game into a classical structure where the attack loses its bite.

hp-e8.spoken: The bishop trade removes one defender, and the remaining bishop is tied down blockading the passed pawn. What looks like an overextended pawn chain is just a target; once the king is safe, the pawn push comes easily and the attack writes itself.

hp-ef.spoken: The move order sets these attacks apart. When Black has already advanced the pawn that prepares the flank expansion, extra options appear. Without that pawn move, the attack works better — Black must waste a tempo on it before starting the flank push.

hp-f2.spoken: The bishop trades on the strong square, opening lines and handing White the attack. If the pawn push comes without backup, the f-pawn advances and the key central square falls under White's control.

hp-eg.spoken: The Lipnitsky Attack is off the mainline, not objectively best, but it brings real practical bite. If White slips, Black equalizes or stands better, yet the attacking ideas stay dangerous and have won games for strong players.

hp-f6.spoken: The knight here is the key defender. If it leaves, White gets tactical strikes that make Black's position difficult. Engine evaluation may say equal, but practical play favors another move.

hp-ev.spoken: The queen steps to the side instead of developing the knight. That passivity lets White start a pawn storm with no fear of the knight trading on the central square.

hp-ee.spoken: The bishop targets the king's weak square and controls the central outpost. This stops the typical central pawn break, forcing the opponent into a different pawn structure.

hp-e7.spoken: The knight drifts toward the kingside. Do not lunge with the pawn — the king will castle there and needs shelter. Push the center pawn, then bring the bishop to bear on that square.

hp-dx.spoken: In a closed Sicilian-style setup, White holds back the knight and supports the center push with the c-pawn and both knights. If Black closes the center, White shifts to a kingside plan with a rook lift and the f-pawn.

hp-em.spoken: The pawn push that weakens the light squares invites a tactical strike. Choose the queen move that answers it directly, not the pawn thrust that lets the bishop press the center and free the opponent's counterplay.

hp-es.spoken: The knight retreats to the edge instead of the active square, and the reply misses the rook lift that keeps the pressure on. The queen step allows the central pawn push, and the defender gains counterplay.

hp-e2.spoken: The flank pawn captures the central pawn, but the trade is worse than in the parallel line where flank meets flank.

hp-dy.spoken: The knight steps into the hole on the queenside because Black's own pawn push has already shut down the fianchetto bishop. And when the pawn lunges forward, capture it — the queen on that file already shields the center pawn, so the response stays flexible.

hp-ed.spoken: The knight development line leaves Black without a clear plan, and the play turns wild and murky. Black must defend while hunting for attacking chances on the queenside.

hp-ec.spoken: The knight develops, and the bishop fianchettoes. If White pushes a pawn past the bishop, the retreat squares close, so the bishop must trade itself. That surrenders the bishop pair, but Black gains play against the weak dark squares.

hp-dz.spoken: The center is closed after the pawn advance, so White has time to prepare either central push or the flank break. Black's natural counter is the same pawn break, and keeping the queen on that file keeps the setup flexible.

hp-ey.spoken: If black gets the bishop to that long diagonal, the kingside attack loses its bite. The center pawn turns into a permanent burden, and white wastes moves defending it instead of pushing the attack.

hp-fo.spoken: The sharper push breaks open the center, the classic Grünfeld approach. Black develops the knight, the queen, and the bishop, all aiming at the d-file pawn.

hp-g1.spoken: The rook develops to a useful file while keeping the central tension intact. When the opponent attacks the unprotected pawn, the capture leaves you temporarily ahead on material.

hp-gi.spoken: The gambit gives up a pawn for quick development and attacking chances, not a trap that wins against the unprepared. Black survives without theory and can easily decline, steering into other openings.

hp-fm.spoken: The queen probes with a check. Trading queens into the endgame leaves the position nearly symmetrical and quiet, with a draw the likeliest result.

hp-fg.spoken: The f-pawn advances to break the shield. If the pawn takes and the bishop recaptures, the rook crashes in and the file opens for a mating attack. Black must never let that file open.

hp-gh.spoken: The c-pawn advance doesn't start a new opening; it just lands you in structures a Sicilian player already knows, like the English or the Botvinnik. Your existing repertoire mostly carries over, with only small tweaks required.

hp-gb.spoken: The exception to the Botvinnik is when the opponent gets the central push in — then the position stays equal but still playable. White's answer is to be ready to trade pieces and simplify.

hp-g2.spoken: The queen grab is a trap, not a threat. The opponent forces the trade and keeps the extra pawn. Better to recapture with the knight, but then the exchange sequence still leaves the opponent a full point up.

hp-g0.spoken: The choice is between taking at once for a slight edge on structure, or pushing the rook to the open file and inviting the gambit. If Black strikes at the center pawn, White can often keep the extra pawn.

hp-fx.spoken: The attack on the queen must come before grabbing material. Capturing the knight with the pawn lets the opponent take the rook for free, and the queen escapes. Press on with the attack instead, and the line forces a queen-for-two-rooks trade, a losing deal.

hp-fq.spoken: The knight steps out, and the bishop pins it to the king. After castling, the queen keeps the pressure. The pawns mirror each other — a four-on-two against a two-on-two on the wings — so passed pawns are unlikely.

hp-g4.spoken: The knight jumps to the weak square left behind by the bishop trade. Black spends moves pushing it back and rerouting the bishop, then uses the extra activity to aim at the weak pawns and pressure them.

hp-fb.spoken: The queen has two similar retreat squares, but one adds pressure on the knight and forces a bishop move in reply. That extra tempo changes the position: Black can then offer a wing pawn to stir up complications, and grabbing the center pawn becomes a mistake.

hp-g9.spoken: The knight retreats to the second rank keeps both setups alive: fianchettoing the bishop or pushing the center pawn. If Black commits the e-pawn, the central push is safe and the position transposes to the Kramnik.

hp-g3.spoken: The bishop pins the knight as the pawn chain collapses. Black gives back the pawn to leave White with three weak pawns and a healthier structure, then turns the pressure on each target in turn.

hp-ga.spoken: The pawn thrust only works if it lands before Black's central pawns are set. Lead with the other push and Black's freeing move is gone, so the target formation is forced. Lead with the wrong push and Black simply sidesteps into a different structure.

hp-fn.spoken: The pawn advance solidifies the center and steers clear of sharp complications—the slowest, safest choice for a calm maneuvering game.

hp-fc.spoken: The knight is forced back to defend the king's wing, and the attack stalls because that defender holds the line.

hp-fi.spoken: The bishop steps out, and the standard reply is the fianchetto — it completes the king's bishop's development and keeps the center under pressure. This move comes before any other plan.

hp-fd.spoken: The king steps into the corner, and the defense holds. That move shelters the king from the mating square, so the pawn can be recaptured safely.

hp-gf.spoken: The center pawns leave a hole between them. The knight is its only guard, and if that knight gets pinned or traded, the hole falls to the opponent.

hp-f7.spoken: The queen lands on a natural square: it guards the pawn, sets up the central break, and keeps the flank push in reserve. It also eyes the weak point if the knight steps away.

hp-fy.spoken: The knight sits defended and safe, not loose. With three minor pieces apiece, the position stays equal — tricky, but playable for Black.

hp-ff.spoken: The bishop often chooses the quiet square over the active one. The active square lets the opponent capture the pawn, and after the recapture, the knight lands a fork that wins material. The quiet square gives up activity but keeps the position solid.

hp-g6.spoken: The pawn thrust is highly committal: it locks the center structure at once and surrenders control of the key central square. Black chooses the game's character by deciding whether that square is challenged later.

hp-fa.spoken: The bishop on the long diagonal eyes the central square, and when the pawn push comes, the center buckles. White instead brings the queen out to support the pawn break.

hp-ge.spoken: After White's first pawn move, if Black declines the open center with a flank pawn, White can push the c-pawn and reach familiar systems. But if Black answers with the central pawn, that same push is a mistake.

hp-fp.spoken: The pawn capture opens the file, and when the queen recaptures, the rook and bishop gain tempi. Material stays level, but Black's queenside lags while White develops ahead.

hp-fv.spoken: The knight is hit four times and held by two defenders, so White must act. Black rallies every piece to the attack, and the quiet pawn structure hides a very sharp fight where one mistake decides it.

hp-fr.spoken: In this symmetrical pawn structure, no one can make a passed pawn, so trading everything down means a draw. The win has to come from piece activity and tactics, not pawn breakthroughs.

hp-f9.spoken: Castling kingside walks into the coming attack. Castle queenside instead, and the normal position stays balanced.

hp-fz.spoken: The rook takes the pawn and offers the exchange. Sacrificing it keeps material equal but sharpens the fight; declining keeps the pawns symmetrical and heads toward a draw.

hp-gd.spoken: Against the king pawn, the c-pawn challenges the center, and whatever Black's defense, the same pawn break leads to the Accelerated Dragon structure.

hp-ft.spoken: The bishop settles on the active diagonal. The queen reinforces the center, and trading there only strengthens the bishop. The knight jumps to the outpost, pressuring the b-pawn, but the defender has more chances to create trouble.

hp-fw.spoken: The knight lands between two pieces. If the pawn takes it, a fork wins a rook. When the other knight recaptures, the king takes back, and the second knight grabs the queen. The rook dare not take it back, so the trade stands.

hp-h3.spoken: The knight's rare reply calls the bluff and shifts the game into a well-known main line. Unprepared, the other side may end up worse.

hp-h1.spoken: The knight offer looks aggressive, but it costs time. Once the queen sidesteps, the knight retreats, then shuffles again, and the wasted tempi make the idea obsolete.

hp-gq.spoken: The bishop slides into a quiet square instead of pressuring, and Black answers with a flexible setup, fianchettoing the other bishop to avoid retreating. The position stays balanced, but Black gets a comfortable game.

hp-h9.spoken: The knight captures the pawn on that central square, and suddenly the pawn break Black was counting on is gone. The bishop at home is trapped with no good squares, and freeing it costs several slow preparatory moves.

hp-hr.spoken: The bishop leaves its defensive post and slides onto a diagonal where it harasses both the knight and the pawn. If the knight goes, the pawn goes, and the opponent's grip on the queenside loosens, making their pawn advance far harder to play.

hp-h5.spoken: Black's bishop reply is a trap with a flaw. Blocking with the knight is stronger. When White takes the pawn, the bishop slides out to hit the queen. But that move chokes the c-pawn, and that cost decides the line.

hp-gy.spoken: The queen grab risks a pawn for activity, and if the offer is ignored, Black stands at least equal. The safer setup puts the bishop on the long diagonal, where it is far easier to play.

hp-ho.spoken: The bishop slides to a strong central square, then advances again, backed by the rook and a fianchettoed partner. Black gains a powerful centralized piece and command over key squares.

hp-gs.spoken: The fianchetto is sound, but it hands White a lasting pull if you slip. The pawn breaks are not easy to arrange; each needs careful timing and preparation.

hp-h2.spoken: The bishop develops to the long diagonal, and Black has many good replies, so White must know them all while Black needs only one. The checking queen move sidesteps that theory but aims lower, and Black equalizes with accurate play.

hp-hp.spoken: The bishop retreats to a square where it controls a key entry point and reinforces the central pawn break — even though it moves twice and gets blocked. That extra tempo buys a real improvement in piece placement.

hp-gp.spoken: The queen slips to a support square, both guarding the pawn and clearing the way for a pawn break. Play that break at once, or the bishop stays locked out of the game.

hp-gu.spoken: The queenside plan starts with the two flank pawns, provoking the c-pawn forward. That locks the queenside and hands Black the a-file as a target. Even if the bishop is blocked from its square, the plan still runs: push the b-pawn, then break with the e-pawn.

hp-ha.spoken: The rook has two retreat squares: one lets the bishop pin the dark-squared bishop against the hanging pawn, stopping the fianchetto; the other avoids the tactic, because if the same pin is tried, the rook stands ready to punish the capture.

hp-h7.spoken: The choice is between grabbing the pawn now or developing first. The immediate capture lets Black push the pawns and start active play. Developing first keeps Black's pawn advance harder to achieve and leaves White with more options.

hp-hk.spoken: The two setups differ: one develops the knight, fianchettoes the bishop, and pins with the other bishop; the other pushes the center pawn. That center push is the rare choice in this opening, and it eases Black's game.

hp-gk.spoken: The knight steps out, inviting the pawn capture, then recaptures to open the file. Black has several defenses, each with its own theory—the pin, the solid bishop move, the central pawn push, or the fianchetto. The opening is theoretically well-developed.

hp-gl.spoken: The bishop stays off that diagonal so Black cannot trade the c-pawn and push the d-pawn with tempo, freeing the light-squared bishop. The queen retreats to support the center instead, though flank development and a quiet bishop setup are also workable.

hp-ht.spoken: The opening lines blur, and familiar setups arise no matter which route the pieces take.

hp-hs.spoken: The pawn push looks like an attack, but the knight just retreats and leaves four black pieces on the central square. A rook lift to reinforce it is answered by a rook on the b-file, hunting counterplay on the queenside.

hp-hi.spoken: This detour dodges mainline Open Catalan theory, yet the risk is real. If the opponent knows the book, White can land in the worse side.

hp-gt.spoken: The queen retreats to safety, and Black's pawn break now fails tactically, leaving an isolated weak pawn behind. The flank push is also met by the bishop stepping in, blocking the intended pin and keeping Black's plan dead.

hp-hu.spoken: The pin offers no real edge—Black castles or sidesteps, and the position stays level. White’s follow-up with a pawn stab and a quiet retreat changes nothing.

hp-hb.spoken: Black has two ways to tuck the rook: one supports the pawn and prepares a push, the other is a quieter square. The active choice invites the bishop to target the c-pawn and leaves the fianchetto unplayable under the queen's threat.

hp-gx.spoken: The pawn push creates a real choice for Black: either spend tempi on the flank advances, or keep the bishop on its home diagonal. The quiet king-side pawn move is prophylaxis against a queen check that would otherwise sting.

hp-gn.spoken: The bishop move to the long diagonal forces a choice. Blocking on the other square abandons the diagonal's purpose.

hp-go.spoken: The bishop fianchettoes on the long diagonal, but that same move also guards a key square. The opponent’s piece steps out to pin and simply neutralizes the setup.

hp-hl.spoken: The king sidesteps to safety, then the rook steps to the central file and the bishop drops back one square. That bishop redeploys to reinforce the key central square and prepare the pawn break.

hp-h4.spoken: The pawn advance is the freeing break, and the knight move prepares it by supporting the push. This sets up a structure like the Slav family, with the same plans and ideas.

hp-hn.spoken: Black's long game is queenside expansion: push the b-pawn, prepare the rook on the b-file. White tries to blunt it with a flank pawn, but Black pushes through regardless. The balance holds.

hp-gj.spoken: White offers the pawn. Black may take, but the engine favors Black after the capture. The main line sees White sacrifice once more, then bring the knight to the center, the bishop to the firing line, and the queen to the kingside, all aimed at the weak square.

hp-hh.spoken: The evaluation is small but misleading. Black's position is easy to play, and in practice Black wins forty-three percent and draws thirty, so White is rarely better over the board.

hp-is.spoken: Black trades off the dark-squared bishop to weaken White's grip on those squares. Then Black's pawns settle on dark squares, boxing in the bishop White has left.

hp-hw.spoken: The bishop is hemmed in by its own pawns, a classic bad bishop. Posting it on the central outpost turns it into an active, valuable piece.
