hp-6ci.spoken: Black's main move here is Nb8-d7, while White often plays a4 to gain queenside space. This known tabiya frequently ends in draws, though practical chances exist for both sides.

hp-6bp.spoken: White's d4, e4, and f4 pawns build a large center and grant extra space. Once Black's bishop reaches b7, development is equal, but that central pawn mass stays a long-term advantage.

hp-6b9.spoken: Black contests d5 to keep White's knight from settling there. The b3 and c4 setup is too slow, since it surrenders d4 and b4.

hp-6br.spoken: After Black pushes c5 and then c4, he grabs queenside space but loses central influence, since that pawn stops pressuring White's center. White answers by slamming d5 and lining up e5.

hp-6bb.spoken: Once the c-pawns come off, White is left with a backward pawn on c2, while Black keeps the bishop pair—that can sting. The engine says equal, but for a human White has no obvious plan.

hp-6c6.spoken: Wait for Black to play e6, protecting the knight and building a solid setup. A common alternative is c6, defending the knight too. After c6, White plays Bc4, saving d4 for later.

hp-6c0.spoken: In the main line, Black often chases the bishop with h6 and then g5, pushing it back to g3. That is Black’s best try, but it usually leads to queenside castling, which hurts because it blocks the c6-b5 and c5 pawn breaks.

hp-6bd.spoken: White castles kingside and expands with f4, steering the attack at Black's king—the standard Pirc plan.

hp-6c5.spoken: Black's knight on d5 has been shifted around several times and now stands strong. White shouldn't chase it with a flashy attack; instead, develop the queenside knight, supporting the center and getting ready to push the d-pawn.

hp-6ch.spoken: If Black faces Nd2, the best reply is h6, forcing the bishop back to h4, then c5, heading toward a hedgehog setup with b6 and Bb7. Strong players reach this position often, and it typically ends in draws.

hp-6ce.spoken: White recaptures with the b-pawn, and Black’s main reply is …b6, aiming the bishop at b7 along the long diagonal. White answers with Bd3, and once Black plays …d6 and castles, we arrive at the key Chase Variation position.

hp-6d6.spoken: White pins the knight with the bishop on g5, a classic aggressive setup, then challenges the center with the e-pawn.

hp-6d1.spoken: Black's queenside majority of two to one creates a potential passed pawn, but White's d5 pawn sits only three squares from promotion, making it the bigger threat.

hp-6d2.spoken: The Grünfeld is an imbalanced fight: White storms the center with e4 and d5, and exchange sacrifices can tip the game into sharp, fast finishes or favorable endgames for either side.

hp-6cm.spoken: White pushes e5, and the structure looks like a French. Black needs h6 to bother the bishop, but it drops back to e3. White's queenside knight hasn't moved, so the extra tempo fuels a kingside attack with f4.

hp-6d4.spoken: In the Grünfeld, this exchange variation is the critical main line. White gets a central pawn majority, while Black gains active piece play.

hp-6d8.spoken: White delays Nc3 to play g3 first, and Black answers with d5. That defines the Neo-Grünfeld, giving White's bishop on g2 more scope.

hp-6d5.spoken: The Russian system starts when White plays Qb3, skipping the exchange and pressuring Black's d5 pawn, which creates a different type of center.

hp-6cz.spoken: In the Grünfeld, Black holds off castling to hit the center at once with c5, targeting the d4 pawn. White’s center is wide but sits two tempi from castling; Black needs only one, and that gap fuels the imbalance.

hp-6d7.spoken: The Brinckmann attack brings the bishop to f4, but here that bishop supports the e-pawn and gives White a firmer center.

hp-6d9.spoken: The Grünfeld is a highly theoretical opening, so memorizing every variation is not realistic.

hp-6ev.spoken: White castles queenside and pushes the kingside pawns, f4 and g3 supporting the storm. The position stays balanced, but White’s attack carries real potential.

hp-6er.spoken: In the Anti-Moscow, Black keeps the extra pawn, but the structure becomes awkward and hard to manage. Dynamic chances run high, and Black must avoid overextending.

hp-6eh.spoken: The tension between the c-pawn and d5 is the heart of the Semi-Slav. Whether Black captures on c4 or not decides the character of the game. If he takes and holds the pawn, White gets sharp compensation.

hp-6e2.spoken: If Black plays Nc6 and then offers the trade of light-squared bishops, the b7 weakness gets solved, but it leaves White slightly better, since White's bishop was the stronger piece.

hp-6ep.spoken: White can sidestep both the Meran and Anti-Meran by playing Bg5, steering into some of the most tangled positions in the game.

hp-6ek.spoken: Taking the pawn on c4 comes with tempo, since White's bishop on d3 hangs. That is the key difference from putting the bishop on e2, where the same capture gains no tempo.

hp-6f5.spoken: Black has three main options here: b6, O-O, or Ne5. The b6 line plans a fianchetto, putting the light-squared bishop on b7 to pressure e4 and the long diagonal.

hp-6ex.spoken: Black’s queen on f6 aims at f2 and b2 while White’s king remains in the center. The direct Qxf2 check is not crushing, but it keeps White unsettled.

hp-6ef.spoken: The queen to a4 combined with the pawn to a4 is the standard treatment of the …Nc6 line, forcing a sequence both players must know cold. The endgame that follows becomes the real battleground, where preparation decides everything.

hp-6dv.spoken: In the line with Nc6, a tactical trick exists. If Black's knight lands on the rook, White answers with Ne1. If Black takes the rook, the knight is trapped and loses two pieces for it, showing White's edge.

hp-6es.spoken: The bishop on c5 is Black's strongest piece, eyeing the center and the kingside. White commonly challenges it with Be3.

hp-6el.spoken: If White delays the bishop and plays b3, Black can't grab on c4 right away, since the bishop still sits on f1. White holds it back to keep the tension and avoid handing Black a tempo.

hp-6e7.spoken: White can hold off castling here and play Kd2 instead, a more active square that keeps the king safe while aiming at c7 and the black king.

hp-6dy.spoken: After …Nc6, Qa4 is White's most practical weapon. It pressures the knight and prepares to win the c4-pawn, keeping a lasting slight edge without heavy theory.

hp-6f6.spoken: In the main line, Black plays b6, then White castles and Black develops the bishop to b7. White’s pawns on f4 and e4 are powerful, while Black’s bishops on c5 and b7 aim straight at the white king, backed by the queen on f6.

hp-6e6.spoken: If Black drops the bishop to d6, White takes the c-pawn with the knight and doubles the pawns. Then Bf4 hits c7, and the knight on d6 is misplaced, forced to move and leaves c4 undefended.

hp-6f9.spoken: The queen’s early trip to f6 leaves the bishop on c5 hanging and the c7 square weak — this position is tactically loaded.

hp-6fj.spoken: White plays h4, Black answers h5, and then White pushes e6. If Black takes on e6, weaknesses appear on d5 and f7 for White to attack. The engine calls it roughly equal, but Black has a hard time handling it.

hp-6fb.spoken: Black faces three main paths on move five in the Classical Scotch, and White chooses which one to play, so Black must know all three.

hp-6ff.spoken: White's g5 pushes the knight to f5, where it rests strong and hard to chase off. No need for g6 to shield it — that wastes a tempo and shuts the square.

hp-6fk.spoken: If Black takes on e6, White plays bishop d3, forcing the queen to recapture. Then White's queen goes to g6 with threats, and Black must be exact to survive.

hp-6gc.spoken: The queen check on a4 works because if Black blocks with c6, White pushes d5. If Black takes, the knight recaptures, and the queen on a4 guards the e4 pawn. With the queen still on d1, that pawn would be left undefended and Black could target it.

hp-6fl.spoken: The engine's first choice after e6 is hxg4, but that leads to a messy position where Black has to push e5 to get developed. White can stop that with queen g5, and Black must go e6 — a tight, cramped setup.

hp-6ga.spoken: Retreating the bishop to f8 looks passive but is actually a solid defensive setup. White's reply is d4, opening the center.

hp-6ge.spoken: Black can decline the Evans Gambit by pulling the bishop back to e7 and castling — a solid choice that sidesteps the sharp lines but gives White a measure of initiative.

hp-6g5.spoken: White sacrifices a pawn for active piece play, a gambit proven sound at the highest level. If Black declines with Bb6, White keeps a comfortable space edge on the queenside.

hp-6fn.spoken: Early f4 is wrong in the queen d6 line because Black's light-squared bishop is still active and can trade itself off, then Black plays e6 and attacks the f4 pawn with the knight jumping e7-g6.

hp-6g8.spoken: White plays c3 to prepare d4 and seize space; Black's bishop has five retreat squares, each starting a different line.

hp-6g3.spoken: The Bayonet Attack is a sharp, faster take on the Caro-Kann Advance, mixing Tal and Van der Wiel ideas. Black can take the pawn on g4 with the bishop at once, but White gains fast development and attacking chances.

hp-6gg.spoken: White reaches a critical moment here. If he defends d4 passively with Qf4, Black is fine. But the sharper Rfe1 allows Black to take on d4, and the game becomes extremely sharp with chances for both sides.

hp-6fg.spoken: Black can pick a French-style setup or keep the Caro-Kann character. The bishop usually lands on g6, and the idea of Bf5-e4 invites White to play f3, a move White often wants anyway.

hp-6fo.spoken: In this Caro-Kann Advance, that bishop on f5 is central. If White advances f4, the bishop gets locked in, which favors Black. White instead steers the f4 square with pieces, letting the e-pawn stand and leaving Black at ease.

hp-6fa.spoken: In the main line, White's e-pawn stays a lasting weakness. The black queen looks active but accomplishes little, while the minor pieces remain locked in sharp central tension.

hp-6hf.spoken: White's last move, Be3, completes the forced sequence of the Steinitz Variation in the Classical French.

hp-6hr.spoken: Black's plan on this side of the board is to push b5 and start a queenside attack. First the c6 knight must move so the bishop on d7 can guard that pawn.

hp-6go.spoken: White is down a pawn, seven to eight, but the activity and piece play give compensation. If the initiative is not converted, the material deficit will tell.

hp-6ht.spoken: After the captures resolve, White comes out a pawn ahead, but Black's bishop pair and attacking threats give real compensation. The engine may favor White slightly, but Black's attack is far easier to play in practice.

hp-6gm.spoken: If Black castles and then captures on e4, White takes back with the d-pawn, and after the exchanges, Qd5 wins material—Black's pieces are overloaded.

hp-6h1.spoken: White must not take on e5, because Black recaptures with the bishop and gets a slightly better position. Instead, Qb6 is strong, hitting the knight and piling on pressure.

hp-6gu.spoken: In this critical spot after Nf6, the most combative try is Nb5, sacrificing the rook for sharp play. Black answers with d5, guarding c7 and hitting the bishop, leaving Black's rooks idle while White's pieces hum with activity.

hp-6hn.spoken: With the bishop on d7, Black covers the c6-knight, so if White takes it, Black recaptures and keeps the balance. An immediate d5 break fails here, because White has enough defenders around the king.

hp-6gk.spoken: White castles first to keep the attack rolling, and Black plays d6 to shore up the center. The pawn takes back on d4, kicking the bishop, which lands on b6—passive and locked in behind the d4 pawn.

hp-6gn.spoken: Black can't safely take on e4 here, because White answers with Qd5 or Qd4, attacking both knights. So after castling, that pawn on e4 isn’t a real target.

hp-6gr.spoken: In the Lasker Defense, once the queens come off, Black keeps the healthier pawn structure. White’s a2 and c4 pawns become targets, and the bishop on b6 stands strong. Defending the e4 pawn is a real problem.

hp-6gz.spoken: After Black plays a6, they're ready to push b5 and start a queenside expansion, a standard French setup. White answers best with Qd2, reinforcing the center and getting ready for Rd1, while Black's f8-bishop still has no comfortable home.

hp-6hs.spoken: After Black plays b5, White must respond quickly with h4 and a4 to build counterplay. The position turns razor-sharp, both sides racing to attack. A zwischenzug like Bxf6 can appear, taking the knight to break Black's coordination.

hp-6hb.spoken: Black should take on e5 rather than play f5. Capturing leaves White with a weak isolated e-pawn, gives Black an outpost on e4, and sets up pressure on the d5 pawn.

hp-6gv.spoken: White gives up the rook on a1, yet the activity of his pieces balances the ledger, while Black's rooks sit passive on a8 and h8. The engine calls this roughly equal, maybe a touch better for Black.

hp-6ie.spoken: If White tries Bg5, Black answers with e6. If White goes Nc3, Black plays g6 — a key branching point.

hp-6hz.spoken: In this critical position, White should not take on b5. Play g5 instead to keep pushing the kingside attack. Black answers with h5 or other ideas to stir up counterplay.

hp-6i9.spoken: White's key idea here is the Maroczy Bind, with the light-squared bishop already traded off—and that bishop is often a liability.

hp-6iq.spoken: This anti-Sicilian approach with Bb5 or Bc4 sidesteps mainline Open Sicilian theory and pushes Black to make choices early. It's a practical weapon that trims the theory White has to prepare.

hp-6i2.spoken: This position is razor sharp and heavily theorized, with countless grandmaster games. Under 2300, it's often smarter to steer away from the most critical lines and pick a more solid setup.

hp-6iy.spoken: If Black pokes with h6, take on f6 and let Black recapture with the g-pawn. White gets a weak h6-pawn to target, and the position takes on a Caro-Kann flavor.

hp-6is.spoken: The Veresov works best against opponents unfamiliar with it, especially King's Indian players. They may not expect Nc3 and the push e2-e4, so White steers the game into unknown territory.

hp-6i8.spoken: If White plays the knight instead of Bg5, Black fianchettoes with g6 and Bg7, reaching a Dragon-style Maroczy Bind setup.

hp-6id.spoken: Black has a solid, Dragon-style setup here.

hp-6iv.spoken: If Black plays e6, White replies e4, turning the game into the French Defense, the Burn Variation. This mainline has thousands of games behind it, so White needs to be ready.

hp-6hy.spoken: Black can try b5, offering a pawn to pull the bishop away and open lines toward the white king. If White takes it, Black gains active pieces and real attacking chances.

hp-6j3.spoken: If White captures on f6 and Black retakes with the e-pawn, that g6 pawn becomes a real problem in this Caro-Kann setup — it leaves the kingside fragile and shuts off the knight's route to f8 and g6.

hp-6hw.spoken: The dark-squared bishop on e3 guards the kingside. Black wants to swap it off with a knight, forcing bishop takes and rook takes back, to blunt White's attack.

hp-6ic.spoken: If White plays Bg5 instead of Nc3, Black’s reply changes.

hp-6im.spoken: The bishop on c8 has yet to develop. The engine may call this equal, but White wants more, since Bc4 on move five usually yields a slight edge.

hp-6if.spoken: White's setup mirrors a Maroczy Bind, with the bishop on c4 playing its typical role.

hp-6i4.spoken: If White castles before playing Bc4, Black gets an immediate d5 in the center, seizing counterplay right away. This is the critical crossroads of the main line.

hp-6k1.spoken: Black's g6 gives White a hook on the kingside — the target for h4-h5, prying open lines against the castled king. Before g6, that attack would be slow and expensive.

hp-6jo.spoken: Black has five solid replies here: h6, c6, e6, e5, or g6. Each one steers the game in a very different direction.

hp-6jx.spoken: Playing Bd3 here is too passive. It breaks the pin but creates no real pressure. Black simply plays d6, and the resulting structure is Slav-like, with easy equality.

hp-6ji.spoken: If Black plays h6 to kick the bishop, White retreats to h4. After e6, White can push e4, transposing into a Rubinstein French — a good choice for a player who knows that line. Otherwise, playing e3 leaves White slightly worse.

hp-6kh.spoken: The move f3 is the soul of the Yugoslav Attack. It builds a pawn chain that props up the center and clears the way for a kingside storm. Skip it, and the game drifts into calmer waters like the Classical or Levenfish lines, where White’s attack loses its bite.

hp-6js.spoken: If Black plays e6, White answers with e4, and after dxe4 the knight recaptures, giving a French-style setup. The position is ordinary, and White can castle queenside and start an attack.

hp-6jc.spoken: Black must castle, since the knight to f6 is unavailable and other development leaves White pressing. If Black develops cleanly, he gets a favorable Caro-Kann structure and stands better.

hp-6jw.spoken: After Nb5, Black must not take the pawn on e4. The bishop on c5 is under attack, and g7 is also exposed — a queen landing on g3 hits both. The Qg4 try is still insufficient.

hp-6j8.spoken: Black’s king is weak after …gxf6. White pushes h5!? to start a strong attack. If Black takes on d4, White gets fast development and more attack. If Black plays …e6 instead, White castles with a clear initiative.

hp-6ki.spoken: Early Dragon masters like Bird, Lasker, and Pillsbury lacked today's theory — White often skipped queenside castling and f3, so games looked like the Classical or Accelerated Dragon with easier development for Black.

hp-6jf.spoken: After the bishop exchange on f6, Black often develops the light-squared bishop to f5. If White trades it off, Black's f7-f5 break gets much harder, and that also weakens support for a knight on e4.

hp-6lo.spoken: Black’s setup targets the knight on c3, which blocks the c-pawn and leaves d4 harder to defend. The bishop on g7 adds pressure to the center.

hp-6kq.spoken: In the Yugoslav Attack, Black’s d6 pawn hangs and needs protection. The rook on f8 is pinned to the f7 square, so moving it would allow checkmate on f7.

hp-6lq.spoken: The Gurgenidze System rarely appears in books, so studying it from print is tough. Annotated repertoires and interactive tools let you learn by playing.

hp-6lg.spoken: The engine calls this line roughly equal, but Black faces the tougher practical task — White's attack is far easier to steer.

hp-6lf.spoken: The critical plan is to push g4 right away. Black has to take that pawn — if they don't, White captures on f6, then follows with h5, ripping open the g-file for a crushing attack.

hp-6kl.spoken: The bishop on b3 is the engine of White's attack. Black's queen on a5 comes too early, letting White castle and launch the assault on the kingside.

hp-6lt.spoken: Black plays h5 to stop g4 and make f5 safe for a knight. The knight travels through h6 to f5, leaving the h-pawn free. This is the key to fighting White's space edge and setting up piece play.

hp-6km.spoken: White's knight on d5 creates a real threat: Nxe7+ wins a pawn and rips open Black's kingside. Black is often forced to trade that knight with the bishop, but once it's gone, taking the bishop on d5 is key — it strips away White's attacking power.

hp-6ks.spoken: In the Prins Sicilian, White aims for a Maroczy bind, but Black sidesteps it with e5, kicking the knight, then follows with d5 to seize active play.

hp-6kn.spoken: In a critical position, Black chooses Rac8 instead of removing the bishop on d5, letting White keep that piece on the long diagonal. The attack then becomes overwhelming.

hp-6ll.spoken: White's d4 keeps the center balanced; the tension between e4, d4, and Black's c6 leads to trades that leave no edge. Black's setup is simpler to handle in practice.

hp-6ls.spoken: The main choice is e5, locking in an advanced Caro-Kann. That stops any quick pressure on d4, grabs space, and builds a solid center. The cost is a weak f5-square, and Black can go after it.

hp-6lj.spoken: If White plays h3 and Black takes on e4, Black can meet with Nf6, and when exf6 happens, that f6-pawn eyes the e5-square. That structure suits Black, cramping White's pieces and anchoring a sturdy center.

hp-6lh.spoken: Black's sharpest reply to d4 is Nf6, hitting the e4-pawn at once. That beats Nd7, which is passive and lets White fortify the center.

hp-6m5.spoken: The Gurgenidze System keeps the game strategically rich and avoids the heavy theory of the mainline Caro-Kann. The real key is understanding two distinct structures—one with e5, one without.

hp-6m8.spoken: Black's pawn on f6 restricts c5 and leaves the bishop passive. The main setup comes with Bg7, and White usually answers with f4 to reinforce the center.

hp-6ly.spoken: If the knight on f5 gets traded, Black retakes with the e-pawn, creating a central pawn majority and opening the f-file. Capturing back with the g-pawn works too, depending on where the king has castled.

hp-6lx.spoken: Playing h5 fixes the pawn structure, leaves White with a backward g-pawn, and locks the knight on f5 in place. If White ever tries g4, Black takes en passant, and the knight keeps its strong post.

hp-6ms.spoken: If White holds off on c4, the position stays quiet and Black keeps building on the kingside. But the moment White plays c4, Black drops the attack and shifts all pressure onto the d4 pawn.

hp-6mb.spoken: If the knight gets taken on f5, the recapture choice matters. If White castles kingside, Black takes back with the e-pawn, opening the e-file and turning e6 into a staging square for a knight coming via a6 and c7.

hp-6lw.spoken: Playing h3 puts the question to the bishop, but Black can keep it active with Nf5, which pressures the g4 bishop.

hp-6m2.spoken: Black's plan is a5, then the knight goes a6–c7–d5, where it sits strong. That provokes c4 from White, weakening d4. If White plays c3 instead, the position stays stable, and Black has a good setup.

hp-6mt.spoken: Nf6 is the more dynamic move here, giving you unique Gurgenidze positions, while Nd7 just heads back into standard Caro-Kann structures that e4 players know well.

hp-6mq.spoken: White's bishop choice is critical: on h2, the queenside stays undefended; on d2, it gains extra security. Black wants it on h2 so the kingside becomes the target.

hp-6mh.spoken: Against Nf3, Bg4 looks tempting since it forces h3, but here it's not good because the bishop isn't on g7 yet. With the bishop on g7, that pin would leave the d4-pawn hanging, but in this position it's safe.

hp-6m6.spoken: Immediate f6 is playable but scores poorly and is harder to handle, since it leaves the tension on e5 unresolved and limits Black's c5 options. White usually answers with f4, supporting the center.

hp-6lv.spoken: Black plays h4 after the knight settles on f5. That move leaves White with a backward g-pawn, locks the structure, and plants the knight forever. If White tries g4, Black captures en passant, and the knight still stands firm.

hp-6mw.spoken: In the Averbakh Variation, after White’s c3, Black can try …Nd7, planning …Bf6 and a rook to e8 to put pressure on d4, much like the Karpov closed line. But since …b5 hasn’t been played, White keeps a big edge here, and that plan isn’t fully sound.

hp-6n5.spoken: After c3, Black usually answers with …Bg4. White can choose between d3 or h3, while d4 is weaker since it lets Black switch into the Yates variation and get easy play. h3 is the sharper option, heading into positions that are more unique.

hp-6mi.spoken: Black could pin the knight with Bg4, but the bishop on f4 already guards d4, so the pin fails to pressure the center.

hp-6od.spoken: In this position, White owns more space, but Black's setup is rock solid and full of counterplay. The engine sees only a slight edge for White, and in practice, the results sit evenly.

hp-6oa.spoken: After d5, c5, and e5, the position stays roughly equal, with White holding only a slight edge. The stats show many draws and plenty of White wins, but Black keeps real counterplay.

hp-6ni.spoken: After Black trades knights on d5, White plays b5, hitting the pinned pawn on c6 and seizing a strong initiative. Black struggles to finish development, and White stands clearly better.

hp-6nf.spoken: The key pattern in every Open Catalan is the push d5, cracking Black's center. That only works while Black's king remains in the middle and his pieces sit awkwardly. Once Black castles and develops naturally, d5 loses its sting.

hp-6na.spoken: Against the Averbakh, Black's natural plan is Bg4. White answers with d3, not h3 — keeping the kingside solid and stopping Black's typical attack with Qd7, castling long, then pushing g5-g4.

hp-6nm.spoken: In the Open Catalan, when Black grabs the b5-pawn with …b5, White faces a choice: play a4 at once, castle, or recapture with Nxb5. The …c6 move supports Black's pawn chain, so White has to pick between challenging it or developing.

hp-6oe.spoken: Black often plays Qb6, aiming at the undefended b2-pawn, which the f4-bishop leaves exposed.

hp-6of.spoken: Playing the knight before the bishop lets Black pin it with Bg4, and if White replies Qb3, the exchange can damage White's pawn structure.

hp-6o5.spoken: If Black takes on d4 and the knight recaptures, White gets the Maróczy bind again with a strong centralized knight. The f-pawn supports e4, and the d4 outpost is powerful. Pushing f4 usually wastes a tempo and weakens the kingside, so skip it.

hp-6n9.spoken: With White's h3 in place, Black can play Qd7, castle long, and push g5-g4, using the h3 hook to open lines. If White plays d3 instead, the h-pawn stays home, so g4 attacks nothing and Black has no counterplay.

hp-6oj.spoken: Black’s early c5 and Qb6 hit the b2 pawn and pressure the center, so White answers with Nc3, defending b2 and holding the middle.

hp-6ok.spoken: Black's main replies to the London begin with d5 or Nf6, each branching into distinct setups. Every path demands a different response from White.

hp-6oz.spoken: The London System gives White a solid setup, and it funnels the game into a narrow group of recurring structures — usually five to ten of them.

hp-6oo.spoken: The London System works against the Dutch Defense too. White plays the same setup, ignores Black's f-pawn, and Black's kingside plans lose their sting.

hp-6oq.spoken: If Black challenges your bishop on f4 with Bd6, do not take. Pull the bishop back and keep the tension, making Black decide. If he captures, you recapture and open the h-file for the rook.

hp-6p0.spoken: The London System rewards you with quick results because it's easy to play well and demands little preparation.

hp-6or.spoken: The London System gives a knight a strong outpost on e5, supported by the pawn structure. Solid as it is, it also carries attacking potential, especially if Black permits e4-e5.

hp-6pi.spoken: White pushes h4-h5, forcing Black to weaken. If the h-pawn takes on h5, f7 hangs; if Black answers with f6, the pawn structure suffers.

hp-6ox.spoken: Here, a London bishop trade on g3 gave White a lever with the h-pawn. White skipped the automatic Bd3, choosing Bb5 to target e5, letting the knight land there.

hp-6ot.spoken: Another pattern: push f4-f5 to crack open Black's structure. Support it by reinforcing e4 with Qe2. If Black plays Re8, White answers e5, using that pawn as a battering ram to split Black's position.

hp-6oy.spoken: The London System offers simple attacking plans, but it plays itself a bit too easily, which can stall your growth. A sharper choice like the Queen's Gambit pushes you to study more and meet a broader range of positions.

hp-6pd.spoken: White just attacked the f7 point, and the natural reply Bf5 is nearly losing. Ng3 chases the bishop back, gaining time and a head start in development.

hp-6po.spoken: Qa4 invites Black's unusual reply, f6, sacrificing a pawn to free the pieces. If White captures on c6, Black recaptures, then plays Kf7, and all the pieces fly out—Black stands better despite the pawn deficit.

hp-6ov.spoken: White's king sits safely behind the pawns, but Black's king remains in the center. The queen on b6 attacks both b2 and d4, yet White can ignore those pawn threats—the king attack matters more.

hp-6op.spoken: Allowing Black to take on d4 twice is fine, though not the classic London. Once Black plays e6, White answers c3 to finish the setup minus the bishop on d3.

hp-6ps.spoken: Black's pawn pushes to d4, hitting the knight on f3. White answers with Qe2, setting a trap: if Black grabs the knight, the queen is lost.

hp-6q7.spoken: Early bishop to e3 or f4 is nothing to fear—Black gets full equality.

hp-6r5.spoken: The Yugoslav Attack against the Dragon produces opposite-side castling, and now both sides race to attack the enemy king. A classic sharp, tactical fight.

hp-6qv.spoken: The Sicilian has been studied since the 16th century and later revived by top players. After a decline in the 1800s, it returned as a fighting choice for those playing for a win.

hp-6qs.spoken: Black’s e5 push attacks the knight on d4 and grabs central space. White’s bishop on c4 looks active, but e5 blocks its diagonal, leaving it misplaced.

hp-6r3.spoken: If White skips the Open Sicilian, the Closed Sicilian with Nc3 keeps the game calmer by holding back d4. The Alapin, with c3, supports d4 in a simple, solid way.

hp-6r2.spoken: After e4 and c5, Black has many solid options: Nc6 for the Taimanov, a6 for the Kan, e6, g6, b6, Nf6, and more. Each choice heads into a different structure and plan.

hp-6qj.spoken: Black has chosen the Rubinstein Variation, and development is fully symmetrical—both sides have knights out, White's on e4.

hp-6q9.spoken: Playing Bg5 pins the knight, and Black answers with b6 and Bb7 to reach a standard setup. White keeps slight kingside pressure from the pin, but the position stays nearly equal. The queen on e2 sits a bit awkwardly.

hp-6qb.spoken: With the pawn structure no longer intact, Black often plays Bb4 to swap off a bishop and cut into White's bishop pair. The game stays balanced, with no clear attacking ideas for either side, and draws are a common result.

hp-6q8.spoken: Black must play c5 to strike at White's center and claim space. Once d5 and Bxe5 settle the structure, the position is balanced—Black's sole concern is the light-squared bishop, which gets out to b7 after b6.

hp-6qd.spoken: In the Fort Knox, taking the knight on f6 lets Black park the knight there, where it does nothing. Ng3 is the better move, holding the knight on a stronger square and keeping Black's knight off d5.

hp-6rb.spoken: The Scheveningen setup with e6 and d6 keeps Black flexible and ready to play d5, but it invites White's f4, and that leads to sharp play.

hp-6ri.spoken: In Sicilian endgames, Black often enjoys the better pawn structure. White’s king gets boxed in by Black’s pawns, while Black’s pieces slip through. Here Black’s king marches forward as White’s king stays trapped.

hp-6rj.spoken: The Sicilian Defense is a family of openings, not one single line. Each variation has its own plans and pawn structures, so no universal strategy works for all of them.

hp-6rz.spoken: The Lasker Defense is simple to play and gives White no real test, but it also asks little of Black. It heads toward quiet, drawish positions, so it’s not advised below 2200–2300 strength – it doesn’t push you to learn actively and can drift into passive play.

hp-6rs.spoken: In this line, if Black delays castling and tries h6 and g5, the immediate g5 is weaker because White can answer Bf4. That move is still no better than Be7, but the missing knight on f3 and the pawn on h6 shift the assessment.

hp-6rk.spoken: For Black, the Sveshnikov is a strong and straightforward Sicilian to learn. For White, the Alapin offers a solid, offbeat option.

hp-6rv.spoken: White’s c-pawn break rips open the center and exposes the black king. After the trades, Black’s king stays trapped in the middle, with no safety.

hp-6re.spoken: If Black accepts the knight on d5, White's other knight leaps to f5, hitting the bishop and keeping the king trapped. This sacrifice hands White the initiative.

hp-6rq.spoken: After cxd5, Black must capture the knight first, or intermezzo moves like d6 allow Nxe7+, losing the queen.

hp-6s6.spoken: If White plays the quiet Nf3, Black can answer with Nf6.

hp-6r8.spoken: In the Sicilian, Black's d5 square is a permanent weakness. White wants a piece on d5, never a pawn, because a pawn there would block the hole and defend Black's backward d6 pawn.

hp-6rt.spoken: The queenside is open and White’s pieces are aimed at the king. Black’s last move lets White strike in the center with real force.

hp-6t6.spoken: Against …c6, White still goes f4. Playing Nf3 instead leaves the position equal, while f4 keeps the game sharp.

hp-6sm.spoken: The Alapin is easy for both sides to remember—the plans are clear and similar in most lines, so it works as a practical weapon for White.

hp-6tr.spoken: White plays e4, heading for the Horwitz Attack. The priority stays flexible, keeping the knight off e4 where it can trade on g5. Castling keeps every option open.

hp-6tj.spoken: If Black trades on g2 and plays c6, the kingside stays solid. White's bishop has no good home on e4 or d3, and pushing e5 just hands over the d5 square.

hp-6to.spoken: After White plays h3, Black chooses g6, controlling f5 and preparing the knight route to e6, g7, and f5. This setup also guards h7, stopping tactics along that diagonal.

hp-6sj.spoken: Black’s knight on e5 stands badly, and the b7-pawn is left weak—White holds a clear edge.

hp-6sq.spoken: White's lead in development and the pressure on f7 leave Black in trouble. Black must play Nc6 to meet the mate threat, but White keeps the initiative.

hp-6tb.spoken: White's light-squared bishop often develops to g5, pinning the knight on f6. Trading on f6 pulls Black's e7-bishop away from defending b4, then White plays b4 to speed up the minority attack.

hp-6v1.spoken: Black's most common reply is advancing the h-pawn, and White's response is a sound pawn sacrifice. If Black tries to hold onto that pawn, White captures on g6 and comes out on top. Black has to pull the bishop back, then White takes the h5 pawn.

hp-6u7.spoken: After g5, Black can try the Paulsen Defense with bishop to g7, pressuring the knight. It's a sideline for good reason—it doesn't fix Black's underlying problems.

hp-6v2.spoken: Black sacrifices a pawn, yet stands equal. The knight on h5 sits offside, and Black picks up tempi. Every Black piece works in harmony.

hp-6tx.spoken: White plays b4 to keep c5 from happening, so Black answers c6, blocking b5, and then a5 to get ready for b5 — the goal is to shut down the queenside and keep things solid.

hp-6uk.spoken: White trades an exchange for the bishop pair and active play, so the engine sees only a slight edge for Black. The position stays playable, and White keeps real attacking chances if Black slips.

hp-6ul.spoken: This opening is the Kieseritzky Gambit, a deeply theoretical line where Black can easily slip up. Over the next ten to fifteen moves, Black feels real pressure, and that is where White’s practical chances lie.

hp-6un.spoken: The knight on c3 does two jobs: it guards e4, so a later g4 leaves the f5-bishop no retreat there, and it props up the center. The cost is that it blocks the c-pawn, so Black's c5 break can no longer be answered by c3.

hp-6u0.spoken: Black delays e5, taking on c4 first to remove White's option to capture on d5 and leave the pawn isolated, then plays e5 with an easy game.

hp-6ui.spoken: Black castles after Bc4 d5. White may capture on f4 with either bishop or rook. The rook capture is safer, since taking with the bishop lets Black's queen take on h4, and White has no g3 resource.

hp-6uy.spoken: White captures on c5, and when the knight recaptures, White's knight jumps to d4, eyeing the a4 to e8 diagonal. Black replies with Nd7, blocking the line and pressuring c5. The position stays balanced—Black's central pawns offset the pawn structure.

hp-6tw.spoken: The critical line runs through Be2: Black takes on c4, White recaptures on f6, and Black must play e5. Then b4 stops c5, c6 stops b5, and later a5 challenges White's queenside pawns.

hp-6vc.spoken: Black gives up the exchange and trades queens, banking on a superior pawn structure and active pieces to make up for it. The d4 pawn stands strong, and Black's pieces sit well.

hp-6wc.spoken: White can regain the pawn or play more ambitiously, letting Black hold the extra pawn while White develops active pieces.

hp-6vp.spoken: In this setup, White builds a Benoni structure minus Black's d6-pawn, so the e4-e5 break stays unblocked. That makes this line a real upgrade over the standard Benoni.

hp-6w3.spoken: White keeps a central pawn majority and holds the e5 square. Black's best try is e5 at once, striking at that center control.

hp-6wh.spoken: White has sacrificed a pawn, but the bishop pair and strong bishops give full compensation. The knight on a3 clears the way for the bishop to fianchetto on b2, and even if the pawn stays lost, the position is worth it.

hp-6vg.spoken: After g4 Bg6, a Black move like Nd7 lets White push h5 and bring the bishop to f3, poking at weaknesses. Black answers a6 to shelter the bishop — if the knight grabs d4, the queen takes back, and both bishops hit f3 and c2.

hp-6vz.spoken: White should not develop with d3 — too passive. Play d4 right away to fight for the center and challenge Black's c5-pawn.

hp-6w5.spoken: If Black plays e5 and White answers g3, then e4 is not dangerous. The knight retreats to g5, hitting the pawn and freeing the bishop.

hp-6vo.spoken: The Van der Wiel Attack favors strategic understanding and attacking skill over rote memorization. Black must be precise to survive, and the Bg2 line gives White rich attacking chances.

hp-6vf.spoken: The knight wants the d4 square, so Black plays c5 then Nd7, tempting f3. After that, a6 keeps the knight off d4. The bishop is safe—it can retreat to e4.

hp-6vj.spoken: Black's knight on f5 looks active, but White can swap a knight for it with Ne2. If Black pushes h4 to hold the knight, that pawn turns into a lasting weakness, pinning down Black's forces.

hp-6vq.spoken: White aims for an Open Sicilian shape, with the d-file opened and ahead in development. Since Black lacks a d6 pawn, the queen can recapture on d4, saving a tempo that Nc6 would otherwise cost.

hp-6w7.spoken: In these Neo-Grünfeld-style positions from the Schultz Gambit, White has the favorable version because Black cannot take the knight on c3. White builds a solid center with the knight and g3.

hp-6ws.spoken: White’s pawns on d3 and b3 lock down the e4 outpost, keeping Black’s knight out of that square.

hp-6wn.spoken: If White captures on d5 early, Black's knight recaptures. That knight stares down White's bishop on b2, and the position can lock up, leaving that bishop with little scope.

hp-6wt.spoken: If Black plays an early d4 to block the bishop, Black likely follows with c5 and e5 to clamp down on the dark squares. White answers with d3 to stop the pawn, e3 to hit it, and a3-b4 to crack the bind on c5.

hp-6xd.spoken: In the Exchange French, playing Nc6 instead of Nf6 avoids the passive setup with c6. That keeps f6 open for the queen and gives Black dynamic chances.

hp-6wj.spoken: In the lines where Black plays Qxc4, Black often pushes b5 to gain space. White strikes back with a4, hitting that pawn and forcing Black to answer. Keep this pattern in mind.

hp-6xu.spoken: The Karpov Variation has one serious weakness: Black must choose the king e7 line and face difficult positions, or allow the queenside pressure described here. Either way, White gets an easy game against it.

hp-6xh.spoken: White can also bring the knight out to c3 on move five, steering away from the usual c3 and Qc2 setup. That changes the character of the game and leads to different kinds of positions.

hp-6xt.spoken: If Black castles kingside, White hits back with g4 and rips the position open. On the queenside, the b6-pawn is a hook for a4-a5, keeping Black from sealing that flank shut.

hp-6wk.spoken: Black can meet the check with c5, setting up b6 and Bb7 for a double fianchetto. The knight sits on d7 instead of c6. White mirrors with b3 and Bb2.

hp-6x8.spoken: White delayed while Black struck first. Castling long, then h5 and Rd2, gave Black full activity. White's plan had to be a3 and b4, opening his own attack before Black's pieces took over.

hp-6xr.spoken: The g5 knight attacks the f6 knight, so Black must first play e6. The bishop belongs on d6 to control e5, not on e7.

hp-6x9.spoken: If Black castles queenside here, the position turns dangerous, because White's attack on that flank can hit hard. On the kingside, Black is not worse, but he must stay alert to avoid a quick collapse.

hp-6xo.spoken: A knight on e5 gives White strong central pressure. It blocks Black's bishop and leaves f7 and e6 vulnerable to sacrifices, so Black struggles to play e6 naturally.

hp-6x5.spoken: Black played a6, b5, and Nb7 to bring pieces out and target the white queen. That queen gets trapped, and Black wins material — a reminder that even a seemingly safe queen can face fierce counterplay.

hp-6x1.spoken: The e-pawn is under attack, and pushing it to e5 opens the center too soon, letting Black simplify into a dull game. Keep the tension with Nc3, a natural developing move that preserves White's edge.

hp-6xp.spoken: The knight on g5 keeps control of e6, so Black's usual h6 can walk into Ne6, with a winning threat. And if Black captures on e6, White has mate on g6.

hp-6xg.spoken: After Bd6, White can instead play Ne2, supporting f4 and preparing f3 to break the pin on the bishop. A subtle but important choice.

hp-6xw.spoken: The knight on g5 is eyeing f7 and e6, so Black must make a decision about the light-squared bishop.

hp-6y8.spoken: Once the sacrifice is refuted, White can try other ideas, but Black is safe if the correct defensive sequence was followed. Even with extra material, the position still holds dangers, so stay alert.

hp-6yx.spoken: If all the pieces come off, the king and pawn endgame heavily favors White thanks to the potential passed e-pawn. Even with the engine calling it a draw, Black has to defend with great precision.

hp-6yk.spoken: Studying theory alone won’t master the Karpov. You must analyze expert games from Karpov, Smyslov, and Geller to grasp the typical plans and ideas.

hp-6yz.spoken: White castles, and Black pins the knight on f3 with Bg4. White's h3 doesn't force a retreat—Black answers h5, and the bishop stays safe.

hp-6yh.spoken: The Karpov Variation gives Black a solid yet passive setup—easier to equalize than to generate winning chances, especially versus lower-rated opposition. The structure stays imbalanced, but converting demands precise play.

hp-6z1.spoken: After d4, Black should capture with the e-pawn. Bg4 is weaker: the f6-pawn blocks Qh4 ideas, and White consolidates with c3.

hp-6z0.spoken: In the Exchange Variation, once Black's f-pawn guards e5, White must play d4 at once. Any delay lets Black push c5, and d4 is blocked for good.

hp-6yj.spoken: The Karpov Variation suits players who value safety over ambition, not those chasing a must-win. It's solid, drawish, and demands deep preparation.

hp-6y1.spoken: Black's queen stays home, because Ne5 attacks f7 and wins. The d4 pawn is not hanging; Black cannot take it.

hp-6yt.spoken: Black plays …Be7, signaling they will avoid the open Spanish and the early Archangel. Both sides follow a forced sequence up to move nine, playing automatically.

hp-6yd.spoken: If White holds off castling and pushes f4, Black hits a dilemma: kingside castling invites White to castle queenside, and the reverse opens the opposite door. White waits more flexibly, so Black holds off castling for now.

hp-6yw.spoken: The doubled c-pawns and the e5 pawn leave Black's structure fragile, so f6 defends e5 but also exposes the kingside further.

hp-6ye.spoken: Black’s king stays stuck in the center while White prepares to castle and start a pawn storm. If Black castles on either side, White castles the other way, picks up a tempo, and leaves Black fighting for a plan.

hp-6yg.spoken: In the Karpov structure, Black aims over the long run at White’s queenside, chiefly the b2 and c3 pawns, plus the weak f2 and g2 squares. If White advances the c-pawn, Black gets pressure along the d-file.

hp-6yf.spoken: If White castles kingside and pushes f4, Black can calmly castle queenside and land in a playable position, though still slightly worse. The plan centers on pressuring the knight on e5 and picking at White's queenside weaknesses.

hp-6y7.spoken: When Black plays h6, White can try the sacrificial Nxe6. If the queen recaptures, Qe7+ wins the piece back. The right defense is taking with the bishop, giving check, then king to e7, not f8, keeping f8 open for the knight.

hp-6xx.spoken: After Black castles, the position is balanced. Black can play knight e4 to centralize the knight.

hp-6yl.spoken: White's bishop on b5 hits the knight on c6, the guard of e5. The direct threat is to capture that knight and grab the pawn, but Black holds several defenses or counterplay options.

hp-6yy.spoken: White's immediate capture on e5 fails: Black recaptures with the f-pawn, and after the queen check and capture on e5, Black's bishop defends and White is down a piece.

hp-6yi.spoken: In the Karpov Variation, White usually carries a three-to-two pawn majority on the queenside, and Black holds a pawn on e6. That structural imbalance makes endgames uneven—though not easy for either side to win.

hp-6zy.spoken: The key to this opening is understanding the strategic ideas, not memorizing move orders. The best way to internalize those patterns is by studying real games.

hp-6ze.spoken: After Black plays Qf6, White must respond with Nbd2 to keep the pawn structure intact. Any random move lets Black capture on f3 and ruin it.

hp-6za.spoken: Black plays f5 to hit e4, and White answers with the precise knight to f4, eyeing g6 and d8. If e5 comes and the rook captures on e5, the knight takes on g6, and Black's pieces hang.

hp-6zj.spoken: White's h-pawn can capture the bishop once the queen steps off the g-file. If Black's queen lands on f5, e6, or e7, White keeps defenses like Nh2 ready against Qh4. The position stays level, but White must play precisely to dodge the tactical threats.

hp-6zc.spoken: The bishop pair is Black's compensation for doubled c-pawns and the damaged structure in this Exchange Variation. Trading queens gives away that compensation, so Black avoids it.

hp-707.spoken: f3 to support e4 weakens the position by opening the dark-square diagonal; once the f6 knight moves, the bishop on g7 can jump to d4 with tactical threats.

hp-703.spoken: In the declined Benko, White can back the c4 pawn with the knight on d2, which also sets up e4. If Black grabs the pawn, White recaptures later, and that knight keeps the e4 push covered.

hp-70h.spoken: Accepting the gambit is fine. White takes the a6 pawn with the bishop, then the king recaptures, keeping a small edge. The black bishop on a6 is traded for White's f1 bishop, so White calmly castles by hand with g3 and Kg2, leaving the king safe.

hp-70i.spoken: The fight centers on White pushing e5 and Black preventing it. Black piles pieces on e5 and lines up heavy pieces on the a- and b-files, turning the bishop’s diagonal and the open files into chaos.

hp-6z7.spoken: Black's c5 makes the knight on b3 a target and could strand it. Moving to e2 keeps it flexible, with the option to reach f4 and pressure g6 and d5.

hp-709.spoken: After Nf3, Black's …Bb7 puts real pressure on d4. If White captures on a6, the rook or bishop takes back easily, and if White pushes e4-e5, the d4-pawn is left exposed.

hp-701.spoken: Declining the Benko Gambit saves White a tempo—no capture on b5—and lets pieces come out, with e4 and a4 fueling the initiative. Avoiding the capture also denies Black the open files and smooth development that acceptance grants.

hp-71e.spoken: In the Czech Slav, Black’s bishop on f5 stands outside the pawn chain, a comfortable and typical structure, much like in the Caro-Kann or Scandinavian.

hp-71c.spoken: After e3, Bf5, and g4, Black plays Nbd7, preparing to take back the c4 pawn and pressure the knight. If White captures on c4, Black recaptures, and the position holds.

hp-71l.spoken: Playing g3 is a risky alternative that sidesteps the immediate challenge to the c4 pawn. It demands deep understanding and is not for practical play unless you have studied it extensively.

hp-71h.spoken: The Alapin Variation with e3 produces sharp, unbalanced play, much like the Semi-Slav. Every move matters and the outcome stays unclear, so Black must be exact or risk trouble.

hp-717.spoken: Black can hold the pawn on c4 in several ways. Playing Bg4 pins the knight, but White answers with h3, then e4, and the bishop can get trapped behind the pawn chain. It works, yet it demands deep positional understanding.

hp-71q.spoken: After Black takes the pawn, White's main move is a4, and the most natural reply is Bf5. It's a straightforward move to grasp, and while this line carries deep theory, mastering it hands Black a serious weapon against d4.

hp-70y.spoken: In the f3 variation, Black need not take the pawn on b5. Develop naturally with g6, Bg7, and d6, following the Benko plan. White's f3 move leaves dark squares weak, so the bishop on g7 gains real power.

hp-71r.spoken: Black often answers with e5. White then plays Nf3, eyeing that pawn. Black's choices are narrow: capture on d4, or check with Bb4+ to pick up a tempo.

hp-713.spoken: In the Zaitsev system, if White plays Bf4 and later captures on e4, Black hits the bishop with g5, forcing it back, and then trades favorably. But if Black recaptures with the knight instead, White gets tactics with Nxd6.

hp-715.spoken: a4 has three drawbacks: it develops nothing, permanently weakens the b4-square, and hands Black the tempo to bring the bishop to f5.

hp-71m.spoken: White's queen check attacks the c4 pawn directly. Black answers with Nbd7 or b5, and b5 is solid — it defends the pawn and prepares development, though it lets White form a fianchetto setup.

hp-70o.spoken: The main line continues with b6, keeping the position closed for a standard Benko setup. Black aims to control c4, denying White’s knight that outpost.

hp-70m.spoken: Playing the queen to b6 immediately is slow, because White develops with tempo and chases it back.

hp-710.spoken: Black gives up a pawn for lasting queenside pressure, mostly down the open a- and b-files. That extra pawn rarely matters because Black's pieces keep it locked down.

hp-70s.spoken: After White takes on a6, Black recaptures with the f-pawn whenever possible, planning d5. That central push gains space and cuts off White’s bishop on e2 from the c4 square.

hp-71i.spoken: Black's extra pawn on c4 comes with a price: White's pieces are active and pressing. The light-squared bishop stays locked behind d6 and e6, and that b-pawn is stretched too far.

hp-71a.spoken: The main move is …Bf5, putting the bishop on its best square. If White plays a4, Black still develops the bishop there, since White used a tempo on that pawn move. White can answer with e3, g4, or the irritating Nh4, which attacks the bishop.

hp-718.spoken: Playing e6 is another option, giving up the c4 pawn for normal development. This reaches a Semi-Slav structure through a different move order, confusing opponents but complicating your own life. It works at high level, but not for club players.

hp-70w.spoken: Black’s bishop settles on b7, aiming down the long diagonal. If White pushes e4, Black answers e6, opens the center, and that bishop turns into a monster.

hp-71u.spoken: Material is level. Black holds a three-to-two edge in pawns on the queenside; White's four-to-three on the kingside is tougher to exploit. White enjoys more space and livelier pieces, but Black's setup stands firm.

hp-70l.spoken: After b6, White gives the pawn back but keeps the queenside shut, so the a-file stays closed for now. Black can push on the queenside or crack the center with e6.

hp-70p.spoken: In the d6 line, White aims for e5, Black must stop it. Black plays Bg4, pinning the knight and easing control over e5. Material is equal, the position is balanced, but Black's extra weaknesses to target make the Benko a strong practical pick.

hp-72l.spoken: White's d-pawn is backward, and every pawn sits on a light square. Black wants to swap the light-squared bishops, leaving White with permanent light-square weaknesses.

hp-730.spoken: White's g5 is a serious mistake, weakening the kingside and letting Black equalize easily. After …Nfd7, Black recaptures on c4 with the knight, gains a tempo with b5, forces the knight to e3, and plays e5, reaching an improved Slav.

hp-734.spoken: White’s pawn on a4 may look slightly overextended, but it is no real problem. The engine calls the position equal, so Black has no pressure here.

hp-72y.spoken: White seals the center, skipping the usual Chameleon ideas. It's a practical dodge of Black's preparation, and the a6 move loses much of its value.

hp-72e.spoken: White has two main ideas here: f3 to hold e4, or Nf3 to surrender the pawn for quick development. The f3 line invites Black's f5 break, unleashing a sharp attack against the white king.

hp-72b.spoken: The Greco Variation with …b5 is a sharp bid for queenside space—risky, but it can produce unbalanced play.

hp-72s.spoken: a4 is the sharper choice. It ends all hope of b5 forever, since axb5 would hang the rook. Black has to switch plans, aiming for c5 or putting the bishop on g4.

hp-720.spoken: After White castles, Black can try an early e5. It looks strange, but it works. White has outposts on c4 and f5, yet Black's passed pawn can challenge both squares.

hp-72h.spoken: The speaker likes …b5, a typical Queen's Gambit Accepted idea to grab queenside space and hit White's bishop. The engine may favor White, but Black still feels comfortable here.

hp-727.spoken: White has nothing more than equality here. If White plays the queen to d4, Black can swap queens, and the game heads toward a dry draw.

hp-723.spoken: White can steer this into a natural sequence where Black must be prepared.

hp-72t.spoken: After a4, Black can choose Bg4, pinning the knight. Nbd7 is White’s reply. The move a5 mirrors the Smith-Morra idea, sending the b8 knight to b4 through a6, but it’s risky — White’s c6 pawn guards b5.

hp-731.spoken: g3 is the engine's top pick, setting up a fianchetto. Black can go solid, or take on c4 and then play g6, Bg7, and c5 — that dissolves the center and equalizes.

hp-72p.spoken: White seals the queenside with c5, leaving Black the main choices of e6, a4, or taking on c4. At club level this stays calm, while masters often settle into quiet maneuvering.

hp-72u.spoken: Black has a big choice here. The risky …a5 is only for players who know these sharp systems well. The standard path is …dxc4, freeing the bishop and heading into the main theoretical battles.

hp-72q.spoken: Natural and best is e6, defending the d5 pawn, preparing the bishop's development, and stopping b5. White likely answers with e3 or b3 to bring the bishop out, since capturing on d5 or b5 favors Black.

hp-72o.spoken: The c5 main line often draws at the top level, but below master play, games stay sharp. Study games from players under 2200 to learn this line properly.

hp-729.spoken: White plays Bc4 only. Taking on e6 lets Black trade queens and recapture with the bishop, keeping the extra pawn, and White loses castling rights.

hp-73y.spoken: White's g4 and a4 push the queen around, but if White plays f4, Black has to strike back in the center with c5. This gives a setup like the French, but with White's pieces still asleep.

hp-73x.spoken: Black's queen on b6 hits b2 and d4. If White pushes g4, the bishop retreats to d7, where it blocks any e6 breakthrough.

hp-73t.spoken: White locks down g5, and Black can't break that bind. So Black's plan shifts to hitting the d4 and b2 pawns; Qb6 attacks both at once, forcing White to spend moves defending instead of developing.

hp-73k.spoken: The Tal variation, with h4, often gets skipped in older Caro-Kann books, and even a classic like "Starting Out" from 2001 omits it entirely—a real gap in the literature.

hp-73e.spoken: In the Chigorin French, White's e3 is a soft move, not the sharpest test. Black must know the right response—if you try to punish it immediately, White plays e5 and you end up worse. Moves like Nf3 or Nc3 are more active, but here the exchange is the key.

hp-73b.spoken: Playing a5 first prepares Bc5, and in these lines White shouldn’t take on d4. With a5 included, Black stands slightly better than without it.

hp-740.spoken: White’s knight to c3 waits patiently, eyeing b5 and d5 and setting a trap if the queen grabs b2. It pushes Black to commit with e6 and then h5.

hp-73i.spoken: The endgame is lost for White—Black is two pawns up. The bishop is under attack, the rook has no escape, and the black king is about to break in on c5. Whatever White plays, material falls or the passed pawn promotes.

hp-73j.spoken: After the pawn push to e5, Black's favorite reply is Bf5, putting the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain. That move solves the bishop's problem before it gets trapped.

hp-73a.spoken: Black can steer toward an endgame and hope to trade down, and the resulting king-and-pawn ending should favor Black, while a knight-versus-bishop ending also tilts Black’s way depending on where the kings stand.

hp-746.spoken: After White plays f4 to block Black's e5, Black's position gets strategically tough. White's pawn on f4 holds e5 and cramps Black's pieces. Black needs counterplay, often by striking at the g4 pawn with the knight.

hp-73w.spoken: The Tal variation plays h4, attacking the bishop directly. Black has three main options: h6 or h5 to give the bishop a retreat square, or delay e6 so it can fall back. Qb6 is also solid, hitting d4 and b2 while slowing White's development.

hp-73m.spoken: White typically answers h6 with g4, and Black replies Be4 to force f3, then pulls back to h7. White’s e5 pawn stands strong, but Black must not take it — capturing with exf5 lets White recapture and leaves Black’s light squares weak.

hp-73v.spoken: With white's knight on f3, black sometimes plays Nh6 and then Ng4, targeting the f2 square. That plan works best if white has castled kingside, where f2 is defended, but a sacrifice on f2 can still create pressure.

hp-73u.spoken: If White castles kingside, allowing him to take the h5 pawn can be fine, since that opens the h-file and leaves his h4 pawn vulnerable.

hp-742.spoken: In this Caro-Kann Advance, Black faces a choice after White’s h4. Playing h6 instead of h5 controls g5 and sidesteps White’s usual plans. It invites g4, which can strand the black king if mishandled, but Black has resources.

hp-74u.spoken: Black had the chance to open the center, but let it slide, and White dissolved the e5 weakness with exd6, wiping out Black's edge.

hp-755.spoken: White’s c4 bishop sets up a discovered check if Black slips, and the king stays exposed in the center. Black can probe with f3 or Bg4, and the e4 pawn falls later.

hp-74l.spoken: After White develops the bishop to c4, if Black captures on d5, White faces no danger. Black can steer toward a calm endgame.

hp-75j.spoken: In the Bishop’s Gambit, Black’s sharpest answer is …Qh4+, and White must answer precisely. The position turns tense, and one slip leaves White in trouble.

hp-74n.spoken: In the Balogh Variation, White's e5 pawn often becomes overextended, just like in the Berlin Defense. That pawn turns weak once pieces get traded off, so White needs active piece play and pressure on f7 before any simplification.

hp-74s.spoken: Playing d5 is playable, but it gives Black's knights room to breathe. White's pawns turn into targets—if f4 comes, the bishop gets locked in, and if b4, Black answers with a5.

hp-74p.spoken: White's knight belongs on e2 instead of f3, because f3 lets Black's bishop come to g4 and pin the knight against the queen, adding pressure on d4. That's the key choice Black's setup forces.

hp-757.spoken: White's king stays on f1 or g1, the rook comes to f1, and Black's queenside sits undeveloped. That leaves White better, a pawn up, even with Black's attacking chances.

hp-754.spoken: Black owns the open h-file, ready to build threats against White's king. Castle queenside, park the bishop on c6 to shield c7, push the f-pawn to strike e5, and double rooks on h-file for the attack.

hp-75c.spoken: White's pawn center and lead in development offset the missing pawn, leaving the position equal but with White holding more ideas and easier play. Black often stays tied to defending the f4 pawn.

hp-74v.spoken: White missed a chance for a winning attack with a knight sacrifice on d7, cutting off the king's escape.

hp-758.spoken: Play Nd7 is Black's usual follow-up here — engines say Black is slightly better, but a pawn up is still a pawn up if White knows how to convert. Qf3 offers a trade, because any endgame favors the extra pawn, even doubled ones.

hp-74x.spoken: Black has options like …a5, …Nc6, and …c5. The main line is …a5, though it loosens the queenside a bit—White answers with a4 to stop Black’s space gain and keep the bishop on b3.

hp-74j.spoken: White's best answer to the queen check on a5 is knight d2, which keeps c4 available and avoids weak points. Bishop d2 or knight c3 instead lets the queen go to a6, putting pressure on the light squares and stopping White from castling kingside.

hp-74z.spoken: Playing …c5 is an offbeat sideline, not recommended, since it lets White capture the knight on b6 and grab a slight edge. The principled main moves are …a5 and …Nc6, which give Black solid chances.

hp-74k.spoken: Black has three solid plans here: queen to b6, h5, or h6. Each creates a different game, though h6 is the speaker's pick — it demands sharp preparation, since the king can end up awkwardly on f7.

hp-767.spoken: The deferred Steinitz mirrors the King's Indian in pawn structure and piece placement, so the two openings complement each other in a repertoire.

hp-76w.spoken: The bishop on g5 pins Black's b5 pawn, so a6 can't reinforce it. White's a4 hits that pawn and stops Black from defending it easily.

hp-766.spoken: Deferred Steinitz doesn't lock Black into a rigid setup. If both sides steer that way, the game can flow straight into mainline Ruy Lopez territory, like the Closed Spanish.

hp-76z.spoken: In the Chabanenko Variation, Black accepts queenside weaknesses like b6 and rarely finds counterplay. If Black never gets e5 in, they stand strategically worse.

hp-76e.spoken: After the trade on c6, Black gets the two bishops, and the light-squared bishop has no rival on the long diagonal. The engine calls it equal, but Black's setup feels far more comfortable and is the one you'd rather play.

hp-76x.spoken: In the sharp line where Black plays Ne5, Black can transpose into the Vienna Variation with e6, sacrificing a piece for three pawns. The position turns very concrete, with both sides forced for the first fourteen moves.

hp-76f.spoken: After Black plays d6, White has two sound move orders: c3 first or castling first. If c3 comes first, White follows with d4. If castling comes first, White can still play d4, or even c4.

hp-75v.spoken: Black's pawn on f6 and knight on f6, together with the g6-pawn, control e4 after …exf6. White's e3 and c4 setup leaves light-square holes, so a pawn cannot easily challenge e4.

hp-76q.spoken: White plays for the Carlsbad setup, posting bishops on g5 and d3. The active pieces give White a small edge, with a tempo up on the similar structures Black usually plays.

hp-75z.spoken: Immediate d4 is a mistake here—Black answers b5, and after the bishop retreats, Nxd4 wins a pawn. If the queen takes back, the Noah's Ark trap springs with c5 and c4, boxing in the bishop.

hp-760.spoken: The exchange here works slightly better for Black than the normal version, since the b-pawn recaptures and d6 keeps the structure solid. White may also build a King's Indian setup with c3 and d4.

hp-77y.spoken: After Black's d-pawn recaptures, White plays a4 to stop the b5 break. That keeps the queenside calm and prevents Black's counterplay.

hp-783.spoken: The pawn on d4 is isolated yet not weak, and the position stands nearly equal with a slight edge for White. This is the critical moment for the Rossolimo Attack.

hp-77f.spoken: White’s pieces sit actively, and Black’s king stays exposed while pieces remain on the board. White eyes Ng5 against e6, while Black seeks to block e5 and lean on the queenside pawn majority.

hp-77x.spoken: If Black pushes e5, White must not take that pawn. Capturing lets Black recapture and White's knight hangs; a desperate Nxf7 only leaves White worse.

hp-78f.spoken: After Black plays a6, White's bishop retreats to f1. Then Black can hit the center with d5, but White must answer with d4 to keep the balance. If White stays passive, Black gets a comfortable game.

hp-77q.spoken: White’s early f5 meets e6, and the position stays about even. The c4-bishop sits awkwardly, since White wants d3, but it can be rerouted later.

hp-78h.spoken: If Black regroups with Ng4-e7, White can pick c3 over Re1, strengthening the center and opening c2 for the bishop. The bishop then goes to a4 and later c2 after b5, aiming along a fresh diagonal at the black king.

hp-77l.spoken: In a line where White gives up the rook for a bishop, the payoff is two pawns and active knights. They get strong squares on e4, g5, and d4, while the dark-squared bishop stays to back the play on dark squares.

hp-77w.spoken: Play h3 before castling, so Black can't pin the knight with Bg4. If the light-squared bishop trades for that knight, White loses a defender of key squares.

hp-786.spoken: If White mistakenly takes on c6, Black recaptures with the d-pawn, opening the d-file and hitting the queen. If White instead defends e5 with the knight, Black simply takes back with the knight on e5.

hp-77v.spoken: Capturing with the d-pawn after Bxc6 opens development lines and locks down the queenside, even without pushing a pawn toward the center — that's Black's strongest reply.

hp-77r.spoken: White can castle, inviting Black to pull the knight back or take the bishop. If Black takes, White trades a badly placed piece—strategically fine.

hp-77m.spoken: The queen often reroutes to e1 in the Grand Prix, where it supports a kingside assault, particularly the h4 pawn push. From e1 it slides over to help the attack, far more useful than staying on d1.

hp-799.spoken: The Open Sicilian is on the board. Black's knight on f6 attacks the e4 pawn and stakes a claim to the center.

hp-78w.spoken: After Qd2, Black's best reply is Rc8, getting ready to pressure the c-file. That move is necessary anyway, and it avoids making weaknesses with early pawn pushes.

hp-79q.spoken: Black's d5-pawn stands exposed, and White's bishop from c1 can develop to pressure it. Black often answers with f6 to block the bishop from reaching g5, where it would pin the knight and break Black's coordination.

hp-79o.spoken: Black can bring the g-pawn to g6 here, and White answers with c4, heading into a Maroczy Bind, just as in the Accelerated Dragon.

hp-78j.spoken: Black can choose d5, a6, or d6. Playing d5 challenges the e4 pawn and grabs central space; if White takes, the knight recaptures and frees the bishop. The a6 move is an unusual approach, while d6 stays solid and sets up d5 after White captures.

hp-78l.spoken: White's d4 and c3 prepare the push to d5, and the center stays tense — neither side should ease it too soon.

hp-78s.spoken: The engines may call this equal, but White's practical chances are far stronger thanks to the permanent outpost on d5 and a clearer attacking plan.

hp-78x.spoken: Black often swings the knight to f5 to bait White into trading the bishop. White answers with h4 and h5, grabbing space and building an attack. Both sides race, and the position stays razor-sharp.

hp-78k.spoken: Black captures with the b-pawn and aims for d5. White holds off and develops with Re1, c3, and a6, driving the bishop back to f1 instead of letting it pressure e4.

hp-78n.spoken: Black's usual reply to White's d4 is taking on d4, entering a well-known sharp line that has seen many strong games, including Anand versus Giri in 2016.

hp-78v.spoken: After White plays Qd2, Black may take on d4. If White recaptures with the bishop, Black trades off his dark-squared bishop, which is usually bad for Black. But the knight on d4 also guards the c2 square, so taking it weakens White's queenside.

hp-79i.spoken: Black has four major setups here: the Classical with …d6, the Four Knights with …Nc6, the Pin Variation with …e6, and the Hyperaccelerated Dragon with …g6. White’s main bid for an edge is Nc3, answering whatever Black picks.

hp-79b.spoken: The Scheveningen Sicilian, with black's pawn on e6, was a big favorite in the eighties and nineties. White has several sharp choices here: the Keres Attack with g4, the English Attack with Be3, f3, Qd2, and castling long, plus setups with f4.

hp-792.spoken: White offers the Smith-Morra Gambit with d4, an aggressive try for an attack. If Black accepts with cxd4, then c3 and Nxc3 give White three pieces developed against Black's one, plus attacking chances that compensate for the pawn.

hp-7ab.spoken: Small inaccuracies like a6 and b3 are not losing, but they hand the opponent chances.

hp-7ap.spoken: White’s knight lands on f3, the key move in the Nimzo-Indian. It clears the way for e4 and guards that square against Black’s knight. The fight for e4 is the heart of this opening.

hp-7b4.spoken: After White plays bishop g5, Black's knight on f6 is pinned, so knight e4 is impossible. Black plays h6 instead, forcing the trade on f6 and securing the bishop pair.

hp-7a9.spoken: White's b3 and later slips leave the c3 pawn weak. Material is even, but Black's pawn structure is better, and the engine's "equal" hides real active play.

hp-7aj.spoken: After Black plays …c5 against most setups, White's Nf3 can lead into either the Rubinstein with e3 or the Romanian with g3, so Black avoids separate prep for the Kasparov line.

hp-7am.spoken: Black's bishop on d6 eyes f4, so White's usual attacking plans get shut down. The d4 pawn sits blockaded and under fire, leaving Black feeling right at home.

hp-7aw.spoken: White often targets e4 with Qc2 and h4 in this Nimzo, but Black counters with h6 and a later c5. If White plays Bg5, Black plays h6 instead of taking the bishop, forcing it to retreat or trade on favorable terms.

hp-7ar.spoken: Black answers c5 with a3 by taking on c3, then after Bxc3, plays d6 to set up Nc6 and b6 against the c-pawn. Sound plan, despite the overextension risk.

hp-7b6.spoken: The bishop on d2 is a modern idea in this Nimzo-Indian line. If Black trades knights on c3, White recaptures with the bishop, keeping the pawns flexible and dodging doubled pawns. That bishop also backs a g3 setup, so it earns its place.

hp-7aa.spoken: Rook to b8 is playable, but the engine prefers the rook to d8. There it pressures the center and supports the c5 push.

hp-7ao.spoken: If Black follows with Bxf3 and Nc6, then e5 is a dynamic choice — it gives up a pawn but wakes up the pieces and targets White's king. d5 is the solid route, yet e5 brings practical chances.

hp-7a6.spoken: h3 beats h4 here because it sets up g4, pushing forward on the kingside while the king stays sheltered. Once g4 lands, the bishop on g2 gains real strength, and White gets ideas like the knight jumping to d4.

hp-7a3.spoken: If Black takes the b2 pawn with the bishop, White answers with Rb1, then b3 and Bxb3, and after swapping rooks on the a-file, Black's attack fades. White has full compensation for the pawn.

hp-79x.spoken: If White pushes h3, Black's bishop just drops back to e6 or g6. The g6 bishop stays active, and a2 is safe because Black's rook is still at home. Instead, White can play Rh2, rerouting the rook toward the center.

hp-7ce.spoken: White still has both central pawns, but they need support — Black can target them.

hp-7bo.spoken: Against c4, Black must not take that pawn—that's exactly what White hopes for. Instead, Black plays e5, stopping d4 and setting up a knight on d4 that no pawn can chase away.

hp-7c9.spoken: White can choose between c4, the Maroczy Bind, or d4, the main line. Playing d4 hits the center at once, punishing Black's flank pawn play, and it's the most frequent move.

hp-7bc.spoken: In this e3 setup, White's pawns all sit on dark squares, so the light-squared bishop on g2 becomes powerful, while Black's bishop on g7 is restricted. Black's c8 bishop outshines White's c1 bishop, and this gives White a theoretical edge in bishop activity.

hp-7bz.spoken: Playing Bf4 in the Miles Variation keeps you out of heavy mainline theory and can unsettle opponents who haven't studied it. If Black responds with the right plans, though, the position runs about level or slightly favors Black.

hp-7c1.spoken: White prepares d4 with c3, and Black can hit the d4 pawn with Nf6. White answers with Re1, and if Black castles, the d4 push loses its bite—the game can go closed, especially if Black follows with e5.

hp-7bq.spoken: The Wing Gambit often builds a structure like the Advanced Caro-Kann, but here Black has won the b-pawn. That extra pawn is real material, so Black stands better.

hp-7bn.spoken: Black shouldn't play e6 here, because White then gets c3 and d4 with tempo, developing easily with a powerful center. Instead, Black plays d5 right away to challenge White's center.

hp-7c3.spoken: Play d4 immediately. It's sharper and avoids closed positions that demand specific knowledge.

hp-7cd.spoken: After Nc3, Black can capture on d4, but White plays Be3, holding the center and exposing Black's queen to tempo gains.

hp-7bs.spoken: Black can respond to Nf3 with Nf6, baiting the pawn push to e5. If White takes it, the knight lands on d5, where it proves almost impossible to dislodge, and Black stands well.

hp-7br.spoken: The Wing Gambit line sees White offer the b-pawn for quick development. With Nf3 on the board, Black strikes in the center with d5, reaching a Caro-Kann-like structure, only now Black owns an extra pawn.

hp-7by.spoken: If Black later plays c5 after the d5 exchange, White can take with either the bishop or pawn, but capturing with the bishop is sounder, leaving a symmetrical pawn structure with no clear winning chances for either side.

hp-7c7.spoken: The Maroczy Bind with pawns on c4 and d4 gives White a strong center, limits Black's space, and improves piece activity. The downside is the light-squared bishop can get trapped behind the pawns, slowing the game down.

hp-7cr.spoken: The same position can come from the Accelerated Dragon or the regular Dragon, so the move order matters for understanding the subtle differences.

hp-7cq.spoken: The engine sees a clear edge for White here, but in practice Black can play it — many strong grandmasters have handled this position successfully.

hp-7cj.spoken: After White plays Bc4 and Black answers with d6, the g7 bishop stays on its diagonal, and White can push d5, creating a Benoni-style structure. White takes space and builds an aggressive setup, while Black’s play flows through the bishop on g7.

hp-7cp.spoken: Taking the knight on c6 gives up the bishop pair, but it dissolves the weakness on that square and simplifies the position, making White's space advantage harder to convert.

hp-7dt.spoken: White enjoys a comfortable space edge in this Exchange Variation. Black's knight on b6 sits awkwardly, so no need to rush with b3—White simply builds pressure naturally.

hp-7d7.spoken: White’s setup is solid, but Black can gambit a pawn with e6, buying activity. The position stays balanced if White is precise, yet Black gets real compensation for any slip.

hp-7da.spoken: Once the position simplifies, Black can develop with d6 and Be6, then castle quickly. White can stay solid with Be2 and d3, without rushing to expand. The game stays balanced, but Black gets real chances if White slips.

hp-7db.spoken: The bishop on e2 develops to its ideal square while keeping the knight free to reroute to e2 later. From there the knight still guards the d4 weakness, though it no longer covers e5, but it sidesteps the Bg4 pin.

hp-7dd.spoken: White's b3 leaves Black's knight nowhere to go but c8, a clumsy retreat. White has every piece out, while Black must waste time bringing that knight back.

hp-7dn.spoken: In a high-level encounter from this exact setup, White's f4 was a mistake. It let Black castle and later build a powerful kingside attack with Bg4 and Nh4, while the push only weakened White's own king side and ignored Black's counterplay.

hp-7co.spoken: White’s e5 pawn grabs space, but the d4 pawn is shaky. Black aims at that weakness and builds counterplay.

hp-7d2.spoken: Black can play …c6 here, heading into the Caro-Kann. The independent option is …e6, the Icelandic Gambit, giving up a pawn for activity; stats favor Black, but with theory, White refutes it.

hp-7d1.spoken: White plays c4, keeping the extra pawn. Black must act at once: c6 transposes to the Caro-Kann, while e6 is the Icelandic Gambit—risky for Black.

hp-7dy.spoken: Delaying the knight's development keeps the opponent guessing how to meet the bishop. A flexible move order creates practical problems at the board.

hp-7ea.spoken: Black's most complex options are …c5, the Vitolins Variation, and …a5, the Mislov Variation. A top expert recommends the Mislov because it keeps the Bogo-Indian character while giving Black solid chances.

hp-7er.spoken: In the Modern Variation, if Black trades off the light-squared bishop and plants a pawn on e5, the structure becomes solid and playable, even if the engine favors White.

hp-7ej.spoken: If White pushes a3 to gain space, Black answers with a timely pawn break—c6, preparing d5. A passive move like Rd8 lets White expand further, and Black lands in trouble.

hp-7eg.spoken: After White pushes e4, Black must answer with e5 at once, or e5 crushes him. That produces a closed center, where Black has to play with energy.

hp-7eh.spoken: If White ever plays e4, Black must answer at once with e5, closing the center. Let White follow with e5 and Black suffocates from lack of space.

hp-7eo.spoken: In the Vitols variation of the Bogo-Indian, Black can fix the knight on b4 to stop queenside expansion, but that surrenders the b5 square and leaves d6 weak, creating lasting positional problems.

hp-7f2.spoken: This is similar to a Sicilian pawn center, but with a queen-pawn opening for White. Black’s bishops have more scope, while White’s knights are better posted. The engine’s plus-one evaluation overstates things.

hp-7f0.spoken: The main line is …d5, stopping e4. After Bxf6 exf6 e3, the position mirrors the Hopton Attack, except the knight already sits on c3. That difference matters—in the Hopton, White breaks the center with c4, but here the center holds firm.
