sl-274.spoken: The knight defends the b-pawn and keeps the bishop on its active square. That single move sidesteps the tactics and preserves the balance.

sl-27g.spoken: The king joins the center to reinforce the attack, and once the rook completes its maneuver, the defense falls apart: bishop dominates knight, rook dominates rook, and the pawn break lands.

sl-26z.spoken: The knight was allowed to slip free, and the promising position turned tricky. White ends up fighting for a draw.

sl-27a.spoken: The defender's king must shadow the passed pawn; once it drifts away, the rook and knight start creating threats that force progress.

sl-277.spoken: The rook pinpoints the weak point and keeps the pressure on, while the natural central file invites a pawn strike that turns the game messy.

sl-27f.spoken: The king must babysit the pawn or it marches on and wins. If the knight leaves to help elsewhere, that side is effectively a piece down.

sl-26r.spoken: White plays the prevention move himself, stopping Black from opening lines. Then he castles and prepares the kingside break with the h-pawn.

sl-27i.spoken: The king walks toward the queenside to drag the rook off its post and take the pawn, or it steps the other way to support the kingside pawns.

sl-27e.spoken: The king is the strongest piece left on the board. A passive pawn push surrenders a key central square, and that square decides the endgame. The king belongs in the center.

sl-26y.spoken: White cannot find a useful move; every option is passive and lets Black improve. Black's pieces are active and can keep generating threats.

sl-273.spoken: The king can also shelter and support the pawn, but that invites a queen check that hands the opponent unnecessary chances. The rook move is cleaner because it avoids all checks entirely.

sl-26i.spoken: Patience turns a small edge into a decisive one. The pawn break is halted, so improve the position step by step, converting the slight advantage into a win.

sl-26q.spoken: The key is to capture, but weaken the king first. A check with the bishop forces the opponent to damage their own pawn shelter, leaving the king harder to defend.

sl-26f.spoken: The knight heads for the weak pawn, but advancing it now lets the enemy fix it and leave it exposed. Play the push first, and the fixing move never becomes available.

sl-26p.spoken: The queen steps back to keep the tension alive, setting up a rook lift that will crush. It looks slow, but it sidesteps the losing material chase.

sl-276.spoken: The queen step leaves the real needs unmet. A rook or knight move would create concrete threats; the queen's support of the pawn is indirect and falls short.

sl-26t.spoken: The queen’s quiet invasion here is even stronger than the obvious move, because the bishop can’t develop to neutralize it. That grants Black total control and fuels the pawn break.

sl-27h.spoken: The king slips around the rear to back the passed pawn while bishop and rook combine on threats. The defender can't stop both the check and the promotion.

sl-26v.spoken: The queen’s square must do two jobs at once: keep pressure on the target while shielding the pawns behind. The rook slides to the open file, hits the pawn at once, and leaves the knight no room to strike back.

sl-2ce.spoken: The king steps toward the center of the action, backing the rook and cutting off the defender’s counterplay. If the opponent takes the pawn, the rook closes in to cage the enemy king or grabs the a-pawn, and the rook endgame turns winning.

sl-2c8.spoken: The king on the sixth rank escorts the pawns forward. If the defender’s king reaches the corner square, the bishop and king coordinate to blockade the pawns forever. But the escorting king controls that square, so the defender arrives too late.

sl-2bn.spoken: The pawn push fails; the knight stops promotion or even takes the pawn. First bring the king up to support the pawn.

sl-2cr.spoken: Get the king to its best square, then seek a trade into a pawn endgame.

sl-2cn.spoken: The king must first stop the pawn from reaching the seventh rank, where it would blockade and draw. So he goes to the square in front of it, not the one beside it.

sl-2cl.spoken: The king's activity decides this endgame, and whoever controls the key squares wins. The extra pawns convert when the defender's king is pulled away from the critical points.

sl-2cm.spoken: The king's reach decides races between passed pawns. When he stands closer to the action, he can take the enemy pawn while his own pawn promotes.

sl-2c3.spoken: The king’s distance decides this rook-versus-pawns endgame. With the defending king far off, the pawn side coordinates king and pawns to force promotion, even at the cost of material.

sl-2cq.spoken: The famous finish is a mirage — the losing side resigned from a drawn position. The king's correct path was not straight ahead but around from behind and the side, which stops the pawn from promoting.

sl-2bz.spoken: A queen by herself can never deliver checkmate. Bring the king forward, or the checks go nowhere and the game ends in a draw.

sl-2dj.spoken: In a queen endgame with extra material, the king joins the attack once pawns shelter it. Active use of the king outweighs saving a weak pawn.

sl-2d6.spoken: The bishop forces the king from the corner, and the king steps in to shepherd the pawn home.

sl-2dl.spoken: The active king decides the outcome. One king advances to support the pawns, the other lags behind and cannot help. That difference turns a draw into a loss.

sl-2cy.spoken: The king's own pawn is doomed, yet the win survives because his king stands close enough to shepherd the remaining pawn home.

sl-2d2.spoken: In the endgame, castling is unnecessary. The king walks toward the center to guard key pawns and connect the rooks.

sl-2du.spoken: The king that reaches the center first gains a tempo edge. Rushing the king forward in king and pawn endgames is decisive.

sl-2d4.spoken: The king gets driven back to the rank where it has no escape squares, while ours stays active with plenty of options—that edge decides the endgame.

sl-2dq.spoken: The bishop is trapped and the king must guard it, leaving it passive. Black walks the king forward, and every step forces White to surrender more material.

sl-2dt.spoken: The king steps over, not the pawn. Pushing the f-pawn lets the opponent grab it and win. Moving the king keeps the defense whole and sets up opposition later.

sl-2dk.spoken: Choosing the king move is the whole game. The natural one fails when the h-pawn pushes, the king leaves the box, and the pawn either queens or forces a draw.

sl-2d5.spoken: The king heads for the b-pawn, ready to snap it up if the rook trades itself for the passed pawn. The other king path is weaker.

sl-2e3.spoken: The kings are the difference in this pawn race. One king covers both pawns and holds the balance; the other stands poorly, and the f-pawn lags behind the g-pawn, so the race tips.

sl-2dd.spoken: The king must escort the pawn. If the pawn sprints ahead alone, the enemy king catches it, takes it, and the endgame is lost.

sl-2dz.spoken: The king is a fighting piece in the endgame. Both sides spend tempi marching their kings toward the center before committing to their long-term plans.

sl-2e5.spoken: The king must hold the right distance from both pawns at once. He picks the square that keeps him within reach of each pawn while also controlling the squares that block the black king's advance.

sl-2d7.spoken: The draw hinges on the defender's king reaching the corner to block the pawn. If the king is cut off and cannot get there, the attacker can still win.

sl-2dw.spoken: The rook owns the open file and the king joins the fight. White's king is trapped on the back rank, so checking sequences keep it pinned there and feed Black's counterplay.

sl-2dp.spoken: The king must race across to stop the passed pawn, while the bishop babysits the other flank. If the king arrives in time, the pawn is neutralized and the win becomes much harder.

sl-2e7.spoken: The rook comes under attack, and the right reply is king to the cage square. A wrong king move lets the white king out and turns defense into loss.

sl-2e0.spoken: The king belongs in the fight. Moving it forward pressures the opponent and shields a weak pawn. When recapturing, using the king is safer than the pawn, keeping it secure from checks.

sl-2e2.spoken: The king, not the rook, is the better guardian for a weak pawn. March the king over to defend it, then step it forward along the path, freeing the rook for active duty.

sl-2d8.spoken: The king's activity decides this ending. Pushing pawns on the kingside creates a passed pawn or drags the defending king off its post.

sl-2cz.spoken: The king’s plan targets a key entry square. Block it by pushing a pawn to deny the approach, and let the bishop cover the remaining route. Once the door is shut, the white king marches over and takes the black pawns.

sl-2dx.spoken: The king must pick the right path to back the pawn. Step wrong, and the rook slips behind the pawn and snatches it, flipping a win into a draw or a loss.

sl-2e8.spoken: The king comes out of hiding in the endgame and becomes an active fighter. One king marches to support its passed pawns, the other rushes to stir up play on the opposite flank.

sl-2dg.spoken: The king slides over to stifle the pawn chain, then the knight covers the weak square. Even a pawn or two down, the king anchors the defense and holds the position.

sl-2da.spoken: The king walks into the pawns' path and locks them down. Black's king activity forces White into zugzwang, and that decides the game.

sl-2de.spoken: The bishop's last move is still a mistake: it lands on the wrong diagonal, letting the white king march in and chase it down with gain of tempo.

sl-2dm.spoken: The king steps to the side to block, and the escape route opens. Hold the king in front instead, and the opponent stays boxed in.

sl-2df.spoken: The king must leave the pawn's file to shepherd it home. Bishop checks only hand tempi, and the attacker answers by keeping the initiative with the king.

sl-2dr.spoken: The king's square decides queen endings on a short clock. Pushing it forward gains activity, and if the queens trade, the pawn endgame may hinge on opposition.

sl-2do.spoken: The bishop endgame hangs on a single choice: which path the king takes to support the advanced pawn. One route wins, the other lets the enemy king catch it.

sl-2d9.spoken: The king steps onto the rank of the loose pawns and snaps them up with zigzag moves. Even with the defending king close, threats earn the tempi to keep picking them off.

sl-2e6.spoken: The king’s first job is to block the passed pawn, but sometimes stepping in front of it is not the best. A more active king move, heading to a central square, creates threats and forces the opponent to react.

sl-2dv.spoken: The king wakes up when the endgame begins. Planting it closer to the center turns it into an active fighter that joins the attack and pushes the pawns forward.

sl-2e4.spoken: The king steps to the edge to meet the pawn's advance, taking away its check and the tempo it would steal. When the pawn finally moves, the rook takes it while the king returns, and the blockade holds.

sl-2db.spoken: The forcing push creates a passed pawn, but the white king steps closer to it, and black must avoid overextending. Black wins a pawn, white takes it back, and the draw holds — the king positions are only marginally better for white.

sl-2dc.spoken: The knight move creates the imbalance: one side gains a central passed pawn, the other a distant one. The enemy king can catch the near pawn, but the far pawn is out of reach, so the king must go hunting.

sl-2dy.spoken: The king must stay flexible, shuttling between both wings as the threat shifts. The d-pawn works as a decoy, forcing the defending pieces to commit.

sl-2di.spoken: The queen endgame rewards the active king and the extra pawn. Threats from the queen force the opponent’s queen onto the defensive, and that passivity decides the game.

sl-2d3.spoken: The king belongs in the fight. Centralizing it opens an escape square, while sitting passive on the back rank wastes its power.

sl-2ds.spoken: The f-pawn is the prize, but grabbing it with the knight gives the king a route to neutralize the advantage.

sl-2d1.spoken: The king's placement decides king-and-pawn endings. One step to the wrong square flips a win into a draw.

sl-2e9.spoken: The king stands on a poor square while bishop and knight are already ideal. Bring the king to a better square, and it joins the mate.

sl-2dn.spoken: The bishop endgame turns on keeping the enemy king boxed in. Once it slips to the queenside and gets active, the defender's drawing chances collapse.

sl-2e1.spoken: The king marches forward to support the passed pawns, and the knights reposition to stronger squares. The enemy bishop sits passive and useless, so trading minor pieces only bolsters the pawn structure.

sl-2fg.spoken: The king on the fourth rank outpaces the opponent's on the third, and the far-advanced h-pawn on a dark square resists capture—that edge decides the endgame.

sl-2f1.spoken: The king must defend in the endgame, not shelter. Bring it forward to guard the pawn while the rooks pound the seventh rank.

sl-2eh.spoken: The black king has no good square, while the white pieces line up against the weak pawn. Black's h-pawn counterplay arrives too late because White's own passed pawn on the kingside runs faster.

sl-2f0.spoken: The king steps off the bishop's diagonal and dodges the checks, so the enemy rook's pressure loses its sting.

sl-2eo.spoken: The breakthrough fails, the pawns get stuck, and the king marches over to take the base pawn. That wins both pawns and the game, with no counterplay left.

sl-2fl.spoken: The passive king stays home while the pawns are there for the taking. His inactivity hands the opponent full control of the board.

sl-2ek.spoken: The active king decides this ending. One king invades and takes the pawns, while the other stays passive and loses.

sl-2f6.spoken: The king steps up to claim the active square, following the rule of maximum king activity. That keeps the extra pawn alive and turns it into real winning chances.

sl-2ep.spoken: The king joins the attack on an edge knight, cutting off its escape squares, and the rook lands the final blow.

sl-2fd.spoken: The king's activity decides this endgame. When one king marches forward while the other sits cut off and passive, the active king forces pawns to fall or mate to follow. A better king turns equal material into an easy win.

sl-2eb.spoken: The king, when forced out by check, often steps to the short side of the diagonal—staying closer to the fight and covering the line that wins.

sl-2eg.spoken: The active king outranks the extra pawn. White's king steps forward and invades, while Black's king can only watch.

sl-2el.spoken: The king walks to the center, backs the passed pawn, and turns a won pawn into a won rook endgame.

sl-2ei.spoken: The rook behind the passed pawn is strong, but the pawn cannot queen alone. The winning plan is to march the king up to support its advance.

sl-2eq.spoken: The king invades the queenside while the kingside pawns advance. The double threat overstretches the defense.

sl-2ev.spoken: The king walks across the board in a rook endgame, climbing toward the enemy side. This long journey activates the king and turns it into a threat.

sl-2f5.spoken: The king picks the wrong side of the board, and the active black king takes over. One king step decides whether the ending holds or collapses.

sl-2f4.spoken: The king stepping onto the square invites the attack. Stopping the pawn's advance held the defense, but the king move hands the opponent a tactic.

sl-2ej.spoken: The king on the fifth and the pawns marching outweigh the extra material. Black's pawns stay put while White's promote, so the active king tips the scale.

sl-2fh.spoken: The king must step where it threatens both pawns at once—blocking the passed pawn while pushing its own toward promotion—and the draw is secured.

sl-2ez.spoken: The pawn steps forward to cut off the enemy king and box it in. Restricting the king's access to key squares is the core idea in king and pawn endings.

sl-2fe.spoken: The king is tied to the weak pawn, while the enemy king escorts the other one. The bishop alone cannot hold both passed pawns, and the moment the king steps away, the pawn falls.

sl-2ea.spoken: The king sits on a vulnerable square, exposed to checks and tactical blows. Getting him to safety first is essential before the mating net can close.

sl-2ef.spoken: The king's activity decides rook-and-knight endings. A king that supports the passed pawn and confines the enemy king forces the defender to find precise moves just to hold the draw.

sl-2f7.spoken: The rook endgame demands the rook stay active. Blocking the king's route in also protects the pawn, so the pawn push does both jobs at once.

sl-2fc.spoken: The rook invades, grabs a pawn, and leaves the king stuck with weak pawns to defend. Retreating only deepens the bind, so the king must find an active path instead.

sl-2en.spoken: A rook advantage usually wins, but king safety can outweigh material. Here the exposed king tips the balance, so the position stays better even once the material is level.

sl-2es.spoken: The king's placement decides the endgame. When the king steps forward to support the pawns, it drives a passed pawn through; a timid king move lets the opponent lock the position and stop all progress.

sl-2ff.spoken: The king stands further up the board and the passed pawn sits on the far edge, on a square the enemy bishop cannot easily take—that edge pawn tips the balance.

sl-2er.spoken: The king, not the rook, targets the weak pawn on the edge. The rook route is too slow, so the king marches over, takes the pawn, and pushes the passed pawns home while the opponent's counterplay lags behind.

sl-2f8.spoken: The king steps up to blunt the checks, then repeats moves on purpose. The opponent dares to hope for a draw, but that hope is the trap. The finish is simple: take the rook, then mate.

sl-2ex.spoken: The bishop plants itself on the long diagonal to lock the white king out of the corner, leaving the pawns there undefended. While the white king stays frozen, the black king walks over and removes them, and the win follows.

sl-2f9.spoken: The king steps close to the pawn to restrain it. The enemy king advances, threatening to break through if the defense slips. The saving move is the same square, the king meeting the advance head-on, and that holds the draw.

sl-2f3.spoken: The pawn's placement decides the endgame. If Black breaks with the c-pawn and then the b-pawn, or trades on the e-file, passed pawns or simplifications raise drawing chances. The actual order lets White keep control.

sl-2fb.spoken: The opposition is everything here. Use it to force the king back, and keep your own king active — but calculate every step, because one slack move lets his king in, and one careless pawn push can turn a win into stalemate.

sl-2ew.spoken: The king and bishop work together, pushing the passed pawn forward while the bishop watches the critical squares. The enemy bishop is frozen, forced to guard the pawn and those same squares, so the fight becomes a slow dance of waiting moves.

sl-2ec.spoken: The attacker’s own king breaks the stalemate by stepping onto a square that unblocks the defender’s pawn, giving them a legal move when bishop and knight alone cannot.

sl-2ed.spoken: The king’s choice of square is decisive. Heading to the obvious spot lets the pawn push with tempo; the other square keeps the king ready to block and join the fight.

sl-2fi.spoken: The king steps to the edge, halting the pawn’s advance while watching the far flank. That single move blocks all progress and turns the pressure back on the opponent.

sl-2ey.spoken: The king's distance from the queenside decides this knight endgame. White's pieces actively attack the pawn and support the passer, so Black's counterplay never gets going.

sl-2fj.spoken: The king's activity decides king-and-pawn endings. Stepping forward to threaten promotion forces a reaction, and that gained time lets the king return to stop the pawns.

sl-2ee.spoken: When the king covers one of the squares on that short diagonal, the enemy bishop runs out of safe squares. If the king stands elsewhere, the defender just shuffles and progress stalls.

sl-2fk.spoken: The king is stuck far from the fight and cannot help stop the pawns. The bishop is trapped, frozen in place to block a breakthrough. With no counterplay at all, the position is practically lost despite the modest engine evaluation.

sl-2em.spoken: Keeping the king cut off is the whole fight. Push the pawn and hold the barrier with the rook, so the king never gets near it.

sl-2gc.spoken: The king must choose between two squares, each with its own risks. One path invites the wrong follow-up; the other holds the line.

sl-2gt.spoken: The king stands too far off to run down the passed pawn, so the breakthrough decides the game.

sl-2gb.spoken: The defender ignores the bishop and slips behind the pawns to hunt the queen. The attacker must refuse any line that trades the rook for the final pawn.

sl-2g4.spoken: In endgames with rooks and minor pieces, the king must defend weaknesses and stay active. When the king is well placed to guard the kingside pawns, it should not wander far.

sl-2gf.spoken: The king belongs in the center of the endgame. From there it pushes pawns forward, boxes in the enemy king, and turns an edge into a win.

sl-2gg.spoken: The king's position decides this endgame. The better-placed king creates threats like a pawn break, while the opponent must guard against infiltration and the loss of pawns.

sl-2fv.spoken: The king flees to the edge to dodge checks, but the attacker just improves position and pushes the pawn. The king is too far away, and the passed pawn cannot be stopped.

sl-2g5.spoken: The king steps in to guard the weak pawn, opens the knight's path, and seals the rank against rook intrusion. That keeps everything solid and avoids the traps.

sl-2g0.spoken: The king steps forward to back the passed pawn, while the rook pressures the pawn in front. That pawn doubles as a shield, blocking enemy rook checks so the break comes through.

sl-2gw.spoken: The rook and knight stand where they belong, so the king must step up to make progress.

sl-2gv.spoken: A king trapped on the back rank is a weakness. The opponent exploits it by checking and driving the king into a worse spot.

sl-2g1.spoken: The king dominates this endgame — no rooks, bishops on opposite colors, knights alongside. Both sides must push their king forward constantly, supporting pawns and blocking the enemy king's path.

sl-2gn.spoken: The king must lead, not linger. Active king play and sound pawn structure decide the outcome, and waiting moves often prove decisive.

sl-2gd.spoken: The king must stand two squares off from the pawn. Any closer, and it will take the pawn instead of letting it promote.

sl-2ge.spoken: The king's activity decides this endgame. Once he penetrates deep, enemy pawns fall and the defense loses coordination.

sl-2fy.spoken: The king wants to support the pawns, but stepping toward them invites rook checks. A direct king move lets the rook snap off a pawn on the far side.

sl-2ft.spoken: The king takes the long way around, not the forcing one. This prophylactic path keeps control of the key squares and keeps the win clear.

sl-2gp.spoken: The pawn structure is symmetric after the queens come off, but the white king stands a step closer to the center, and that edge decides the endgame.

sl-2g7.spoken: The king's activity decides this rook endgame. If the black king reaches the edge, the white king gets boxed in and zugzwang loses the game. White must control those two key squares to stop it.

sl-2fw.spoken: The king steps forward to a safe square, where it also blocks the passed pawn. The knight remains badly placed, and that piece is still a major weakness for Black.

sl-2g6.spoken: The rook and king must hold the rank against a king that wants to invade. Sideslipping along the back rank looks natural, but it lets the enemy king step in and take control.

sl-2gj.spoken: The king must pick the right square to keep the cage shut. One step lets the enemy king slip out through the corner, so the correct move slides over to seal the escape and preserve the net.

sl-2gh.spoken: The king first cuts off the enemy king's escape. One legal move remains, and each one walks into its own ruin.

sl-2g3.spoken: The rook endgame turns on one extra pawn, but it only decides if the attacking king can break through. The defender's king tries to blockade, so first build a barrier that stops him from crossing to halt the pawn.

sl-2gs.spoken: The king's presence alone can block the break, so White must look for other plans. A quiet king move improves its square and keeps every option alive.

sl-2ga.spoken: The king's activity matters more than the bishop's placement. A bishop that keeps the enemy king cut off creates real pressure, while a quieter square lets that king march forward and take charge.

sl-2gq.spoken: The passed pawn decides it. White just takes pawns and marches the king up to support it. Black’s counterplay is too slow — White gets there first.

sl-2fz.spoken: The king marches up the kingside, but must not abandon the pawn behind. The opponent answers with a pawn thrust that blocks the king's path and leaves that pawn weak.

sl-2fs.spoken: The knight circles to the outpost that controls the key square, backing the passed pawn's march. The king steps off the edge—staying cramped there invites a cage, with the enemy king closing in from three sides to lock it in.

sl-2fn.spoken: The bishop sits on a square where it already stops the king's path. Once the king finds a way around, the pawn falls. The fix is to shift the bishop so it still watches every route the king can take to reach the pawn.

sl-2g9.spoken: The rook endgame plan is to march the king forward while the rook makes threats. A rook check along the rank hits the bishop and forces a defensive reply, letting you keep improving your position.

sl-2fr.spoken: The king stepping into the hole left by the missing pawn wakes up the whole side. With the white king cut off from the pawns, that activity buys the draw.

sl-2gi.spoken: The king must reach the square in front of the pawn's advance. Whether it gets there by one route or another, the goal stays the same: lock the enemy king in place so it cannot slip away.

sl-2g8.spoken: The rook endgame turns on king safety. The king hides on the edge to control crucial squares and dodge mate. If the enemy king advances, the rook checks him and opens an escape square.

sl-2gx.spoken: The material is equal, yet the position is winning on activity and a fixed kingside that carries two lasting weaknesses.

sl-2fo.spoken: The king becomes a decisive fighter when only rooks and pawns remain. Once the rook is planted on the seventh rank, the next move is marching the king into the action.

sl-2g2.spoken: The king looks active on that square, but it is worse than it appears — it blocks the rook's escape route, and that lets the attacker keep pushing forward.

sl-2gu.spoken: The king steps up as a fighter in the endgame. Turning an edge into a win demands exact technique — the king and pawns must work together.

sl-2fu.spoken: Push the passed pawn with king support while the rook guards the file. The defender's rook stays glued to blocking, and any attempt to take the pawn opens a decisive check.

sl-2gm.spoken: In a pawn-race, the king defends weakly because a check drives it off, and the piece it guarded falls.

sl-2gk.spoken: The king is boxed in by his own pawns, and the attacking king must pick the exact path to deliver mate. One wrong step lets the enemy king slip out, so the precise route is everything.

sl-2go.spoken: The bishop is taken, the pieces come off, and a pawn endgame appears. White's king stands active and breaks in to take the pawns, while Black's king stays passive.

sl-2fq.spoken: The knight recaptures on the central square, but the king must stand beside it, not behind it. Staying close to that key square keeps the counterplay alive.

sl-2fp.spoken: The pawn is bait, not dinner. Capturing it hands Black a pawn wall that locks the white king out. With the board nearly empty, the king's activity decides the game; if it never gets inside, the win slips away.

sl-2gr.spoken: With the extra f-pawn, the stronger side wins no matter whose move it is, as long as the defender's pawn hasn't already left its starting square. The king walks over, and the f-pawn escorts the h-pawn forward.

sl-2hh.spoken: The king stays central with the passed pawn instead of castling, and pieces settle on squares the enemy bishop cannot reach.

sl-2i3.spoken: After the key check, Black can take with king or queen, and each capture demands a specific reply to hold the draw.

sl-2h3.spoken: The defending king's square decides everything. One step wrong lets the enemy king support the pawn to victory; the right square forces the draw.

sl-2hd.spoken: Both kings should march to the middle of the board. Centralization decides the endgame.

sl-2hm.spoken: The king's choice decides it. From one square, the king forces the queen off her post and the passed pawn promotes. From the other, the rook is overworked and the defense holds for a draw.

sl-2ha.spoken: The pawns are connected and passed, and the bishop keeps them rolling. But the king is far off and stuck on the back rank, and that distance gives the defender real chances to hold.

sl-2hg.spoken: The defender's king can slip into the critical squares and force a draw, because the stronger side has no way to make progress.

sl-2i9.spoken: The passed pawns race against the queenside threats, and every move shifts the evaluation between drawn, winning, and losing. White must calculate precisely to see whose pawns promote first.

sl-2ho.spoken: The king is a piece in the endgame, not a spectator. March it toward the center to back the passed pawn and keep heading for the queenside. Steer clear of awkward squares so the enemy finds no counterplay.

sl-2hn.spoken: The king sits on the far edge, safe from checks and holding the defense together, so White struggles to break through.

sl-2hb.spoken: The king must join the fight at once. Marching it toward the far side supports the rook, forcing the enemy pawn forward — any other reply lets the rook pick off pawns.

sl-2hl.spoken: The king must cross the center before hunting the knight. His activity matters more than the capture; taking now only wakes the enemy king.

sl-2i4.spoken: In a queen endgame, a pawn push and queen infiltration force the opponent to find the only move or lose on the spot.

sl-2hj.spoken: The king steps toward the center to back the weak pawns, while the enemy king is locked out by the pawn chain.

sl-2h7.spoken: The king must be close enough to stop the passed pawns. Chasing the pawn with the king instead of improving his position lets the pawn advance, and the king is suddenly too far away to catch it.

sl-2hc.spoken: The king wriggles toward the corner, but the bishop controls the escape squares and holds him in the pin.

sl-2h5.spoken: The advanced pawn turns from strength to weakness once the enemy king joins the fight. Trade off major pieces, bring the king closer, and the pawn falls.

sl-2gz.spoken: A passed pawn and an active rook can hold the draw, even against an extra pawn and a king that has entered the game. When the king is too far to stop the pawn, the rook handles it alone, and the position stays level.

sl-2hp.spoken: The bishop is frozen in place, defending one key square. The king strolls up to control the critical squares, shoves the enemy bishop onto worse ground, and the win follows.

sl-2i1.spoken: The pawn looks safe to defend, but the quiet move lets the opponent set up a blockade. The win demands exact calculation, not a patient retreat.

sl-2i6.spoken: The material edge is real, but it does not excuse carelessness. That checking pawn push looks tempting because it drives the king, yet it also drops the pawn to the rook and hands White counterplay.

sl-2h8.spoken: The bishop retreats to watch the pawns, while the king steps up to back the center. Black's queenside push is stopped cold.

sl-2hs.spoken: The king steps forward and becomes a fighter. A pawn goes to open lines, and the king walks through to the sixth rank — a classic winning idea in rook endgames.

sl-2h9.spoken: The king is a fighting piece in the endgame — bring it forward. Advancing the king, not grabbing material, supports the passed pawn and confines the defender.

sl-2h2.spoken: The king can't guard two separated pawns at once. Push both, and when the king commits to one, the other advances — the king stays in front and wins.

sl-2hx.spoken: The knight is protected by the king-and-pawn ending it creates. If the king captures it, the opposing king steps across, and the passed pawns are out of reach.

sl-2gy.spoken: The king stands poorly placed, so the rook's activity is choked off. The defender's setup holds like a fortress, and the win nearly slips away.

sl-2i5.spoken: The king must find the one square that keeps both threats alive: stopping the passed g-pawn while supporting the b-pawn. That square alone preserves the draw.

sl-2he.spoken: The king marches over to eat the pawns, but even a winning side must stay precise. The active defense forces a fresh calculation, and only exact play keeps the win.

sl-2h1.spoken: The bishop that must guard a pawn becomes a wall in front of its own king. When it is pinned to that duty, it blocks the escape square, and the opponent's king acts like an extra piece.

sl-2hz.spoken: The king steps in first. Capturing right away lets the knight be deflected and the pawn promote. When the king forces the bishop away, the knight controls the squares that matter, and the pawn marches through.

sl-2hv.spoken: The winning line demanded a forced sequence of only moves, ending in a sacrifice to clear the pawn’s promotion path. Even the best can miss that narrow a win when the clock is tight.

sl-2h4.spoken: The king must pick the one square that both guards the knight’s exit and keeps the passed pawn in check. The safer-looking square lets the pawn run; the correct one does the same job but gains a tempo with check.

sl-2hy.spoken: The defender fights back with tricky moves, but the attacker calculates every line. The killer idea is often a pawn sacrifice for opposition or to pull the king away.

sl-2hq.spoken: The king belongs in the center, active and fighting. From the advanced square it attacks the pawn and eyes the next key point. The passive square leaves the king a bystander, not a participant.

sl-2i7.spoken: The key move frees the position. Play it first, or the pawns lock down and the opponent breaks through. Once it's on the board, their push is met by your own pawn, and the rook covers what remains.

sl-2hr.spoken: The king's centralization and connected passed pawns outweigh material in the endgame. The rook stays active, but the king's position decides.

sl-2i0.spoken: The evaluation hinges on a single tempo, so calculation alone decides it. Count the pawn race and the king's path to the end.

sl-2hu.spoken: The pawn grab is the turning point. White has one move to keep the fight alive, and both sides must calculate every line precisely.

sl-2hw.spoken: The board may be nearly empty, but the endgame is still hard. Fewer pieces do not mean fewer ideas. Go move by move: test every candidate, answer each with the opponent's best reply, and only then choose.

sl-2i2.spoken: The pawn advances to the edge, boxing in the knight. The attacker must check every knight landing square before pushing on to queen.

sl-2hk.spoken: The outside passed pawn looms, but deny all counterplay. A pawn move clears the king a path to the center, and that royal march decides endgames.

sl-2i8.spoken: The c-pawn offers Black counterplay, but White can meet it with rook checks that drive the king back. Still, the line lacks full conviction, so the knight reroutes to a stronger square instead.

sl-2h6.spoken: The king steps to the key square, hitting the bishop and denying the enemy king an escape. The opponent must shed material, and the endgame turns winning.

sl-2ht.spoken: The king is herded to the rim, and a final check drives it to a fatal square, where mate or material loss follows.

sl-2j4.spoken: Calculation is the engine of endgame technique. Great players lose that sharpness with age, not from forgetting the ideas, but from the nervous system losing the ability to sustain focus.

sl-2jg.spoken: Count the moves before you touch a pawn. One wrong capture turns a winning race into a lost one.

sl-2jd.spoken: The pawn push invites a trade, but the rook move was a miscalculation. The right defensive resource is the pawn advance that forces favorable trades.

sl-2jb.spoken: The mating threat still stands even if the defender tries a pawn push. Either capture it or ignore it, then recalculate the forced line and confirm no counterplay rescues them.

sl-2id.spoken: The king's direct march to support the pawn is too slow; the defender's rook wakes up and creates complications. Only the precise tactical sequence forces the win.

sl-2jh.spoken: The endgame forces the issue with few branches, so a strong player can calculate far. For less experience, intuition must fill the gaps.

sl-2ib.spoken: The choice is between capturing the knight into a rook endgame or retreating. The endgame looks lost, but the black king's exposed placement gives White real drawing chances.

sl-2iy.spoken: The key move hides because you check it in some lines, not the critical one. Systematic search guided by the two-weaknesses principle finds it.

sl-2if.spoken: The choice between king and bishop decides everything: one leaves Black with the edge, the other hands it to White. The bishop move unlocks a tactic that gives Black real counterplay.

sl-2jl.spoken: Pushing pawns too soon and leaving the king idle are the classic endgame errors, and they cost games at every level.

sl-2ig.spoken: In complex endgames, one move decides win, draw, or loss. The natural king move loses at once; a careful alternative holds. Calculation alone finds the difference.

sl-2ip.spoken: The king must pick a route to the pawn while watching Black's own pawns. Find the plan that blocks counterplay, then advance.

sl-2io.spoken: The rook lands as a sacrifice, but the opponent cannot take it — a discovered check would drop the queen. The rooks then coordinate, and the king has no escape: checkmate.

sl-2je.spoken: The single extra pawn with little material left does not make the win automatic. The position stays sharp, and only precise calculation keeps the chances real.

sl-2jj.spoken: The evaluation swings wildly with a single move. One candidate loses, another draws, and a third wins — even strong players misjudge this position.

sl-2il.spoken: The pawn push only works if the king can slip through every check. The queen may have to guard a pawn along the way while the king escapes through the center.

sl-2ie.spoken: The rook endgame is rich with chances, but every one must be calculated to the letter. A single inaccuracy gets punished, and even strong players miss the best defense.

sl-2j0.spoken: Calculate the entire line before you strike. The defender may have hidden resources, so finish every variation to the end before committing.

sl-2ij.spoken: The final phase runs on checks, but one key check is missed at first — the one that keeps the opponent from slipping away. Find that check and it wins the queen or ends the game.

sl-2j9.spoken: The rook trades down into a king and pawn endgame, but the result must be calculated exactly. A rook move that rescues the pawn turns that endgame into a win.

sl-2ik.spoken: Both sides have passed pawns, and the race turns tactical. A pawn capture that looks natural can let the opponent promote with check or weave a mating net, so calculation decides the outcome.

sl-2ix.spoken: In a pawn race, weigh every capture and how the opposition falls after it. At times a straight push skips the long line and simply wins.

sl-2im.spoken: Every forcing line must be played out to the end. After the knight moves, the capture forces you to weigh which recapture square your king stands on.

sl-2iu.spoken: The pawn grab into the endgame is a misstep — the rook should shift first. Once the king steps wrong, what was a win slips into a draw.

sl-2ih.spoken: The defender rushes the king over to stop the pawns, but checks push him off course, and each step costs another pawn. The attacker counts every move carefully to turn the edge into a win.

sl-2j2.spoken: Two checks present themselves, but the rook check fizzles once the king sidesteps. The queen check first keeps the pressure on and sets up the rook to join the attack, netting the enemy queen.

sl-2iw.spoken: The hardest part is the calculation: you must weigh every option the defender has, including the non-obvious one of ignoring the recapture and pushing a pawn instead. The verdict on the position rests on those precise lines.

sl-2jf.spoken: The king move first lets the rook escape and the pawn endgame slips away. The transition must be timed, not rushed — play it now, before the rook can answer.

sl-2j7.spoken: The opponent will resist with their best defensive tries, not just sit still. Expect a long, precise solution — this is a study, not a quick tactic.

sl-2ia.spoken: The attack on the flank falls short when the capture resolves into a pawn endgame with the black king ruling the board. The knight must retreat to a passive square, and the black king walks in to take the h-pawn.

sl-2iv.spoken: The bishop looks tempting to stop the pawn, but the pawn simply captures and keeps pushing — not enough. Trapping the rook at the edge also fails, because the pawn promotes with check.

sl-2it.spoken: The king must pick the right square. If Black heads one way, a direct approach draws. If Black heads the other, the obvious moves fail — one lets the pawn through, the other hands Black the opposition.

sl-2ji.spoken: Pawns decide the endgame long before promotion. General principles guide the play: hold the enemy pawns back, simplify to one pawn against the queen, and press a two-on-one advantage to pick the queening file. These patterns shrink the calculation.

sl-2iq.spoken: The bishop steps to the center to provoke a pawn advance. Then it checks, forcing the king out, and the captured pawn falls. The line works only if the knight's counterplay is calculated first.

sl-2is.spoken: The king must be coaxed, not challenged. Advancing the pawn a single step first forces the opponent's king into the fatal square, where it blocks its own path and hands you the stalemate. Delaying the advance is the only precise move.

sl-2ic.spoken: In a pawn race, exact calculation decides. Weigh the defender’s best resources and map the winning plan to the end.

sl-2jc.spoken: The pawn push looks natural but only draws — the defender hides a resource. The king must take a quiet path to make progress.

sl-2j1.spoken: Calculate only until a position you know is won or drawn. Stop there.

sl-2jk.spoken: In a king and pawn endgame, the exact sequence decides everything. Step the king forward first, then capture with the pawn, and the opposition guarantees the winning race.

sl-2j6.spoken: The pawn taking the rook might hand the opponent a draw: they sacrifice their rook back, grab the pawn, and the game slips away.

sl-2j8.spoken: A concrete plan beats random pawn pushes. Force the king toward a bad square, then close the net or use the stalemate resource.

sl-2ii.spoken: The rook check looks tempting — it guards the pawn and eyes the kingside — but the defender’s f-pawn advance breaks the net, and the draw holds. The real question is whether that counterplay arrives in time.

sl-2iz.spoken: The king cannot march to the mating square, for the defender's own queen meets it and the endgame turns against the attacker. The rook must come down and the king step back to hold the draw.

sl-2ir.spoken: Passed pawns make rook endgames razor-thin. A single miscalculation flips a win into a loss.

sl-2j5.spoken: Every move must be checked before choosing. Several lines hold the draw, but only one keeps the win.

sl-2ja.spoken: Push the pawn only after calculating, not on reflex. Playing early can toss the win, because the king walks over, forces the trade, and the endgame turns drawn.

sl-2jy.spoken: The knight seals the escape squares around the cornered king. A quiet bishop move then leaves the king no choice but to drift toward the target corner.

sl-2k3.spoken: The rook belongs one file over, beside its king, ready to answer checks. That spot keeps the bishop protected while the rook slides across to a new file.

sl-2kd.spoken: The king needs a safe square, but pushing it to the center is risky while the edge holds a tiny but persistent edge.

sl-2k8.spoken: The knight must stay near the king. If it wanders, it becomes a target. The rook slides in behind the lines to keep the cut and push the knight to worse squares.

sl-2ke.spoken: The king sits exposed and a pawn is weak. Solidify first, bringing the bishop to defend that point, before any other plan goes forward.

sl-2ka.spoken: The bishop steps in to defend the pawn, and that frees the rook to leave its passive post and target the opponent's weak pawns.

sl-2ku.spoken: Dynamic pieces can outweigh a three-pawn deficit. Even with material hanging, the exposed kings keep the balance equal.

sl-2ko.spoken: The king has lost its pawn shield, so the pieces must serve as bodyguards. With the queen harassing and the king exposed, consolidation comes first.

sl-2jp.spoken: The endgame runs long and both sides err under the clock. The defender had winning chances but lets them slip, and the result is a draw.

sl-2ju.spoken: Time pressure hides resources from both sides. The opponent missed a drawing defense, and the winning side missed a tactical reply in the same scramble.

sl-2jo.spoken: Even grandmasters can misjudge a winning position under time pressure — a position that looks clearly winning can actually be a draw.

sl-2ks.spoken: The queen step forfeits castling and strands the king mid-board. With the rook already on the open file, White gains attacking chances.

sl-2kb.spoken: The king sits safely while the loose pawn falls, yet the fight stays unclear — the enemy pawn stands better protected.

sl-2kn.spoken: When the king has no pawn shelter, his own pieces must stand guard — and that duty pins them down.

sl-2jw.spoken: The knight is a fortress on that square, controlling key points and fueling the attack. Rook and knight work together to force the defender into constant reaction.

sl-2kj.spoken: Black offers a return of material, but it changes nothing. The white king stays exposed, and Black’s active pieces and strong pawns keep the attack alive.

sl-2kq.spoken: The king is wide open, and every white piece is aimed at the squares around him. That exposure is the real advantage, and it outweighs the deficit in material.

sl-2kh.spoken: The king shuffles sideways to step out of the line, or the side gives back material — both trade a little to cancel the mate threat and keep the position playable.

sl-2k7.spoken: The king flees toward the corner, so the knight closes off the escape squares while the bishop shuts down the diagonals. Together they box the king in and force it toward the edge.

sl-2kx.spoken: The bishop and pawn clamp the enemy king in permanent danger. Every black piece is pinned to duty, fending off captures and the pawn’s march forward.

sl-2jz.spoken: The king tries to flee the corner, but the bishop and knight lock the escape hatch. The bishop owns the light squares, the knight owns the dark ones, and together they hold every exit.

sl-2kv.spoken: The exchange sacrifice forces the recapture, and the queen reclaims the minor piece. A tempting square for the bishop invites a queen-and-knight attack that creates weaknesses and leads to a fast collapse.

sl-2kl.spoken: The rook becomes a weakness when it creates a target for a pawn push that exposes the king. The pawn's only defender is the rook itself, and that defender gets attacked again, so the position slides downhill.

sl-2kf.spoken: The king steps off the back rank and lends support to the weak pawn, a typical improving move. But it gains little and may walk into checks later.

sl-2k9.spoken: The bishop and knight drive the king out of the wrong corner by sealing off its escape squares, forcing him back toward the mate.

sl-2k4.spoken: The rook and bishop work as a pair, each move keeping them in touch so the threats stay alive. The king is pushed back, and the coordination decides the endgame.

sl-2ki.spoken: The center pawns open lines and leave the white king exposed, while the black king stays safe. That safety lets black attack the king side and grab pawns on the queenside, and a safer king outweighs any passed pawns white can make.

sl-2kw.spoken: The king needs a bolt-hole before the pawn push lands. Securing the escape square first lets the king flee the checks, and only then does the attack on the pawn go through.

sl-2kg.spoken: When the opponent throws that pawn forward to rip the position open, taking it invites trouble with the f-pawn and the knight landing on a strong square. Instead, the king steps quietly to the corner, sidestepping the storm before it breaks.

sl-2kk.spoken: The move with no flashy follow-up may still be the stronger one if it plants long-term weaknesses. Here, the bishop exposes the king on its new square, a permanent wound to be exploited later.

sl-2jt.spoken: The rook slides onto a rank, eyeing the pawn through the enemy line. Many sound replies exist, yet the sheer range of options weighs on the defender, especially when the clock is short.

sl-2jx.spoken: The king steps out first, trading time for activity. Only once the king is placed does the bishop slide to its diagonal, freeing the rook to seize the open file with decisive force.

sl-2kc.spoken: The queen attacks two pawns at once, and the bishop joins in with a direct threat on one of them. White has exactly one reply: the knight jumps in to block the bishop’s diagonal and covers both squares under fire.

sl-2jv.spoken: The extra pawn is no fluke—it comes from real pressure. After the first capture, the follow-up grabs a second, often with a check in between. The defender crumbles under the clock, and the extra material decides.

sl-2k0.spoken: Coordination wins these endgames. A knight on a strong square dominates, and the rook supports it to build threats.

sl-2jr.spoken: The h-pawn marches, then the bishop slides in front of the enemy king to cut off its escape and the win follows.

sl-2jq.spoken: The bishop endgame is drawn on the board, but the clock makes it hard. Low on time, White must find the exact defensive moves to hold.

sl-2k2.spoken: A queen and rook cluster around the bare king and the net tightens. The rook slides in to finish, and the defense has no piece to answer.

sl-2jn.spoken: Time pressure and a complex position hid the defender's chances to grab pawns or force a draw. The attacker still had to find exact moves to keep the win.

sl-2kt.spoken: The king sidesteps to dodge the pin, but a natural developing move is better. The discovered check hangs the bishop, and Black wins a piece. Both kings sit exposed, Black up three pawns, yet the position stays equal.

sl-2kp.spoken: Control the king’s escape squares, not just the piece in front of it. Taking with check looks tempting, but it opens a flight path and drags the game out.

sl-2kr.spoken: The queen is boxed in by her own pieces. One escape square is guarded by a pawn, so a sacrifice removes that pawn. When the king recaptures, the knight jumps in anyway, pulls the king into the open, and the mate follows.

sl-2k6.spoken: The bishop and knight weave a net around the fleeing king, cutting off escape squares. The attacking king must climb the board to join them before the trap closes.

sl-2k1.spoken: Rook and knight combine to threaten, yet the defender's rook often cuts the king off or harasses the knight. Piece placement decides everything.

sl-2km.spoken: Choosing the king move over the pawn move keeps the kingside solid and keeps every defensive option ready for what comes next.

sl-2jm.spoken: Choose the central check first. It keeps the king pinned near the middle, where both flanks stay in reach.

sl-2k5.spoken: Knight and passed pawn defend each other: the knight guards the pawn, while the promotion threat keeps the enemy king away from the knight. This mutual protection makes it tough to win either piece.

sl-2kz.spoken: Castling into the attack hands the king to waiting pieces. The defender's natural move becomes fatal because the attacker's forces are already coordinated against the exposed king.

sl-2lx.spoken: The king sits exposed in the center, the pawns are broken, the bishop is trapped, and the rook is idle. That shape alone shows the defense is already compromised.

sl-2ky.spoken: A weak king is its own deficit. Even a defender up the exchange can fall when the king has no shelter, and that weakness alone turns into a decisive attack.

sl-2la.spoken: The king has few legal squares and the enemy controls the exits, so danger is real even before the checkmate lands.

sl-2l8.spoken: The king-safety swing matters more than material or structure. With the dark-squared bishop gone, the queen slips in close and the king has no cover.

sl-2l2.spoken: The position is sharp, and the natural king move is tempting but probably not best. The defense is logical, and whether it holds is unclear.

sl-2l3.spoken: The long castle leaves the king exposed to a kingside assault, and while a closed position forgives errors, it does not cancel the danger.

sl-2li.spoken: The castled king is thin on defenders, so the attack must land before reinforcements arrive.

sl-2lw.spoken: The king is exposed with queens still on, but trading them leads to an endgame Black prefers. The pawn structure and piece activity leave the position compromised.

sl-2m0.spoken: The king is exposed, so checks and threats push it deeper into the open. That chase wins material or ends in checkmate.

sl-2lk.spoken: Pushing the g-pawn is tempting but unjustified: it cracks open the king's shelter and the g-file, yet the rook arrives too late to exploit it. The king weakens with no concrete payoff.

sl-2lz.spoken: The king is safe, but the opponent's is exposed to open lines. The cost was the exchange, so this attack cannot fizzle out — it must finish the game.

sl-2l5.spoken: The king pawn push is a maximalist choice: it weakens the kingside but opens squares for friendly pieces. The opponent tries to punish with knight or bishop sorties, but White accepts the risk because the initiative outweighs the damage.

sl-2lj.spoken: The pawn push creates weaknesses around the king and opens holes for the opponent to exploit. Better to improve the queen's placement and then use a pawn break to open lines.

sl-2le.spoken: A piece sacrifice cracks the king's shelter, and the exposed king cannot find safety. The defender's army sits frozen on the back rank while the attacker's pieces dominate the board, turning a material lead into a strategic nightmare.

sl-2l1.spoken: The king's long march burns the attacker's initiative — once the king finds safety, the threats lose their sting, and the attack dies on closed lines.

sl-2m2.spoken: The pawn thrust weakens the king’s shelter, and even a well-placed knight cannot hold the position once the attack breaks through.

sl-2l0.spoken: The king step is a wasted tempo, but it sets up the bishop’s retreat to defend the attack. If the bishop sat elsewhere instead, a sacrifice would open the line for the queen to finish the game.

sl-2lo.spoken: The king stands exposed with no pawn shield after that push, and with pieces already aimed at it, the attack gains real force.

sl-2lm.spoken: The king is exposed to checks, so the first job is to find shelter. A pawn advance creates a safe square, letting the king breathe and the position improve.

sl-2m7.spoken: The king steps to a light square, keeping the dark-square bishop from checking. A check there would be deadly while the knight still hangs.

sl-2lg.spoken: The king hides safely behind the pawns, and the bishops keep their pressure down the open file. When the opponent tries to chase the knight, the bishops simply prove too strong.

sl-2ls.spoken: The king on one side hides in safety while the other stands exposed. The pawns race toward promotion, and every defender is nailed to its post.

sl-2lu.spoken: The king's castling is restricted to one side only. That single legal option narrows his choices severely and leaves the position hard for him to handle.

sl-2l6.spoken: Pushing the pawn in front of the king weakens the castled position and creates lasting holes. That move invites a direct attack the defender cannot easily meet.

sl-2ln.spoken: The queen check forces the king into a response, and the defender’s exposed king can’t afford to hand the attacker a tempo. If the reply is careless, the active queen turns that tempo into material or a mating attack.

sl-2lq.spoken: The king stuck in the center faces a castled rival whose army opens the middle. With pawns gone and pieces pressing, the attack breaks through when the defender’s pieces sit passive, parked on the back rank after chasing with the queen.

sl-2ly.spoken: The queen sidesteps the rook and escapes the bishop's line, readying active play. White's bishop pair already points at the king, and with no knight on the kingside to help, the black bishop stays locked in.

sl-2m4.spoken: The king is trapped in the center while the queen up side is frozen. The opponent's threats—pawn pushes and a bishop on the long diagonal—set up discovered checks and mating nets.

sl-2l7.spoken: The queen steps to a square where the enemy queen captures a crucial pawn, doubling the pawns and stripping the king's shelter. That pawn was the king's shield, and losing it costs real safety.

sl-2ll.spoken: The rook pressures a pawn, and a knight lurks nearby. Pushing the pawn to defend only cracks the king's shield. Instead, a piece steps in to block the rook's line and harass the knight at the same time.

sl-2m9.spoken: The rook owns the open file, and the bishop hovers behind it. The pawn push was a mistake—it lets the opponent grab it and feed the bishop. With the king tucked in the corner, that diagonal bears down on it.

sl-2m5.spoken: The king sits in the center as the enemy prepares pawn breaks that open lines against him. He must carve out an escape square before the mating net closes.

sl-2ld.spoken: The king belongs where the attack cannot reach. With the queenside hard to open, center and queenside offer safety, while the kingside is under fire and exposed.

sl-2lh.spoken: The king sits exposed, few pawns left to shield him, and every attacker hovers close. Trading queens or forking fails because either move only opens the king wider.

sl-2m6.spoken: The queen overextends herself, and the pin turns toxic. With the king exposed along the back rank and diagonals, an undefended queen lets the bishop deliver mate on the spot.

sl-2m8.spoken: The king's pawns have all advanced, leaving no shelter. Your own king sits safely tucked in after a single pawn push, so the attacker has nothing to strike back with.

sl-2lr.spoken: The king sits exposed behind the weakened pawn, and the active bishop supplies compensation for the missing piece. The defensive try is to pull the queen back for cover, but the rook slides across to join the attack and it is over.

sl-2lf.spoken: The pawn break stays on the board as a constant threat, so Black must stay vigilant. After the push, the king steps in to defend the pawn and back up the knight's recapture, while the rook bears down on the c-pawn from the side.

sl-2m1.spoken: The king looks exposed but is safe; the real threat falls on the other king, whose pieces are under pressure. A prophylactic bishop move stops the knight from reaching its outpost and holds the balance.

sl-2lv.spoken: Capturing on that square begins the sequence, forcing a favorable exchange while the exposed king and the loose pawn stay under pressure.

sl-2l9.spoken: The pawn push weakens the dark squares in front of the king. With extra material, the priority is king safety, not hunting pieces.

sl-2l4.spoken: The queen settles on the long diagonal and dominates the board, pressing against the opponent. Pushing the flank pawns opens lines and only speeds the attack.

sl-2lp.spoken: The queen is attacked while the king still sits in the center, and her escape squares shrink because she must also shield the king. Every move leaves something exposed, and the king's openness turns the position critical.

sl-2lc.spoken: The knight trade would hit the g-pawn too. A pawn push denies the exchange, and the king can walk to the other side since the rook already stands ready and the king stays safe.

sl-2na.spoken: The king is unsafe on those light squares, and with opposite-colored bishops, there is no defender to cover them. That leaves the king exposed to checks and mating threats.

sl-2mw.spoken: The king's safety doesn't require a full three-pawn shield. Any pawns standing in front of him can serve as protection.

sl-2nb.spoken: Material lead means nothing if the king falls. The opponent may pry open lines against it, so defend first while still pushing your own ideas.

sl-2mx.spoken: A check that feels natural can be a favor. When the enemy king sits awkwardly, forcing it to move may grant it the exact square it wants. Skip the check, and the king stays trapped.

sl-2n2.spoken: The bishop sits behind the pawn chain instead of guarding the king. That leaves the file open, and once the center opens, the rook points straight at the king with no shield.

sl-2ni.spoken: The exposed king is chased by checks into a worse square. Each step the defender takes must avoid the mating net closing around it.

sl-2mm.spoken: The king steps to a safer square, sheltered by pawns, while the enemy queen sits far off. That single move develops and defends at once.

sl-2mq.spoken: The pawn move cracks open the king's shelter. The light squares soften, the king sits exposed, and the pawn itself turns into a permanent target.

sl-2mh.spoken: The extra pawns mean little when the king sits in the center and development lags. Active pieces and a safer king give the edge.

sl-2ne.spoken: The king's shelter is gone, and even a defensive move does not repair it. When the bishop steps out to guard, the king stays exposed, and the game is beyond saving.

sl-2ma.spoken: The pawns before the king are shields. Voluntarily moving them exposes the king. When the bishop comes under attack, a pin neutralizes the threat without retreating.

sl-2mb.spoken: The center opens after the pawn capture, and the opponent's pawn push exposes the king's vulnerability. With the king still in the center, the advancing pawns create immediate threats.

sl-2ms.spoken: The rook is a healthy advantage, but the exposed king turns it into a liability. One careless move can hand White mate or the return of the material.

sl-2mz.spoken: The king must step to safety before the enemy check lands. Tucking into the corner behind the pawn removes any perpetual check danger.

sl-2me.spoken: The pawn march chases the knight away, and when the king steps forward, the queen slides in with threats — hitting the bishop or stirring tactics against the king.

sl-2mt.spoken: In a sharp position, king safety comes first. Stepping the king to a quieter square may look passive, but it dodges tactical tricks and readies the defense.

sl-2nc.spoken: The rook checks, and the king must choose. The corner offers shelter but few exits, inviting a mating net. Staying central keeps escape squares open, even at the cost of further checks.

sl-2n3.spoken: The knight is pinned and attacked, so keep piling on pressure rather than capturing. If the defender tries to escape the pin, castle to safety and keep the attack rolling.

sl-2n4.spoken: The king must pick the right escape square. One wrong step lets the queen and knight close in for mate. Find the safe square, then march the king up the board and bring him home again.

sl-2n5.spoken: The pawn thrust drives the bishop back, but it costs a pawn and tears open the king's shelter. The bishop retreats, and the opponent's position cracks.

sl-2mu.spoken: Pawn storms on the flank with the king still in the center carry real risk. Solid central play lets Black open the position, and the uncastled king becomes a target.

sl-2mj.spoken: The king still sits in the center, and White strikes before castling gets done. Black grabs another pawn, but White keeps the initiative, chasing king safety and piece activity.

sl-2mv.spoken: The king is exposed, black has a knight and two pawns for the rook, and piece activity is overwhelming. Black's pieces nearly own the board while the king stays vulnerable.

sl-2ng.spoken: The rook slides in and both bishop and queen train on the same square, but the queen still guards it. The rook then hits the queen, driving her back, and the bishop falls back too.

sl-2nf.spoken: Opening the position is risky — it exposes the weak king. Hidden tactics lurk beneath a calm surface, and the queen move is only one of several ideas, not the best.

sl-2mg.spoken: A rook on the king's file threatens a pin. The queen steps off the file to dodge it and hits a pawn at the same time. The king then has to move onto a file where enemy major pieces stand, and that exposure costs.

sl-2nk.spoken: The pawn storm tempts, but the queen rakes the g-file target. Before pushing, the king steps to the corner—the precaution that keeps the attack alive.

sl-2n6.spoken: The pawn and bishop both train on the same square, shielding the knight from capture. Forced to step the king away, choosing the far corner keeps the rook from being boxed in.

sl-2n8.spoken: The queen steps out early to press the bishop and knight. When the knight is captured with check, the recapture wins a pawn, but the king stays in the center — a serious liability.

sl-2ml.spoken: The king is exposed after the sacrifice, and survival comes first. Defensive moves may look natural, but they lead to terrifying positions. The practical choice is to return material to reach safety, then hold on with the extra piece.

sl-2mf.spoken: The knight retreats to the center, keeping the position razor-sharp. The rook cannot cross to that square, because the bishop covers it from the diagonal. The real worry is the white king's safety, not the pawn. Later, that knight targets the central pawn.

sl-2nj.spoken: A tiny pawn push can decide a whole tactic. Giving the king an escape square turns a back-rank mate into nothing, so even one quiet move can change whether a sequence works.

sl-2mp.spoken: The king sits exposed after the queen steps out with check, yet that queen dominates the center, controls key squares, and ties down enemy pieces. Black's knights are well placed, and one wants to leap forward to threaten a fork that strikes the king.

sl-2mc.spoken: The king marooned in the center is no weakness when the center is strong and the bishops rake the board. With the enemy queen stranded offside, the attack builds at leisure—castling is a luxury, not a need.

sl-2mk.spoken: The king is forced to a worse square because the other escape allows capture. Once the pawn chain is fixed in place, a critical choice appears between pushing and playing around it.

sl-2mr.spoken: The queen gives check, and every king move walks into a new trap — one square lets the queen in for mate, another invites a decisive blow. The safe square is the one where the king can shelter behind its own queen and dodge the checks.

sl-2nl.spoken: The king sidesteps instead of defending, and the queen checks, forcing the king further out. A capture then wins the knight. With the king exposed in the center, a pawn push opens lines and brings pieces out with tempo, keeping him under fire.

sl-2nd.spoken: Castling removes the immediate check danger that made the advance risky, so the king’s safety turns a dangerous move into a reasonable one.

sl-2n1.spoken: Castling first puts the king to safety and connects the rooks, leaving the position sound. Watch for tactical tricks like a pawn push, but the real danger is a pin that costs the queen.

sl-2mi.spoken: Three extra pawns, yet the king sits in the center — a fatal flaw. With active coordination, those pieces turn the exposed king into attack chances that outweigh the material edge.

sl-2mo.spoken: The pawn break exposes the king to diagonal checks. Capturing on that square and checking forces the king into the corner, where the queen dominates and the knight prepares a decisive leap.

sl-2mn.spoken: The center opens, Black's pieces wake up, and White's king still sits in the middle. White picks between moving the king to safety or using it actively — stepping it forward sets up artificial castling, while the queen stepping out is another option.

sl-2n7.spoken: The knight on the great square dominates. Castling kingside looks safer since that bishop doesn't bear down on the king, but the pawn storm can still rip the position open. Queenside castling guards the b-pawn, though that alone may not justify it.

sl-2md.spoken: The bishop pair and space advantage set a simple plan: push the h-pawn, castle long, storm the kingside. Black's king has no safe home—center stays dangerous, queenside is exposed, and the kingside faces the pawn wave.

sl-2n9.spoken: The king steps up before the attack, and the pawn goes to the second file to keep the bishop's diagonal clear. When the defender moves a bishop off a key square, the rook drops to the seventh rank and breaks through.

sl-2nr.spoken: The king never got to safety, and the checks keep coming. With the initiative, you keep creating threats and force him to stay in the center.

sl-2no.spoken: The king is exposed and under a rain of checks. Every escape square is covered because the attacking pieces work together to hold the net closed.

sl-2ns.spoken: White is castled and the king still sits in the center. Crack open the middle with pawn breaks to turn that exposed king into attacking chances.

sl-2nn.spoken: The king is exposed, so advancing looks reckless—yet up the board can be safer than back. Pushing forward dodges the mating net that retreat walks into.

sl-2nm.spoken: The exposed king in the center is the target. Black trades pieces willingly to keep it there, blocking both castling and retreat. The king's danger outweighs any material cost.

sl-2oi.spoken: The king steps to safety before the tactic begins—a prophylactic move that removes back-rank threats and sets up the pawn grab.

sl-2od.spoken: Black's king sits exposed in the center, so White's material deficit buys real compensation. The count means less than the king's danger.

sl-2o4.spoken: A queen is strong, yet among many pieces it can fall to checks and forks. Moving the king elsewhere keeps it safe and sidesteps stalemate traps.

sl-2o5.spoken: The king sits exposed, and the attacking pieces coordinate for a decisive finish. Chasing pointless checks only lets the target off the hook.

sl-2np.spoken: The king's walk to the center is not a choice—the opponent's shocking castle forces the capture of the queen, stranding the king in the open. In hindsight, a quieter king move holds, but the surprise makes the best defense hard to find.

sl-2op.spoken: The queen steps to safety and opens a flight square for the king, dodging the knight's immediate check. That is prophylaxis in action—king safety before everything.

sl-2o6.spoken: The queen stands awkwardly, inviting a knight fork. The plan: castle long, bring the rook to the open file against her, and strike in the center toward the enemy king.

sl-2oe.spoken: The king stands alone, stripped of defenders, while White’s forces converge from every side. Even the rook that seems close to the king is not actually guarding it.

sl-2om.spoken: The knight is the king's only shield. Once it is pulled away or traded off, the king's shelter crumbles and the attack breaks through.

sl-2nu.spoken: The safer king makes the queening race unequal. When both sides push pawns, the exposed one pays the price.

sl-2or.spoken: The king stays in the center while pawns advance on the flank, and castling waits until much later. It works because the opponent has no counterplay to punish the delay.

sl-2ot.spoken: The queen and knight sit far from the action, exposing the king. Meanwhile, the opponent's king stays sheltered behind a bishop. With queens and rooks on the board, that imbalance decides the game.

sl-2ov.spoken: Keep the king trapped in the center and the pieces undeveloped. Hold the pressure and never let them castle.

sl-2oh.spoken: The king has only one safe square from the queen check, since every other escape lets the bishop give check. Trading queens is worse, because the opponent has two attackers on that piece and you would lose material.

sl-2nz.spoken: The pawn push exposes the white king. After the capture, the reply opens the b-file and leaves the king with no refuge: kingside is sealed by advancing pawns, queenside is impossible, and the center is unsafe.

sl-2o2.spoken: The king is exposed, so safety comes first. Consolidate the king before grabbing pawns, or the greed hands the opponent counterplay.

sl-2ob.spoken: The knight reroutes to a stronger post, and the bishop slides out with an eye on the long diagonal. King safety comes first—castle even if it means a fork that drops a pawn.

sl-2nw.spoken: The king sits exposed with enemy threats in the air — checks and captures that can end in mate. A random move hands over the time those threats need.

sl-2o8.spoken: The king steps to the corner for safety, but without the light-squared bishop the shelter leaks. Enemy pieces target those light squares, and the king's refuge becomes a weakness.

sl-2o1.spoken: The bishop grabbing that edge pawn is greed, and it throws the advantage away. King safety comes first, and with the white king exposed, black gains counterplay against it.

sl-2of.spoken: The king still sits in the center, but the attack can begin anyway. When the opponent's pieces sit passive and yours stand active, the king is safe there as long as the strike lands fast.

sl-2o7.spoken: The pawn falls, but it opens the files beside the king. Now Black owns long-term attacking chances against that king, even while it sits in the center.

sl-2nv.spoken: Keep the king safe and the army coordinated. Walking the king forward holds every defense, while a bishop move here, though not losing, leaves the kingside loose and invites discomfort.

sl-2nx.spoken: The bishop move looks natural but invites the pawn push that opens the rook's line. Once the king steps over, the rook joins the attack, and the pinned bishop leaves the enemy king trapped in the center with no good move.

sl-2o9.spoken: The king shuffles toward the corner, seeking safety, but each step forfeits castling and exposes a shortage of useful moves. As your pieces regroup, your mobility grows, and once the position shifts, central pawn breaks become worth exploring.

sl-2oq.spoken: The king's safety decides everything here. A pawn push to open luft or chase a piece looks natural, but it opens the door to concrete tactics that lose material on the spot.

sl-2ny.spoken: The king shelters behind a solid pawn shield, while the opponent's king sits exposed. A pawn up, you press with active pieces against a fragile defense, and the opponent has no counterplay.

sl-2os.spoken: The queen sits off to the flank, the king stands exposed, and threats hit both rook and king at once. Black's defenses stay tricky, but they fail unless found with perfect accuracy.

sl-2on.spoken: The knight is the white king's shield here — it alone guards the critical square. Both kings are exposed, but black's is weaker because the white knight still holds the defense together. That shield may not last forever.

sl-2oo.spoken: Pushing the g-pawn opens the door to the king. Once the enemy king tucks away and the f-pawn advances, the attack gathers real force. A weak central square means little when the center is sealed and the real fight is on the kingside.

sl-2og.spoken: The defender's king looks safer on the corner square, but that's exactly where the file can open against it. The king sits there comfortably while the attacker, with equal material, brings the rook straight down that file—and the "safe" spot becomes the trap.

sl-2ok.spoken: Advancing the pawn in front of the king invites danger. It weakens the squares around the king and lets the opponent target the defender of a critical square.

sl-2oc.spoken: The pawn is bait. Rescuing it while the king still sits exposed trades safety for material, when the real priority is casting and finishing development.

sl-2nq.spoken: The king stays in the center and every plan feels tight. Pushing a central pawn opens lines while the king sits exposed, and the opponent pounces on the missing castle.

sl-2o3.spoken: When Black tries to shield the king with a pawn move, the bishop takes that pawn directly. If Black recaptures, White takes back, and the king stays exposed. That shows the defense does not hold.

sl-2nt.spoken: The king has castled, yet open lines and pawn weaknesses still leave him exposed. White coordinates threats on the king, and any try to cling to the extra material walks into a mate.

sl-2oa.spoken: The queen checks, and the king steps to the corner — not to dodge, but to prepare the rook lift.

sl-2ou.spoken: The king has no safe corner: pawn weaknesses and threats like the h-pawn march make castling queenside a trap and leave the f-pawn hanging. Their position is already lost.

sl-2oj.spoken: The pawn grab gains material, but the king pays the price. The enemy bishop checks and develops with tempo, opening lines straight at the king.

sl-2ol.spoken: The king steps to guard the weakened pawns, and the bishop on the open diagonal becomes a monster, controlling the key squares. The other bishop, though boxed behind its own pawn, keeps latent pressure alive.

sl-2o0.spoken: The knight jump is a trap. Taking that pawn uncovers the bishop against the king, and the rook behind it wins the queen. Castling long invites the pawn storm and a wild game where White gambles.

sl-2ox.spoken: The bishop locks the king in place. Bring the queen and knight up to the same wing, and push the f-pawn as a break. Any pawn attack gets defended simply, and when the exchange happens, the opponent castles believing all is safe.

sl-2pg.spoken: Pawn storms toward your knight expose the king they were meant to shield. Each advance creates weaknesses worth exploiting.

sl-2p8.spoken: Pushing the pawn opens the g-file and puts both kings on the same line. The calm game turns sharp, and king safety becomes the deciding factor.

sl-2pi.spoken: The fork forces a choice between two squares. One square lets the queen slip behind and deliver mate, so the other is the only safe retreat.
