sl-6j2.spoken: A pin to the king makes the pinned piece unable to move legally. Hitting the pinner with pawns and pieces forces the defender to give ground, and the pressure becomes decisive.

sl-6j7.spoken: The bishop is pinned and attacked twice, yet the king and pawn defend it twice. The pawn cannot recapture, because it is pinned, so the bishop remains under siege.

sl-6ip.spoken: The queen sits pinned on the king's diagonal. Attacking her directly fails since she can capture, but she cannot step off the line without exposing the king.

sl-6ji.spoken: The knight is pinned and outnumbered three to two. Every black piece is tied down — the knight shields the pawn, the queen guards the knight, the rook stays frozen — so Black runs out of useful moves.

sl-6ia.spoken: The bishop pins the knight and hits the bishop behind it. That one move pressures the kingside and threatens a trade that wins material when the pawn recaptures. Simple to play, but it builds a dangerous attacking structure.

sl-6o7.spoken: Back-rank checkmate makes even a queen-for-rook trade worthwhile — delivering mate is worth any price.

sl-6o5.spoken: Back rank mates never go away—they just get buried deeper. The same motifs, from double attacks to pins to back rank mates, show up at every level, only wrapped in more layers.

sl-6ov.spoken: Black's quiet bishop move lets White's queen step out and complicate things. The follow-up knight move walks into rook and queen pressure, and Black trades down to an endgame a pawn up but with a weak pawn to defend.

sl-6pu.spoken: The knight travels to the central outpost to double the pressure and wake up the dormant pieces.

sl-6px.spoken: The knight reroutes to a strong outpost, but the bishop slides in to block its path and challenge the plan.

sl-6p4.spoken: The bishop and queen load up on the weakest square, forcing the king into a mating net.

sl-6q3.spoken: The knight lands on the target square and forks king and rook, forcing the king back to defend, and the pawn is lost.

sl-6pm.spoken: The knight sits deep in White's camp, immune to pawn kicks because White's own pawns are loose. White wastes tempi shuffling the knight back while Black develops the bishop and grabs space.

sl-6pb.spoken: The target is a knight-file square that no piece currently attacks. Double the rooks, open that file, and the weak pawn falls.

sl-6pz.spoken: A knight that lands in the center creates threats, often forking the king and queen. When the opponent misses the immediate danger, the fork lands and decides the game.

sl-6pl.spoken: The knight leaps to the central outpost, hitting the queen and creating threats too dangerous to ignore—the opponent must spend a move responding.

sl-6p0.spoken: The doubled pawn is the target, but the queen cannot reach it yet. Preparing the queen's path turns the weakness into a real threat.

sl-6pn.spoken: A knight planted on the central outpost dominates the structure. It backs every pawn break in the middle and hammers every weak square around it.

sl-6po.spoken: The knight lands on a square defended twice, so capturing it loses nothing and gains nothing. That move only works when the target is undefended or guarded once.

sl-6p7.spoken: The knight that just lost its defender, and the hole beside the king — both are permanent. Apply piece pressure and the weaknesses do the rest.

sl-6q1.spoken: The knight sits strongly on its outpost, backed by its partner and covering key central squares. The opponent's pawn push is inaccurate and hands White a small edge.

sl-6q7.spoken: The knight leaps deep into enemy territory and makes threats, but it can get stranded without support. Harass it with pawns and pieces until it is trapped.

sl-6p9.spoken: The pawn thrust threatens to capture and strip away a key defender, opening the door for a follow-up strike on the same square that can end in check.

sl-6pv.spoken: The knight leaps into the center to block the bishop's line and seize squares the enemy knight used to guard. That shift redirects the fight toward dark-square control.

sl-6q8.spoken: The knight leap to a strong outpost tempts Black, but pushing the pawn beside it invites a pawn reply that leaves lasting holes.

sl-6oy.spoken: The pawn advance leaves a permanent hole behind it. Don't rush into the outpost—first improve your pieces, developing the bishop to pressure that pawn and contesting the rooks, and only then take the square.

sl-6q4.spoken: The knight leaps forward, attacking the queen and eyeing the escape squares. The queen is boxed in, with no safe flight, and the threat wins decisive material.

sl-6pj.spoken: The knight sits on its outpost, supporting two different jumps that each create a fresh threat. Black's position turns shaky, and White's attack builds into something decisive.

sl-6pr.spoken: A knight planted on that square becomes a battering ram, hitting key points and feeding the attack. When the opponent's pieces sit badly and yours swarm the board, that knight makes the attack real.

sl-6q0.spoken: Black's rook prepares a knight outpost that would threaten the position. The bishop retreats to hold the key square, and the queen's withdrawal confirms the plan works.

sl-6pp.spoken: A knight leap to the center dares the opponent to capture it, but taking often costs a tempo. The move also baits careless play, and if the opponent bites, the initiative flips.

sl-6pk.spoken: The knight jumps in to attack the bishop, and the follow-up jump aims to harass it again. The opponent's pawn push stops that plan but readies a pawn storm against the king's flank.

sl-6pw.spoken: The knight eyes a dominant outpost. Moving the pawn first clears the path, then the knight hops through an intermediate square to reach it. This precise maneuvering raises its activity and can decide the game.

sl-6p5.spoken: The knight jumps into the weak square, and the threat lands on the defender. If the opponent captures, the queen suddenly hangs. That one move sets up a mating net in the corner.

sl-6pa.spoken: The pawn move leaves a hole, and the knight that lands in it loses its defenders. Black targets that knight, and when the queen joins the attack, the pressure forces White to bend.

sl-6pi.spoken: The player spots an outpost for the knight, but exchanges open the file and the knight falls to a capture. The queen slips away safely because taking the knight would lose her.

sl-6q5.spoken: The knight retreats to defend the rook and break the pin, while also setting up a jump to an outpost. With the pawn still unmoved, that outpost is solid, because the pawn can come forward to kick the knight out, giving the defender extra options.

sl-6pc.spoken: The weak square cramps the defender's options, quietly discouraging piece sacrifices. When a knight presses on that weakness and trades land, the defender cracks open the position with a pawn push, and the game stays balanced.

sl-6pe.spoken: The pawn push opens a hole behind it. That hole becomes a fork square where the knight hits queen and rook at once, since nothing guards it. The opponent's pawn thrust gains strength by piling on threats and overloading the defender.

sl-6p8.spoken: The bishop and rook both point at the same weak pawn in the enemy camp. When the queen joins in, she also hits the rook.

sl-6pg.spoken: The pawn advance creates a permanent hole at the center. The enemy's entire plan is to occupy and control that square, with knight and bishop already aimed at it.

sl-6q9.spoken: The outpost knight threatens the queen and rook together. When the opponent stops the fork, do not push it if the knight falls in return.

sl-6q2.spoken: The knight leaps to a central outpost, breeding fork and check threats. The opponent's pieces crowd together, stripped of their freedom.

sl-6q6.spoken: The knight sits on its outpost, anchoring the position and narrowing the opponent's choices. The bishop move that would challenge it fails to tactics.

sl-6p1.spoken: After castling, the rook guards the kingside pawn in front of it, so that attack loses its bite. The real target is the pawn next to the king, defended by nothing but the king himself.

sl-6p3.spoken: The bishop on the long diagonal looks awkward. The knight hops in to pressure it, and that outpost becomes a recurring theme for the whole game.

sl-6pd.spoken: The bishop aims at the king’s only defender, the weakest point in the opening. When the opponent blocks, you trade bishops and then check along the diagonal.

sl-6pt.spoken: The king tucks into the corner, and the pawn push looks natural but can backfire. The bishop, queen, and pawn breaks each carry drawbacks, while the knight sits powerfully in the center.

sl-6pq.spoken: The knight sits on its outpost and aims at the rook from afar while adding pressure on the tender square behind the king’s wall. With both rooks on the opponent’s second rank, the heavy pieces dominate the position and threaten a decisive breakthrough.

sl-6py.spoken: The plan pushes the pawn and bishop to provoke weaknesses, aiming to plant the bishop deep in enemy territory. The knight is the defender's key piece: it pressures the center and supports queenside counterplay that can halt the attack.

sl-6ph.spoken: The knight sits like a monster, impossible to dislodge, and rules the whole position. Every move the opponent makes to create pressure just weakens his own setup and lets White improve.

sl-6p2.spoken: The e-pawn advance abandons its guard over the central square. That square turns into a permanent knight outpost for the opponent.

sl-6qy.spoken: The attack is on, but the central pawn push challenges the knight and forces complications.

sl-6qq.spoken: The knight jumps into the mating net, and the king has no escape.

sl-6ra.spoken: The knight on the outpost dominates while Black's pieces sit passive. Any counterplay—pawn pushes or piece rerouting—arrives too slowly and only creates weaknesses.

sl-6rd.spoken: The knight lands on the outpost after the capture, and that piece becomes the backbone of the advantage.

sl-6rc.spoken: The knight is a key defender, covering critical squares and stopping captures through mating threats. The queen creates multiple threats while the king steps forward to escape checks.

sl-6qc.spoken: The knight has three squares to aim for, but the route to the outpost is best. From there it supports both central and queenside play.

sl-6rg.spoken: The knight takes the long way around, but the route ends at the perfect outpost to press the queenside, targeting the weak pawn on the b-file.

sl-6rj.spoken: The knight sits strong on its outpost, and the enemy king's wander has cost tempi, giving us time to improve our position.

sl-6qu.spoken: The knight lands on that square to guard the pawn, but the square is unstable—a pawn push kicks it away. That push is a standard resource, not a surprise.

sl-6qx.spoken: The knights are beautifully posted, gripping key squares and cramping Black. Pressure builds on both wings, and the squeeze tightens.

sl-6ri.spoken: The knight leaps to a fork, striking two targets at once. The queen falls back, the knight gets chased off, and the repetition ends the game in a draw.

sl-6rb.spoken: The knight's power lives on the central outpost. Chasing the flank pulls it out of play and leaves the key squares too far to reclaim.

sl-6r4.spoken: The knight sits aggressively, hitting several squares at once. It supports pushes that win the bishop, shore up the center, and open a route to a stronger outpost.

sl-6rh.spoken: The knight rides to the outpost, where it attacks the bishop and anchors the attack. The opponent's long think uncovers a defensive resource — the threat is real, but it does not decide the game.

sl-6r9.spoken: The knight plants itself on that outpost, and the threat against the rook is real. When the queen drops back to block the fork, the defense cracks and a mating attack opens up.

sl-6qt.spoken: The knight travels to the outpost, eyeing the castled king's pawn shield. The rook waits behind the pawn that will advance to pry open the file for the bishop.

sl-6qv.spoken: The knight jumps to the key square, aiming at the enemy king's doorstep. It pressures the vulnerable point and supports a bishop sacrifice there, unleashing a decisive attack.

sl-6qe.spoken: The knight plants itself deep in the center, griping key squares and choking the opponent's coordination. Both enemy knights sit on the rim and on the back rank, far from the action.

sl-6qf.spoken: The knight's jump looks active, but the bishop retreats and leaves it with no good squares—every route is cut off. The knight is stranded, and that hands the opponent a clear advantage.

sl-6qd.spoken: The knight lands on the central outpost, and the rook on the seventh rank becomes a mating threat. From there the knight also leaps to the other key square, and the position is nearly decisive.

sl-6rk.spoken: The knight heads for the outpost, where it teams with the bishop and builds pressure. That rerouting is a standard idea in this pawn structure.

sl-6ql.spoken: The knight sits idle on the edge; a single jump to the center turns it into a threat. From that outpost it attacks the enemy bishop while supporting the rook down the open file. One move, and the piece goes from passive to dominant.

sl-6rf.spoken: A knight posted deep in enemy territory invites a pawn challenge. The pawn push forces it to retreat or trade, and when the opponent lashes out with a sacrifice, a calm simplification or counterattack refutes it.

sl-6r8.spoken: The bishop steps out to a central square, eyeing a weakness in the enemy camp and preparing a knight leap. That leap forks the queen and rook at once, and the only try to block it fails when the queen checks back, so the fork is the real threat.

sl-6r2.spoken: A knight planted deep in enemy territory is a thorn that is very hard to remove. The opponent's attempts to activate pieces or defend pawns often ignore the knight's real strength.

sl-6qh.spoken: The pawn shield keeps the defender alive, but once it advances, the square in front of it becomes a permanent knight outpost. From there the knight dominates the position.

sl-6r7.spoken: An idle knight with no useful squares is a real liability. The active knight keeps creating threats, forcing the opponent to respond and stay tied down.

sl-6qz.spoken: A knight planted on an outpost square becomes the foundation of a tactic. It hits the queen, pushes it to a worse square, and that sets up the combination that wins material.

sl-6qa.spoken: The pawn advances, and the knight is suddenly misplaced. Answering by attacking that pawn gives the knight a clear path to a strong outpost.

sl-6qb.spoken: The knight heads for an outpost on the queenside, probing the weak squares in Black's structure. The other piece routes are alternatives, but this maneuver is the typical plan here.

sl-6qn.spoken: The knight heads for the outpost, its presence alone stopping the pawn break that would free the position. A patient, long-term plan.

sl-6r1.spoken: The recapture with knight instead of pawn may look like a concession, but it pries open the e-file and sets up a knight route to the key outpost. The aim: get both knights to that square.

sl-6qw.spoken: The knight lands on the outpost as planned. When the pawn advances to drive it back, the missing defender on the other wing makes itself felt. The result is only a slight edge for White, not a clear win, but enough to nurse toward conversion.

sl-6r6.spoken: A knight planted deep in enemy lines is hard to dislodge because its threats pile up. If the queen is taken, a second knight leaps in to deliver mate, showing how the pair cooperates to dominate the critical squares.

sl-6qk.spoken: The knight sits on a square with latent attacking ideas, eyeing two forward jumps and a third that kicks the bishop. Black must keep the knight off that third square, or it wins a pawn.

sl-6re.spoken: The knight jumps forward, but first point out that once it lands, the rook on the other side cannot move—the queen hangs. If the pawn captures the knight, the tactical resource keeps the attack alive.

sl-6qg.spoken: With the center open, the knight leaps to the strong square and presses hard. If the king castles, plant the knight there, back it with rooks on the open files, and attack the weakened pawns.

sl-6r0.spoken: The pawn advance prepares the knight's reroute to a natural outpost. If the opponent bolsters the center with a pawn, their own knight sits poorly and no piece is ready to occupy the key square, leaving a favorable version.

sl-6qs.spoken: The pawn advance weakens the dark squares and invites long-term problems. Blocking with the bishop allows the knight to land, and that creates too many threats.

sl-6qi.spoken: Push the pawn, and if the knight tries to contest the center, meet it by stepping the knight forward. If it captures, the bishop opens, but the knight still protects. The pawn stays, shielding and guarding the king.

sl-6qo.spoken: The knight on that square attacks multiple targets at once. That makes it the best piece for the job, and the result is winning material or a crushing attack.

sl-6sl.spoken: The knight blocks the bishop's protection and threatens mate, so the opponent must take it. That capture exposes the king and lets the rook join the attack.

sl-6ry.spoken: The knight is strong after the bishop trade and eyes a central outpost. But stepping there invites checks, so first safeguard the king.

sl-6rt.spoken: The knight sits strong on that outpost, guarding key squares and easing the bishop's path. The bishop aims to provoke pawn weaknesses, but Black refuses the capture.

sl-6rs.spoken: A knight on a strong outpost can support a mating attack, forcing the defender onto precise moves to block the kingside.

sl-6so.spoken: The knight stands strong in the critical spot, and that alone gives White a comfortable edge. Black's push with the f-pawn fails to fix the trouble.

sl-6sq.spoken: The knight finds a stronger square, striking two key points at once. A safe, flexible repositioning works well when the opponent may not expect it.

sl-6sn.spoken: The knight lands on a square that no pawn can touch, but only after every piece that could challenge it is removed first. That makes the outpost permanent and dominant.

sl-6sd.spoken: The knight hops in to trap the king, herding it onto a single square. That barrier turns bishop and knight into a net, and the king has no way out.

sl-6si.spoken: The knight leaps to the outpost, grabbing the pawn and leaving that bishop sealed behind a pawn wall.

sl-6s7.spoken: The knight eyes the outpost, the queen backs it. Black's bishop aims to trade off the light-squared defender, clearing that square for the knight.

sl-6s2.spoken: The knight on the outpost is supported by a pawn, and its threat to jump and fork king and rook locks down the defense.

sl-6sv.spoken: The knight sits strong on its outpost, so the defender pushes a pawn to chase it back. But as the knight retreats, the pawn is won, and that new weakness decides the game.

sl-6sj.spoken: The knight sits deep in enemy territory, guarding the pawn and cutting off the queen's path. White must deal with it now, or Black's threat wins material.

sl-6sp.spoken: The knight strikes a pawn, and if the pawn recaptures, the queen leaps to a strong square, freeing White's pieces. Black must stop that.

sl-6sc.spoken: The knight sits deep in enemy territory and hits the rook, bishop, and more all at once. No matter how White tries to defend, the attack is too much.

sl-6s4.spoken: A strong knight sits deep in enemy territory, generating threats that Black must answer. Even with perfect defense, the pressure builds until the position collapses.

sl-6sb.spoken: The knight sits on an active outpost, controlling key squares and pressuring the opponent. Retreating it to a passive square abandons those posts and hands back the initiative.

sl-6sh.spoken: The knight leaps to the outpost, hitting the queen. She must flee, and that flight strands a pawn as an island and leaves the bishop doing nothing.

sl-6sf.spoken: The knight holds a pawn back when it camps in front of it, and the pawn on its file keeps it company. Keeping the bishop rather than trading it preserves pressure on the opponent’s king side.

sl-6rx.spoken: The knight belongs on the advanced square: it eyes the critical central point and leaves the bishop's diagonal clear. From the passive square it would block that line and stiffen the position.

sl-6s3.spoken: The knight takes, then royal checks look tempting but fizzle — the enemy king finds shelter in the center. Move the knight to the outpost instead, pressuring the pawn and covering the escape square, sealing the king in.

sl-6sm.spoken: The knight plants itself on a central outpost and dominates the board, chaining enemy pieces to defensive tasks and cramping their activity. Its presence makes captures impossible, because every take walks into a tactical threat.

sl-6s9.spoken: Trade off the piece that guards that square, and the knight that lands there becomes a permanent powerhouse. Even with no direct target, it dominates the opponent's camp and stifles their activity.

sl-6ru.spoken: The minor-piece trade bleeds the queenside of targets, so White commits freely on the kingside. The knight sits offside on the rim where a central post would have kept the pressure alive.

sl-6s6.spoken: A knight that jumps deep into enemy territory cuts off castling, harasses the queen, and ties down the opponent's pieces. Even when down material, that bind lasts long after the sacrifice.

sl-6sr.spoken: The knight eyes a strong outpost, but delay hands Black the turn. Once Black plants the knight and pushes the pawn to attack, the bishop joins in and Black stands well.

sl-6sw.spoken: The knight jump looks natural but misses the sharper plan. Retreating to the edge sets up a pawn thrust and a queen lift, creating threats with the bishop and a return to the strong square.

sl-6s5.spoken: The knight jumps to the center, eyeing the fork square. When the defender covers that square with a queenside knight, the recapture on the other side follows and leaves the position comfortable.

sl-6rr.spoken: The knight planted deep in enemy territory pressures critical pawns and cramps the opponent's play. They often must trade it off before they get overrun, but before you commit, check that your queen is not left loose—tactical blows tend to target her.

sl-6rq.spoken: The knight sits deep in enemy territory, and the rook is active on the seventh. The passed pawn looks dangerous, but piece activity is the compensation. Trading queens into a rook-and-knight ending favors White because every piece is perfectly placed.

sl-6st.spoken: The centralized knight threatens a deep outpost that binds the opponent. Even without landing the jump, the mere threat of it grants full control.

sl-6rv.spoken: The knight heads to the ideal square, where it feeds both the queenside attack and the central plan through the f-pawn.

sl-6s0.spoken: The knight retreats to a hub square, from where it eyes both of Black's weak pawns.

sl-6rm.spoken: A knight landing deep in enemy territory creates mating threats on both adjacent king-side squares, and the smothered mate lurks behind them. One piece, many tactical ideas.

sl-6rw.spoken: The knight steps in to shield the bishop and back later pawn pushes. It lands on a lively square, eyeing two weak points, while the center pawn stays fragile and demands constant cover.

sl-6ro.spoken: The knight on that square is unstable. If the pawn advances to attack it, the knight either retreats and loses something, or stays and gets captured.

sl-6sx.spoken: The bishop-versus-knight endgame offers a recapture choice. The knight take strands it awkwardly among pawns with no useful squares. The king take lets the knight leap to a strong central outpost.

sl-6sk.spoken: Once the knight lands on that square, it becomes a monster: it covers the whole board, no bishop can touch it, no enemy knight remains, and no pawn can drive it off. The only way to remove it is to throw a rook at it.

sl-6sa.spoken: The plan shuffles knight and bishop to reroute the piece, but the defender must watch for the knight landing on the weak square, forcing the pawn move to block entry.

sl-6rz.spoken: The knight lands strongly after both flank pawns advance. When the queen attacks one pawn, the other pushes forward. Capturing lets the recapture hang the center pawn and drags White into an unpleasant line.

sl-6s8.spoken: The knight reroutes to the stronger outpost, while the direct route invites a trade. If the recapture is made by the pawn, that key square is sealed forever, and the other outpost gets harder to hold.

sl-6rp.spoken: The knight wants the outpost, but the queen sits on it. Reposition the queen, and the knight takes the square.

sl-6t0.spoken: A knight planted on a strong outpost and backed by pawns and rooks can decide the game. The opponent's underestimation turns defense into a struggle.

sl-6sz.spoken: A free knight on a strong central square controls key points and hammers your weak spots. You must answer that piece immediately.

sl-6tz.spoken: The king tries to close in on the pawn, but the queen must cut off its path or drive it back—that's what wins the race.

sl-6tw.spoken: The knight sits in the center like an octopus, reaching eight squares at once. Its power is huge, but only one move is safe—the one where the queen stands behind it.

sl-6u4.spoken: The passed pawn looks like a win, but if the defender can neutralize it, the game often fades to a draw. The real fight is about restricting pieces and maneuvering.

sl-6tk.spoken: The knight jumps to the center, attacks the rook, and forces White to respond. That reaction hands Black the time to improve their position.

sl-6t6.spoken: The knight leap to the outpost attacks the bishop and sets up threats on the rook. Whatever square the rook flees to, tactics still find it.

sl-6t9.spoken: The knight jumps to the outpost square, landing with real pressure. The pawn move gains space but leaves the pieces passive.

sl-6ti.spoken: The knight hops to a better square and eyes a fork against the king and queen. Black has to answer that threat.

sl-6u6.spoken: Black's passed pawn and active rooks outweigh White's passive pieces. Trading queens and centralizing the king is sound, yet it falls short against exact defense.

sl-6tf.spoken: A knight heading to the square that attacks the bishop turns that square into an outpost, neutralizing the bishop's strong diagonal.

sl-6u5.spoken: The passed pawn is the whole game. When the defender tries to trade it off, keep it guarded, then bring the king up to drive the rook away—and the pawn decides the ending.

sl-6u1.spoken: The rook endgame hinges on the a-pawn. Keep that pawn alive and push it; trade it off and the win often evaporates into a draw. The rook earns its keep on an active file, backing the pawn's march.

sl-6tx.spoken: The passed pawn is the real threat, but White holds a three-to-two majority on the other side. He must move fast — either generate his own counterplay or block the pawn before it runs.

sl-6sy.spoken: The knight sits deep in enemy territory, but it is cut off and doing nothing yet. The opponent's blocked piece is the real problem — once it gets out, your weakened pawns start to hurt.

sl-6tv.spoken: The knight jumps to a square where it hits the rook and bishop at once. The other route attacks the bishop and threatens the same fork next move.

sl-6ta.spoken: The knight is a serious threat, and once the pawn advances, it jumps to an even stronger square. Trading the bishop for that knight removes the danger entirely.

sl-6ty.spoken: Do not grab the pawn. Black’s trick is to let you take it, then push on and queen. Let that happen, and Black’s extra queen and pawns finish the game.

sl-6tm.spoken: The knight takes and takes again, landing on a square where it is misplaced. White can exploit it. Pushing the pawn first would have forced the knight back to its original square, avoiding the poor placement.

sl-6tu.spoken: The knights cooperate to reach a powerful central square. If that square is well-defended, remove a defender before the centralization lands.

sl-6tg.spoken: The knight aims for a strong outpost, but the path reveals the intent. An edge square looks weak, yet it can be a stepping stone when the real target sits centrally ahead.

sl-6t5.spoken: Plant the knight on the weak square. When the rook defends the file, the knight darts to a new outpost, then captures the pawn — and the position turns in your favor.

sl-6u2.spoken: Passed pawns come first when judging an endgame—here neither side has one or any immediate way to make one, and that pushes the position toward equal. Still, one side may edge ahead on smaller things like piece activity or pawn structure.

sl-6tn.spoken: The knight rides toward a central outpost, with the endgame target deep in enemy territory. Pawns advance to harry the bishop and clear the path.

sl-6ts.spoken: The knight that lands on the central outpost dominates the position. The opponent's weakened flank pawns become targets, and while the king is safer, the active pieces and sounder structure tip the balance.

sl-6t4.spoken: The knight heads for that strong outpost. Pushing the pawn to stop it just gives the knight a new target on the weakened square. Blocking the outpost square with a knight is the solid answer; a pawn thrust to the flank is premature.

sl-6tc.spoken: The knight heads for the outpost that locks down the g-file, cutting off the rook's highway. A check from the rook forces the king out of the way, but the knight still lands on its target, and now the king must face the threat.

sl-6tj.spoken: The weak square in Black's camp is the target. A knight posts itself where it eyes that hole, and when the pawn lunges to drive it off, the knight takes the pawn — and if the recapture comes, the pin on the bishop wins material.

sl-6t8.spoken: The knight trades itself off to land in the center, where it attacks the pinned piece and makes defense nearly impossible. If the defender tries to retreat, the knight leaps in and delivers forced mate.

sl-6tl.spoken: A knight landing on that edge square often turns out awkward and offside, with no clear future. The ideal homes for that piece are strong central outposts or a solid advanced square where it pressures the opponent.

sl-6t3.spoken: The knight lands on the central square and cracks the pawn structure. Black must give up the bishop for it or tuck the king somewhere unsafe. Tucking the king invites a double attack, and shuffling it into a manual castle costs time and leaves it exposed.

sl-6tt.spoken: The knight is Black's main defender. Push the pawn to attack it, then take it. With that knight gone, Black cannot push the pawn to shield the king, and the position collapses. Even if Black grabs the pawn on the flank, the attack is overwhelming.

sl-6u0.spoken: The d-pawn turns into a protected passed pawn, with the bishop ready to back it. Black’s rooks cannot stop its march, especially once the bishop finds a powerful diagonal.

sl-6u3.spoken: Create a passed pawn — the e-file is the classic route — and turn the bishops loose against the enemy king. Pawn pushes are part of it, but the real winning try fuses pawn advances with king threats.

sl-6u7.spoken: A passed pawn is a distraction as much as a threat. Pushing it forces the opponent to divert pieces to block, and that buys you freedom to improve elsewhere.

sl-6th.spoken: The knight fork looks tempting, but it lets the opponent plant a knight on a central outpost. After the bishops trade, that outpost knight proves far stronger than your misplaced one.

sl-6tb.spoken: The knight plants itself on a dark square and controls key dark squares from there. It also threatens a jump that would be terrible for Black, while Black must constantly watch the dark-square weaknesses White can exploit.

sl-6to.spoken: The king is exposed, and the attack lands on the two pawns in front of it. The knight sits powerfully in the center, ready to leap forward, hit one of those pawns, and open the line for the rook.

sl-6t2.spoken: The knight plants itself in the defender's path and shuts down their counterplay entirely. With the defender frozen, attention turns to a soft pawn, and the rook joins in to finish the assault.

sl-6u9.spoken: The kingside offers the breakthrough, since the queenside blockade stalls all progress. The king marches to support the pawn, and the passed pawn pushes through.

sl-6te.spoken: The knight sits strong, and pushing the h-pawn secures it while the a-pawn starts a storm. Black's g-pawn thrust only tears open the kingside.

sl-6u8.spoken: The rooks and material are level, but the king stands better, the rook is better placed, and the passed pawn is safe and can be taken whenever White chooses. The point is not to grab the pawn at once, but to spend the tempo improving the king's activity.

sl-6tq.spoken: The knight sits strong on an advanced square, backed by a passed pawn that cannot be caught. White wants to push the kingside pawns to dislodge the knight, but with queens still on the board that push opens lines the black queen will exploit.

sl-6uv.spoken: A knight blockades a passed pawn well, but once the pawn advances too far, the knight can get trapped and lose its mobility.

sl-6v4.spoken: The bishop is tied down, so the queenside pawns become a cage. A sacrifice on the flank creates a passed pawn that the bishop cannot stop, and the advance wins.

sl-6ur.spoken: The passed pawn races forward, not sideways. Push it two squares toward promotion, and the opponent must answer at once.

sl-6us.spoken: The bishop is tied to guarding the promotion square, so the king can walk the pawn up. The enemy bishop has no useful squares, and the win plays itself.

sl-6ve.spoken: A passed pawn that reaches the last rank can win material—once it promotes, the new queen may capture a piece outright.

sl-6ue.spoken: The king must push to the seventh rank to back the pawn home, but the enemy king and bishop throw checks and roadblocks. Time the king's march with the pawn's step, and use a check to buy a tempo when the path tightens.

sl-6uw.spoken: The passed h-pawn is a real advantage, but the deeper threat is the rook sliding to the back rank — a near mate that the opponent must answer.

sl-6uu.spoken: The extra pawn is blockaded and dead weight. A pawn push breaks the blockade, opens lines, and creates a passed pawn — that is the only way forward.

sl-6ub.spoken: The bishop pair’s long reach stops passed pawns from the distance, while tactical tricks turn defense into a decisive attack, even on a bare board.

sl-6vk.spoken: The bishop builds a bridge so the rook can back the passed pawn. With an extra piece, precision still wins the endgame.

sl-6v1.spoken: The king and rook escort the passed pawn forward, and resistance collapses as the pawns roll on.

sl-6v0.spoken: The passed pawn, backed by the king, ties the defender down. The pawn advances, forcing the rook to sit passively, and the defender has no active plan.

sl-6ul.spoken: The passed pawn in a rook endgame does not guarantee a win. The correct plan is what matters: push the pawn and bring the king up to support it.

sl-6vf.spoken: The queen race ends in checkmate. Whoever queens first is irrelevant when the other side has a mating net already calculated.

sl-6ut.spoken: The rook wins because the knight is chained to stopping the passed pawn, and the bishop alone answers for the other pawn. A knight’s short steps make it useless against a runner.

sl-6ui.spoken: The outside passed pawn alone is not enough. Without an open file to invade on, the position tends toward a draw — the entry point makes the win possible.

sl-6ux.spoken: The king's distance decides the race. A far-off king cannot catch the passed pawn, and that pawn marches through to win.

sl-6ua.spoken: The bishop parks itself on the passed pawn’s path. The passed pawn is worth more than the extra pawns on the far side, and the active bishop is what holds it back.

sl-6up.spoken: The passed pawn is a prize because it stands one step from promotion. Two enemy pieces guard the queening square, so the task is to remove one defender.

sl-6uo.spoken: The passed pawn is the priority, not the cheap capture. Pushing it keeps the win alive, while grabbing the pawn on the side lets the advantage slip.

sl-6vi.spoken: The pawn push forces the king to step aside. Once he takes it, your king walks over to collect the h-pawn and escort the f-pawn home.

sl-6vb.spoken: The passed pawn and the knight work as a pair: the knight denies the queen her checking squares, and the pawn marches forward. Even a temporary sacrifice is fine while the knight keeps control.

sl-6va.spoken: The rook and bishop must hold back advanced passed pawns while pushing their own. The pawns threaten to promote, so White must stop them without abandoning his own runner.

sl-6v8.spoken: The passers need a clear road. Push the pawn, and keep the knight off the blocking square — that stops the fortress and secures the promotion.

sl-6uq.spoken: The pawn is nearly home, and the defender's rook tries to block it. The knight cuts off the rook's path, so the pawn's advance is unstoppable. That leaves a choice between grinding out the win or grabbing the simpler material gain.

sl-6v9.spoken: In this endgame, a pawn races to promote while the defender's bishop steps in to block it. That block pulls the bishop out of the mating net, so the defender must weigh stopping the pawn against keeping mating chances alive.

sl-6vd.spoken: Two passed pawns can be a trap. When one of your own pawns blocks another, neither is truly passed. A single true passed pawn, running free, is the clear advantage.

sl-6uk.spoken: The king-side pawn push looks like a direct way to win the e-pawn, but the defender's own pawn advance can throw the plan into complications.

sl-6vl.spoken: The king must time its approach to the pawns correctly. If the black king rushes over, the white king should not grab the pawn at once, but first push a pawn of its own—the same idea, and the draw holds.

sl-6ug.spoken: The passed pawn is the direct road to victory, especially when enemy pieces are bound to defense.

sl-6v7.spoken: The queenside passed pawn pins the rook to passive defense, while the king and pawns manufacture winning chances. Best play holds the draw, but the practical pressure belongs entirely to Black.

sl-6vc.spoken: The surest road to a won endgame is a pawn that reaches the far rank. In both games, a passed pawn queened, and that decided the result.

sl-6uf.spoken: Keep the pieces on the board. The outside passed pawn and weak points in the opponent's camp turn every trade into a loss of pressure and every exchange into a step away from conversion.

sl-6uj.spoken: The method uses the kingside pawns to manufacture a passed pawn or pull the defender's king away. Captures are never forced, so progress must come from maneuvering, not from threats that cannot be refused.

sl-6v5.spoken: The pawn up in a rook endgame is real, but the passed pawn sits far back and can be halted before it crosses midfield. With the enemy king locked out, the edge shrinks toward a draw.

sl-6ud.spoken: The rook endgame turns on the passed pawn: once it reaches the fifth rank, nothing stops it. The rook seals the king off from behind, the enemy bishop pair owns the light squares, and the knight just watches as the pawn marches to promotion.

sl-6v6.spoken: The pawn sits one square from promotion. When the defender can neither blockade nor conjure a counter-trick, that pawn decides the game.

sl-6uz.spoken: A passed pawn is gold, but only when backed up. Left unsupported, it gets blockaded and captured; with the rook and king behind it, it becomes a real threat.

sl-6un.spoken: Black pushes kingside pawns to create passed pawns, and if White's blockade breaks, they become unstoppable. The rook on the f-file joins in to support them.

sl-6uh.spoken: Two passed pawns decide this endgame. One stands deep in enemy territory and cages the knight, leaving it no useful square. That makes White effectively a piece up, and with no dangerous black passer, the win is clear.

sl-6um.spoken: The kingside pawn majority turns the game around. Pushing the f- and g-pawns creates a passed pawn in the center, which drags the defender away and sets up a winning rook endgame.

sl-6wu.spoken: A pawn ahead, the winning recipe is two steps: create a passed pawn, then trade off the rooks.

sl-6wd.spoken: The passed pawn and the active king are the two top priorities in the endgame. Weigh both before every move.

sl-6w8.spoken: A passed pawn that cannot advance is no advantage. Blockaded and stuck, it is worthless, while the opponent's active pieces and kingside majority decide the game.

sl-6vn.spoken: A passed pawn exists to advance. When the key squares are controlled, pushing it is the natural path to convert the win.

sl-6wo.spoken: The a-pawn becomes a shield and a decoy. When Black's king tries to invade, pushing the pawn creates counterplay and obstructs the breakthrough.

sl-6ws.spoken: The passed pawn reaches the seventh rank and decides the rook endgame. The attacking king walks over to back it up, and more material falls.

sl-6w5.spoken: The passed pawn, backed by its king, forces the opponent to sacrifice a rook to stop it, and that loss ends the game.

sl-6vw.spoken: A passed pawn plus extra material gives you more than one road to the win. Push to promote, or give the pawn up to strip every enemy pawn from the board.

sl-6wt.spoken: The queenside pawn decides it, not the kingside attack. Swing the rook to the seventh rank first, and the king is forced to the edge—worse for him than the other square.

sl-6wh.spoken: The king and knight are too far away to catch the passer. The pawn runs home while the black pieces give chase in vain.

sl-6wf.spoken: The knight wanders too far, and the bishop seizes the diagonal. One tempo decides it: the pawn's promotion becomes unstoppable.

sl-6vx.spoken: A knight sacrifice attacks a pawn and forces an answer. Refuse it, and the pawn falls — then the passed pawn promotes.

sl-6wg.spoken: The passed pawn is the stronger one, because the knight can block the enemy passer while nothing on the other side can stop our own. That edge turns a material deficit into a winning endgame.

sl-6wa.spoken: The king is stranded far from the action. The rook checks and then slides in front of the pawn, so White must surrender the pawn or lose the game.

sl-6wv.spoken: The passed pawn is the whole game. The white king is stranded offside, the white rook chases a mate that never lands, and the pawn just keeps rolling to promotion.

sl-6vz.spoken: The passed pawn is one step from promotion, so the rook heads behind it to halt the queen. White's own passed pawns move too slowly, and the enemy king and rook work together to round them up. The result is already decided.

sl-6wc.spoken: The pawn cannot queen because the rook will take it, and the rook endgame that follows is drawn — so every attempt to push it is futile.

sl-6wp.spoken: The d-pawn is stopped for now, so the fight turns to making progress. White cannot abandon that pawn, and Black can exploit its constant pull to build winning chances.

sl-6vr.spoken: The h-pawn races ahead, far from the action, and becomes a passed pawn that decides the game. The central pawn is worthless—the king already has it covered.

sl-6wl.spoken: The protected passed pawn ties down the enemy pieces, so centralize the king and attack the weak pawns—your opponent must watch both fronts at once.

sl-6wb.spoken:
The rook's place is behind the passed pawn—it pushes
the pawn forward and boxes in the enemy king. Leaving
that square or trading rooks throws the advantage away.

sl-6vu.spoken: A passed pawn on the far wing is decisive when the opponent's king and knight are both pinned to their defensive duties. The pawn runs while the defenders stay glued to their posts.

sl-6w4.spoken: Two bishops are active while the opponent's king is caged by the passed pawn. Material is level, but the pressure is nearly decisive—the defender must block the pawn and trade pieces to ease the squeeze.

sl-6we.spoken: The bishop must be denied the diagonal that stops the pawn. Once the bishop cannot capture, the enemy king has to come alone, and that opens the door for your own king to break in.

sl-6vo.spoken: The rook endgame turns on a single passed pawn. One side pushes it forward while the other scrambles to block. The pawn's owner uses the rook to shield and escort that pawn toward promotion.

sl-6wi.spoken: The passed pawn ties the rook to the back rank, so it cannot defend actively. The king marches to support the pawn, and every rook move off the rank allows promotion. No counterplay remains.

sl-6w3.spoken: The rook gives check, and if the king grabs the pawn, the d-pawn turns dangerous. The knight leaps to block the enemy rook's defense, and the pawn rolls forward.

sl-6wn.spoken: The rook and bishop work together behind a passed pawn. Plant the rook on the promotion file to support it, while the bishop and king clamp down on the defender's activity. That coordination secures a winning edge.

sl-6w9.spoken: The pawn advance meant to keep the bishop off its best square only loosens the king's shelter. The reply turns the bishop into a monster and halts the passed pawn cold.

sl-6w1.spoken: The push on the a-file creates a second passed pawn and wins the king-and-pawn endgames because the black pawn trails behind. The b-pawn push wastes time, since Black's reply forces the same problems without gaining an extra passer.

sl-6w7.spoken: The extra pawn on the central files, not the wing, is what turns this knight endgame from a draw into a win. A passed pawn that can be supported and pushed decides the fight.

sl-6wj.spoken: The knight blocks the passed pawn, but a check from the f-file shatters the mating net, and the king arrives too late to stop promotion.

sl-6vv.spoken: The pawn break creates a passed pawn the opponent cannot stop. With material level, that pawn plus the active king decides the game.

sl-6wq.spoken: Push the pawn and the plan plays itself. The enemy rook is glued to the promotion square, and their king cannot interfere. Even under check, step forward and the win holds.

sl-6w2.spoken: The outside passed pawn is a lure, not a prize. While the opponent rushes to block or trade it, the side with the pawn wins material on the other wing, turning a positional edge into a decisive one.

sl-6wr.spoken: The pawn pushes to the last rank and freezes the enemy king, which dare not step off its square or face checks. The rook must stay on the pawn's file to block, yet it still finds room to check from behind.

sl-6ww.spoken: The bishop trade costs a pawn, yet the win remains: the passed pawn threatens and the king joins the attack. White’s defensive bishop can’t hold the barrier — the black king still marches through the weakened squares to decide the game.

sl-6vt.spoken: The better bishop dominates the stranded knight, and the plan is clear: push the passed pawn. That pawn no enemy pawn can stop, so every advance forces the opponent to respond and ties their pieces down.

sl-6vp.spoken: A passer far from the enemy king decides the endgame. The king can only stop it if close enough; too far, and the pawn promotes.

sl-6w0.spoken: A bare bishop and knight can still force checkmate, but it takes precise technique. Two knights alone cannot checkmate at all. So Black must find a win before the board is stripped down to that.

sl-6vm.spoken: The passed pawn must reach the back rank. The defending king posts up in front of it, so the attacking king steps forward to escort the pawn home.

sl-6wk.spoken: A pawn on the seventh is a threat the defender cannot handle with normal moves. Stopping it demands extraordinary measures, even a sacrifice of material.

sl-6vs.spoken: In this rook endgame, the goal is a passed pawn on the edge, far from the center, making a second weakness. The central pawn matters less because the king already controls it well.

sl-6wm.spoken: The passed a-pawn cannot be stopped. The enemy bishop has only one long diagonal, but the king escorts the pawn forward, and that single diagonal cannot cover both key squares.

sl-6xd.spoken: A passed pawn is a decisive advantage when the king and bishop back it up.

sl-6x9.spoken: The rook drops in behind the passed pawn on the seventh rank, on the queening file. That placement stops the pawn from promoting.

sl-6xb.spoken: In a rook endgame, an active rook move looks tempting, but it often lets the opponent push a dangerous passed pawn. Weigh the activity gained against the pawn weaknesses it creates.

sl-6xa.spoken: Pushing the pawn up the board creates a passed pawn with promotion threats. That forces the opponent to respond, and you gain active play in the meantime.

sl-6xp.spoken: The pawn is bait, not a gift. If the rook grabs it, the pawn advances and promotes — a passed pawn's endgame power.

sl-6x0.spoken: The extra pawn becomes a passed pawn, and with no counterplay against it, the rook supports its march and wins.

sl-6y2.spoken: Black's pawn thrust creates a passed pawn, opens lines for the bishop, and denies the white knight its key square that would block the pawns.

sl-6y8.spoken: A passed pawn is a threat the rook must answer. Push it, and the rook is forced to deal with it, leaving the other pawns undefended.

sl-6xx.spoken: The passed pawns race, but the kings decide. Black’s safer king and the stronger passer offset the extra pawn — the position holds a draw.

sl-6x1.spoken: The queenside pawn break is the path to a passed pawn. Push forward and trade, and one of your pawns runs free — the others do not.

sl-6y0.spoken: The pawn trade is left unfinished, and White's majority starts rolling. Once it promotes, the game is over.

sl-6xe.spoken: Black's extra pawn on the queenside means two against one, so he can create a passed pawn. White has no way to make his own passer, which leaves Black with the better chances.

sl-6x7.spoken: A centralized queen behind a passed pawn is a fortress. The king alone cannot halt her, so the pawn marches on — and the king may end up mated.

sl-6xy.spoken: The king alone cannot always halt the passed pawn. Sometimes the knight blocks it better, and choosing the right defender is the precise resource that saves the endgame.

sl-6xi.spoken: A strong passed pawn looks dangerous, but pushing it forward makes it weaker and easier to blockade. Once stopped, the rook slips behind enemy lines and wins it.

sl-6xr.spoken: The g-pawn sprint begins now, and Black has the head start. The rook takes the f-pawn, leaving just the g-pawn to clear, and the race is won.

sl-6xv.spoken: The rook and pawn is a clear win if you play simply. The passed pawn is far advanced and the knight guards it, while the rook owns the only open file and locks the defender out.

sl-6x4.spoken: The sacrifice gives Black a far passed pawn and a kingside majority. The knight must retreat all the way to the edge to stop the runner, and that passivity decides the game.

sl-6xn.spoken: The passed pawn is the whole game here. Push it, and bring the king up to guard it — that path leads to promotion and the win.

sl-6y9.spoken: In a rook-and-pawn ending, king placement decides the result. Drive the enemy king off with checks, gaining tempi, so your own king can escort the passed pawn home.

sl-6xj.spoken: The passed pawn in an opposite-colored bishop ending is the real advantage, not the material balance. It ties down the defender's pieces, and that restraint turns a drawish position into a decisive win.

sl-6y3.spoken: Every natural move hides a trap. Search for the defensive resource before you commit — the evaluation turns on one subtle tactic.

sl-6wy.spoken: The race decides this ending: both sides push for promotion. The b-pawn wins because it is the safer candidate—harder to attack and quicker to become a passer, especially since the bishops exploit the knight's clumsiness.

sl-6y1.spoken: The king sits between the back-rank corners to cover the two pawns in front of it, but the h-pawn breaks that setup. White pushes the h-pawn forward and creates a passed pawn that will promote.

sl-6x5.spoken: The opponent's connected passed pawns look strong, but your own passed pawn is the real threat. When the rook parks itself on the promotion square to block, but instead drifts elsewhere, that opens the door to a forced win.

sl-6xm.spoken: A passed pawn looks urgent, but the push can wait. First bring the king or rook up to support it.

sl-6xc.spoken: The rook must strike the pawn at once, forcing the knight to take and clearing the path for the pawn's advance. The enemy king is far off, yet the knight alone may still try to halt it.

sl-6xq.spoken: The bishop must be kept alive — it is the pawn’s escort. Sacrificing it without immediate compensation strands the passed pawn, and the enemy king just parks in front and blocks promotion.

sl-6y6.spoken: The king steps toward the pawn, but that lets the rook capture on the h-file. The passed d-pawn is unstoppable, so White takes material first and then brings the rook up to shepherd the pawn home.

sl-6xg.spoken: The passed pawn is the imbalance, advanced and backed by the king. The enemy pawn is far behind, and the knight sits offside, unable to touch the passer. That leaves the weak pawn on the flank as the target.

sl-6xt.spoken: The bishop is pinned to its duty against passed pawns. Once it is driven off, the pawn promotes, and the king arrives too late to stop it.

sl-6x2.spoken: Sharp play hangs in the balance. The side with the extra material must stay precise, because the opponent's easy draw has vanished.

sl-6wz.spoken: The pawn on the sixth rank is a decisive advantage—it chains the black king to its defense while the white king walks in freely to win material.

sl-6x6.spoken: Black gives up the h-pawn to make a far-advanced f-pawn with king support. That pawn's quality beats White's extra material—it is closer to queening and strongly backed.

sl-6x8.spoken: The passed pawn far from the kingside outweighs two pawns on the other wing. In queen endgames, what matters is how far a pawn has advanced—a deep runner decides the game even against a pawn majority.

sl-6y5.spoken: The extra pawn is not enough if the rook can build a fortress. Push the pawn first, create a passed pawn, and gain tempi — that wins.

sl-6xo.spoken: The pawn rolls forward with king and bishop behind it. White's bishop is frozen — it can't block the pawn, because every move it makes leaves checks or other pawns hanging.

sl-6xw.spoken: The method is simple: push the h-pawn, trade down, and suddenly a passed pawn appears on the kingside. Every exchange Black agrees to only clears the board and brings that passer closer.

sl-6y7.spoken: The a-pawn queens no faster for being passed — it stands alone on the far wing. White's king walks over to meet it, while black's king stays chained to the c-pawn. That chain breaks, and the game with it.

sl-6xs.spoken: The pawn falls to the defender, but the attacker checks and drives the king to the edge. The rook then steps to the third rank and cuts the king off, so the defender must escort the pawn with the king while the rook gobbles whatever it can.

sl-6y4.spoken: The h-pawn push cramps the enemy king and manufactures a passer, yet it often only earns an edge, not a win. The defender must yield ground or give something up.

sl-6xl.spoken: The passed pawn looks dangerous, but the king's activity and the knight's return keep the game level. Only one rook check holds the draw—it forces a fork that wins the knight, then the exchange buys off the pawns.

sl-6z6.spoken: The passed pawn and extra material tip the balance, but the enemy rook’s activity keeps counterplay alive.

sl-6yr.spoken: The pawn push forces the issue, and when the black king moves to defend, a rook check drives him off and the rook falls.

sl-6z2.spoken: The majority creates the passed pawn, and the active king guards it. That frees the rook to slide along the rank and push the pawn forward.

sl-6z5.spoken: The extra pawn demands precision. With the king pushing the passed pawn and the rook guarding, the side down material still generates real counterplay.

sl-6za.spoken: The rook endgame turns on three factors: the more advanced passed pawn, the better king, and the better rook. Black holds all three, and that decides the result.

sl-6yw.spoken: The king escorts the pawn home after first fixing it on its file. The enemy knight cannot intervene because the bishop controls the critical squares.

sl-6zh.spoken: The passed pawn on the far wing is the defender's counterweight. When the stronger side's king marches inward, the defender's own passed pawn balances the threats and holds the draw.

sl-6z3.spoken: The passed pawn plus a helpless opponent is a simple win. Their only hope is to trade into a king and pawn endgame a pawn down, and that still loses.

sl-6ys.spoken: A passed pawn sits on the seventh rank, ready to promote, but the enemy queen and king coordinate to threaten mate. Pushing straight ahead fails; the king must first address the mating threats before the pawn can advance.

sl-6yq.spoken: The defender sits on the promotion square, so White throws the other rook at it from elsewhere. The deflection forces the black rook away, and the passed pawn marches through.

sl-6zg.spoken: The king struggles to attack those pawns from the front. Push the h-pawn instead to create a passed pawn. That forces the opponent to respond, and the counterplay comes from that pressure.

sl-6ym.spoken: An extra pawn that is not passed rarely wins; accurate defense should hold the draw. But if the pawns are split or the defender has weaknesses, the attacker can generate real pressure.

sl-6yk.spoken: The h-pawn falls, and suddenly White owns a decisive passed pawn. The bishop is helpless, stuck on the wrong-colored squares, and the enemy king is too far off. White's king escorts the pawn home for promotion.

sl-6yo.spoken: A distant pawn can act as a decoy. When the enemy king must stop it, your own pawns gain time, and even an advanced opposing pawn may not decide the game.

sl-6yg.spoken: The rook takes the f-pawn, then lands on the seventh rank, where it creates mating threats and clears the path for the pawn's advance. The king joins in, piling more pressure on the enemy king.

sl-6yv.spoken: In the endgame the goal is to create a passed pawn from the central mass. Push the side pawns first to lure the defender's pieces away, then advance the central pawn through the gap and win.

sl-6z4.spoken: A far-advanced passed pawn forces the opponent to park a piece in its path, and that piece is then stuck—its activity is spent holding the line instead of helping anywhere else.

sl-6yp.spoken: The advanced passed pawn is the only life left in this endgame. Push it back a step, and the position turns completely drawn with nothing left to fight for.

sl-6yz.spoken: The pawn marches forward, and the bishop settles on a protected square that blocks the rook's key escape route. Cut off from support, the enemy pawn is forced onward, and the passed pawn promotes.

sl-6ze.spoken: The passed pawns demand the black king's attention, but when the white king lends support, the black king runs out of moves and the pawns roll forward.

sl-6yj.spoken: The h-pawn looks stopped, but White still finds the path to queen. Black refused a draw in an equal position, overpressed, and lost — the danger of declining when the position is level.

sl-6zl.spoken: White's king marches to the center to guard the passed pawn and drive it forward. Black's rook stands pinned to its defensive duty, so White improves the position at will. A pawn push gains space and tempo, but the earlier push was the stronger choice.

sl-6z7.spoken: A passed pawn wants to advance, but pushing it blindly can walk into a perpetual check. Before committing, see if the opponent's checks can force a draw by repetition.

sl-6ya.spoken: The pawn must reach the seventh rank to win. Then the king walks to the sixth and the bishop has no answer. If the pawn falls short, the bishop holds the draw by sacrifice or blockade.

sl-6yt.spoken: The passed pawn looks ready to promote, but the enemy bishop waits on the diagonal to stop it. A preparatory move first—forcing the king to step aside—clears the path, and then the pawn promotes.

sl-6z0.spoken: The rook endgame's real prize is the passed c-pawn, not the open files. Exchange off the c-pawn with the opponent's d-pawn, and that file opens while your c-pawn runs free — worth more than any pawn majority.

sl-6yb.spoken: The king knight advances to hit the knight and eye key squares. If White bolsters the kingside pawn instead, Black's pawn push creates a weakness on the edge. If the knight jumps instead, Black trades into a knight endgame where precise play draws.

sl-6zk.spoken: The passed pawn stands one step from promotion with the king behind it, so the position is winning again.

sl-6yn.spoken: The defender's rook belongs behind the passed pawn, halting its march. The attacker's rook works from the front or the side to push it through.

sl-6zi.spoken: The pawn is the winning asset, so push it instead of trading. Keeping it preserves chances and locks the opponent down.

sl-6zd.spoken: The passed pawn marches, the queen backs it, the king sidesteps every check — and the defender's checks run dry.

sl-6z1.spoken: The passed pawn is the real prize in a rook endgame. A majority that produces none is far less dangerous, so making one is often the whole fight.

sl-6yu.spoken: The pawn push removes the bishop and leaves a passed pawn. With the next push, the bishop is forced to flee, and Black wins material or promotes.

sl-6ye.spoken: The pawn's advance keeps the enemy king at a distance. If the rook comes to defend, the white king steps in front of the pawn, and pushing it forward demands far more support.

sl-6yh.spoken: A passed pawn can look like a draw when your king trails it. Forget promotion — push it as a decoy, drag the enemy king away, and sprint your king to the other wing to eat the remaining pawns.

sl-6yx.spoken: The knight plants itself on the key square and dominates the board. White's extra pawn and king support make the passed pawn a slow but certain threat, leaving Black only slim chances to survive.

sl-6yl.spoken: The king must commit to the winning route. If he hesitates, Black sacrifices a pawn and the g-pawn outruns him — White cannot afford that race.

sl-6yd.spoken: Pawns that close in on the promotion rank become almost unstoppable, especially when the queening squares are guarded. A quiet pawn push on the kingside kills the opponent's counterplay, and once the advance cannot be halted, the game is over.

sl-6yf.spoken: The pawn push probes the kingside. When the bishop captures on that diagonal, the rook cannot recapture, because doing so leaves the pawn on the other wing undefended—and that pawn promotes.

sl-6yi.spoken: The race between connected pawns and separated pawns turns on one question: can the king step in front of the passed pawn, or can the other side hold it off?

sl-6z8.spoken: The passed pawn is the whole game. Black parks the queen with check, then marches the king up to stop it. Queen and king together take the pawn before White's king can get there.

sl-6z9.spoken: Black has three isolated pawns to none, yet may stand better: his passed pawn and blocked majority leave White unable to create a passer, while Black's king enters the game more freely.

sl-6zb.spoken: The extra pawn turns the endgame when the defender's rook is stuck and cannot halt the passed pawn. Even a pawn deficit can win once that pawn is far advanced and queening while the enemy rook just watches.

sl-6zc.spoken: The far-advanced passed pawn queens because the king hides on the pawn's square. One rank back, the king has no shelter and the rook checks forever, drawing.

sl-6zm.spoken: The recapture choice decides this endgame. Central pawn takes are a habit, but here the f-pawn creates the passed pawn, and that outweighs the rule.

sl-70l.spoken: Rooks belong behind passed pawns, not in front of them. That single rule decides which rook move is correct: the rook supports the pawn from behind.

sl-6zw.spoken: The passed pawns are the threat, but the bishop holds them from a distance. Create a decisive passed pawn and strip the bishop of its defensive square in the same move.

sl-704.spoken: The pawn threatens to march and win. The defender must calculate exactly, finding counterplay or perpetual checks to hold the draw.

sl-70b.spoken: The passed pawn is the whole advantage, so push it. Force the king away to defend, then step in and take the weak pawns.

sl-70d.spoken: The passed pawn must be blockaded by the bishop while the king stays confined. If the opponent trades bishops, the pawn endgame may no longer be winning.

sl-70v.spoken: The rook cuts off both the king and knight, so neither can stop the pawns. With the king backing the advance, the endgame is winning.

sl-70q.spoken: Push a passed pawn on one wing, then create another on the other side to overload the defender. But that second push can backfire if it wakes the opponent's pieces up.

sl-70a.spoken: A check that targets the promotion square forces an answer. If they capture, your pawn promotes with checkmate or a winning game.

sl-70k.spoken: The passed pawn reaches the seventh rank, and promotion is the threat. If the rook takes the pawn, a rook check follows, and the black king's bad position decides the game.

sl-70p.spoken: The rook on the back rank is the only practical stopper for the passed pawn. Every step the pawn gains becomes a bigger problem, so the rook must sit directly in its path.

sl-6zz.spoken: The king is stranded on the far edge, so the pawn is safe by distance. The promotion goes through without resistance.

sl-708.spoken: The h-pawn reshapes the whole position, and its threats outrank the material. The rook on the seventh and the pawn's advance weave a mating net, while the pinned knight is a decisive weakness.

sl-6zs.spoken: Pawns against a rook fight by pushing for a passed pawn. Once the pawns are many and far advanced, the rook's reach shrinks and they become unstoppable.

sl-70i.spoken: The rook must not chase pawns here. That tempting capture fails when the knight forks rook and king, and even after grabbing the pawn, the bishop halts the pawn's promotion—sacrificing the knight to force a draw.

sl-6zx.spoken: The king marches around the pawn, not through it. Ignore the hanging pawn and drive the g-pawn forward; the king's path up the board is the fastest way to back the promotion.

sl-6zr.spoken: The bishop pair is gone, leaving a pawn race. The kingside majority runs faster than the king can cross, so counterplay must come from the far wing.

sl-6zy.spoken: The pawn is safe because the enemy king is too far to reach it. White can simply promote it or use it to win material.

sl-70u.spoken: The rook outvalues two minor pieces here, but extra pawns do not win by themselves. Push a pawn on either flank to make a passer; the knights are short-range and cannot cover both sides.

sl-70j.spoken: A passed pawn can decide the game even when the opponent seems to hold drawing chances. Precise calculation decides whether it promotes or drags the enemy king away.

sl-70n.spoken: The rook stops the passed pawn before it can create chaos. Blockading it early keeps the rook free for active play instead of chasing a distraction.

sl-707.spoken: A pawn push can decide a rook endgame. A single step forward creates a passed pawn that nothing can stop, while any lesser move lets the defender trade rooks and escape.

sl-703.spoken: Black keeps the extra pawns and passed pawns, yet the fight stays sharp. White's attack fails against Black's precise calculation and grip on the central squares.

sl-706.spoken: The passed pawns on both wings tie the enemy king to their defense. Trade the bishops, and the pawn ending is simply winning.

sl-70m.spoken: The rook aims at the passed pawn on its march up the board. While Black is forced to stop it, White invades and creates counterplay, turning a lost position into a fight.

sl-701.spoken: The a-pawn pulls the knight away from its outpost. Once the knight is glued to stopping it, the f-pawn drops. The bishop roams free while the knight sits stranded on the rim.

sl-70w.spoken: The rook endgame draw works by pushing a passed pawn on one side, then trading that rook for the enemy's passed pawn on the other side. The result is a king and pawn endgame that holds.

sl-70r.spoken: Push the passed pawn to the seventh rank. The enemy rook must stay glued to the side, the king gets boxed in, and queening threats take over the board.

sl-70s.spoken: The pawn push forces White to capture, and once that trade happens, the passed pawn cannot be stopped. Black decides which pawn advances, but the goal stays clear: keep the white king out of reach, and promotion is guaranteed.

sl-6zu.spoken: The pawn threatens to promote, but the defender has a resource: a pawn move that covers the key squares and sets up a fork if the knight jumps in. That resource must be spotted before pushing the pawn.

sl-70c.spoken: The choice between two knight squares is decisive: one path works, the other lets the enemy knight block the h-pawn. Pushing the h-pawn at once is critical to deny that knight its strong squares.

sl-70o.spoken: The king heads over to back the connected passers. A rook blockades to halt their march, then the king relieves the rook so it can rejoin the fight.

sl-705.spoken: The rook holds the fifth rank, covering the escape square and shutting down the counterplay. The king stays cut off, and the queen's attacking ideas never get off the ground.

sl-70f.spoken: The extra material and the passed pawn do not end the care. The king must walk the pawn forward, the knight stays active, and the blockade is still a threat to stop.

sl-6zn.spoken: The knight ending hides a resource: push the pawn to lure the opponent's pawn forward, then plant the knight to create a target. Later, the knight sacrifice clears the path, and the passed pawn promotes.

sl-709.spoken: A passed pawn must advance. Pushing it creates threats and confines every enemy piece, and once it reaches the seventh rank the defense collapses.

sl-70e.spoken: The bishop arrives too late to stop the pawns. One push of the h-pawn leaves it behind, and the king is out of the square as well.

sl-70g.spoken: The passed pawn is the whole game. If it dies, the win goes with it. The rook must hold the file and keep the pressure on.

sl-6zq.spoken: The king drifts toward the queenside, and the rook cannot stop the passed pawn and guard its own pawn at the same time. That split is the draw.

sl-700.spoken: Queenside pawns gain tempi and push toward a passed pawn that pins the white king in place. With the king tied down, Black breaks through freely on the kingside.

sl-6zt.spoken: The race decides everything when passed pawns run. Even sacrificing one may fail if their pawns are too fast, and the king, too far away, cannot join the block.

sl-70x.spoken: The defender's passed pawn on the kingside forces the attacker to push pawns to block it, even if the king takes one. What remains are passed pawns far apart, and the defense collapses.

sl-702.spoken: The piece is given up to halt the passed pawn. The endgame still turns in the attacker's favor because the pawn is far advanced and the defending king is sealed off from the action.

sl-6zo.spoken: The rook endgame hangs on two passed pawns, each racing to promote. The white rook sits pinned and loose, while the black king stands near the pawn. If the bishop gets a moment, it can cover the queening square, so white must strike now.

sl-71o.spoken: The king stepping off the back rank removes the checking resource, so when both sides queen, the race ends in a draw instead of a loss.

sl-71x.spoken: The fifth-rank pawn beats the sixth-rank pawn and wins even against opposition — unless it sits on the rook file, where the result is a draw.

sl-71p.spoken: When both sides race passed pawns, count the moves before calculating. Blocking the enemy pawn costs the defender tempi, and those wasted moves hand the attacker the win.

sl-71h.spoken: The rook and the passed pawn work together to force the win; the combined threats of check and promotion leave the opponent no defense.

sl-71w.spoken: A rook sacrifice opens a race to the critical square. The defender holds the draw if the king arrives in time, but any imprecision costs the point.

sl-727.spoken: In a pawn race, a check buys a tempo. And when the opponent believes they are safe, a cross-check seizes the initiative and flips the result.

sl-71f.spoken: The pawn push creates a passed pawn that forces the opponent to react. If they capture it, the recapture comes with check and wins material. If they ignore it, the pawn simply takes their pieces.

sl-71v.spoken: The king's shortest route is not always the straight line. A diagonal path matches it in tempi, and the same move can serve a second purpose at once.

sl-71a.spoken: A passed pawn can pull the enemy king away from the defense. Once the king chases it, your own king walks in and takes the remaining pawns.

sl-71s.spoken: The defender has one saving pawn move, and it must come now. Capturing instead hands the opponent a promotion with check, and the game is lost.

sl-71z.spoken: The careless pawn advance lets the enemy king slip between the pawns, and the win turns into a draw. The right push keeps the king out and ends the game on the spot.

sl-71g.spoken: The knight sits strong on its outpost, hemming in Black's army, while the passed c-pawn waits to push forward, seize space, and claim key squares.

sl-71e.spoken: A far-advanced passed pawn can make piece trades into a winning pawn endgame, but only if the king arrives in time to support it.

sl-729.spoken: The king's rank decides the race. When the defender steps off the back rank, the queening pawn skips check, so both sides queen and the game draws.

sl-718.spoken: A passed pawn on the verge of promotion that cannot be stopped is decisive; it fails only if captured on the path to the final rank.

sl-714.spoken: Push the passed pawn as far as it will go. When the enemy king comes to block, your own king or pieces back the pawn, and the advance forces promotion.

sl-710.spoken: Pushing a passed pawn can drive the enemy king to a worse square, and that weakness creates tactical chances.

sl-719.spoken: The rook and pawns work as one, and the pawn keeps marching. White's checks do nothing, and nothing can stop the promotion. Black is in no hurry and just wins.

sl-715.spoken: The king takes the pawn, then escorts the passed pawn up the board. The knight's short legs cannot catch it from across the board, but the bishop's long range keeps it supported.

sl-712.spoken: The central break first clears the path, then the pawn capture and the push turn the wing pawn into a passed pawn.

sl-722.spoken: The king's placement decides this pawn race. Putting it one way lets the enemy pawn advance with tempo and flips the result. A pawn in front blocks the queen's diagonal check, which would otherwise halt the rook.

sl-71k.spoken: A passed pawn plus active king can tip an endgame between a draw and a win. With the extra pawn, choose between playing for victory or settling for safety, and sometimes keeping things messy is the most practical call.

sl-71d.spoken: The race to queen decides the game. The king that stays off the passed pawn while the rook defends buys time, but the side that calculates the exact tempo wins.

sl-720.spoken: Two pawns can outrun three when the opponent's structure is awkward—a blocked king or stale pawn formation leaves them short on tempi.

sl-721.spoken: The king must pick the exact square, not just any near one. The wrong step lets the pawn queen with check, and the queen falls. Only the precise spot holds the draw.

sl-713.spoken: In a pawn race, the more advanced passer usually holds the edge, but exact counting decides whether promotion can be stopped. Sometimes the rook must be sacrificed to block the enemy pawn.

sl-71j.spoken: The rook grabs the passed pawn, then the other rook slides behind the remaining one. That's the standard technique. But the pawn is far advanced, and it ties down the enemy rook to stop promotion, so the position turns sharp.

sl-71n.spoken: The sacrificed pawn is a trap, not a gift. Taking it can lose because the enemy pawn promotes with check, buying time to stop yours. The defender must measure the race before accepting.

sl-70y.spoken: The king is cut off, so he can never reach the key squares. White's pawn creeps forward, the king slides over to block any detour, and the bishop props up the pawn — it's a win.

sl-716.spoken: The pawn races ahead, and the knight cannot stop it alone. When the bishop guards both pawns, the king is too far off to catch the passed pawn. Even trading the knight for that pawn leaves the other one running free.

sl-723.spoken: The pawn race decides this endgame. After the knights come off, count which side promotes first, and whether the king can catch the pawns when they are disconnected or nearby.

sl-726.spoken: The pawn race favors the side with the more advanced pawns—that side queens first. So the player who is behind must steer clear of any trade that turns the ending into a pure race.

sl-71b.spoken: A rook-and-pawn endgame can hinge on which pawn remains. Four against three may be drawn when the extra pawn is blocked and the king has no entry, but when that pawn is passed and the king can invade, the win becomes straightforward.

sl-71c.spoken: The enemy push cracks the position open. Capture first to forge a passed pawn, then drive the f-pawn forward and force the rook away.

sl-71y.spoken: Every tempo counts in the pawn race. The king must choose its square to support the pawns and dodge checks—staying safe outweighs grabbing a pawn.

sl-70z.spoken: The rook slides along the rank to block the pawn’s advance, and that defense can stall promotion—know how to break through.

sl-71q.spoken: The pawns are too many to halt, even at the cost of the bishop. The distant passed pawn is no real threat — too far from promotion — while the closer pawns are already within striking range.

sl-711.spoken: The rook is sacrificed for the knight, and then the passed pawn marches through. The pawn's control of the key square keeps the enemy rook from blocking the promotion.

sl-71t.spoken: The f-pawn advance is no threat while it sits blockaded on its dark square, stuck forever. White lets it be, concentrates on shutting down the e-pawn, and the extra material decides.

sl-71r.spoken: The breakthrough pawn offer forces a choice. Decline it, and the kingside pawns march forward to forge a decisive passed pawn. Accept it, and a pawn race begins that demands exact calculation, since both sides may promote with check.

sl-71l.spoken: Four pawns versus one, two of them passed, and the enemy king is too far off to help. His approach burns tempi, while your central pawns support a quick march forward. Material is equal, but your pawns are far ahead — that is the edge.
