sl-ag8.spoken: Black has no useful moves left; the bishop is trapped on the rim, while White improves the king. Black's bishop covers key squares but also locks down its own army, so White maneuvers freely and the position is lost.

sl-agw.spoken: The perfect defensive setup becomes a liability when it is that side’s turn to move, because any move must disturb the harmony. That is zugzwang.

sl-ag6.spoken: The winning move is precise — White has three king retreats, and one resists longest by steering toward stalemate if the pawn rushes to queen too soon.

sl-afs.spoken: The king stands in zugzwang: every legal move worsens the position, and the only escape leads to mate. His own pawns are the trap—remove any one and the defense holds, at least to a draw.

sl-ags.spoken: The passed pawns make this a race decided by zugzwang. When the enemy king is forced back, the extra tempo lets the decisive pawn push through and win.

sl-agt.spoken: The king-and-pawn endgame turns on who holds the power of choice. When the defender's pawns sit further back, triangulating with the king forces them into zugzwang—they must eventually push, and that push gives you the target.

sl-afy.spoken: The king steps into the dominant square while the rook pins the pawns from behind, freezing them in place. Black must create counterplay now or slip into zugzwang.

sl-agr.spoken: The pawn endgame rewards the side that keeps a reserve pawn on its starting rank. Moving it one square or two buys a tempo, and the opponent, stuck in zugzwang, must give way.

sl-ago.spoken: The rook cuts the enemy king off while the pawn races toward promotion. The rook squeezes the king's space, and zugzwang forces the defender to move, losing the key squares and the game.

sl-ag5.spoken: The king steps onto its most active square, and the pawn push becomes the key to the breakthrough. King and pawn together control the squares around the enemy king, who is forced back by zugzwang.

sl-agv.spoken: The rook is tied to the pawn's defense. Offer the pawn anyway—when the rook takes it, the king slips in on the kingside and the pawns roll.

sl-ag4.spoken: The king stepping onto that square looks natural, but it is a land mine. A pawn check from the side forces the king into zugzwang, the pawn gets in front, and the win slips into a book draw. Stay off the poisoned square.

sl-afn.spoken: The king must lead the attack in minor piece endgames. March it into enemy territory. Here the knight sits trapped on the rim, unable to escape, yet direct attacks fail — the enemy king covers the critical squares.

sl-ag1.spoken: The bishop runs out of room on the sixth rank. It cannot both watch the key square and keep its pressure, so the defender is stuck. Move the bishop and the pawn promotes; move the king and the key square slips away. Zugzwang decides.

sl-afu.spoken: The king is bound to guard that pawn. Step one way and the pawn drops; step the other and the far-side pawns race through. Either move loses, so Black is in zugzwang.

sl-afm.spoken: The kingside holds the winning plan, but Black's extra pawns there demand care. If his own passed pawn gets rolling, the win turns hard. Zugzwang is the key: Black cannot guard the trapped knight and the kingside at the same time.

sl-ag9.spoken: The bishop is pinned to guarding a square, so the enemy king cannot take. That leaves the defender no moves for king or bishop, forcing a pawn push — and the pawn move weakens the position into zugzwang.

sl-afp.spoken: In locked positions, the better-placed king decides. Once the file is sealed, the opponent has no entry points, so passing and waiting wins.

sl-agk.spoken: The king marches to the far side and breaks in. White’s pawn moves run out, and zugzwang hands Black the win.

sl-age.spoken: When the opponent has nothing useful left, zugzwang can force a good piece to trade for a bad one, and the pawn endgame that follows is won.

sl-agu.spoken: Cramp the king to a handful of squares and kill its options. Once it is boxed in, the side to move picks a pawn push that leaves the opponent with no good move — zugzwang.

sl-afv.spoken: The king is forced off the pawn's path, and once the blockade breaks, the pawn advances. The bishop's diagonal is what drives the king away.

sl-ag0.spoken: The king walks the pawn home, and the enemy king is cut off. Every move he makes leads to checkmate or promotion, so the net never closes.

sl-agl.spoken: The pawn push invites the king in — he steps forward and hits the pawn, forcing your king to defend, and then opposition or zugzwang wins the pawn. Or, if your king goes the other way, his king breaks in on the queenside.

sl-agf.spoken: The king is pinned to defending the pawn, and the knights are so tangled that any move drops material. With bishops covering the key squares, Black has no constructive moves left.

sl-afz.spoken: The rook creates a real threat. Black's pawn moves are not passes, because White improves the king while Black shuffles. When the pawns run out, Black is in zugzwang. Steer clear of such positions.

sl-ahm.spoken: The king and rook get tied to their pawns, defending them. Force the opponent into that bind, and they run out of useful moves.

sl-ai9.spoken: In a pawn race, every tempo decides. Force the opponent to step first into zugzwang, and the advantage turns decisive.

sl-ah3.spoken: White is in zugzwang: every move loses. Push the pawn, and the black king is faster, takes both pawns. Move the king away, and the pawn falls.

sl-ah6.spoken: The king steps to the side, forcing the enemy king to give ground. Now Black is in zugzwang: any pawn move drops a pawn, any king move lets White improve.

sl-ahf.spoken: The pawn captures with check. If the pawn recaptures, the rook falls. If the king takes the rook instead, the pawn advances and traps the rook, forcing a zugzwang.

sl-ah0.spoken: A bishop stuck guarding a diagonal can be driven off by zugzwang when it runs out of safe squares, and then the pawns roll forward.

sl-ahy.spoken: The defender's king is pinned to the passed pawn. Zugzwang forces it to abandon the critical squares, and the pawn promotes.

sl-agz.spoken: The rook cuts off the bishop's best retreat, leaving only poor squares. Any move the bishop makes now worsens its position — that is zugzwang.

sl-agy.spoken: The rook harasses the bishop wherever it hides, forcing it onto worse squares. Eventually the defender runs out of moves, and zugzwang decides the endgame.

sl-ahg.spoken: The king lends support while the pawn marches. The rook is tied to blockade duty, and if the defender's king steps away, the pawn promotes.

sl-ai7.spoken: The king is tied to defending the rook, and the rook has no safe square. Every move worsens Black's position — the forced pawn push gets captured, and the zugzwang holds.

sl-ahj.spoken: The rook is the only piece that can move; the knight, king, and pawns are frozen. Every move worsens their position, a zugzwang-like bind.

sl-aht.spoken: The pawn on the seventh changes everything — stalemate is no longer the defender's threat. Instead, the defending king may face zugzwang, forced to a worse square, and the queen slips in to take the pawn.

sl-ahv.spoken: The active king dominates the rook endgame. Centralize it to create zugzwang—the enemy rook is pinned to its pawns, and every move it makes loses material. With no safe squares left, the defender can make no progress.

sl-ahn.spoken: With the f-pawn still on the board, the result flips to a win. White forces it off through zugzwang, since black's rook is pinned to both guarding that pawn and covering the promotion square.

sl-ai4.spoken: The king is boxed in and the bishop is pinned down, so the pawn must advance. The bishop blockades it, black runs out of useful moves, and the knight delivers checkmate.

sl-ai1.spoken: The queen uses the king as backup to put the rook in zugzwang. The defending rook is forced to a passive square, then must abandon its defensive post.

sl-ahe.spoken: The rook is pinned to the passed pawn, but the bishop severs its escape squares. The defender runs out of moves, and zugzwang decides the game.

sl-ah4.spoken: The protected passed pawn is a shield and a sword. Put the defender in zugzwang, and any move they make worsens their position. Force their king to move, and the pawn falls.

sl-ahc.spoken: The rook on the seventh rank tears through the pawns, and the king is exposed. Every move falls into mate or loses the rook, leaving a king-and-pawn endgame that is simply lost.

sl-ahk.spoken: The bishop is boxed in on a short diagonal, with your king covering one exit. Leave the diagonal and it falls; stay and the pawn promotes — the defender has no answer.

sl-ah2.spoken: Pushing the pawn invites the reply that ignores the capture. Taking the pawn lets the defender escape with a draw, but the quiet thrust forward puts the defender in zugzwang, drives the king backward, and secures the win.

sl-ahi.spoken: The pieces are frozen — the rook can't step away without dropping material, and the king has no escape. That's zugzwang: every move makes things worse.

sl-aha.spoken: The king marches toward the knight, and the rook must pick a task. It cannot both halt the king and guard the knight, and the defender falls into zugzwang where every move loses.

sl-ai8.spoken: The bishop blockades, stopping the pawn push from arriving with tempo. Forcing it anyway lets Black regroup, and White must watch the clock of moves. Careless pawn advances can tip into zugzwang and hand Black the draw.

sl-ahx.spoken: The defender’s queen is bound to stop checks, so the attacker creates zugzwang to force it off its post. Once the queen must move, it steps to a square where the king can attack it.

sl-ai0.spoken: The capture looks natural, but taking the knight leaves the black king boxed in and stalemate threatens. The rook must watch both the knight and every escape square, squeezing Black into zugzwang.

sl-ahr.spoken: The king must take the precise path, using shouldering to block the opponent's route, then zugzwang forces them to yield the pawn.

sl-ai5.spoken: The bishop check forces the pawn to block, and now black's rook is trapped with no safe squares. The king is boxed in, and every move costs material — zugzwang wins the game.

sl-ahq.spoken: The knight is stalemated, locked down by the stronger knight. Black is left with only king moves or pawn moves on one flank, which gives limited options. White can burn reserve tempi to outmaneuver and take over.

sl-ahh.spoken: The defender's bishop holds the long diagonal and covers too much ground. Force it onto a shorter diagonal where the squares run out. Control the key squares along the path, and the defender runs out of moves—zugzwang decides, winning the bishop or the pawn.

sl-ahz.spoken: The spare pawn move is the weapon. It forces the defender's king to step onto a losing square, and the zugzwang decides the endgame.

sl-ahw.spoken: Both kings are chained to their pawns, and every move one side makes loosens its own grip. That mutual tying turns the endgame into zugzwang.

sl-ah1.spoken: Black must avoid zugzwang. With no kingside pawn moves left, White drives the black king back, trades off the f-pawn, and marches to the queenside to clear the rest.

sl-ah8.spoken: In this endgame with same-colored bishops, the turn to move decides everything. If it is your turn, you may face zugzwang and be forced into a concession; if it is the opponent's turn, the blockade holds.

sl-ah7.spoken: The bishop has everything covered—the key pawn, the invasion square, and the restraint on the enemy king. Any move breaks something, so zugzwang forces Black to weaken his own position.

sl-ahp.spoken: The rook trade leaves White with a waiting move that forces Black to weaken. If the king steps aside, a check wins a pawn; if the rook leaves, the pawn comes under attack. The waiting move is pure zugzwang.

sl-ai6.spoken: Two defensive ideas: guard the pawn's path, or step around it. Either way, White's pawns shrink the king's space until zugzwang decides.

sl-ai2.spoken: The defender's king is chained to a pawn, so every waiting move forces it to yield. That zugzwang hands over the pawn, and the win follows.

sl-ahu.spoken: Zugzwang: every move Black has makes things worse. Any pawn move lets White take it, and any bishop move lets White push the h-pawn forward.

sl-ah5.spoken: The bishop drops to the long diagonal and forces Black to advance pawns. White then builds a fortress, Black’s king hits zugzwang and cannot approach the f-pawn, so White collects the pawns and escorts the f-pawn home.

sl-aig.spoken: Fix the weakness, improve slowly, and the defender reaches zugzwang: every move damages their own position.

sl-ajl.spoken: The king is the decisive piece in opposite-colored bishop endgames. It drives pawns forward and locks down the defender, overpowering the drawish nature of the position.

sl-aik.spoken: The bishop freezes the enemy king in place, then the king marches over to back the pawns and finish the job.

sl-aiu.spoken: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, a draw is common, but piece activity still decides. If the defender activates the knight and creates counterplay, they can hold.

sl-aif.spoken: Rook pawn and bishop pawn against rook pawn follow the same principles. The stronger side wins by advancing the rook pawn one square or two, keeping the defender in zugzwang.

sl-aj7.spoken: Rooks and opposite-colored bishops together is not the pure bishop endgame, so the trade into it is no easy call.

sl-aih.spoken: The fortress is a trap, not a fact. Promoting at once may only draw, so find the move that passes the turn instead — zugzwang forces the defender to weaken their own position.

sl-ajh.spoken: Opposite-colored bishops and a mirror pawn structure turn the position into a dead draw — neither side keeps any winning chances.

sl-aj9.spoken: The knight is trapped, crippled by the closed position, and the king cannot come to its rescue. Trading the bishop for that knight risks opposite-colored bishops, which would turn a win into a draw.

sl-ajj.spoken: The king and bishop lock the dark squares, and the bishop covers every entry point. Black must drive one piece back or find play on the other side to get anywhere.

sl-ajk.spoken: The bishop of the wrong color cannot help the pawn promote once it is blockaded. Set the blockade on the light squares, and trade rooks to cut down White's winning chances.

sl-aj3.spoken: The extra pawn, the isolated pawns, and the attack on the king give Black a clear edge. Opposite-colored bishops often draw, but not here.

sl-aiy.spoken: The knight and bishop form a perfect blockade against the passed pawn, while the opposite-colored bishops keep the king at bay.

sl-aji.spoken: The extra pawn is the f-pawn, worthless here. Black’s two connected passed pawns loom, but opposite-colored bishops hand White defensive resources that same-colored bishops would never allow.

sl-ail.spoken: Two connected passed pawns face an opposite-colored bishop. If the defender plants that bishop directly in the pawns' path, the enemy king freezes in place — but the attacker must still crack the blockade to win.

sl-aib.spoken: The rook and knight work together to box in the queen, and every escape square gets covered. The queen has almost no safe squares, so Black runs out of moves and the position collapses.

sl-aip.spoken: The bishops rule opposite colors, so the defender’s bishop can never fight for the squares the attacker controls. That lets the attacker’s king slip in while the defender’s king stays tied down.

sl-aj6.spoken: Opposite-colored bishops make this endgame tricky — the defender can stop passed pawns on their bishop's color. But three extra pawns still leave Black clearly winning.

sl-aiv.spoken: The rook and the bishop belong to different colors here, so the extra pawn still gives real winning chances. The defender's pawns sit exposed, and the attacker can crack open multiple weaknesses to convert.

sl-aia.spoken: The knight dies in the corner. A waiting move puts the opponent in zugzwang, forcing pawn pushes until the knight runs out of squares.

sl-aj2.spoken: The dominant bishop and the passed pawn give White a nearly decisive edge, yet one wrong move can forfeit the win. Precise maneuvering is what turns the advantage into the full point.

sl-aie.spoken: The king steps aside quietly, avoiding all checks and passing the turn. The enemy king is boxed in, so the queen must move, but she cannot hold that key square without losing material.

sl-ajf.spoken: The king stands before one pawn while the bishop patrols the long diagonal to hold the other. Together they restrain both pawns and keep the enemy king out.

sl-aid.spoken: The opponent has no good move—zugzwang forces them to damage their own position. Every pawn push or piece step opens a weakness, and once a key square is exposed, the knight jumps in and traps the queen.

sl-aix.spoken: The bishop colors split the board, and passed pawns run on both wings. A distant pawn pulls the defender away, and then the far-side pawns roll forward.

sl-aim.spoken: The pawn break is the whole game here. Push it only when the enemy bishop cannot give itself for the pawn, and let the king back it up while your own bishop keeps the defender off the key blockading squares.

sl-aje.spoken: The king's activity looks real but may not decide anything here. The weak pawn can be held if the king gets near it or another piece covers it.

sl-aio.spoken: The bishop owns the diagonal and freezes every white pawn in place. Bring the king up now, but step carefully so White never finds counterplay.

sl-aiz.spoken: The rook recaptures to keep the pawn chain whole, turning the c-pawn into a fixed target. From the adjacent files, Black's rook pounds that pawn from both sides.

sl-aii.spoken: The queening square is a trap — it ends in stalemate or a fortress. The bishop alone keeps winning chances by covering the critical squares and dodging those drawing mechanisms.

sl-aj1.spoken: The bishop is pinned to a defensive duty, and that duty is the whole position. Any move that relieves it lets the passed pawn advance, and any capture lets it promote. The defender loses either way.

sl-ajd.spoken: Opposite-colored bishops make extra pawns treacherous — the endgame turns drawish when the defender's bishop controls squares the pawns must cross. A favorable pawn structure keeps the win alive, but every move must be exact.

sl-ajc.spoken: The extra pawn alone cannot decide this locked opposite-colored bishop ending because Black has no weaknesses to attack. The task is finding a plan that creates a second weakness.

sl-aic.spoken: Zugzwang: the opponent must move, yet every legal move worsens their position until the queen is trapped or mate lands.

sl-ais.spoken: The defender's bishop stays on the diagonal that cages the enemy bishop. Once that bishop slips free, the game is drawn even when the pawn falls.

sl-ajb.spoken: The bishops are an obstacle, not a fortress — opposite colors lock the position, but the outside passer and active rook keep real winning chances. Put the rook on the seventh.

sl-aja.spoken: Rooks and opposite-colored bishops usually suggest a draw, but not when one side is better. The rooks sharpen the attack, and the opponent's weak pawns become fixed targets.

sl-aiw.spoken: The d-pawn looks dangerous but is actually weak. The real fight is the bishops: if the white bishop reaches the central outpost it dominates the board, while the black bishop stays passive.

sl-ait.spoken: Opposite-colored bishops turn a two-pawn advantage into a draw. The defender builds a fortress by putting the bishop directly in front of the pawns while the king supports the blockade.

sl-aj4.spoken: Do not assume this ending is a draw. The extra pawn, the passed pawn on the sixth, and the more active king give White genuine winning chances.

sl-aj5.spoken: A bishop that cannot attack the king's square is toothless. The defender parks the king on the opposite color, and the bishop can only watch while its own pawns are held.

sl-aj8.spoken: Rooks in opposite-colored bishop endgames change everything. That extra piece manufactures threats and counterplay no bishop alone can match, so what looks drawn can turn sharp for the defender.

sl-ajg.spoken: The rook lunges forward, but that is not the winning idea. It lets Black swap rooks and land in a drawn bishop endgame. The pawn on the rim is the real defense — it buys Black just enough counterplay to hold.

sl-aj0.spoken: A protected passed pawn anchors the attack. When bishops are opposite-colored, the active bishop shields the pawns while the enemy bishop sits passive, and the rook-and-bishop pair overwhelms the defender.

sl-ajy.spoken: Three connected passed pawns outweigh the drawing tendency of opposite-colored bishops.

sl-ajn.spoken: The further-advanced passed pawns and the more active king tip the balance. Opposite-colored bishops favor the attacker—the defender's bishop simply cannot fight for the key squares.

sl-akf.spoken: The extra pawn counts less than piece activity in opposite-colored bishop endgames. Safety and activity decide more than material.

sl-aka.spoken: When down a pawn, hunt for opposite-colored bishop endgames — the extra pawn often cannot win, and the draw is within reach.

sl-akp.spoken: In opposite-colored bishop endings, a pawn deficit is not defeat. Active counterplay holds what passive waiting would lose.

sl-akl.spoken: Separated pawns stand on different-colored squares, so they cannot cover each other. The defender attacks each one alone, and the draw comes easily.

sl-ajm.spoken: The extra pawn is neutralized. The bishop blockades the passed pawn, and the king comes up to defend, so the win evaporates into a draw.

sl-ajt.spoken: The bishop is trapped on its side of the board. Keep it boxed in—if it reaches the key diagonal, the defense holds and the position is drawn.

sl-akm.spoken: The defender’s king sits centrally and the bishop stands behind the pawn, so the attacker’s king cannot push through the middle. Progress demands another route around the solid setup.

sl-akn.spoken: The bishop holds two fronts when the pawns sit close, but once they spread apart, one bishop cannot guard both sides at once.

sl-ajz.spoken: The bishop swap grabs a pawn and steers the game into an opposite-colored bishop endgame. The extra pawn and the active king tip the balance, and the final bishop move seals the win.

sl-aku.spoken: The bishop stands wrong on that diagonal, letting the enemy king slice through to the queenside. It belongs on a line that controls the entry square and blocks the king's path.

sl-ak5.spoken: The bishop alone holds the defense. Its job is to keep the black king off the key square that wins the pawn and the game.

sl-akx.spoken: The bishop holds the draw from a square where it both guards the pawn and keeps checks available. From a poor square, the defense collapses and the win becomes reachable.

sl-ako.spoken: The rooks keep this opposite-colored bishop ending alive. A pawn up with rooks on the board offers real winning chances, where a pure bishop endgame would drift toward a draw.

sl-ak8.spoken: Opposite-colored bishops make this look drawn, but the blocked pawns are the real story: none can queen, and the lone passed pawn is easily stopped. The engine calls it a draw, yet a human can still find winning chances.

sl-akc.spoken: The position stays level because the pawn structures match and the bishops work on opposite colors. Those bishops steer the game toward a draw, so even after the tactical fights, the assessment stays even.

sl-ak9.spoken: The bishop's color decides the endgame, not the board position. A good bishop supports the passed pawns when the promotion square matches its color, turning what looks like a draw into a win.

sl-ajq.spoken: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, the defender's pawns sit on squares the bishop can guard, so one weakness is never enough. You must create a second weakness or pile attackers onto the first.

sl-akj.spoken: The advanced pawns create tactical threats, so the defender stays alert. A king step toward them looks tricky, but a precise reply holds the draw. Moving the bishop away surrenders the pressure and lets the pawns run.

sl-aks.spoken: The bishop belongs in front of the pawns, not behind them. From there it eyes the key pawn and holds the chain back far more effectively.

sl-akt.spoken: The bishop’s best square flips with the task. Against connected passed pawns, place it in front to block their march. When hunting enemy pawns, put it behind them to strike from the rear. These two rules pull in opposite directions, so judgment decides.

sl-ajv.spoken: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, an extra pawn often only draws, but mistakes make it miserable for the side with the edge. Control of the open file and a dominant knight give the stronger side lasting initiative.

sl-ajo.spoken: The bishop endgame looks winning, but the extra pawns do not guarantee the point. With the black pawns fixed on the bishop's color, they are hard to touch, and the black bishop can blockade the connected passed pawns, holding the draw.

sl-ake.spoken: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, pawns on the enemy bishop's color get blockaded, so keep them off that color. Win by checking the enemy king from afar, then marching the pawns up with the king behind them.

sl-akv.spoken: The bishop must stand on the right square to meet the pawn push. From the correct diagonal, it controls the key squares and holds the draw; from the wrong square, the pawns roll forward and win.

sl-akh.spoken: The bishop must defend both squares at once: the point where the pawns stop and the backward pawn behind them. That pressure keeps the enemy king from escorting the pawns forward.

sl-ak1.spoken: The defender's king must hold the critical squares to block the attacker's king from breaking in. Pushing the h-pawn is the precise resource—it fixes the pawn structure and locks the enemy king out of key entry points.

sl-akk.spoken: The defender's own bishop gets trapped when the king moves forward and the enemy king steps in to cut off its escape. Keep the bishop back on the safe square, and the blockade holds.

sl-ak7.spoken: The bishop pins Black down on both wings. It holds back the pawn break, the king stays chained to defense, and if Black tries to march the king to support the pawn, White's king slips in on the other side. The material edge demands exact play.

sl-ak6.spoken: The bishop stands guard on the diagonal, blocking the enemy bishop's path to its key square, and the draw is secure. Or park it on the other diagonal, and opposite-colored bishops make the draw dead, since neither can challenge the other's critical squares.

sl-ajw.spoken: Opposite-colored bishops raise drawing chances dramatically, even a pawn down. Simplification lets the defender hold, with the bishop covering the critical squares.

sl-ajs.spoken: The king and bishop dominate the board, and the lone pawn drives the opponent into a mating net — opposite-colored bishops and thin pawns cannot save them.

sl-aju.spoken: The pawns may outnumber, but the defender plants them on the bishop's color and holds. Here the win comes from a mating net, not from pushing the pawns through.

sl-akb.spoken: With no pawns on the board, opposite-colored bishops alone cannot force a win. Only precise queen play can convert—by exploiting the exposed king and the bishop's short reach.

sl-ak3.spoken: The defender’s bishop blockades the passed pawn and holds the key diagonal shut. Force that bishop aside or trade it off, and the blockade breaks, letting the pawns roll.

sl-akr.spoken: Material advantage means little here: the defender blockades the passed pawn and trades away attacking chances, turning the engine's plus score into a fortress draw.

sl-ak4.spoken: The dark-squared bishop is worth more than that knight. Trading it leaves opposite-colored bishops, a routine draw where the defender parks the king and uses the bishop to shield the pawns, making progress impossible.

sl-ajx.spoken: The weak pawn is the only target, and every other pawn is blocked. The defender's king does more work from the far side: it covers the entry squares and guards the weak pawn far better than from the nearer square.

sl-aki.spoken: Failure to attack the backward pawn lets the enemy king come up and push the pawns, creating winning chances. Yet a blockade may still be possible if the pawns haven't advanced too far.

sl-akd.spoken: The bishops work on opposite colors, so the defender can hold a draw while down material. A fortress forms when king and bishop cover the squares the pawns must cross, and the opponent's bishop can never touch them.

sl-ak2.spoken: A passed pawn on the fifth rank is nearly home in opposite-color bishop endings. The defender’s first try is to attack it from the front, not from the side or behind.

sl-ajr.spoken: Connected passed pawns on the sixth rank decide the game. Let them advance unblocked, and the bishop cannot hold them back — the endgame is lost.

sl-akw.spoken: The bishop parks on the diagonal to watch the critical squares and wall off the king. That same square also stops the knight from landing the decisive check, making it the ideal post for the variations.

sl-akg.spoken: Two connected passed pawns meet opposite-colored bishops: the defender wants them blockaded on the lighter squares. Pushing them to the darker squares costs nothing for the attacker, yet that path runs into a blockade and turns a win into a draw.

sl-ala.spoken: The pawn’s key square is the one the king must attack to force the pawn forward. Once the king gets there, the push wins a black pawn no matter where the black king stands.

sl-alo.spoken: A rook for a knight can turn winning when the opponent is boxed in — with the king, knight, and pawn all trapped, only one legal move remains.

sl-alc.spoken: The pawn on the sixth rank decides the endgame. The attacking king steps in front, drives the defender away, and the pawn marches on while the bishop blocks checks. One square shifts the verdict from draw to win.

sl-am7.spoken: The bishop strikes the pinned piece, and once the pawn recaptures, the rook slides to the back rank for unstoppable mate. The king’s checks are only spite before the net closes.

sl-alx.spoken: Sacrificing a piece to stop a pawn from promoting is only worth it if the resulting position gives real counterplay.

sl-al8.spoken: The king eyes the entry square, but stepping in early lets the opponent push the pawn and seize the opposition. From the adjacent rank, the king keeps both entry paths alive, and the defender runs out of useful moves.

sl-am0.spoken: Material sacrifices can be risky, but in the endgame, the chance to promote a pawn can justify the cost.

sl-ald.spoken: The bishop guards the entry square the rook needs. While that square stays covered, the opponent can’t break through, and the position stays frozen.

sl-al4.spoken: The passed pawn fixes the enemy king in front of it, blocking its path. White’s king tries to approach, but the black king opposes and refuses to yield. Correct maneuvering uses outflanking or a spare pawn move to force the black king to give way.

sl-akz.spoken: The bishop takes away the squares the king needs to reach the corner. With that escape cut off, the king is boxed in and the win follows.

sl-al0.spoken: The bishop must choose the right diagonal: one move blocks the enemy pawn's promotion, the same move clears the path for our own pawn to advance.

sl-am4.spoken: Sacrificing the pawn with the recapture creates a triple pawn on the file. Counterintuitive, but it draws: the opponent must spend pawn moves that break their own plan.

sl-aky.spoken: The exact drawing square decides the result. On one rank the position holds, on the next it may collapse. The bishop must sit on the square that controls the key points and locks out the enemy king.

sl-al9.spoken: The rook drives the lone king toward one of two key squares, and from either one the king backs the pawn while staying safe from bishop checks.

sl-ale.spoken: The four squares that wrap around the king are the key to the mating net. Any square farther away is too distant, so the king cannot reach them in time.

sl-am6.spoken: Black offers material to stir up counterplay: the king steps forward, the knight recaptures and reroutes, and a pawn is sacrificed for activity.

sl-alr.spoken: The knight sacrifices itself on the critical square; the bishop must take it and leaves its post. The pawns roll forward with nothing left to stop them.

sl-alb.spoken: The king holds the escape square, so the check cannot be dodged there. The pawn's absence keeps the neighboring square open for the king's route.

sl-am9.spoken: The king is boxed in, but stalemate looms. Sacrifice the bishop to force a capture that unblocks the defender, then the mating net closes again.

sl-al2.spoken: The study demands a precise move order: the defender's drawing setup must be stopped before it forms. Force the pawn forward or turn the advantage decisive before the defense settles.

sl-alk.spoken: The extra pawn means little with opposite-colored bishops — the draw is always near. But the king can infiltrate on the queenside and pick off the weak pawn there, while a kingside attack goes nowhere.

sl-alz.spoken: The attacker spends pawns to build the mating net or push a pawn home. Sacrificing pawns drags the enemy king into position, then the bishop delivers mate and the defense must answer the threat.

sl-alu.spoken: The rook faces two bishops in the endgame. Trading the rook for a bishop loses, but giving up a pawn to reach a drawn fortress is the right defense.

sl-alv.spoken: The rook offers itself to the enemy rook. If the offer is taken, the bishop recaptures, and the king-and-pawn endgame that follows is winning when the opposition can be secured.

sl-alp.spoken: The b-pawn is a sacrifice that awakens the rook and turns it toward the undefended kingside pawns. That attack produces two connected passed pawns, and the position is winning.

sl-ali.spoken: The king must choose his route with care. Heading to the natural square lets the enemy keep the opposition, but stepping to the correct side first approaches the pawns from the right angle and wins it.

sl-al6.spoken: The key square must win from any reasonable enemy king placement. One square may fail if the king can force a retreat, while another wins because it guarantees progress.

sl-al3.spoken: The king wants out through its one free square. Seal that square so the piece stays trapped — if it escapes, the win becomes a draw.

sl-am5.spoken: The rook gives up the a-pawn to bring the king to life. Once the king joins the kingside, the pawns link up, take the h-pawn, and roll forward as connected passed pawns that win the game.

sl-alt.spoken: The bishop lands with check, and the opponent must capture it. That capture removes a defender and opens the line for your pawn, making it the key resource that stops the enemy pawn from promoting.

sl-al1.spoken: Each side of the pawns is a different fortress. When the bishop stands on the wrong diagonal, the king chases it off, and the pawn walks through to promotion.

sl-all.spoken: The drawing plan starts with a pawn push that blocks the white king’s invasion route. That stop matters more than trading pawns, because the white knight can deal with the outside passer if given time.

sl-aln.spoken: The bishop sacrifices itself on the mating square to drag the king forward. Your king then steps through the gap the bishop opened, and once it settles there, the enemy cannot easily drive it out—the result is a decisive advantage.

sl-am2.spoken: The knight is one step short of mate. Pushing the pawn clears the path and opens lines, forcing a capture that hands the knight its mating square.

sl-al7.spoken: The king's square decides the win. If the attacker stands one file short, the enemy king forces a retreat and the win slips away. From the stronger file, the win holds no matter where the defender stands.

sl-aly.spoken: A knight sacrifice for a pawn or a passed pawn tempts, but fails when the opponent blockades and consolidates. Then the loss is material without compensation.

sl-am8.spoken: Activation is worth more than a pawn. Trade the material to bring your pieces to life, rather than stay passive while the opponent strengthens their position.

sl-am3.spoken: The sacrifice deflects the enemy bishop and clears the pawn's path. If the bishop accepts, the pawn rolls forward to promotion.

sl-als.spoken: The side with the extra rook still must act. A bishop sacrifice that pulls the defender’s pieces away turns a fragile advantage into a decisive threat.

sl-alf.spoken: The rook pawn changes things: the comfortable key square shifts, but even the less ideal one wins, because the critical square lies just one step further. The winning idea stays the same.

sl-alh.spoken: The king route matters: stepping through the center keeps the defender's bishop off the key diagonal. Take the other path, and the bishop slips in and the win turns into a draw.

sl-alg.spoken: The pawn sits too far back and the defender locks the key squares with checks and bishop shuffles. The king can never be forced out, so the win slips away.

sl-alj.spoken: The king circles wide to reach the critical square, and the defender runs out of moves. With the rook trapped and no safe square left, zugzwang decides the game.

sl-alq.spoken: Sacrificing the bishop for the final pawn turns a losing race into a draw, as long as the king can reach the queening square in time.

sl-am1.spoken: Sacrificing the rook on that square pulls the enemy rook away, then the check lands and the loose bishop or the pawn about to promote falls.

sl-alm.spoken: The king marches toward the kingside, climbing through g-file squares to break in on the flank. A pawn distraction on the other side buys the time needed. Once the king enters, the defense collapses.

sl-ams.spoken: The bishop must stay on the diagonal that hits the pawn from behind. That pin keeps the passed pawn frozen in place.

sl-amr.spoken: The bishop acts as a fence, controlling key squares along its diagonal. A simple shuffle along that line keeps the enemy king from breaking through.

sl-amg.spoken: The knight gives itself up to pull the defender away, and the h-pawn runs free. Once the king is dragged out of place, the pawn cannot be stopped.

sl-anl.spoken: Advancing one square defends the pawn; advancing two lets the attacker capture it for free.

sl-an2.spoken: The bishop locks the long diagonal and cages the enemy king. Then the king walks over and takes the pawns.

sl-amh.spoken: The rook is pinned to the back rank, so the bishop offers itself to deflect it or buy a tempo. Once the bishop is captured, the king chases the rook down and the pawn promotes.

sl-amm.spoken: Give up a pawn to push a passed pawn far up the opposite wing, and the defender can't stop it.

sl-amj.spoken: In a complex rook endgame, the side to move gives up a pawn to rip open lines and aim real threats at the enemy king and rook. A deep combination, but it rests on one simple tactical pattern.

sl-amv.spoken: Trading pawns on the kingside helps the defender by shrinking the rook's targets. One passed pawn against two offers more drawing chances than none against one.

sl-amk.spoken: The rook gives itself up to pull the king onto a square where the follow-up check wins material or forces mate. The sacrifice creates a threat the opponent must answer, and the king's new position is the whole point.

sl-anc.spoken: The king walks in and forces the bishop to flee, then grabs a pawn. If the bishop recaptures, the king steps forward and takes more pawns.

sl-amf.spoken: The knight sacrifice for a pawn looks reckless, but it creates a passed pawn that cannot be stopped. The knight strikes an enemy knight that is pinned in place and unprotected; if the capture is taken, the pawn recaptures and pushes forward.

sl-amp.spoken: Doubled pawns usually hurt, but in a passed-pawn race they can help. The front pawn can sacrifice itself to capture the enemy bishop, and then the trailing pawn takes over the march to promotion.

sl-amn.spoken: The fork forces a blocking move, and the king steps into a key square to weave a mating net.

sl-amq.spoken: The trap collapses when the king marches to the rescue and shoves the pawn forward to break the cage. The doubled pawns that remain are a draw, because the advanced pawn hands the defender a fortress.

sl-amw.spoken: Trade the pawns away and the extra one vanishes — the win goes with it. The opponent's whole plan is simplification toward a draw.

sl-an0.spoken: The king or rook sidesteps fail—the rook either takes the pawn with check or holds the draw. Board geometry decides: squares that look distant can be equal in chess distance.

sl-an4.spoken: The bishop locks the diagonal that guards the pawn’s escape square. To free the pawn, the rook must either block that diagonal or drive the bishop off it.

sl-anf.spoken: A capture opens the position but splits the pawns into three islands, cutting the f-pawns off from the queenside. That weakens the structure and leaves those pawns hard to defend or push.

sl-an6.spoken: The bishop is perfectly placed, guarding every vital square. Cut off the king’s route so it cannot interfere with the black king’s advance.

sl-amx.spoken: Trading pawns shrinks the defender's material and raises drawing chances. Even a pawn move that looks ugly works, because it forces exchanges and steers into a more comfortable endgame.

sl-amd.spoken: The bishop lands on the square that attacks the king's escape. The king retreats, and now the defender of the knight is overloaded. Giving up the bishop deflects that knight, and the passed pawn rolls forward.

sl-ang.spoken: The pawns are split into multiple islands, which is usually a drawback. But the position earns its keep through initiative and active pieces aimed at Black's weak points.

sl-ank.spoken: Pawns shuffled before the king look risky, yet they hide a plan to double rooks on the open file. But they also pin the knight: if it steps away, the rook behind it falls.

sl-an1.spoken: The king's path matters more than the pawns. Heading the wrong way lets the bishop sit on its key diagonal and freeze them forever. The king must circle to the queenside, sidestepping checks that drag it back to guard the pawn.

sl-an7.spoken: The attacker must march the king over to block the rook from reaching its drawing square. Only that king move wins, while any other move lets the defender set up the Vančura fortress.

sl-an9.spoken: The pawn on the fourth rank forces the stronger side into a dilemma: keeping the enemy king off the h-file blocks a fortress, but that same guard duty pins down their own king. The two tasks collide, and progress stalls.

sl-amo.spoken: The h-pawn is a dead end. Grabbing it instead of the central pawn leaves too little material to convert, and the defending king forces stalemate or perpetual check.

sl-anb.spoken: The king must not approach the pawn. The wrong first move lets him reach the sixth rank, where the stalemate defense appears. The right move keeps him at distance and converts the win.

sl-ame.spoken: Giving up material to freeze the opponent's knight turns the endgame into a holding pattern. That restriction cancels their activity, making the position easier to draw or win.

sl-anh.spoken: The bishop retreat is a trap, not a defense. Capturing the pawn hands the opponent counterplay by exposing your own pawn, and holding the line with the bishop invites a tactical sequence that drops material.

sl-amt.spoken: Trading pawns cuts your winning chances when too few remain. Capturing here bleeds the position dry and turns a win into a draw.

sl-amu.spoken: The bishop sacrifice for the final pawn is a classic defensive trick in opposite-colored bishop endgames. If the opponent grabs that pawn, the king wakes up and generates counterplay, so that winning attempt fails.

sl-amc.spoken: The rook on the edge is a sleeping piece. Sacrificing a pawn wakes it into active duty. The defender gains checks, the enemy king is driven across the board, and counterplay erupts while the opponent's rook stays passive.

sl-an8.spoken: The position wins theoretically, but the technique is delicate. Force the enemy king away from the pawn — if it stays close, it defends against promotion.

sl-ama.spoken: The knight checks near the king, forcing the king to take it, and the king then mates on that very square. The king stands in front of the bishop to cover the escape squares, and that control makes the mate work.

sl-an5.spoken: The bishop on this diagonal pins two enemy pawns to their advance squares at once. The king marches over to block one while the bishop holds the other.

sl-amb.spoken: The rook is thrown in as a sacrifice, deflecting the bishop or forcing capture. Either way the pawn promotes, and the threat also keeps the bishop off the queening square.

sl-amy.spoken: A central pawn traded for a flank pawn can win if it sets up a later trade that leaves two passed pawns far apart. That gap makes the defender's bishop helpless against both.

sl-ami.spoken: The rook is under attack and the pawn is one step from queening with check. White must start with a forcing rook check that gives up the rook, turning the threat into the key.

sl-ana.spoken: When a rook endgame leaves the defender's king trapped on the back rank, the stronger side must bring their own king forward. If that king stays passive, the position leans toward a draw, as the defender's rook can generate perpetual checks or pick off pawns.

sl-an3.spoken: The bishop retreats along the same diagonal to stop the enemy king from crossing. The rook checks, then attacks the bishop, but the king must not step toward it—stay near the pawn, and the bishop holds the line.

sl-amz.spoken: The king must take the precise route, not the direct one. Going straight in lets the defender build a fortress, with the king tucked in the corner and the bishop shuffling to sacrifice for the pawn. Instead, cut off the king's access to that drawing zone.

sl-ani.spoken: The pawn push opens the position to strike at the e-pawn. The reply keeps everything closed, turns that pawn into a protected passed pawn, and plants a weakness in return.

sl-aoi.spoken: Closing the position hides the opponent's weaknesses, but it also traps his bishop for good — a heavy positional price.

sl-aoq.spoken: Black seals the kingside, and White's breakthrough chances vanish. With a pawn up and threats on the queen side, Black keeps the pressure.

sl-aoe.spoken: The rook belongs on the more promising file. In this closed structure the d-file rarely opens, while the c-file offers real chances after the usual pawn exchanges.

sl-aou.spoken: The knight steps back instead of pushing the pawn, anticipating a closed center. In King's Indian structures, trading the light-squared bishop favors White.

sl-aos.spoken: The bishops outshine the rooks in this closed position, giving them the long-term edge. With the dark-squared bishop gone, the kingside turns fragile.

sl-aog.spoken: The wrong rook slides to the g-file, leaving its twin passive and the center unguarded. One more strategic slip stacked on the earlier ones.

sl-ao2.spoken: The rook looks to the open file, but the better square guards the pawn and backs the pawn break. The obvious choice is natural; the right one is subtle.

sl-aod.spoken: The rook belongs on the file that is likely to open, not the one that stays closed. Place it where future captures or a piece trade will clear the path.

sl-anz.spoken: The rook parks on the third rank, shielding the weak pawn and guarding the key square so no enemy knight or queen can land there. It also clears the way for the queen to slide onto the file when needed.

sl-ao6.spoken: The rook opposes the queen directly, and the move looks so odd the opponent suspects a blunder. That suspicion alone provokes mistakes.

sl-aok.spoken: In this locked position, the attacker doubles rooks and pushes the b-pawn to blast through, while the defender runs out of useful moves and can't stir up counterplay.

sl-aov.spoken: In a closed structure, the central pawn grants White lasting space. There is no immediate win, only a patient improvement of the position.

sl-anw.spoken: A rook that pushes deep into enemy ground without backup can turn into a liability, especially when it sits far from the action.

sl-ao8.spoken: When doubling on an open file, pick the rook whose pawns can move in front of it. A rook stuck behind a fixed pawn has less flexibility.

sl-ao4.spoken: The queen's aggression meets resistance, but the rook's placement decides the fight. On the back rank it blocks the queen's retreat and keeps tactical answers ready, so the opponent's counterplay falls flat.

sl-anp.spoken: The queen hits the pawn from the side, but the rook shifts over, ready to slide along the b-file. Then the rook comes back to the same file it left, admitting the first move was wasted.

sl-aor.spoken: Sacrificing the rook on the closed square opens dark-square dominance. After the recapture, knights and bishops take over while the rooks stay useless.

sl-anr.spoken: The rook owns the open file and backs a pawn break. If that break comes, the capture opens the diagonal and leaves the bishop hanging.

sl-ao1.spoken: Development gives White a small edge, but the plan matters more. Target the sixth rank, where Black’s pawns are weak. Rooks on the seventh rank find nothing there.

sl-aof.spoken: The rooks belong on the central files to finish development and back up the pawns and pieces. When Black pushes the queenside pawn, White answers on the same wing, but the supporting pawn must step first so no weakness appears.

sl-ant.spoken: Rooks slide onto the central files where pawns are about to clash, ready for the files to open. One rook steps between, breaking the pin on the knight and setting up the double-rook battery.

sl-aon.spoken: White has castled, so the center is his to open. Black's bishop presses the king, but the defense holds fine — no panic, just the long-term cost of Black's misplaced time.

sl-ao7.spoken: The first rook had a defensive job. Moving it opens a hole in the kingside. The other rook was the one to activate—keeping the defender on the back rank preserves the pawn.

sl-ao5.spoken: The rook steps onto the same file as its partner and blocks the road. The file is opened later, but this move gets there too early and caps the rook's potential.

sl-ano.spoken: The choice of rook to the open file is decisive. Bringing the far rook over leaves the other one idle and exposes the kingside to knight and pawn attacks. The near rook keeps every piece active and shields that weakness.

sl-ao0.spoken: The rook you move to the open file decides your defense. The far-side rook keeps the near-side rook at home, ready to shield the king if the file opens or pressure builds. The tempting rook looks stronger for attack, but the quiet one holds the fort.

sl-anq.spoken: The rook sits on the fourth rank to block the opponent's pawn break with tempo, while aiming at the king's files. That pawn becomes the target, and winning it is the only path to victory.

sl-aoj.spoken: In this French structure, White keeps a slight edge by holding the center closed while Black hunts for counterplay on the kingside. White's job is to refuse the opening, keep the pawn chain intact, and maneuver pieces behind it.

sl-aoa.spoken: The rook slides to the middle file, a quiet move that props up the bishop and trains its sights on the central pawn once the opponent pushes their flank pawn. Watch for the enemy bishop left loose on the long diagonal—some lines hang it.

sl-aop.spoken: In semi-closed positions knights outshine bishops, and the fianchettoed bishop stands especially poorly.

sl-aoh.spoken: The rook belongs on the open file, where it backs the push. With the knight pinned and the king still at home, that placement is the whole point.

sl-aom.spoken: In closed positions, bishops often sit useless behind their own pawns while knights hop over. When the bishop becomes a target, the opponent trades it off and leaves its owner at a lasting disadvantage.

sl-anx.spoken: The rook commits to the wrong file and keeps the pressure alive. The other file fights for the key square and could crack the opponent's position open.

sl-anv.spoken: The rook pins itself to the pawn and the capture square at once. If the pawn is taken, the recapture comes with the pawn, and the follow-up push breaks through.

sl-aob.spoken: Rook to the open file backs a pawn capture that leaves the opponent with hanging pawns. If they trade in the center, the recapture lands cleanly, and the rook stays pointed at their queen and the doubled target.

sl-anu.spoken: The bishop trade leaves White's fianchetto bishop unopposed. The pawn advance shores up the kingside, then the rook doubles pressure on the open file, aiming at the weak pawn at its base. The other rook stays ready to support a central break.

sl-ao3.spoken: The f-rook looks natural, sliding off the bishop's line, but bringing the other rook is the precise choice.

sl-aox.spoken: The closed position keeps Black worse but not lost, since entry points are scarce. White must find a breakthrough, yet direct tries can backfire.

sl-ao9.spoken: The rook belongs on the open file, but the other square readies the f-pawn break. The h-pawn thrust tempts, yet the enemy rook simply slides over to meet it.

sl-aoc.spoken: The bishop stands well, but the rook sits awkward on an open file. Moving it to the back rank to support a kingside push keeps the file open for pressure.

sl-aoo.spoken: Black closes the kingside, and that hands White firm control of the key square in front of it. The knight drops in behind the pawns, the king tucks safely next to it, and the center is ripe for opening.

sl-ans.spoken: The rook earns its place on the open file by guarding the pawn that wants to advance and leaving the other rook ready to back a pawn push on the opposite wing. With no immediate threat, the rook sits safely where it is.

sl-apx.spoken: Repeating moves or playing without commitment feeds the opponent time and information.

sl-aq4.spoken: Deny the opponent's desired plans at every turn. When they fail to block your ideas, the advantage builds itself step by step.

sl-ap3.spoken: In a closed position, mistakes cost less because tactics move slowly. Still, principled play—development and castling—remains the goal.

sl-aq8.spoken: The game was won by refusing to rush and watching for any hint of counterplay, then shutting it down every time.

sl-aq9.spoken: Pressure, inch by inch, piles up until even a super grandmaster cracks.

sl-aoy.spoken: In a closed position, castling loses urgency. Both sides improve piece placement and seize space instead; pawn pushes on one wing expand, while the bishop and rook on the same file prepare counterplay.

sl-apd.spoken: Closing the position with the pawn push is principled when development lags, because it shuts down the opponent's attacking lines and buys time to finish mobilizing.

sl-apc.spoken: A knight stuck on the rim is not a weakness if it can be rerouted. Black wants piece trades to relieve the pressure, but White has a better plan than swapping everything off.

sl-apu.spoken: Keep their pieces dead. Even with a winning position, if the opponent's pieces come back to life, mistakes happen — so leave them no moves.

sl-apz.spoken: Anticipate the opponent's plan before choosing your move. Stop what they want to do first, then act.

sl-apn.spoken: In equal positions, even strong players often sit back and let the opponent press slowly—when the right move is to find active play and fight for the initiative.

sl-apf.spoken: After the capture sequence, White advances the c-pawn, but Black answers by pushing the d-pawn, shutting the center and blunting White's development edge.

sl-api.spoken: A move that looks like a pawn blunder is actually a trap. If the pawn is taken, a rook fork wins material outright. Even strong players lean on tactics like these to hold the balance.

sl-apk.spoken: The knight forges ahead to the outpost, and from there it eyes the weak pawn while backing the central push.

sl-apj.spoken: The knight can go for a tactical fork or simply capture. The capture trades into an endgame where Black's bishop is bad and the knights dominate.

sl-apt.spoken: Patience itself becomes the weapon. Quiet developing moves put the burden on the opponent to find a plan, and hasty pawn pushes tend to backfire over time.

sl-aq5.spoken: The enemy never interferes with the plan, so each idea goes through unchallenged.

sl-ape.spoken: The center is locked, so no pawn break will open it. White's edge in development is useless unless it finds another way through.

sl-aph.spoken: The rook looks tempting, but the trap is set — stepping in lets it get cornered. Avoid the complications and strike at the structural weaknesses instead.

sl-ap4.spoken: A slow position forgives slow moves. Rerouting the knight to a stronger square costs several tempi, but that is fine here — even if the opponent stops it, making them respond spends their time, not yours.

sl-aq6.spoken: Prophylaxis is the mark of a world-class player: spot the coming threat and prevent it before it exists. A quiet pawn move now stops the opponent's pawn advance, cutting off their counterplay before it starts.

sl-apb.spoken: The knight sits on a deep outpost that costs the opponent too much to dislodge. If the bishop ever steps away, the queen turns to the light squares or the pawns, and Black's advantage becomes crushing.

sl-ap5.spoken: The bishop trade leaves Black's pawns damaged, but the closed position shields the king. White needs a breakthrough, and a sacrifice may be the key to open lines.

sl-aps.spoken: The knight finds a strong square, eyeing the long diagonal where Black's bishop holds the position. From there, a bishop move to the center becomes powerful, and a queen swing to the flank targets the rook and stirs up threats.

sl-apa.spoken: The pawn push slams the door shut, stranding the knight on the rim. Black stays cramped, while White keeps a lasting space edge and attacking chances.

sl-apy.spoken: Even with a winning position, the opponent can still have sacrificial threats. Prophylaxis means seeing those ideas in advance and stopping them before they appear.

sl-aq2.spoken: The a-pawn advance stops the bishop from pinning the knight, a key modern idea that works no matter how the opening was reached.

sl-apm.spoken: The c-pawn advance creates a target and abandons a key square, killing Black's counterplay. Retreating with the b-pawn shows hesitation, giving up the active push that would have freed the c-pawn and kept drawing chances alive.

sl-ap2.spoken: In a closed opening, the center locks down and direct attacks stall. The key is repositioning pieces to stronger squares, not forcing tactics.

sl-aq1.spoken: The bishop pins the knight to the king, and the queen joins the attack on the same diagonal. The defender must interpose with her own queen, but that only delays the mate — the threat is renewed on the next move.

sl-ap8.spoken: The knight steps out to offer an opening instead of the pawn. Black pushes the pawn, and when White answers, Black's reply gains tempo while keeping the position sealed. Black's job stays locked on containment, never chasing its own pawn breaks.

sl-ap0.spoken: A quiet developing move gets challenged on the spot and looks awful. Play something active instead and force the opponent to make an immediate choice.

sl-ap6.spoken: Pushing the pawn to attack the knight leaves a hole behind it. After the knight retreats and reroutes, that weak square stays vulnerable. In a closed position, the lost tempo is no punishment.

sl-apg.spoken: Closed positions allow slow, unhurried preparation; open positions demand quick development. Here, the slow push is safe because the position stays closed and the opponent's setup remains unresolved.

sl-apw.spoken: When the board quiets, players drift. The same rules still hold: no threat from them, find your weakest piece and bring it forward.

sl-ap9.spoken: In closed positions neither side breaks through easily, so the work is restriction. A pawn move on the flank is less a plan of your own and more a lock on the opponent's activity.

sl-aq3.spoken: The knight jump looks aggressive, but it fails when the opponent gains center pressure. The better path pairs the attack with prophylaxis.

sl-apq.spoken: The queen steps into the attack and threatens the pawn, forcing a defense. Once the pawn falls, the two-versus-one majority on that flank becomes the real prize, because those pawns can roll forward.

sl-apr.spoken: The queen offer attacks the pawn, forcing Black to respond. The other tries — the bishop route and the pawn storm — create pressure, while the knight move is slowest, giving Black time to develop.

sl-apo.spoken: The knight belongs on the active square, not babysitting a pawn that needs no defense. Swing the rook to the c-file instead, ready to double on the open line.

sl-aq0.spoken: The win came from relentless pressure, not a single blow. Constant problems made the position awkward and narrowed every option.

sl-apl.spoken: The knight's natural square is passive. The active choice opens the center, gives the knight more scope, and invites a pawn fight even at the cost of defending the e-pawn.

sl-apv.spoken: The pawn controls a key square, shutting the knight out of its best post and leaving the opponent short on activity.

sl-app.spoken: The king and bishop have sharper options than quiet retreats. A bishop can come out actively and settle on a strong central square, while a pawn sacrifice opens lines for a knight jump that gives real play for the pawn.

sl-aql.spoken: Natural moves can carry hidden traps. Improve the piece, set the threat, and strike if the opponent overlooks it.

sl-aqb.spoken: In slow endgames, think beyond your own setup—imagine how your opponent will attack it, and seek improvements for both sides.

sl-aqi.spoken: The game shows the classic grind: create a weakness, deny counterplay, and convert the edge at a slow, relentless pace.

sl-aqv.spoken: The king's move does double duty — it prepares a useful square while quietly neutralizing a threat that only appears after a precise sequence.

sl-aqa.spoken: Constant pressure breaks balanced positions down. The defender stays alert for tactics, while the attacker piles on threats and quietly improves the position.

sl-ar6.spoken: Castles are not a luxury. Leave the king exposed and even strong tournament players can be gone in a handful of moves.

sl-aqe.spoken: The pawn move earns its keep not by starting a storm, but by denying the enemy a key square, narrowing their choices.

sl-aqc.spoken: The pieces barely cooperate, yet the win is there. Squeeze the position dry and deny the opponent any hint of counterplay.

sl-aqf.spoken: Random moves let the opponent strike back and mate your exposed king.

sl-ara.spoken: The locked structure suits the player who knows prophylaxis. Black wins not by flashy ideas but by quietly stopping White's plans while the bishops stay hemmed in.

sl-ari.spoken: The exposed king tempts you to check at once, but the hasty check often fails. Wait, find the real idea, and strike when the pattern is fully formed.

sl-are.spoken: The king move that answers a check can act as a waiting move: it costs the opponent a tempo, because their threat evaporates and they must start over.

sl-ar5.spoken: The stronger idea wins: stop the threat, not just play your own plan. When the opponent's danger is real, defense outranks your move.

sl-ark.spoken: Build the position piece by piece, provoke a weakness, then strike. The pressure alone cracks the opponent, and even the endgame that follows is already lost.

sl-arh.spoken: Patience wins blocked positions: maneuver your pieces until the opponent errs, rather than forcing a breakthrough.

sl-aqu.spoken: The position turns without a single flashy move. One side stacks small edges, and the opponent’s natural replies slowly sink the position until it is lost.

sl-aqy.spoken: Ignored threats come back as punishments. Leave a problem untreated and the game turns into a loss.

sl-aqj.spoken: The bishop retreat looks passive, but it earns its place through the coming pawn push. Its pressure is prospective, not immediate.

sl-ar0.spoken: The player sees only his own attack and ignores the opponent's threat—that blindness decides the game.

sl-aqx.spoken: A winning position must not allow counterplay — especially a queenside passed pawn that could turn the tables.

sl-aqh.spoken: The slow squeeze trades nothing for everything: each small gain stacks until the opponent is tied up and bleeds material without a single tactical blow.

sl-ar7.spoken: The king takes the pawn, the pin stays, and the extra material converts. No rush to grab the other pawn; the pin is worth more than the pawn.

sl-ar4.spoken: The king is boxed in the corner, and the threat is the pawns joining forces. One prophylactic pawn move keeps them apart and holds the bind.

sl-aqs.spoken: The dominant position asks for no forcing line. Find the piece doing least work and bring it forward; the tactics will come on their own.

sl-arc.spoken: The solid, passive side must suffer under sustained pressure. Even the best defenders crack when fatigue or the clock joins in.

sl-ar1.spoken: The piece shuffles back and forth, baiting White into pushing kingside pawns. Those tempi are a fair price for the structural damage they inflict.

sl-aqn.spoken: Patience is a weapon. When both sides are locked down, the opponent often cracks first and tries something risky — that move becomes your opportunity.

sl-aqt.spoken: When the opponent has no active threats, stop searching for deep calculation. Their pieces can only shuffle, so the task becomes recognizing that and finding a plan.

sl-arf.spoken: The king is already on its way in, and moves like these just rearranged the furniture. They ignore the penetration and leave weak squares behind.

sl-aqr.spoken: Fixing the weakness only works if the bishop gets there first. Otherwise the pawn becomes a target that ties you down instead of a strength.

sl-ar2.spoken: A quiet, lasting edge is all you need. Improve piece by piece, no tactics required — just the right plan and steady pressure.

sl-aqm.spoken: The knight was meant to reach its strong square in time, but the delay let the opponent's knight leap forward first. The punishment is still there: capture and transform the pawn structure in your favor.

sl-aqw.spoken: The pawn push cramps the opponent's queenside and shuts down their counterplay before it starts. It also makes the defensive square on our own side far less appealing, so the whole flank stays quiet.

sl-ar8.spoken: The rook slides sideways, not forward — a quiet move that neither checks nor captures. The natural push looks stronger, but the lateral square keeps more options alive, preparing the next step along the rank.

sl-ard.spoken: The opponent’s pressure never lets up, offering no counterplay and no path back into the game. Even when the position is not clearly losing, the defender is left to grope for moves with no relief in sight.

sl-aqd.spoken: When winning, look for your opponent's ideas before your own. That guard against traps is what keeps the advantage yours.

sl-arg.spoken: No threats on the board and Black nearly paralyzed means White owns the clock. Improve the position methodically, and there is no reason to rush into complications.

sl-ar9.spoken: If the opponent has no moves, grabbing material is not always best. Take only if you can clear their pieces—otherwise, leave them paralyzed.

sl-aqz.spoken: The problem on the board must be answered now. Delay lets it grow into punishment; here, the b-pawn advance would drive the knight back and eventually win material.

sl-arb.spoken: The structure holds and the bishops stay passive, so the long-term outlook is sound. The task is to block White's play, not to start your own.

sl-arl.spoken: The win is not in flashy tactics—black's position is already worse. Apply steady, lasting pressure instead of slow maneuvers.

sl-aqo.spoken: When a pawn steps forward, it may not be defending anything—it may be clearing a square for a piece. The opponent wants the square, not the pawn.

sl-aqg.spoken: The space advantage lets one side shuffle pieces, refining the setup while the opponent waits with no useful plan.

sl-arj.spoken: Stopping a move your opponent would never play wastes a tempo. Worse, the pawn structure change can actually make that move good for them.

sl-aqp.spoken: The endgame itself was the surrender. Reaching it forced the defender to find one long, exact line just to draw — a result that should never have been required.

sl-as9.spoken: A bishop trapped behind its own pawns contributes little. Active pieces coordinate attacks.

sl-as1.spoken: When the bishop owns the long diagonal and the pawn storm is no real threat, the defender calmly tucks the king to safety and then strikes at the center.

sl-as5.spoken: The bishop gains a powerful diagonal once the pawn advances, pressing Black's setup and forcing concessions, possibly including an exchange.

sl-as3.spoken: The bishop stays safe and holds its diagonal, so we can keep developing our other pieces. If the knight advances to challenge it, we still have answers.

sl-ase.spoken: The bishop tucked behind the pawn chain sits idle. The one on the active diagonal aims at the enemy king, ready to check and feed the attack.

sl-arr.spoken: The pawn advance controls the critical square, stopping the knight from jumping in and harassing the bishop. That is prophylaxis — it keeps the light-squared bishop active.

sl-aru.spoken: In quiet, boring positions, the stronger player leans on memory and experience instead of calculation. The weaker side should avoid that kind of game.

sl-arv.spoken: The key to the position is not brute calculation but reading the real danger—king safety. Only one quiet move wins, and it is far from obvious.

sl-arm.spoken: The threat comes first. Answer it, but if you can answer while keeping your own threat alive, the initiative stays yours and the pressure never lifts.

sl-asi.spoken: The bishop lands deep in enemy territory, perfectly placed. The rook lifts to the seventh rank, and mate threats follow one after another.

sl-asc.spoken: The bishop owns the long diagonals. Because the pawn stands one square forward, the knight finds a way in, and Black's pieces stop working together.

sl-arp.spoken: The queen steps early to dodge a pin that never lands, reading the bishop's threat and answering it before it exists.

sl-asm.spoken: The bishop stares at a wall of pawns, biting on granite with no useful targets. Regroup the knight to the strong center instead, softening the loss of the other bishop.

sl-asq.spoken: The bishop retreats off its natural diagonal. Keeping it on that line keeps pressure on key squares and stops the opponent's bishop from landing on its best square.

sl-as8.spoken: The bishop finds a safe home on the strong diagonal. Black faces a critical choice: trade queens or keep them on, and that decision shapes the whole middlegame.

sl-as2.spoken: The bishop is clearly the better piece—it presses on many squares while Black's stays home. The a-pawn is a target, but not one that can be taken right away.

sl-asl.spoken: The light-squared bishop is the player to watch — it reaches active diagonals with real pressure, while the rival bishop stays passive and struggles to find useful work.

sl-arn.spoken: The rook slides to the first rank to close the door on the queen's landing square. That is prophylaxis—stopping the opponent's plan before it starts.

sl-ars.spoken: Over-defend every piece and seal every entry point, then march the king forward. The defender runs out of useful moves and can only wait, and that waiting breaks them.

sl-art.spoken: Trading into an endgame works when you know the position better, not when you are rated higher. It means steering the game to the ground where your understanding gives you the edge.

sl-asg.spoken: The bishop change reshapes the whole board. When one side’s bishop sits weak and the other’s commands a strong diagonal, the weak side wants to trade—but the strong side dodges the exchange.

sl-arx.spoken: The pawn push leaves the dark-squared bishop stranded. White's pieces step into ideal squares, and a knight on that central outpost bears down on both key weaknesses.

sl-asr.spoken: The bishop lands on a passive square where it does little. With the center square denied, the way out runs along the long diagonal, and the bishop should head there instead.

sl-asw.spoken: A bishop buried behind its own pawns waits for a pawn break. One push opens the diagonal, and suddenly the bishop stares down the line at the enemy king.

sl-arz.spoken: The bishop lands on a passive diagonal. It attacks nothing and cannot retreat to cover key squares. Black's pieces are frozen, tied to defending pawns, and the position becomes zugzwang.

sl-arw.spoken: The knight is stuck behind its own pawn, and that blockage is the whole point. This line has been played by the very best, and the idea runs through countless top-level games.

sl-ash.spoken: The bishop takes that pawn, and when the recapture comes, White's bishop takes control of the light squares, dominating the queenside—even if Black grabs a few pawns in return.

sl-asf.spoken: The bishop holds the key squares together. If it gets traded, Black’s weaknesses fade. So keep it, or offer the trade only on your terms—swap it while keeping the pressure on.

sl-ass.spoken: The knight reroutes to a stronger square, but the pawn push exposes the bishop to attack. If the bishop takes the pawn, the enemy pawn and knight combine to win it back or leave lasting weaknesses.

sl-asv.spoken: The bishop slides to the far corner, commanding the diagonal and fueling the attack. White stands better on both wings, with a stronger king, rook, minor piece, and an extra pawn.

sl-asu.spoken: The bishop retreats to a passive square and abandons the queenside. A better square keeps it active, but that active post invites a pawn push, and the intended recapture with the knight fails to tactics.

sl-asx.spoken: A knight posted forward looks active, but it stands exposed to being chased off or caught by tactics aimed at it. Its apparent threats are hollow, because the opponent answers with a strong move that turns the knight's own position against it.

sl-as4.spoken: A bishop planted in the center can disrupt White's harmony, the way it does in Catalan setups. That piece becomes a stronghold, and Black may follow by challenging the queenside with a pawn push.

sl-asn.spoken: The pawn advance looks tempting, but it blocks the bishop’s long diagonal and hands the opponent a comfortable outpost. The quieter push keeps the bishop’s line open, so the knight develops and the bishop slides into its fianchetto afterwards.

sl-arq.spoken: The bishop retreats as a prophylactic move, stopping the pawn break by preparing a clamp on it, and keeping the bishop off the bad diagonal. If the pawn advances anyway, White takes it and leaves the opponent pinned on the file, losing material.

sl-asp.spoken: The bishop to the more active square presses on the king's weak point along the long diagonal. The defender's natural block creates doubled pawns, but the opponent can simply castle first and leave that offer on the board.

sl-asj.spoken: The bishop stands on an open diagonal with real prospects, while the rival bishop stays locked in. That imbalance grants Black lasting freedom of movement.

sl-as6.spoken: Black's setup is strong, yet the knight eyeing the central outpost demands respect. The pawn chain suits Black, but the light-squared bishop bites on granite behind its own pawns.

sl-aro.spoken: Chasing flank play lets the opponent seize counterplay on the opposite wing, and that activity may be just enough to hold the game.

sl-asd.spoken: The active bishop outshines the passive one. It stands on strong squares and influences the board, while the enemy bishop sits back and does little.

sl-asa.spoken: The light-squared bishop is boxed in until the pawn break opens its diagonal. Once free, it bears down on the enemy kingside and queenside, while the opponent's dark-squared bishop stays passive.

sl-ast.spoken: The bishop finds a strong diagonal and presses on the king. Pinning by putting the bishop there forces the opponent to give up that diagonal.

sl-aso.spoken: The bishop heads for an open diagonal, and the defender slides a piece in to block. When that block is driven off, the advancing pawns and the king join the attack, and the game ends fast.

sl-att.spoken: The rook takes, but the queen simply steps away, and the capture fails because the queen no longer guards that square.

sl-at3.spoken: The knight's attack on multiple points looks dangerous, but a pawn push questions it. Forced to retreat, the pressure evaporates and the threat dies.

sl-atg.spoken: The bishop pins the knight and pressures the king. The queen chooses between two squares—one invites a trade that helps the opponent, the other stays safe.

sl-atw.spoken: The queen is the hardest piece to place. Put it on a safe square where it still controls the open files, out of reach of attacking pieces.

sl-atp.spoken: Early queen activity turns reckless when enemy pieces share her line, handing over discovered attacks and checks.

sl-atv.spoken: The knight trade leaves the queen stranded on an open file where rooks can challenge her. She needs a safer square.

sl-ati.spoken: The queen is not forced to retreat — Black answers one attack with another, but the counterattack fails to defend, and the queen is simply captured, losing material.

sl-at2.spoken: The rim knight has only four squares to choose from, while the central knight has eight. Posting it on the edge shrinks its control over the center, and the opponent seizes the initiative with a central pawn push.

sl-at5.spoken: The knight on the rim is offside and cramped, while the same piece on the central file has flexible routes into the game and stands better placed.

sl-atz.spoken: Moving the queen when it is attacked often concedes tempi and improves the opponent's position, turning a small threat into a worsening situation.

sl-atn.spoken: The bishop attacks the queen, and blocking with a knight fails—two pawns guard the bishop, so the recapture is lost. Pushing the b-pawn opens lines, which hands Black's bishops targets.

sl-at1.spoken: The knights sit stranded on the rim, unsupported and exposed once the center cracks open. The bishop is loose too, but grabbing it with a knight only opens lines, lets the pawns roll, and hands the attack more fuel.

sl-au6.spoken: The attacker activates everything while the defender has no counterplay. Losing the light-squared bishop here creates lasting problems, even when the damage is not immediate.

sl-aty.spoken: The queen's aggressive check is only sound if other pieces back her up. She never goes on a solo mission.
