sl-asy.spoken: A knight out on the rim is usually badly placed and can't pressure or protect the critical pawns. The two fixed pawns sit side by side, weak together — when one falls, the other typically goes too.

sl-atl.spoken: The queen looks trapped, but retreat is not the only answer. The stronger resource wins another piece instead of saving her, and the material advantage grows.

sl-at8.spoken: The knight lands badly, and the pawn advance punishes it. A better square would have kept the central pawn in check while the knight stayed safe.

sl-at6.spoken: The knights sit exposed to pawn pushes that drive them back. Once they retreat, the weak pawn loses its defenders and falls, leaving a lasting structural edge.

sl-atc.spoken: The king steps correctly, and the knight's options shrink. It can sit on squares that block the pawn's advance, but that leaves it tied to guard duty. White keeps pushing and forces the knight to stay put.

sl-au7.spoken: The knight still isn't free — that pawn push becomes a target. You ignore it and proceed with your own plan, eyeing the weak square it left behind.

sl-atf.spoken: The queen sidesteps the e-file pin and eyes the open file. Greedy pawn grabs invite trouble—the queen gets trapped or hands Black dangerous counterplay.

sl-atb.spoken: The knight is misplaced on the edge—the outpost it eyes is blocked by its own pawn, so the move merely stops a knight from landing there, and that landing was never a genuine threat.

sl-ats.spoken: The queen is attacked after the capture. Retreating it is right, but one safe-looking square is a trap — the knight jumps in and forks king and rook.

sl-asz.spoken: The knight sits poorly on the rim, and the pawn push looms. Black chooses whether to fix the knight now or deal with the threat later.

sl-atj.spoken: The rook harasses the queen, but the queen sidesteps to safety, still free to flee. The fight stays sharp, yet Black holds the winning plan.

sl-at9.spoken: A knight on the rim can look active, but without pawn support it is easily chased. A rook pawn push drives it back, and the square it wanted becomes unreachable, leaving it stranded.

sl-ato.spoken: The queen steps onto the open diagonal, and White eyes it as risk. Black pushes the pawn to make room for the bishop, but the bishop belongs on the other square — defending the pawn that now hangs.

sl-ath.spoken: The queen is chased to a cramped square because stepping to the natural escape square lets a pawn push open the position, attacking the queen and unmasking a second threat against the king's pawn.

sl-au8.spoken: The center pawns look powerful but are fragile. Once the pawns trade off, the rook slips through the gaps. The bishops and knight are alive, so the central advantage is an illusion.

sl-at7.spoken: A knight stranded on the rim is not dead, but it must find a way back in. The weak squares around it let the opponent build pressure and turn the misplaced piece into a real advantage.

sl-atd.spoken: The knight on the rim looks trapped, but a retreat squares it away for later. Meanwhile, the bishop occupies the center and the knight reroutes through a quiet square to rejoin the fight.

sl-au5.spoken: The misplaced knight has no good square, so it cost the opponent positionally. The practical try is to centralize your own knight, even into a tactical line that gives up a pawn and keeps the bishop pair.

sl-atr.spoken: The queen may grab that pawn, but the board is hostile. A knight or bishop can chase her down, and with a rook waiting on the open file, the pursuit turns fatal.

sl-atu.spoken: The queen tucks behind the knight and pawns to guard the piece and set up castling. When White harasses the queen, watch the diagonal for checks and threats—sharp play follows, with mate tactics in the air.

sl-au3.spoken: The queen's raid on the pawn looks tempting, but a pawn push traps her on that file. With no safe retreat, she gets boxed in, and the bishop slides over to sidestep any perpetual check.

sl-atk.spoken: The pawn thrust strikes the queen and the king at once. If the king captures, the rook checks from the corner and the queen falls, so the queen must flee to a safe square, and every retreat carries its own hidden cost.

sl-au2.spoken: The queen steps forward to a risky square, chasing a phantom threat instead of castling. She sits exposed in the open, where every tempo spent harassing her is one the opponent gains.

sl-au0.spoken: The queen must find a safe square after the sequence. Placing it where it pressures a vulnerable pawn is better than a passive retreat, because it keeps the opponent’s pawns under fire and sidesteps immediate threats.

sl-au4.spoken: The queen sits badly on the rim, opening the door for a pawn push that wins material. The file beside her is a trap — a rook behind the pawns supports a queen invasion that boxes her in.

sl-au9.spoken: The pawn push cracks the kingside open and makes the e-pawn a target. The knight jumps in to hit that pawn and the h-pawn square at once. When the defender blocks one threat, the h-pawn advances to tear the shelter apart.

sl-atx.spoken: The queen stands exposed on a file shared with the rook while pieces remain crowded. A safer square ends that vulnerability.

sl-ata.spoken: The knight is the key attacker, aiming at two weak squares and keeping the pressure on. The pawn push fails to answer it, so the knight keeps its outpost and the target stays real.

sl-atq.spoken: The pawn push forces the queen to choose between two squares. One lets the rival queen slip in behind the king, so she takes the other, staying active while closing the door.

sl-at4.spoken: The h-pawn push is the most popular answer because it kicks the knight back and keeps the position closed. Developing instead lets the opponent advance the f-pawn and stir up threats.

sl-atm.spoken: The knight shields the queen. Castle first, then push the pawn to chase the bishop. Black's pawn break aims to trap it, but trading bishop for knight is often better—the bishop has little future behind dark-squared pawns.

sl-au1.spoken: A queen that lands exposed can be chased and trapped. Keep it on safer squares like the back rank, where it stays secure.

sl-av7.spoken: The attacker must plan around the defender's pawn break — a forward push can carve an escape hatch for the king, unraveling the net.

sl-aut.spoken: Two weak pawns sit on opposite flanks, hard to defend together. Threats against both force the defender into difficult choices.

sl-av5.spoken: The queen alone cannot finish the job. Bring the rook or knight in to cover the escape squares and turn pressure into mate.

sl-av1.spoken: The bishop gives up the key diagonal, and the queen steps in to attack the exposed pawn from a dominant square.

sl-avb.spoken: Three pieces stack on the same file, and the bishop guards the mating square. The queen is the strongest piece for the finish, but she must be brought in with care.

sl-aum.spoken: The first target gets defended, so White switches to the next weakness. The pawn near the king is exposed, and that becomes the new point of attack.

sl-av3.spoken: When the king sits exposed, the scoreboard stops mattering. Three pieces swarming the king can force mate without ever evening the material count.

sl-av0.spoken: The pawns on both flanks are falling, and the bishop pair dominates. Black's pieces are simply better.

sl-aur.spoken: The king is exposed and several pawns hang loose. The opponent holds control, trades only when it serves them, and keeps the pressure on. Every option left is a lesser evil.

sl-aui.spoken: The bishop is active and the rook pressures the weak pawns. Together they create threats down the file and along the diagonal, and the opponent's structure cannot hold.

sl-avj.spoken: The king is exposed and the heavy pieces are ready on the open files. The rook threatens mate on the h-file, forcing a response, while a pawn push opens more lines and keeps the attack rolling.

sl-aup.spoken: The pawn capture creates two pawn islands to attack, while White keeps a single island. The knight could have held the tension, but now the structure is fixed and vulnerable.

sl-ava.spoken: The defender reaches for tactical tricks like pins to hold off the attack, but the attacker accepts material losses. The pieces develop to create mating threats that cannot be stopped.

sl-auc.spoken: The pawn advance opens a hole in the kingside and invites attack. The queen and rook swing into action, while the knight sits pinned and the queen must stay glued to defending it.

sl-avk.spoken: The king is boxed in on the kingside with few escape squares, so mating threats loom. The bishop retreats to cover the key checkmate square, keeping the attack alive while shutting down the rook's threat.

sl-avg.spoken: The pawn push opens a mating net around the trapped king. One rook waits passively while the advancing pawn threatens a decisive mate on the next move.

sl-avf.spoken: The bishop checks, forcing the king to the back rank. The rook checks again, driving it to the corner. Now the bishop slides over, cuts off escape squares, and threatens mate.

sl-auo.spoken: The rook lift to the second rank can leave the f-pawn exposed, especially when the f-file is open. The other rook may end up stuck or out of play.

sl-aua.spoken: The pawn advance on the queenside is a weakness, not a threat. It lets White push the g-pawn as a tempo, driving the queen back, and suddenly the a-pawn matters more than the one on the other wing.

sl-av6.spoken: The queen checks, forcing the king to its only legal square. The knight is then sacrificed to dominate the back rank and seal the escape squares, leaving the king just two squares to shuffle between.

sl-avc.spoken: The queen captures on the edge of the board. Black cannot grab the knight, because the bishop climbs to the diagonal and mates — a standard puzzle finish.

sl-aux.spoken: A queenside pawn push leaves holes behind it and a soft pawn on the edge. The knight jumps into the empty squares, attacking the pawn and the weakened outposts.

sl-auk.spoken: The weak pawns and active pieces are the story here — Black's king is exposed, the knights and queen dominate, and the position rewards White with a steady edge.

sl-auz.spoken: The pawn thrust in the Stonewall weakens the light squares around the king. The knight hops in to hit the holes on both flanks, and once the king steps out, the bishop joins the attack and the exposed monarch pays.

sl-aue.spoken: The passed pawn alone may not break through—solid defense can hold it. When progress stalls, attack other weaknesses on their side, like a pawn left exposed on the edge.

sl-auv.spoken: The pawn structure is cracked and the bishop is shut out, leaving Black uncomfortable. White piles onto the weak pawn, then advances the f-pawn and plants a knight to squeeze harder.

sl-av4.spoken: The quiet move sets up an unstoppable mate threat: the pawn advances to deliver mate. If the king retreats, a fork punishes it; if the queen is captured, a skewer check wins her back.

sl-auu.spoken: The pawn move opens the king’s flank but offers no target to seize. With White’s pieces already trained on that side, the advance hands over new squares to strike.

sl-ave.spoken: A king trapped in the corner with an open file and a queen hovering creates an immediate mate threat: the knight removes the defender, and the queen delivers mate on the last rank. The opponent must answer it at once.

sl-avd.spoken: The king shuffles to the corner to stay clear of the queen's path to the edge. White opens the h-file, then the queen steps in, the knight clears the defender, and mate lands on the back rank.

sl-aub.spoken: The pawn push and trade cracks the structure, leaving both pawns stranded and weak. The knight is boxed in by the enemy pawn, the bishop has no road. The position is broken open and White's pieces come alive.

sl-auy.spoken: The pawn advance looks like solid defense, but it quietly abandons the bishop and leaves a permanent hole. Stopping the queen's squares is tempting, yet those long-term weaknesses outweigh the short-term gain.

sl-av8.spoken: The pawn push looks tempting but fails, because it lets the enemy give a check that gets captured. The right idea is a bishop move that cuts off the rook's protection, so the enemy king has no escape square to that flight.

sl-auj.spoken: The queenside pawns are exposed and Black's pieces hold the activity. The bishop sits idle while the rooks slip in. White is uncomfortable, though not lost.

sl-aun.spoken: The c-pawn push opens a hole, and the queen slides in to attack the pawn and eye the weak square the knight wants. The knight sits awkwardly, and if it shifts, the queen checks from the open file and keeps the pressure on.

sl-avl.spoken: Queen and rooks coordinate to force the king from the center with checks, driving it to a worse square, and the mating threats become unavoidable without chasing material.

sl-aud.spoken: After the pawn break, Black stands active and comfortable. White carries weaknesses on both queenside pawns, and Black's knight sits in the center as a monster.

sl-aus.spoken: The bishop can give check from the diagonal, and when the enemy answers by pushing a pawn, that advance weakens the queenside and hands you a target.

sl-auh.spoken: The inaccurate rook trade leaves black with weak pawns and a cramped king. The pawns restrict the king, while back-rank threats loom — weakening pawn moves only make it worse.

sl-auf.spoken: The pawns sit exposed and hard to guard, while the one across the board resists attack because defenders return quickly. The opponent lines the queen up behind a piece to bear down on those weak points.

sl-auw.spoken: The rook move abandons the pawn behind it. When White pushes the b-pawn, that pawn falls, and the knight settles on the central outpost, leaving Black with a weak structure and nothing to do.

sl-aug.spoken: The rook harasses the pawn while the enemy rook moves. White takes, restoring material, and Black's weak pawns cannot all be defended at once.

sl-av2.spoken: The dust settles with material even, but White's problems remain: weak pawns, an exposed king, a passive rook, while Black holds the bishop pair and a solid center. A quick push and a bishop swing aim straight at White's weak queenside.

sl-awk.spoken: The knight seals the escape square, boxing the king in for a back-rank mate.

sl-awa.spoken: The bishop still guards the escape square, so even if the pawn recaptures, the same mating pattern works and the king has no way out.

sl-awp.spoken: The exposed king has no escape squares, so the attacker spreads a mating net. The pawn holds vital squares and locks the king in place.

sl-avs.spoken: The pawn push creates mating threats instead of taking the pawn. The bishop joins the attack, closing in on the exposed king.

sl-avo.spoken: In a mating net, your king's escape squares may look open, yet enemy pieces can still control them.

sl-awr.spoken: The bishop, backed by a pawn, locks down the king's escape squares and joins the attack to weave a mating net.

sl-avp.spoken: The queen sacrifice buys coordination, not just material. The black pieces work together to keep the white king exposed, forcing mate or a bigger win.

sl-awn.spoken: The king slips away to the edge, and the checks dry up. The rook and queen weave a mating net, and the opponent's counterplay comes too late.

sl-awx.spoken: The king flees to dodge the mating net, and the queen slides into position with a quiet threat of back-rank mate, turning calculation into execution.

sl-awm.spoken: The mating threat forces a weakening pawn move, and the queen then takes the central pawn while keeping the net intact.

sl-aw2.spoken: The queen threatens to break in and mate with the rook's help. The defender must slip the king to a safer square to escape the net.

sl-aw9.spoken: The king is trapped, but one careless capture lets him slip out. Pick the mate that seals the escape square first.

sl-avz.spoken: Your own pieces can cage your king. When the rooks block the escape squares, the king has no air, and the defender's army becomes part of the mating net.

sl-aw7.spoken: The direct capture only wakes the rook, and planting the queen there makes no real threat. The key is moving her onto the long diagonal, where she threatens mate on the corner square.

sl-avy.spoken: The knight on the rim and the queen work together to weave a mating net, while the lead in development and exposed king leave the defender with no escape.

sl-avn.spoken: The pawn push creates a double threat. If the bishop is taken, the queen delivers mate; if the king steps aside, the other square is mate.

sl-awi.spoken: The pawn push creates an instant mate threat that the queen delivers on the back rank. Nothing can block the queen's path, and even capturing the bishop fails because the mate lands first.

sl-avq.spoken: The queen and knight work together to threaten mate, forcing Black to shed material just to survive. The finish comes with a queen check, then a bishop delivers mate.

sl-aw6.spoken: The pawn offer guards the king and menaces mate. Capturing walks into the pattern, and the king can't recapture because the pawn is protected.

sl-awe.spoken: The rook and bishop pin down the king while the queen applies pressure. The king has no shelter, and the pieces coordinate to force mate or win material.

sl-avu.spoken: A material edge does not win by itself if the opponent still has active pieces. A mating net can end the game faster, even when the moves are precise and hard to find.

sl-aww.spoken: The queen and bishop work as a pair, creating mating threats that force the defender into weakening moves. Each defensive response buys time but only digs the position deeper.

sl-awv.spoken: The bishop trade strips the king's guard, leaving the monarch exposed. The queen slides to the mating square, and the defender has no adequate answer, so the game ends.

sl-awq.spoken: The queen slides to the edge and eyes two mate squares at once. A pawn block slows nothing — the queen steps forward and the net tightens.

sl-avv.spoken: The sacrifice buys more than check — it strips escape squares and closes the net. A bishop that holds the king in place outweighs one that merely checks.

sl-awb.spoken: The bishop has two squares that both force mate with rook and queen on the seventh rank. One square is the computer's first choice for precision, but the other is equally sound.

sl-aw5.spoken: The bishop steps in to defend, but Black keeps the pressure with knight and queen moves that renew the attack and threaten mate on the king’s doorstep.

sl-awu.spoken: The queen on the mating square delivers decisive threats, forcing the opponent to create weaknesses. The rook slides along the file to reinforce, and the queen shifts along the same rank to keep the net closed.

sl-aw8.spoken: The bishop retreats to prepare the queen's attack on the king's fortress. The h-pawn blocks the immediate mate, but if the opponent advances the g-pawn to shield the king, that h-pawn becomes a target.

sl-aw3.spoken: The queen parks on an open diagonal against the exposed king, threatening mate on the corner square while the e-pawn hangs. The opponent's defenses are stretched too thin to cover both.

sl-aw4.spoken: The knight stays put while the queen slides over to join the attack, putting mate above material. Forcing moves follow, and the rook lands the final blow, showing what coordinated pieces can do.

sl-aw0.spoken: The knight is headed for the mating square, but the direct route fails—the rook deflects it. The right path goes around, stepping first to the side, still aiming at the same deadly target.

sl-avt.spoken: The threat to break through in the center and then rip open the king's shelter is decisive because the king is trapped. The only defense is a pawn push to create luft, though it weakens the kingside.

sl-awh.spoken: The knight captures, the rook takes the bishop, and now both rook and bishop hit the queen while a mating threat looms. Forced to recapture with the knight, the defender still falls: rook takes, queen recaptures, and the final queen strike delivers mate.

sl-awt.spoken: The rook slides behind the queen's line, preparing twin threats on the king's flank. If the king has no escape square, those threats converge into mate.

sl-awj.spoken: The rook is under fire, but the queen's mating threat outweighs it. Address the mate first; saving the rook comes second.

sl-awd.spoken: The mate looks forcing, but a single defensive resource can spoil it. After the check, the defender blocks or guards the mating square, so the attack must stay precise.

sl-awo.spoken: The queen threatens mate on the back rank while the rook covers both escape squares, cutting off the defender's resources. The bishop sits behind its own pawn, so counterplay stays blocked.

sl-awc.spoken: The queen lands on the decisive square, attacking the pawn and threatening mate at once. The rook cannot be captured, because the mate threat remains unstoppable. That is how an attack converts into a win—by keeping threats alive.

sl-aw1.spoken: A dying attack is your only real chance. The bishop strikes the critical squares, forcing the enemy queen to choose between guarding the promotion and guarding the king.

sl-avr.spoken: The knight leaps into enemy territory, menacing the king and forcing an answer. When the queen slides out to counter, the rook lifts along the back rank, and mate threats become unavoidable.

sl-awf.spoken: The g-file assault breaks through. Rook and queen line up for mate, and the queen cannot be traded because the rook behind controls the escape square. When the defender swaps rooks, the recapture keeps the mating net intact.

sl-awl.spoken: The knight jumps to the edge of the attack and the bishop steps out to push it back. White answers with the rook, building a mating net: the knight delivers the final check, and the rook lands the mate on the back rank.

sl-aws.spoken: The rook slides to the back rank, then the bishop joins the attack, and the rook delivers mate on the fifth rank. If the defender tries counterplay with a rook lift and pawn push, first give a rook check to drive the king off, then continue the pawn advance.

sl-axa.spoken: The knight is attacked, but the queen’s strike at the weak squares near the king is decisive, forcing mate on either of two squares.

sl-ax6.spoken: The rook and queen line up on the seventh rank against the king, and the mating threat is decisive. That makes the tempting capture unattractive.

sl-axd.spoken: Once the king is pushed into the corner, extra attackers join in and the mating net tightens.

sl-ax2.spoken: Sometimes the only defensive move still loses. Stopping one mate lets in another, and no good move exists — the attack is simply overwhelming.

sl-awz.spoken: The queen and pawn form a classic mating net against the king. Every defensive try fails because the threats stay alive.

sl-awy.spoken: The rook slides to the back rank, threatening mate on the spot. White has no choice but to trade the queen for two rooks, and Black finishes with a forced mating sequence.

sl-ax5.spoken: The queen checks along the diagonal, driving the king to the edge. The rook then sacrifices itself on the square beside the king, and the attack ends in mate.

sl-ax3.spoken: The sacrifice removes the defender and exposes the king. Even when the opponent finds a defense, the mate threat on the king's square keeps resurfacing.

sl-ax1.spoken: The king is exposed, and a forcing sequence of checks drives him into a mating net. If he retreats, the queen slides in to deliver mate, every escape square covered.

sl-ax8.spoken: The bishop slides to the key square, cutting off the king's escape and clearing the path for the rook to join the attack. The queen checks, the rook lifts, and the net closes for forced mate.

sl-axf.spoken: The rook and queen combine against the h-file pawn, and when the knight controls the escape squares, the h-file mate lands.

sl-ax7.spoken: The queen and bishop aim together at the same dark square, threatening mate. Black can defend, so White must pick exact moves to keep the initiative.

sl-axb.spoken: The rook slides into the third rank to lift the mating net, the knight joins it, and the king, still trapped in the center behind broken pawns, has no escape.

sl-axx.spoken: The hidden mate begins with a scare: the rook must reach its mating square even if the path looks illegal. Once the knight clears the way, the queen steps onto the protected square and delivers checkmate.

sl-axi.spoken: The queen circles back to renew the threat, and the opponent must answer. Meanwhile the rook slides away, opening the king's escape route. When the queen finally reaches the far corner, the mating net is unstoppable.

sl-axl.spoken: The knight grabs material, then the queen slips into the net. If the knight takes the rook, the other knight leaps forward, and mate on the back rank looms.

sl-ax0.spoken: The queen returns to offer herself again. If she is taken, the back rank is undefended and it's mate. If she is refused, she takes the other pawn, and the bishop's protection delivers mate.

sl-axq.spoken: A mating threat on the king’s doorstep is what keeps the attack alive. Without that concrete finish, the assault runs out of steam and stalls.

sl-axu.spoken: The first move forces the king toward the corner, shrinking its escape squares. Then the queen steps in to deliver mate, while controlling the key square that blocks counterplay.

sl-axg.spoken: The bishop opens fire from a distance, and the close-range threat is immediate. Every defense is met with a counter-strike, and the one that seems to block the mate steps into a discovered check that collects the queen.

sl-ay1.spoken: The bishop slides in to smother the king after the forced recapture, and the mate threat that follows cannot be stopped.

sl-axn.spoken: The knight slides to the rim, and the quiet move sets a net. Multiple mates threaten, and the opponent must give up material to survive.

sl-axr.spoken: The knight sacrifice forces the rook to take. That capture opens the king and leaves the defenses scattered, so the follow-up checks and threats crush the position.

sl-axe.spoken: The knight leap plants itself in the heart of the position and turns the queen's threat into a launching pad for mate. Even the defender's sharpest replies, like grabbing the queen, walk straight into a mating net.

sl-axo.spoken: The knight lands on the key square and threatens mate on the adjacent square. The defender's only reply is a particular move that stops nothing, because the queen still joins the attack.

sl-axw.spoken: The bishop checks from a distance, cutting off one escape square. The queen then slides in to narrow the king's cage, trapping him where he stands.

sl-axv.spoken: The king is chased by checks and forcing moves into a vulnerable spot. The mating net closes while the queen stays on the board, avoiding trades that would break it.

sl-axz.spoken: The rook falls, and White is lost — Black keeps mating threats on every king move, the bishop and queen both waiting to strike.

sl-ay9.spoken:
The rook shuffle looks active, but the king move is the natural choice.  
The position stays sharp, with no forced win in sight.

sl-ay2.spoken: The king expects the loud check, but the quiet bishop check is the trap. It forces the king to one square, the bishop pulls back to check again, and the queen delivers mate from close range.

sl-axy.spoken: The king sits exposed while the queen and rooks coordinate the mate. The final blow lands on the seventh rank, and Black's defenses fall apart completely.

sl-axt.spoken: The bishop delivers a mating threat, and the king has no shelter. Every white piece already points at it, so the attack runs itself.

sl-ay6.spoken: The opponent pushes pawns on the kingside while you keep your pieces home and make simple, safe moves. You survive the storm, and their clock pressure hands you the blunder.

sl-axp.spoken: The queen guards the mating square, so both the queen and rook deliver mate threats. The king is forced to the edge with no escape, and mate follows in three.

sl-ay7.spoken: Champions blunder under the clock like anyone else. The real skill is not avoiding the mistake but bouncing back from it.

sl-axs.spoken: The bishop lands on the dream square, cutting off the king's flight paths and creating a mating threat in one move.

sl-axc.spoken: The pawn move creates a mating threat. If the queen takes it, the rook lifts across the rank and mate on the corner becomes unstoppable.

sl-ay0.spoken: The knight leaps into the mating net, and the queen is suddenly trapped. The king is boxed in, and the escape route is gone.

sl-axk.spoken: The queen settles on the mating square, and the rook delivers the final blow. Each time Black answers the threat, the rook slides back and renews it, forcing Black to keep responding.

sl-ay3.spoken: The king flees toward the queenside, so the attacker seals the escape routes. The bishop steps onto the long diagonal, covering critical squares, and the king cannot slip away.

sl-ay5.spoken: The opponent, short on time, drops one pawn, then another, leaving you two up with the better game. Taking the first would have opened the long diagonal and finished—so they avoided it.

sl-ay4.spoken: The pawn push is the defender's one escape from the mating net. Sacrifice a piece onto that square to pin or block the pawn, and the net closes.

sl-ayo.spoken: The double attack strikes two targets at once, and since the opponent answers only one threat per move, defending both at once is nearly impossible.

sl-ayv.spoken: A double check gives the king no choice but to move, since blocking or capturing one checker leaves the other threat unanswered.

sl-az7.spoken: Sacrificing the pawn back unlocks the pieces and turns the deficit into a strategic edge: a passed pawn and grip on key squares.

sl-ayf.spoken: Pins, forks, and discovered checks keep reappearing in king hunts and across the board, so spot them early.

sl-ayz.spoken: A double check is a discovered check where both pieces give check at once. Neither block nor capture can answer it—the king must move.

sl-azd.spoken: Black has the material edge, but the extra pawns stay put. Grabbing them too fast hands White counterplay and space.

sl-ayt.spoken: A double check hits the king from two pieces at once. The king must move, and every escape square is usually bad.

sl-az5.spoken: The pawn stays untouched because grabbing it would trade queens and blunt the attack. Development with the knight instead builds activity and keeps the initiative.

sl-azl.spoken: Taking the pawn wakes both bishops; chasing the bishop with a pawn move instead keeps them quiet.

sl-ayn.spoken: The queen steps in and hits two pieces at once, a double attack, and the opponent cannot defend both.

sl-azg.spoken: Taking the offered pawn is a must, not a choice. Refusing lets the opponent push the center pawn forward, and that advance becomes strong.

sl-ayx.spoken: The king is boxed on the back rank behind a rook and bishop. A double check forces the king to step, and with no safe square, it is mate.

sl-ayw.spoken: A double check is when one move attacks the king with two pieces at once. Two threats from one move cannot both be blocked or both captured, so the king is forced to move.

sl-ayh.spoken: The pin is only a threat when it targets something real. If the opponent can simply defend, the pin has no concrete payoff.

sl-azi.spoken: The rook grabs the bishop but wakes up the d-pawn. That pawn's potential outweighs the piece, so the capture is the wrong deal.

sl-ayu.spoken: The king and another piece stand on the same line. Strike them together with one tactic, and the opponent can only answer one threat at a time.

sl-ayy.spoken: A double check comes when one move lets two pieces check at once. Since the opponent cannot block two lines of attack, the king is the only piece that may move.

sl-ays.spoken: A double check is always discovered: both lines open at once, so the king must flee. No move can give three checks at the same time.

sl-azh.spoken: Black is down a pawn but his pieces stand active, White's sit passive. Pushing the pawn forward cramps the knight's squares and drives it backward.

sl-az0.spoken: In a double check, only the king can answer—nothing blocks or captures both threats. That forced move drives him toward the corner, where knight and rook finish with mate.

sl-ayg.spoken: A pin can unsettle you, but challenging it beats enduring it. When the bishop pins your piece, meet it head-on rather than suffer passively.

sl-ayk.spoken: The double attack strikes two targets with one move, often a mate threat and a hanging piece, forcing the opponent to respond to the greater danger and lose the other.

sl-azc.spoken: The queenside pawns are a lure, not a lead. Black ignores the deficit and plays for activity, and if White bites on the b-pawn, the queen walks into a trap. Development and piece activity pay for the missing pawn.

sl-aya.spoken: The queen retreat is the one move that holds every line and keeps the extra pawn. Any other square invites dangerous counterplay in time pressure.

sl-aza.spoken: The queen sacrifice leaves you down a pawn for the queen, but the deficit alone is not the verdict. The opponent's threats still decide the game, and they can outweigh the extra material.

sl-azj.spoken: The knight is snatched, and the recapture unleashes a storm of threats. Better to develop and hand over material than to take the piece and leave the position cracked open.

sl-ayi.spoken: The pin, fork, and skewer all hit at once, and each capture removes a defender. Every way Black answers, a piece falls, so the attack wins outright.

sl-az9.spoken: The queen sits offside, and the three-point edge is not the whole story. The computer sees a smaller advantage because her exposed position invites forcing attacks that can win material back.

sl-azb.spoken: The extra pawn means nothing while development stalls. The human eye sees a clear edge, even when the engine calls it only a slight plus. Winning still demands careful study.

sl-ayd.spoken: The bishop offer is a trap in disguise. Declining the trade keeps the position complex, because simplifying would make defense easier for the opponent short on time. Keeping pieces alive increases the clock pressure.

sl-aze.spoken: The bishop's early retreat releases control of the escape squares. Black pushes the pawn through, and once the bishop captures, the king slips out. Down to two bishops versus one, the win fades to a draw.

sl-ayb.spoken: The queen steps in and hits the bishop while eyeing entry squares. The reply is the best try, but the damage is already done and the defense stays hard.

sl-aym.spoken: The double attack strikes both bishops at once, and the opponent must surrender one of them, so their bishop pair is gone for good.

sl-azf.spoken: The bishop sits on the diagonal, holding the position together. If White grabs the piece, the rook recaptures and keeps everything solid—while the tempting rook capture on the other side would crack the defense and hand White the initiative.

sl-az8.spoken: Keep pressing forward. The opponent refuses to take the hanging piece because it opens the back rank for the rook, and that leads to forced mate. The material deficit is real, but the initiative and constant threats are the compensation.

sl-ayc.spoken: When the opponent is short on time, skip forcing lines that give them easy replies. Pick the move that forces them to stop and think instead.

sl-ayj.spoken: The bishop goes to the advanced square, hitting both rook and bishop at once. The rook cannot guard the bishop, so the double attack wins material.

sl-ayr.spoken: The double check lands hardest—king must move, queen and rook stay put, and the bishop falls while the passed pawn stays frozen.

sl-az1.spoken: Double check attacks the king with two pieces at once, so the king must move. When no square exists, it is checkmate.

sl-az4.spoken: The pawn that remains after the exchange is bait. Taking it at once invites counterplay, and the king and pawns are too fragile for the rooks to cover everything.

sl-az2.spoken: Recapturing with the bishop keeps a dangerous passed pawn and leaves you hope, while taking the pawn leads to a dead loss with no counterplay.

sl-ayl.spoken: The queen lands on the line where she attacks bishop and mate together. One piece, two different threats, and the bishop is suddenly outnumbered.

sl-ayq.spoken: The queen slides to the third rank and strikes the rook and bishop at once. Black's pawn moves have weakened the long diagonal, leaving both pieces vulnerable to the double attack.

sl-aye.spoken: The bishop is pinned because it stands between the pawn and its promotion square. Move it, and the pawn queens — so black can take it freely.

sl-ayp.spoken: The bishop and queen line up on the long diagonal, hitting the rook and the bishop at once. When the pawn chain breaks, the diagonal opens wide and the double attack wins material.

sl-az3.spoken: A knight is given up to castle, and the queen stays boxed in. Down material, but the active army and the jailed queen make White's winning chances real.

sl-b0q.spoken: Taking the pawn rouses the opponent's dormant pieces. The knight and rook wake up and create counterplay.

sl-b00.spoken: The engine returning material signals trouble—either a direct threat forces the return, or it has no useful moves left and just shuffles pieces.

sl-b0t.spoken: The undeveloped bishop and the unmoved d-pawn leave the king exposed. White spends tempi and sacrifices a pawn to speed the assault, a fair price when the mating threat is real.

sl-azm.spoken: The pawns vanish from the board, leaving material level, but activity tells the tale—White keeps a slight edge.

sl-b04.spoken: A sacrifice offers a poisoned gift. Check first whether giving the material back lands you in a comfortable position, before clinging to the extra pawn at any cost.

sl-b0h.spoken: The passed pawn and the exposed king outweigh the scoreboard. The threat is faster than the pawn count, and a slow move hands over the game.

sl-azr.spoken: The extra pawn means little while the opponent's pieces are active. A misplaced knight and a powerful bishop give the opponent real compensation.

sl-b0a.spoken: The rook is gone for two pawns, but the pieces stay active and the enemy king stands exposed. The material debt is real, yet king safety and piece activity decide the truth.

sl-azw.spoken: Winning the knight feels clean, but the position that follows tells the real story. Even with extra material, the result is only good if the weaknesses it creates are worth the gain.

sl-azu.spoken: The attack must land before the material deficit decides the game. If the mating threats fizzle, the position collapses.

sl-azy.spoken: The exchange is worth less than the attack here. White's king is safe, Black's is exposed, and Black can give up material to keep the initiative alive.

sl-b0u.spoken: The queen's pawn grab looks active, but developing the bishop is the stronger plan. When the opponent's moves fix your king safety and free your bishop, the position turns in your favor.

sl-b05.spoken: The pawn march rips open the shelter around the king. White has the extra rook, but his pieces are scattered, and the exposed king turns that advantage fragile.

sl-b0k.spoken: The extra exchange counts for nothing when Black owns the light squares. White’s pieces cannot hold the key squares, and the attack is not ready.

sl-b03.spoken: The recapture looks natural, but walking into a blocked diagonal is the trap. Chasing the pawn lets the opponent shut the bishop out and leaves your pieces sitting passively.

sl-b0r.spoken: Black is down a pawn, and the instinct is to trade pieces to simplify, but here trades are a mistake. White's queen offers the exchange, yet Black keeps queens on to preserve attacking chances against the king.

sl-azz.spoken: The knight is a tempting pawn grab, but it trades into an opposite-bishop endgame with no clear win. The two bishops outweigh that pawn.

sl-b0v.spoken: The player with the advantage eyes the pawn, but taking it hands the opponent active play. He picks a stronger move that keeps the bind and leaves the weakness fixed in place.

sl-b0c.spoken: The knight's capture is a trap, not a treasure. It rips the position open, exposing the king to a storm of tactical blows the opponent cannot answer.

sl-azo.spoken: When the opponent offers material, do not grab it on reflex. Ask what the threat is behind the gift—here, taking the rook would invite a crushing attack, so the right choice is to decline.

sl-b02.spoken: The queen captures on the edge, winning a pawn and freezing the enemy's rook and bishop in place. Those pieces cannot move while the queen presses them, and Black's defense collapses under the pressure.

sl-b0m.spoken: The trade on the corner wins two pawns but gives up the long-diagonal bishop, the key piece in this setup. After the exchange, Black takes over the light squares, and the king, still in the center, has less shelter.

sl-b09.spoken: The pawn is a lead, not a license. Black's active pieces and the exposed king give compensation, so the material edge demands care, not confidence.

sl-b0g.spoken: Black trails by a piece but the attack is real. The defensive pawn push forces trades, easing the pressure, and the white king sits exposed, so the attack cuts both ways.

sl-b07.spoken: The knight grab looks tempting — it nets two pawns and makes passers. But White's counterplay comes alive: a flank push, the knight re-enters the fight, and the rook penetrates to the seventh, putting Black on defense.

sl-b0n.spoken: The pawn falls, but their king sits in the center and their pieces stay at home. Material matters less than king safety and development.

sl-b0s.spoken: Greed for a pawn backfires when development gets ignored. Compare the positions before grabbing material — the solid choice often beats the flashy one.

sl-b08.spoken: The engine values central control over grabbing that pawn. Retreating the knight inward and then forward to a central outpost prioritizes piece activity. The opponent's corner rook stays passive, and that activity is the compensation for the material.

sl-b0j.spoken: The sacrificed pawn costs White little because both bishops are active, one eyeing the kingside and one stripping the black king's defenses. Even with the rook retreating, the initiative outweighs the material deficit.

sl-b0x.spoken: The opponent's plan is a slow build, not instant mate—like advancing the pawn to open a line for the queen. The defender can either shed material to simplify or hold everything and reposition the rook, but the pawn break demands constant care.

sl-b0d.spoken: The f-pawn is a fair price for counterplay. White gives it up willingly to push the pawns and bring the rook to life.

sl-b0o.spoken: The pawn push looks timid, but taking the offered pawn with the rook opens the long diagonal. The enemy queen and bishop line up there, aiming a deadly battery at your queenside.

sl-b01.spoken: The defender takes the bishop only when mate looms, not earlier when it would reach a favorable endgame. Taking it sooner is no advantage, because the king can step to either central square and gain activity.

sl-b0w.spoken: The rook is offside, the king sits in the center, and White trades a piece for a lasting attack. Rook to the eighth and queen to the fifth strike two targets at once.

sl-azv.spoken: Tied-up defenders on the queenside make a material deficit meaningless — the king stands exposed and the initiative decides.

sl-b0i.spoken: Trading two pieces for rook and pawn is only nominally ahead, but with your pieces trapped and the opponent's lead in development, the activity costs more than the point difference.

sl-azn.spoken: The bishop takes the pawn and gives up a piece for it, trading down to a rook endgame where White's extra material means nothing because Black's kingside pawns are connected and passed — they decide the game.

sl-b0e.spoken: Black trails a pawn but owns the position: doubled isolated pawns, no activity, no space, a fragile king. White’s lead in development and piece play outweighs the material, so Black is clearly better.

sl-b06.spoken: The extra pawn cost Black real concessions—the queen shuffled out and back, and a center pawn stayed back instead of fighting for space. Now White owns the central pawn duo and every piece works.

sl-b17.spoken: The solid move beats the flashy one when it keeps every piece guarded and sets up the pawn storm without leaving anything hanging.

sl-b0y.spoken: The exchange is not a shield when the king is bare. Black's active pieces and four pawns for the rook outweigh any material edge, and the attack is unstoppable.

sl-b1n.spoken: The queen steps in to block the mating bishop, but the rook lifts along the file and every move gives check. The king is dragged forward, the queen falls, and the bishop delivers mate on the diagonal.

sl-b1a.spoken: Retreating to a safe square is often the simplest answer to an attack, instead of complicating the position.

sl-b1h.spoken: The queen on the diagonal faces the bishop. The bishop simply takes her, and the game is done.

sl-b1c.spoken: The rook trade is a trap. Losing the knight leaves two rooks facing a queen and pawns, and that endgame is far harder to win.

sl-b1y.spoken: The queen checks, but the rook guards the escape square. The attack only succeeds once that defender is deflected or captured, so the mate can land.

sl-b15.spoken: The king is driven across the board, and the defender rejects a knight move because that knight would hang — the pair must keep protecting each other.

sl-b18.spoken: Before a piece moves, ask where it lands. A free capture is bad; losing a higher-value piece on the spot is worse.

sl-b1l.spoken: Two bishops on crossing diagonals form a mating net: one owns the light squares, the other the dark, and the enemy king has no escape.

sl-b1f.spoken: The pawn advances and attacks the knight, forcing it to move. Once the knight retreats, the queen steps off the open file, dodging the tactical tricks.

sl-b1s.spoken: The promotion leads to a mate with the pawn push, but the chance is missed and a rook is taken instead. The mate is found later.

sl-b1r.spoken: The double check forces the king onto the one square, and the bishop mates there. Its own pieces block every escape, and the rooks cannot come to the rescue.

sl-b25.spoken: When the position is lost, the only way out is a creative resource—and that pressure is exactly what produces brilliancies.

sl-b19.spoken: The knight is under attack and Black tries to guard it with the bishop instead of moving it. The capture still wins the knight, and the pinned queen falls next.

sl-b1z.spoken: The bishop checks and forces the king onto a square where mate follows. Material deficit means nothing when the attack lands first.

sl-b1b.spoken: The pawn break frees the bishop, but the square is exposed. A knight can chase it off, and the enemy bishop slides in to pressure the pawn behind it.

sl-b1t.spoken: The bishop takes the pinned knight and lands on a powerful square, the rook shifts, and the king stands exposed. The queen then delivers mate on the weak diagonal.

sl-b26.spoken: The desperate rook lift and knight maneuver create nothing but noise. White's activity is already too strong, so the calm capture simply ends the attack and leaves White's threats standing.

sl-b1g.spoken: The rook hangs while the queen checks. The rook must flee or find pawn cover, and that pawn move gains a tempo and sets up discovered threats.

sl-b1m.spoken: The knight lifts away and the discovered attack threatens mate, while the rook joins in. Two minor pieces alone rarely finish the job; the queen and rook must lead the charge.

sl-b22.spoken: The bishop forces the knight to block the file, and the knight now stands between the rook and the mating square. The recapture that seemed natural leaves the defender in the way.

sl-b28.spoken: The pawn storm is a gamble when the position is already slipping. Pushing pawns on both flanks creates chaos, but every advance is also a fresh weakness.

sl-b10.spoken: Grabbing the pawn looks tempting, but white's pieces dominate the board while black's army sits at home. Overindulgence here makes the position collapse.

sl-b1j.spoken: A queen sacrifice can force a defender away or clear the path to the king. When the defender's own pieces crowd the escape squares, every capture and block becomes a chance to tighten the net.

sl-b1p.spoken: The pin ties the queen to defense, so the rook checks force the king into the open. Sacrifice the queen to clear the mating square, and the rook delivers mate.

sl-b29.spoken: The knight leaps into the middle of the board. If White takes the queen, it is checkmate. White must guard that key square and still watch the other knight check. So the queen steps back calmly, keeping the rook boxed in.

sl-b12.spoken: The rook grab looks tempting — a pawn gained and more pressure on the pinned knight. But the rook slides in behind, the pin breaks, and the knight jumps to the outpost. White keeps only a small edge from activity.

sl-b24.spoken: A rook check on the far rank drags the king to the rook. When the king takes, the queen checks from the other side, forcing the king back, and then the queen mates on the diagonal square, guarded by a pawn.

sl-b1o.spoken: The bishop delivers the final blow on the king's guard. If the king steps toward safety, the rook checks along the open file and the game is over — the king has no shelter left.

sl-b1v.spoken: The bishop captures, and now the queen's landing square decides everything. One step sideways lets the game drift on, but when the king retreats, the same piece that forks also covers the escape—so mate lands immediately.

sl-b1q.spoken: The king is harried by a stream of checks from knight and queen, each one clearing a square for the next. White is herded to the edge, and once the king reaches the corner, the queen and knight close in for the mate.

sl-b1e.spoken: The bishop is loose, and the knight wants to land again. Pushing the f-pawn shields the bishop and keeps the threat alive. When the pawn chain advances on the flank, the defender’s reply stops the break and locks the kingside.

sl-b21.spoken: Precision is the price of a mating attack. One careless check can hand the defender a way out or a block.

sl-b27.spoken: The knight dives in as a desperate gamble, attacking the queen. But the rook simply takes it, keeping the bishop defended, and the material loss is decisive.

sl-b11.spoken: Material is not sacred when the opponent's pieces are active. Giving it back can simplify the position and steer toward a favorable endgame.

sl-b23.spoken: The bishop moves to hit the rook and threaten mate at once. One move, two threats, and the opponent must answer both.

sl-b1w.spoken: The knight lands on the king’s doorstep, creating an unstoppable mate threat. Black resigns, the attack overwhelming and the defender’s pieces boxed in.

sl-b1d.spoken: In a mating attack, watch for your own hanging pieces. The attacked knight can bait the opponent or slide to a stronger square without losing steam.

sl-b1i.spoken: The queen is loose, and the bishop rakes a dangerous diagonal. Pushing the pawn to defend creates luft but may expose the king.

sl-b1k.spoken: The king has no shelter after the sacrifice. Saving the knight lets the queen line up with the rook for mate, and the escape square is cut off, forcing mate.

sl-b20.spoken: The king hides in the corner, but taking the pawn rips open the shelter, and the queen delivers mate on the adjacent file. The bishops own the long diagonals, so the king has no escape square.

sl-b0z.spoken: Material favors White: four pawns beat a knight. But the knight's partner, the bishop, has no scope, and Black's position moves: the queen menaces a soft pawn, the f-pawn advances to open a diagonal for a check, and a rook enters play on the open file.

sl-b13.spoken: The queen takes the pawn with check, forcing the king to recapture. Then the knight fork lands and wins material. The flashier threat looks tempting, but the opponent's decisive reply refutes it.

sl-b1u.spoken: The rook and bishop close the mating net. If the king flees there, checkmate follows, and taking the bishop only opens another mate. The rook cuts the board, and even the best check changes nothing — the passed pawns finish it.

sl-b32.spoken: The king must guard the promotion square himself—pushing the pawn alone lets the defender take the opposition and hold the draw.

sl-b30.spoken: Distant opposition draws the endgame. The king stands at a distance so the opponent cannot force progress.

sl-b2c.spoken: The defender must not take the opposition too close. Getting behind the pawn gives the opponent the outflank and forces the win, so keep the distance that maintains the opposition.

sl-b3c.spoken: Keep the opposition and hold the back rank. Chasing the pawn directly lets the enemy slip behind it, push the king away, and win both the pawn and the game.

sl-b2e.spoken: The king takes the opposition to force the enemy king aside, then steps forward to clear the path and shepherd the pawn home.

sl-b36.spoken: The queen cuts off escape squares, driving the lone king toward yours. That route to the corner is faster than chasing it.

sl-b2k.spoken: Kings standing one square apart face each other in opposition. That barrier locks both kings in place, and the defender uses it to halt the pawn's march.

sl-b3i.spoken: The defending king seizes opposition and the win slips away. The attacking king must choose the penetrating path carefully.

sl-b3d.spoken: The king steps to the side to keep the opposition, refusing to let the opponent escape. This demands exact calculation.

sl-b2f.spoken: The king that must move breaks the opposition. A pawn thrust cracks the static wall, forcing a concession that may decide the game.

sl-b2y.spoken: The defender is stuck shuffling while the attacker maneuvers. By triangulating or simply out-waiting, the attacker seizes the opposition.

sl-b3k.spoken: The king aims to break through, but the defender holds the draw with opposition and triangulation. The right king moves keep the opposition and block all progress.

sl-b2d.spoken: The king steps onto a key square and forces the opponent to move. Taking the opposition turns the position into a win.

sl-b2v.spoken: The kings stand face to face with one square between them. Whoever must move loses ground, letting the opponent step through or seize the opposition.

sl-b2h.spoken: The king's distance shapes the opposition — a knight's move apart or further. Read the gap, then pick the king step that reaches your goal.

sl-b3a.spoken: In king and pawn endgames, triangulation hands the move back to the opponent while the position stays the same, buying a vital tempo.

sl-b2j.spoken: The king must control the promotion square after the pawn falls. One precise king move draws; any other move loses.

sl-b2t.spoken: The defender faces a fork in the road. Only the king move straight backward holds the draw; any other step lets the attacker's king get in front of the pawn and win.

sl-b38.spoken: The defender steps diagonally instead of straight back, and that error hands the attacker the opposition. The attacker drives the king away and the pawn promotes.

sl-b3e.spoken: The defender's pawn on the second rank faces an attacker's pawn beside it. Sliding the king over to cover the queening square leaves the tension unresolved, forcing the attacker to commit first, and then a pawn move grabs the opposition.

sl-b2n.spoken: The king must pick the right square to hold the draw. The wrong square lets the enemy king support the pawn and win; the right square keeps the opposition and forces the draw.

sl-b34.spoken: The king must not grab pawns blindly—capturing can surrender the opposition and the game. Keep the opposition, and take only when the capture is safe.

sl-b2p.spoken: Opposition is the lever in a king and pawn endgame. The king steps forward to push the enemy king aside, then the pawn falls, and the win follows from precise king moves that hold the opposition.

sl-b3l.spoken: The side to move decides everything here. With the move, the defender takes the opposition, wins the pawn, and the position flips.

sl-b2i.spoken: The king needs to hold opposition while the bishop slides between the two kings, covering the escape squares ahead. That keeps the enemy king retreating.

sl-b2l.spoken: The pawn marches to the seventh rank. If the defender steps sideways, the enemy king steps in front and escorts it home. Only stepping straight ahead, keeping the opposition, holds the draw.

sl-b2g.spoken: The king must pick the right opposition square. If he steps to one side, the defender matches the file, not the diagonal, because the entry is not sealed and the attacker can slip around the other way.

sl-b2x.spoken: The rook trade leaves the pawn weak. When it falls, the king steps in and blocks the enemy king out. That opposition ends the game.

sl-b3f.spoken: The king claims the opposition, so you step aside with a pawn move. That waiting tempi forces their king to yield, and the opposition comes back to you.

sl-b39.spoken: The opposition is a tool, not a promise. Misapplied, it only draws. The winning method is to shuffle the king, always ready to step forward the moment the defender retreats.

sl-b2z.spoken: The pawn push gains a tempo but never wins. As the white king edges closer, the black king is squeezed until no legal move remains — and what looks like pressure becomes stalemate.

sl-b2o.spoken: The king and pawn endgame comes down to one question: who takes the opposition. The first move is diagonal opposition, then convert it to the regular form and walk the enemy king away from the pawn.

sl-b31.spoken: The passed pawn on the seventh is a knife at the throat. A natural king move can let it queen with check and lose the game. Slide the king quietly into the corner instead, keep the opposition, and the draw holds.

sl-b33.spoken: The king must keep the opposition and walk toward the critical square instead of pushing the pawn. Control of that square stays the aim, and opposition forces the defender away.

sl-b2r.spoken: Mirror their step: left for left, right for right. Keeping the opposition this way forces the win.

sl-b3j.spoken: The king is far from the corner, the win stays alive. Cut off the road to the corner, and the bishop backs the pawn through to promotion.

sl-b2q.spoken: The extra rank is the margin between victory and a draw. With sufficient room to maneuver, the defender takes the opposition and halts the pawn’s advance.

sl-b2u.spoken: Kings staring through a single square: whoever is not to move holds the opposition. That grip shoves the enemy king aside and clears the road for a pawn to promote.

sl-b2b.spoken: The defending king must retreat along the queening file and give ground only when forced.

sl-b2s.spoken: The opposition and zugzwang decide this ending. Whoever moves often loses, since any king step lets the opponent break in or take the pawn.

sl-b2a.spoken: A pawn check is the desperate resource. It buys nothing but time while the pin holds, the pawn stays lost, and the rook remains under fire.

sl-b3h.spoken: The king steps forward, and if the pawn advances, it is simply taken. In a king and pawn ending a lost pawn usually means a lost game, so the defender must find a way to hold the draw.

sl-b4l.spoken: The king must follow the pawn, not chase the king. Staying near the pawn is what stops it from promoting.

sl-b3y.spoken: The opposition decides between a draw and a loss. When the attacking king steps forward, the defender's exact square choice is what keeps the game alive.

sl-b40.spoken: The bishop may have to be sacrificed for a pawn, leaving a pawn race. King activity and opposition decide whether the draw holds.

sl-b3x.spoken: The king must step to the opposition square, not the side. That choice holds the opposition and keeps the h-pawn safe.

sl-b3p.spoken: Choose the king move that keeps the opposition. A natural step looks right, but the wrong one hands the opponent the opposition — and the win.

sl-b44.spoken: Some squares are landmines: step on them first and you win, step on them second and you lose. Whoever claims them gains a decisive advantage.

sl-b4k.spoken: To take a pawn outright can hand the opponent the opposition and turn a win into a draw. Hold the opposition first, then take.

sl-b3r.spoken: The king trails its own pawn to the edge. Once there, opposition forces a choice: step away and drop the pawn, or push and hand the defender stalemate.

sl-b46.spoken: The king must pick the right side to pressure the pawn. Choosing the wrong side lets the enemy king seize the opposition and force a draw; the correct side keeps the pressure and wins.

sl-b4i.spoken: When the rook trade is offered, taking it may be right if the king and pawn ending is drawn. After the exchange, opposition gives the defender the draw—or even the win of the pawn.

sl-b42.spoken: The king faces the pawn. Stepping straight ahead lets the enemy king take the opposition and draw. Step aside first to seize the opposition, force the enemy king to move, then step in front and keep it.

sl-b4n.spoken: The decision to trade rooks into a pawn ending rests on two hidden assets: a barrier that locks the enemy king out of the kingside, and a pawn break ready to launch.

sl-b4o.spoken: The h-pawn push alone loses a tempo when the enemy pawn blocks it. March the king forward first to support the pawn's path to promotion.

sl-b4q.spoken: One side can still play for a win in a drawn position — by steering into a favorable pawn endgame or by threatening to grab a pawn.

sl-b4d.spoken: The defending king seems to block the pawn, but the attacker holds the opposition, forcing the defender aside, and the pawn promotes. Precision decides the outcome—one hasty move throws away the win.

sl-b43.spoken: The king's defensive move keeps the opposition and blocks the enemy king's path in. Once the pawn advances, the bishop gains a longer diagonal and the advanced pawn turns into a target.

sl-b4c.spoken: The pawn push looks natural but fails — the enemy king walks over and takes it, and the game ends in a draw. Place the bishop on the key diagonal instead, and the king can never block the pawn.

sl-b3s.spoken: The king steps in front of the pawns and uses opposition to force the defender back. The extra pawn is a reserve tempo that narrows the defender's choices and secures the win.

sl-b3u.spoken: The defending king must stay close to the action and keep opposition alive if the queens come off. Drifting toward the flank lets the opponent force a favorable trade.

sl-b47.spoken: The king must choose correctly under pressure. One wrong step hands over the opposition, and the opponent converts that into a win.

sl-b3o.spoken: The knight's path to the h-pawn decides the endgame. The defender's king holds the opposition, blocks the attacker's king from entering, and the win slips away.

sl-b3t.spoken: The king steps into opposition, and the opponent must yield ground. That forced retreat lets your king break through and take the pawn — slow, methodical, decisive.

sl-b3m.spoken: The king must step precisely to keep the opposition. That one move locks White's king in place and lets Black take the pawns; any other step lets White slip free.

sl-b4s.spoken: The extra pawns only win if conversion stays precise. The defending king is active, so the pawns must advance with the king's support.

sl-b3w.spoken: The opposition is a powerful weapon: keeping it lets the defender freeze the attacker's king, even a pawn up. Any flanking attempt fails because the defender's pawn is further advanced and stops the break.

sl-b45.spoken: The rook chooses its square to hold the opposition and block the pawn. The patient rook waits one file back, losing a tempo while staying active. The hasty move lets the pawn step forward and hands the king the opposition.

sl-b49.spoken: The kings face off in opposition, and every king move is delicate. One careless step hands the opposition away, and the opponent seizes it, wins the pawns, and converts.

sl-b4t.spoken: The bishop pair plus the better king decides the pawn endgame. With rooks traded, White's knight stands badly, the king trails, and Black's advanced king becomes the winning factor.

sl-b41.spoken: When the king leads the pawn, opposition decides the outcome. Kings face off with one square between them, and the player to move must yield. Take the opposition, force the enemy king aside, then outflank and bring your king forward to escort the pawn home.

sl-b48.spoken: The extra square gives the defender more options, but most still fail. The attacker uses the additional space to outflank.

sl-b4f.spoken: Win the pawn first, then take opposition to promote. When the opponent holds opposition, advance the pawn; when they step off, advance the other pawn.

sl-b4r.spoken: Fix the pawns on one color complex, and the advance stalls — the defender's precise move is the only one that avoids the loss.

sl-b4p.spoken: Win the enemy pawn first, then promote your own. But taking the pawn does not guarantee the win — the defender's drawing technique can still hold.

sl-b4e.spoken: The king steps in front of the pawn and the draw holds. The side with the pawn must choose: push it or bring the king forward first.

sl-b4a.spoken: The king holds opposition to keep the enemy king out of the key square. Once the enemy king must step aside, the bishop is freed and the pawn advances.

sl-b3n.spoken: The king must match the tempo of the pawn shield. If the pawn advances, the king steps back to hold the opposition and force zugzwang, but the correct square shifts with structure and turn.

sl-b4h.spoken: The defending king sits on the pawn's path, and if it is near enough, it reaches the pawn in a single move — but only when the attacking king is off elsewhere. Push that king away with opposition and checks, and the pawn survives.

sl-b3v.spoken: Approach with the far side. Moving straight forward lets Black take the opposition and hold the draw. Coming around the other way forces the pawn forward, trades it off, and lands the king on the same rank as the weak pawn to take it.

sl-b4x.spoken: The extra pawn wins only with precision. Grabbing the pawn at once is not best; improving the king or the pawn structure first is stronger. When the opponent misses that capture, the winning pawn promotes.

sl-b4m.spoken: The rook endgame favors the side with the pawns only if they judge the rook trade carefully. The enemy’s distant passed pawn wins any pure pawn race, so forcing the exchange of rooks is not automatic.

sl-b5q.spoken: A closed center leaves the light-squared bishop a prisoner behind its own pawns.

sl-b5o.spoken: In a closed center, one key square becomes the battleground. Plant a piece there, and the opponent suffocates — especially when that piece backs a passed pawn.

sl-b59.spoken: The c-pawn push is the key lever: it drags both kings toward the e-pawn, and everything then turns on that pawn.

sl-b53.spoken: The queen trade is only winning if the endgame is played precisely. Hold the pawns back and bring the king forward instead.

sl-b5t.spoken: A bad bishop still commands long diagonals, while a knight touches at most eight squares. Paired with a rook on the other half of the board, their reach smothers the enemy knight.

sl-b5y.spoken: Central pawns cage the same-colored bishop, turning it into a passive piece and letting the opponent act freely.

sl-b56.spoken: The king escorts the passed pawn forward. When the enemy king commits to block, waiting moves force them into zugzwang.

sl-b5j.spoken: The extra kingside pawn decides the endgame. The defender's rook pawn becomes a liability, not a resource, and the extra pawn wins.

sl-b52.spoken: The connected pawns hold the draw against the separated pawns, even when one black pawn is passed with the king behind. One wrong move turns the draw into a loss.

sl-b60.spoken: The flank attack looks scary, but random moves lose the game. Meet it with a concrete plan.

sl-b5d.spoken: The extra pawn changes nothing about the winning plan, it just adds cover. The attacker still drives his own pawns forward and stays in charge.

sl-b69.spoken: The opening balanced out with both sides holding opposite pawn majorities. The plan is not to force a decisive edge, but to activate the king and clamp down on the opponent's pieces.

sl-b5f.spoken: The knight trade into a pawn endgame looks tempting, but the resulting structure decides everything. Black still has kingside counterplay, so the conversion is far from automatic.

sl-b58.spoken: The rook trade leaves a pawn endgame where the black queenside pawns are frozen by the b-pawn, and the white kingside majority decides the game.

sl-b5x.spoken: The bishop sits on the long diagonal doing nothing while White's pieces press forward. That gap in activity decides the game.

sl-b5l.spoken: A rook check that also eyes the pawn sets a trap: if the king takes it, the defender has no legal moves and the game is a stalemate.

sl-b5g.spoken: When the defender’s h-pawn still sits on its starting square, the ending is a draw. Once that pawn advances, the stronger side wins by walking over and taking it.

sl-b5k.spoken: The attacking king sidesteps to threaten the pawn. If the capture is safe, the defender must take it — declining the pawn loses the game.

sl-b61.spoken: Copying your opponent move for move looks clever, but it ignores strategy. Match the plan, not the pattern, or the position collapses on its own.

sl-b5n.spoken: In a closed center, the side with more space holds a structural edge, yet the blockade forces play to the flanks.

sl-b5v.spoken: A bishop that looks "biting on granite"—stuck behind its own pawns—still counts as developed if it guards the king, watches the center, and holds a later plan, like a minority attack pushing the b-pawn.

sl-b66.spoken: Both sides need a plan here. White intends to challenge the bishop and pressure the c-file, while Black holds firm and aims for equality.

sl-b5u.spoken: A bishop that looks harmless can turn into a real liability when the opponent locks it out of the game. Forced onto a dead square with no prospects, it becomes a permanent weakness.

sl-b5s.spoken: The bishop on the long diagonal goes mummified once the pawn shuts the door. With no pawn breaks left, its diagonal stays sealed and the piece has no future.

sl-b5b.spoken: The rook step is a commitment, not a threat—it may steer the game into a pawn endgame. If the enemy king circles in to support the pawn, the pawn holds, White finds no way forward, and the game ends drawn.

sl-b4y.spoken: The king outruns the opponent to the queenside, and the extra pawns decide it even if the enemy promotes first.

sl-b54.spoken: The king has two candidate squares to halt the passed pawn. The f-file square is correct, because the e-file lets the opposing king slip past, while either f-file square locks the escape route shut.

sl-b55.spoken: The pawn's square decides the outcome. If it sits one step further out, the defender's king cannot step in front, and the fortress fails. The king must pick the right file to block the pawn.

sl-b5i.spoken: The king was just in time to reach the critical square, so taking the pawn only leads to a draw. The defending king catches the passer before the opponent's king can support it.

sl-b4z.spoken: The passed pawn needs protection from being challenged. A pawn push to block the opponent's advance keeps the defender from striking, and the pawn stays safe.

sl-b5c.spoken: In pawn endgames, deep calculation is practical, unlike in tangled middlegames. The player trusted positional judgment, not full lines, knowing two pawns on the queenside hold the enemy pawns back, and that structure alone decides the win.

sl-b5w.spoken: The bishop is a liability, not a strength: passive, sealed out by the closed center, and never touches the action. That handicap outweighs ugly pawns, so Black's advantage stands.

sl-b65.spoken: The defender drifted into the endgame with no plan, and a pawn push hands the opponent a target. Black then strikes on both flanks, and every reply is a forced, uncomfortable defense.

sl-b5a.spoken: The pawn endgame was the losing call. Trading rooks leaves a king-and-pawn fight where the h-pawn is a runner, the king breaks in, and the passed pawn decides.

sl-b5m.spoken: The rook keeps a checking square alive. If White tries to remove it, Black slides the rook behind the bishop's reach, and the capture leaves stalemate. White must see the trick and play around it.

sl-b63.spoken: Pressure the bishop until it abandons control of the key central square. Once it yields, the knight steps into the outpost, and the pattern is a piece-improvement plan, not merely a pawn-structure idea.

sl-b62.spoken: Spot the weaknesses first, then ruin the pawn structure that guards them. After that, reposition slowly, avoid exchanges, defend the weak pawns, and only then advance.

sl-b68.spoken: The attack was staged many moves earlier, waiting for the moment it could land. The opponent missed one defense, yet the threats alone were already overwhelming.

sl-b5p.spoken: A closed center makes king-side pawn pushes safe. When the center is locked, those advances no longer expose your king because the opponent cannot open lines to strike back.

sl-b5r.spoken: A single pawn push can cripple two pieces at once: it slams the door on the bishop’s diagonal and leaves the knight without its best support.

sl-b5e.spoken: The king must aim for the corner, not the edge. From the fifth-rank g-pawn, stepping to the near side allows stalemate after the push; the king must go to the far corner first, then the corner square, then push the pawn twice.

sl-b51.spoken: One square decides everything here. Put the defending king on the right side and it's a draw; a single square off and it's a loss.

sl-b57.spoken: Only the side with a pawn can win this endgame. The defender must find precise moves to hold the draw or steal the win.

sl-b6b.spoken: A plan assumes cooperation; a refutation is the opponent's answer. Shape every idea against their best defense.

sl-b6g.spoken: A two-move idea is not a plan. A real plan targets the king, cracks the pawn structure, or invades on the queenside.

sl-b6z.spoken: The bishop-for-knight trade leaves White with the pair but a weak pawn. Defending it with the rook invites a bishop exchange that neutralizes White's advantage.

sl-b6h.spoken: Judge the position in front of you, not the opening that produced it. The engine sees no history—only the pawn structure—and neither should you.

sl-b6c.spoken: The move is only half the answer. Back it with a plan that leads to a concrete win.

sl-b6j.spoken: Commit to the minority attack once it starts. Changing course mid-plan only wastes the tempi already spent.

sl-b6d.spoken: The plan is an investment. Once you commit to it, changing course mid-game just loses your gains.

sl-b7g.spoken: Two bishops crisscross the board while White’s pieces fail to coordinate. That mismatch hands Black the initiative, and White’s stray pawn just hangs as a target.

sl-b7c.spoken: The bishop pair is an asset, so don't trade it off cheaply. Retreating the attacked bishop to its old square wastes time — find a new active diagonal instead.

sl-b7h.spoken: The pawn thrust chases the bishop and forces a retreat. Capturing with the pawn surrenders the bishop pair and loosens the kingside.

sl-b74.spoken: Capture the active bishop first. That wins the bishop pair and frees the black king from its pressure, while the intended knight move only leads to a flawed follow-up.

sl-b6u.spoken: With a bishop pair against you, activity is everything. Bring the worst piece, that stranded knight, into the game before it turns into a permanent liability.

sl-b6f.spoken: A plan needs patience. Stop and ask: what blocks the plan, how do I remove that block, and how does the opponent prevent it?

sl-b7a.spoken: Trading bishop for knight gives up the bishop pair, a real concession. In open positions, the two bishops are an edge, and this position stays open, so the pair keeps its value.

sl-b6t.spoken: The bishop pair and a passive knight leave Black tied down. The light-squared bishop controls the queenside pawns, and the king steps to safety while the central pawn majority advances.

sl-b78.spoken: The two bishops pay off over the long term, especially when the position opens up. So the bishop side seeks open lines, and the opponent keeps things closed.

sl-b75.spoken: The bishop pair thrives in open positions. Push pawns to open diagonals for the bishops, while Black fights to keep the position closed.

sl-b6o.spoken: The queen steps to the blocking square, the knight joins her, and the pawns march to pry open the enemy king. The plan is not flawless, but a clear idea crushes a positionless reaction.

sl-b6l.spoken: The pawn breaks through by sacrifice. Give up one pawn to clear the road for another, turning a blocked position into a promotion race.

sl-b7d.spoken: The bishop pair and a sound pawn skeleton give White the lasting edge. With the bishop rerouted to the long diagonal, the long-term pressure builds.

sl-b6p.spoken: The long-diagonal bishop is active, while the opponent's is walled in by its own pawns and shut off from the open file. The bishop pair loses its edge.

sl-b6x.spoken: The bishop pair is a long-term asset, but losing one to a bad trade changes the endgame. When the tactic strikes, the material loss becomes decisive.

sl-b6s.spoken: The bishop pair rules once the defender's bishop is gone. The surviving bishop controls the entry squares, keeps the knight out, and backs the pawns forward.

sl-b6a.spoken: Black's early shuffling costs the initiative. Stopping development lets White build up freely and take over the game.

sl-b70.spoken: The bishop pair is an asset, but Black's structure is sounder and the weak pawn must be defended. After one bishop is traded off, the remaining bishop has no good squares and stays passive.

sl-b7j.spoken: The bishop takes the knight, and Black chooses between two roads to equality. One trades down into a level endgame; the other pushes the f-pawn to challenge the bishop.

sl-b79.spoken: The raking bishops control both long diagonals, so White can sacrifice the queen. The queen's deflection and the pin against her let the attack roll on, no matter the material cost.

sl-b7f.spoken: The bishop sortie surrenders the pair for nothing. After the pawn chase and the trade, White is happy to keep both bishops.

sl-b71.spoken: The centralized bishop dominates the board while Black's other bishop sits passive, unable to develop without dropping a pawn. White's edge is pure activity—one piece doing real work against two that cannot.

sl-b6v.spoken: The chronic weakness on the queenside is a permanent target. The king stands near, and the bishop slides in to add pressure. With Black's pieces passive, the bishop pair secures long-term winning chances.

sl-b7l.spoken: The bishop is overextended, guarded by a lone knight and ripe for attack. Pushing the pawn and recapturing with the queen keeps the dark-squared bishop from being traded away, preserving the bishop pair.
