sl-elf.spoken: The pawn steps forward before the knight would claim that square, which looks strange. But it starts a chain, and when the next pawn extends it, the pair fights for the center.

sl-el0.spoken: The knight jumps to the outpost, then to the kingside, and Black's deep grasp of the position wins fast. White runs out of moves and resigns, down three pawns.

sl-ems.spoken: The trade fails because Black answers with a pin, keeping the pressure on.

sl-emc.spoken: Trading a knight for a bishop is only sound when it supports your center. Here the trade hands Black a stronger center and opens the f-file for his rook.

sl-emg.spoken: The opponent keeps pieces on the board and dodges trades, holding pressure so the defender never gets a moment to regroup.

sl-en8.spoken: The piece is lost, but the activity remains. The attack stays live, and Black must walk a knife's edge to survive.

sl-enb.spoken: A practical defense can still work even when technically losing, if it tempts the opponent into a rushed, flawed decision.

sl-en1.spoken: Exchanging material under pressure can ease the attack, but the simplified position sometimes favors the attacker even more.

sl-emj.spoken: The bishop has done its job and now trades off cleanly. The knight eyes the weak square, keeping White from settling there.

sl-emf.spoken: When space is tight, trades help. Swapping that bishop, even the strange one, cuts the opponent's attacking power and frees up your defenses.

sl-enf.spoken: In a rook endgame, a solid but passive defense may hold the draw, yet constant pressure still creates practical problems for the defender.

sl-en6.spoken: The extra pawn and active rooks look strong, but the win is not yet clear. The knight sits badly, and the mating threats are real, yet the defender still holds resources.

sl-en3.spoken: The forcing line wins bigger, but the simple one still collects material. The queen-and-knight checks are sharper, yet the practical choice keeps the win without the risk.

sl-emw.spoken: When the opponent’s active piece causes trouble, trading it off neutralizes it—especially when you already stand better.

sl-emx.spoken: A material lead grows when pieces come off the board. Each trade cuts the opponent’s counterplay and steers the game toward a winning endgame.

sl-emr.spoken: The strong bishop gets traded, and the position locks up. The knight settles in and becomes a blockade. The attacker's pieces lose activity, the open files close, and the breakthrough disappears.

sl-enl.spoken: The position is already bad, so a desperate move like pushing the g-pawn gets played — not because it works, but because every alternative is just as unappealing.

sl-emv.spoken: Trading pieces with a space advantage is usually wrong, but here it's right: the rook trade steers Black into a favorable endgame.

sl-emz.spoken: The knight steps into the center offering trades. It sits well defended, so swapping everything off strips White of any attacking chances.

sl-enk.spoken: The queen drops into the heart of the position, and the defense has no answer. Even if the engines find no forced win, the pressure is overwhelming and guarantees at least a draw.

sl-emb.spoken: The knight jumps in to trade, and the attack thins. The danger is not a draw, but the initiative slipping away and the position going flat.

sl-emm.spoken: Break the position open at once, and the weak pawn falls again. Other routes rip open the queenside while the opponent wastes time on pawn moves.

sl-en4.spoken: The bishop is bait. Taking it walks into the pin, and the pin loses material. Let it stand, and the tension stays yours.

sl-ena.spoken: The knight steps forward to hit the weak pawn and settle the pieces, and White is simply lost. It is a simpler, more practical choice than the razor-thin rook endgame lines.

sl-emi.spoken: Black must not trade pieces too freely; that only helps White. Holding the tension keeps the messy position playable, while moves like the knight to an outpost or the rooks to open files are fine. The real danger is grabbing the central pawn.

sl-en9.spoken: The exchanges leave the position near equal, but probing for weaknesses still has value. Moves that create tension force the opponent to make decisions, even with the balance intact.

sl-eni.spoken: The rook takes the aggressive file instead of the safe one — a calculated gamble. With Black short on time, White bets that the sharper move creates practical problems.

sl-emt.spoken: Trading pieces when ahead sounds like a rule, but the real question is which piece you give up and which you keep. And if queens come off, ask whose king stands safer.

sl-emq.spoken: The engine's top line is nearly impossible to spot in blitz. A patient rook lift activates the piece and sets up a slow, surrounding attack on the king — no immediate check required.

sl-en5.spoken: The initiative demands a choice: cash in material for a direct attack, or keep the pressure on without risking what you have. Sacrificing the queen or rook can end it, but solid play often wins just as cleanly.

sl-ene.spoken:
The rook steps into a practical square, setting a trap for the clock.  
If the opponent misses the single saving reply, a pawn falls.

sl-enh.spoken: Weak pawns are an endgame asset: the king marches in and feasts. But in the middlegame, activity and attacking chances keep the position messy, and the pawns' weakness is hard to exploit.

sl-ema.spoken: The knight's hop looks tempting—it hits the pawn and grips the dark squares—but the pawn takes back, and the knight lands on the worst square on the board. Worse, the trade would loosen the cramped side's bind, so the move is discarded.

sl-emo.spoken: The bishop sidles over to pile pressure on the pinned knight, but the choice to prevent the pawn breaks and chase the rook off is deeper. The engine may call it clearly winning, yet the position resists easy conversion—the exact move order decides everything.

sl-emd.spoken: The queen and bishop support the center pawn and set up attacking chances, including a possible sacrifice on that square. The enemy knight sits in the center, pressing against the bishop and breaking White’s coordination.

sl-en2.spoken: In a losing or equal game, prioritize practical, tricky moves over the engine's top line. A queen move that creates threats invites errors, especially when the clock is short.

sl-emu.spoken: The enemy knight sits active in the center, menacing the queenside. Swapping it off clears the board and strips away a real attacking force.

sl-en7.spoken: When normal play drifts toward a slow loss, complicate with a piece sacrifice. It is a practical choice: losing positions justify a risky move that hands the opponent a chance to err.

sl-emn.spoken: The board is chaos: pieces hang on both sides, one bishop is pinned, and even the engine's slight edge does not reassure. A human simply struggles to find a move.

sl-en0.spoken: Trading the d-pawn for the c-pawn frees Black's bishop and helps his development. Taking with the other pawn lets Black recapture, and White swaps his c-pawn for a weak pawn—no real gain.

sl-emh.spoken: Taking that pawn helps White recapture with the knight and brings the bishop to life. Keeping pieces on keeps the isolated pawn a target, since tactical chances remain.

sl-emy.spoken: The knight leaps forward only to meet a counter-offer of trades. If pieces come off, activity fades and structural strength takes over.

sl-end.spoken: The rook joins the fight, keeps the tension and eyes the pawn break that frees the bishop. If the rook is taken, the recapture restores the bishop's activity. The queen tries to hold things together, but White keeps playing freeing moves.

sl-emk.spoken: A bishop that seals off the king is a powerful piece. Giving it up for a quieter piece, like one that hasn't moved yet, is usually a blunder.

sl-eop.spoken: The knight is defended twice, but one defender just stepped away and left it hanging.

sl-enq.spoken: A deep tactic hides near the time control, easy to overlook when the clock is tight.

sl-eos.spoken: Remove the knight’s protector first, then take the knight itself. The queen’s defense falls apart, and the defender is left paralyzed.

sl-ens.spoken: Quick decisions under the clock bring mistakes that slower play would avoid.

sl-eoo.spoken: The attack removes the defender — the bishop that shields the queen. When the queen is forced away, the bishop is left hanging and falls.

sl-enp.spoken: Time pressure hides the simplest moves. A player can spend half the clock on a losing move and still miss the winning defense available the whole time.

sl-eor.spoken: The bishop is the only guard of a vital square. Sacrifice the queen to take that bishop, the guard disappears, and the knight leaps in to fork.

sl-eov.spoken: The opponent ducks the queen move because it lets a pawn step forward and drive off a key defender. With that defender gone, the queen falls for a rook and the material swing is decisive.

sl-eou.spoken: The rook steps in to cover the fork, but the queen is now the sole defender. Attack that queen with a pawn, and the defender must abandon the rook again.

sl-enm.spoken: The trade and equal trade leave the position objectively level. Play now with renewed energy — this is a practical fight, not a forced win.

sl-eo3.spoken: The knight and rook are both loose, and one move attacks them at the same time. Since Black cannot defend two undefended pieces at once, the double attack wins material.

sl-eob.spoken: Loose pieces invite double attacks. When your opponent leaves pieces unprotected, look for a fork or a single move that hits two targets at once.

sl-env.spoken: When in check, three options exist: move the king, capture the attacker, or block the line. Blocking is easy to miss, but it is always a legal path that deserves consideration.

sl-eny.spoken: The fork is there, but not yet. First make a preparatory move that loosens two white pieces, then the fork lands and wins material.

sl-eo8.spoken: The bishop is loose, a tall pawn waiting to be taken. Attack it with the queen, then bring the bishop in behind to create threats that win material.

sl-enw.spoken: Loose pieces invite tactics. An undefended rook can be targeted, where a defended square would keep it safe.

sl-eo9.spoken: The king comes first. Even when enemy pieces look loose, secure your own position and connect your pieces before chasing targets.

sl-eon.spoken: A piece is lost in the trade sequence because the bishop was left undefended. The opponent simply captures it and wins material.

sl-eo4.spoken: The queen steps in to guard the key pawn, so the direct push is neutralized. Dropping pieces onto loose squares turns them into targets, so that idea is bad.

sl-enu.spoken: Time pressure hides tactics that observers see instantly. That is natural, and naming the miss is about learning, not judgment.

sl-eom.spoken: The bishop attacks a pawn the queen protects. Trade off or drive away that defender, and the pawn falls for nothing.

sl-eo2.spoken: The knight and the advanced bishop hang by a thread—only the queen defends them. Chase the queen, and when she retreats, she still has to guard the knight. That pressure creates tactics.

sl-eoq.spoken: The defender is the key. Attack it, force it away, and the piece it protected falls.

sl-eot.spoken: The opponent's pawn advance weakens the kingside. Capturing the knight that guards the key square removes the defender, and the fork lands.

sl-ent.spoken: In time trouble, the goal is not the best move but the playable one. Solid moves that keep the tension force the opponent to burn the clock, while speculative complications only give them a chance.

sl-eo5.spoken: A loose piece invites tactics. Here a fork by the knight attacks the king and queen together, and however the king steps aside, the queen falls.

sl-eok.spoken: The queen eyes the mating square, but the knight guards it. The knight advances to attack the defender, and once it is captured or forced away, the mate lands.

sl-eof.spoken: The bishop captures and then slides to a line where it hits the rook and keeps itself safe. The king's exposure turns every loose piece into a target, since any check can cost the rook.

sl-eoh.spoken: The queen and king sit on the same line, ripe for a discovered attack. A rook gives check, and when the king steps aside, the queen falls.

sl-enx.spoken: One loose piece is a warning; two is an invitation. When White’s pieces sit unprotected, a single fork lands on both at once.

sl-eol.spoken: The bishop grabs a pawn that is defended as often as it is attacked. First remove a guard instead, and the target falls for nothing.

sl-eo1.spoken: The bishop retreats from the knight's attack even though no immediate tactic looms, spending a tempo. That move is part of a wider plan to cut down on loose pieces, since undefended pieces invite tactical blows.

sl-eo7.spoken: The bishop is loose, unprotected, and ripe for a tempo attack. Black strikes in the center, even while behind in castling. If White takes, the recapture leaves the bishop still hanging.

sl-enr.spoken: Time pressure and complexity invite mistakes, and both sides trade inaccuracies freely.

sl-eo6.spoken: The bishop takes on the king's doorstep, a sacrifice that punishes how loose Black's pieces sit. If Black grabs back, the queen delivers check, and when the king retreats, the knight leaps in with a discovered attack on the exposed queen.

sl-eod.spoken: Take the loose piece. The pawn break looks tempting, but it risks handing the attack to the opponent — the capture is solid and safe.

sl-eoe.spoken: The knight lands on the outpost and hits the queen while the other knight sits loose. An unprotected piece turns the position tactical, even when nothing falls at once.

sl-enz.spoken: The bishop hangs loose, and the pawn in front of the king guards the open file. Grabbing that pawn invites counterplay that bares the king and costs material.

sl-eoc.spoken: The bishops stand without pawn cover, guarded only by the king. That invites checks and attacks on them, and the king cannot answer everything.

sl-eow.spoken: The pawn advance that looks natural can backfire when it lets the opponent push past and embarrass the bishop. Better to strike the center instead, giving the bishop a retreat square where it gains activity and eyes key central and kingside squares.

sl-eog.spoken: The knight is trapped, so the defender tries to buy time with a developing move, often the bishop. The attacker simply protects the knight and then targets that loose piece, keeping the pressure on.

sl-enn.spoken: The pawn break looks tempting, but the bishop stays strong, and even after the invasion, the queen slides into place to set up a fork that wins one of the rooks. Trading queens simplifies the board and drains the attack.

sl-eoj.spoken: Taking out the piece that guards a stronger one clears the way to grab material—the defender falls first, and a rook follows.

sl-eo0.spoken: The knight stands unprotected, inviting the classic Greek gift. The bishop takes the h-pawn with check, and the loose knight makes the sacrifice work.

sl-eoa.spoken: The knight lands on a square that hits the bishop, leaving it undefended. Retreating the bishop to a king-protected square removes the target and ends the tactic.

sl-eoi.spoken: The pawn thrusts loosen Black's kingside, and the knight on the rim turns into a loose piece. White captures in the center, then brings the queen over to hunt that knight down.

sl-eno.spoken: The queen finds the one square that saves the bishop and starts two threats at once. Every other queen move leaves the position hanging. Black cannot pressure the bishop, and any queen check gets met by the pawn, so White keeps time to rescue the rook.

sl-epb.spoken: Total seriousness in every game, even against weaker opponents, turns routine wins into maximum results.

sl-eq8.spoken: The attack hits so hard that even a grandmaster can miss the defense. Black's position is already near collapse, and White's advantage is decisive.

sl-epe.spoken: A draw claim for insufficient losing chances can be overturned when the arbiter errs, and the resumed game may end in a win.

sl-epw.spoken: The queen looks active, but one careless step can walk into a rook attack that harasses her and costs a pawn.

sl-epx.spoken: The careless capture opens the door for the central pawn push, and suddenly the position turns equal or better for the second player.

sl-epr.spoken: The player looked for a rook move but overlooked that the bishop defends the queen, so a queen trade was available. That miss leads to a worse move, and the opponent pins the knight.

sl-epu.spoken: The knight threatens a fork that wins material. Black must answer by trading it off or moving the queen to safety.

sl-epd.spoken: Tournament rules apply to everyone, regardless of rating or fame. A forfeit for not keeping score shows that scorekeeping is mandatory, not optional.

sl-eps.spoken: The bishop retreats to safety, refusing the opponent's invitation to complicate. Those aggressive moves aim at sacrifices; stepping back denies them extra tempi and keeps the position calm.

sl-ep4.spoken: The bishop steps out to attack the knight, developing with a threat. When the bishop must leave, trading it off beats retreating to a worse diagonal.

sl-epy.spoken: The queen's pressure on the diagonal outweighs a free pawn. The pawn-grab would be a distraction; the opponent's attack on the bishop fails to answer the real threat.

sl-eoy.spoken: The bishop belongs on the active diagonal, where it pressures a pawn. A quieter square may be safe, but it wastes the piece's potential.

sl-eph.spoken: The theory runs deep here, and both sides castle on opposite wings, each storming the other's king. Whoever knows this structure better holds the edge.

sl-epv.spoken: A queenside break must be timed with care. If the knight jumps to the edge, it attacks the pawn and ignites counterplay of its own.

sl-eq5.spoken: The queen retreat is criticized here for what it allows: Black builds serious pressure and the king grows vulnerable.

sl-ep0.spoken: The bishop sits behind its own pawn, sealed off from the center. Pushing past it would only let the pawn run into a wall that is already well defended.

sl-eq4.spoken: The queen retreats along the back rank to defend, and the bishop retreats to cover the key square. That holds the balance and steers into a drawish endgame.

sl-ep5.spoken: The early bishop move makes it a big pawn, sitting behind its own pawn and eyeing nothing. The same piece belongs on the active diagonal, where it points at the king's weakness.

sl-epj.spoken: The pawn advance forces the knight to retreat, and with no good squares left, it is effectively out of the game. Capturing the pawn is no relief, because it opens lines for the bishop and the rook.

sl-epa.spoken: Black angles to play the bishop to a strong diagonal, attacking the queen and trading off the dark-squared bishops. That bishop thrives on open diagonals, so Black targets it for exchange.

sl-epg.spoken: White forgoes sharp tactics for a steady buildup, placing pieces on natural squares. The slow setup leaves Black with a key choice: whether to push the b-pawn forward.

sl-eq0.spoken: The bishop hangs under attack, and castling can walk into a capture. Retreating it to safety first keeps the material intact.

sl-eq1.spoken: White's next move must be careful. A bishop to that square faces tactical replies from the opponent that open counterplay, so the goal is to keep the opponent out of a comfortable position.

sl-epi.spoken: The pawn push is not a positional mistake here because the usual refuting knight jump is unavailable. Both the bishop and the knight are en prise, the light-squared bishop is powerful, and Black wins material with the bishop pair.

sl-ep2.spoken: The bishop steps out in front of the pawn chain to keep its lines open. Black reinforces the center and aims to bring the other bishop out, but White's queen stops that plan by eyeing a weak pawn on the flank.

sl-eq6.spoken: The rook darts out for counterplay, but rushing the pawn lets the attack back in. Better to drop the rook back first, keep control, and let the pawn advance on your terms.

sl-epm.spoken: The queen trap was missed because the king fled to safety before the knight arrived. Moving the knight uncovers the trap: the queen has no escape, and the only capture that waits is not enough.

sl-epn.spoken: The knight hop to the outpost looks tempting, but first weigh the bishop's activity and the damage to the pawn structure. If the bishop wakes up or the pawns crack, the penetration costs more than it wins.

sl-eq3.spoken: The pawn move quietly closes the door on Black's freeing break — the break is met with a tactic. Black wisely declines it, develops the knight instead, and keeps the position solid.

sl-epp.spoken: The outpost knight sits securely, and the plan is to back it with a pawn while the queen prepares to join. But the opponent can strike back with a pawn of their own. Tactics are always on the table, even in a positional game.

sl-eq9.spoken: The aggressive bishop moves look sharp but both fail. One is answered by castling, the other lets the queen give check, forcing a trade that hands Black the initiative.

sl-epo.spoken: The push opens a door. Once the pawn advances, both knights leap forward and the pressure on the weak square becomes crushing. If the queen tries to snatch a pawn, the knight jumps in with check and traps her.

sl-ep6.spoken: The knight grabs the pawn, but the recapture chases it off. The pawn advances and kicks that bishop off its best diagonal, and now tactical threats loom over Black's position.

sl-ep7.spoken: The knight dominates the bishop in the closed position, a classic winning edge. White tries to build a fortress, so Black must add pressure without opening lines for the bishop.

sl-eq2.spoken: The rook turns the tables. Without it, a calm king move wins for Black. With it, Black is forced to block on a bad square, and the tactic decides.

sl-epz.spoken: A winning position can vanish in one blow. A sacrifice that starts a counterattack can flip the game and pull the position back to near equality.

sl-ept.spoken: A recapture can turn a winning trade into a losing one. If the defender sees the trick and sidesteps with a king move toward the center, the sequence fails.

sl-eoz.spoken: The bishop's post looks inviting, but that piece can turn into a target; the king sits safer here, yet the bishop may not earn its square.

sl-epf.spoken: The early flank pawn move is rare but thematic, preparing the advance that challenges the bishop and seizes the central square. This game is the model for executing that plan.

sl-epk.spoken: The queen steps forward and creates threats, but the defender answers with her queen, leaving a central square unguarded. That lets White push there, supporting the knight, attacking the enemy knight, and freeing the bishop.

sl-eq7.spoken: The rook sneaks to the third rank, setting up checks that drive the king back or force perpetual. Pushing the pawn straight away allows those tricks and turns a win into a draw.

sl-epl.spoken: The rook lift and bishop retreat look natural, but the pawn advance frees the e-file and kicks the bishop. The piece that looked active is now misplaced, and the attack gathers force.

sl-epq.spoken: The queen attacks the knight, and the threat to trade queens wins it. But the hidden resource is a perpetual check from the enemy knight, so the win is not clean.

sl-eqr.spoken: The development lead buys compensation, but it is borrowed time. If the opponent catches up, the advantage vanishes.

sl-eqg.spoken: White keeps the edge with simple defense. Black's tricks amount to nothing, and the win stays safe.

sl-er6.spoken: The bishop steps out early in this rare opening line. It is playable but shows up less often at higher levels.

sl-er9.spoken: The player hunts for a win no matter the rating, while others settle for draws. That mindset produces more victories and earns respect.

sl-er1.spoken: Rely on patterns in the endgame, not calculation from scratch. Known techniques win the clock and the game.

sl-eqs.spoken: Even top players can slip in the opening and fall behind in development. That lead must be pressed actively, and exploiting it is rarely automatic.

sl-er4.spoken: The Baltic Defense is a sharp, offbeat opening that dodges main lines and creates practical problems. White's checking queen disrupts Black's development.

sl-era.spoken: The fighter refuses early draws and plays for the win even against a stronger opponent, while the pragmatist accepts the offer when outmatched.

sl-erd.spoken: The center belongs to White, but the queenside is Black's playground. The b-pawn break challenges the center and lights the fuse for counterplay.

sl-eqe.spoken: The attack on both knights is a phantom—Black grabs a pawn and no recapture follows. The defensive move is unnecessary and hands White the right to castle.

sl-eqk.spoken: The desperate tries are not real threats. The knight is not a genuine resource here because the pawn and king stand in the way, so Black refutes calmly.

sl-eql.spoken: After winning material, a quick central queen move invites a tactical reply that strikes two targets at once. The position stays winning, but the carelessness hands the opponent counterplay.

sl-eqn.spoken: Before the plan, look for danger. Black can strike the pawn and the knight, and a bishop landing on that square prepares to trade itself for the rook in the corner.

sl-equ.spoken: The queen and rook join forces to overload the defenses. A queen check drives the king away, and the rook swoops in to take the knight.

sl-er2.spoken: The king heads for the third rank, and the draw is agreed. The pawn push was known from the books, the position a standard draw.

sl-er3.spoken: Endgame patterns matter because fatigue and time pressure make calculation unreliable. Familiar shapes save clock and mistakes.

sl-eqz.spoken: The pawn push removes the defender of the mating square, turning the rook's threat into a forced mate. The bishop backs that threat, and the king's attack on the rook makes it a double attack.

sl-eqf.spoken: The queen's advance is risky: it lets the rook capture on the seventh rank, creating a dangerous pin that shifts the game's character. Even if Black recaptures, the rook sits awkwardly and White gains active play.

sl-er7.spoken: The bishop steps out early, and White answers by attacking the pawn on the queenside. That probe targets a weakness while the game still takes an unusual shape.

sl-eqo.spoken: The bishop’s placement is bold, but taking it lets the rook slide down and the queen deliver a check from the corner. White must weigh the capture against the threats it unleashes.

sl-eqt.spoken: The king's defenders are all watching from the far side, taking no part. That disarray invites a spectacular sacrifice, because the coordination to answer it simply is not there.

sl-erc.spoken: The knight plants itself on the outpost, and the bishop captures the weak pawn. Black's pieces are left misplaced, with no freeing plan.

sl-eqc.spoken: The bishop looks to cover the queenside, but that misses the sharper idea. When the knight leaps forward, the bishop must leave its diagonal, and then a sacrifice opens the king's flank, unleashing serious threats.

sl-eqw.spoken: The rook's activity is the whole point. When the bishop steps forward, the rook attacks it and threatens mate in the same move — one piece doing two jobs is what wins in the endgame.

sl-eqh.spoken: A fork may be the opponent's last trick, not their best plan. Stay alert and refuse the bait, even when the material looks free.

sl-erl.spoken: The h-pawn and knight step forward to seize kingside space and free the bishop's diagonal, setting up a pawn break against the center. Meanwhile, the bishop presses the backward pawn, forcing a response.

sl-erg.spoken: The knight's flexible development aims for a stronger square where it pressures the center and supports a thematic pawn break. If that break lands early, it gains space and activates the pieces.

sl-erj.spoken: The pawn push opens the queenside for Black, whose pieces mass there to storm forward. White must block that expansion and strike in the center instead.

sl-er8.spoken: The queen steps out early to hit the b-pawn, and the main reply pushes the e-pawn in the center. That move is the book answer, found after a few earlier tries.

sl-er5.spoken: The bishop trades itself for the knight, and that exchange disrupts the opponent's natural development. After the recapture and the check, the opponent regains the piece with a pawn in hand, but the resulting structure demands care.

sl-erk.spoken: The knight parks on the kingside to launch pawns at Black’s castled position. Black answers with the h-pawn, chasing the knight back and claiming space, then reroutes the other knight to clear the bishop’s line and free the f-pawn to strike at the center.

sl-eqv.spoken: The double attack hits rook and pawn, so pushing pawns loses the advantage. Protecting the pawn with the rook keeps winning chances alive.

sl-eqb.spoken: The rook's move is a trap, not a threat. A winning side must not chase the bait, or the back rank will deliver the mate.

sl-eqy.spoken: The queen on that diagonal checks and hits the pawn behind the king. The king cannot abandon the pawn, so it steps back, and the attacking king moves in.

sl-eqd.spoken: The bishop trade tempts, but exposing the pawn makes the knight retreat to guard it.

sl-er0.spoken: The rook and bishop against the lone rook is a rare but critical theoretical endgame. Even strong players can be shaky here, and it often decides the full point.

sl-eqj.spoken: The rook stepping forward is tempting, but it walks straight into capture. The bishop is posted precisely to punish that idea, so the move is flawed.

sl-eri.spoken: The bishop on the long diagonal weakens White's hold on the central square, so White often advances only one step instead of two. That dodges the tactic of the knight capturing the pawn, but it gives up the central grip the main line enjoys.

sl-eqi.spoken: The bishop fork fails here: the opponent captures the rook with check, then takes the queen, leaving them up a rook.

sl-erb.spoken: Fighting chess draws crowds. Win or lose, the tension is real. But the scoreboard still decides the prize, and brave losses do not pay.

sl-esi.spoken: The kings stand in distant opposition, a form that matters when they are far apart. Black must pick a plan now: queenside, kingside, or straight ahead.

sl-esk.spoken: The lone drawing move steps the king aside, away from the pawn, taking distant opposition so the enemy king cannot slip behind and win.

sl-esd.spoken: Distant opposition is one case of corresponding squares. Corresponding squares are the deeper idea.

sl-erz.spoken: The rook strikes the pawn, and any greedy capture on the far side walks into a knight fork that picks up the rook. The defender is forced into passivity.

sl-erw.spoken: The king stands without pawn cover, wide open to attack. A rook slides onto the open line to join the assault, doubling the pressure on the exposed monarch.

sl-err.spoken: The bishop heads to the long diagonal, with pawns preparing to support it. The setup stays flexible, and many moves remain viable.

sl-erx.spoken: The rook climbs its file, then slides sideways to the rank that matters—choosing the right floor. From there it aims at the weak point and attacks.

sl-esw.spoken: The king move decides the endgame. Let the enemy king escape the corner, and the win is on; trap it there, and stalemate turns the win into a draw.

sl-es8.spoken: Black trades a pawn for a lead in development and a castled king. The extra pawn is real, but the uncastled king stays safe behind its pieces, and the active bishop gives full compensation.

sl-ert.spoken: The rook climbs to the third rank, shielding the bishop and aiming at the d-file. That path also blocks a tactical blow on the h-pawn that would hand the opponent counterplay.

sl-esg.spoken: The kings stand three squares apart on the same file, and the side to move can make no progress — that is the distant opposition. The defender keeps that opposition to hold the draw.

sl-es0.spoken: The rook check forces the king aside, and the blocker falls. That is the whole motif — a passed pawn, a blockade, and a check that breaks it.

sl-esj.spoken: The extra pawn only wins the pawn endgame if the kings are placed right. The method: take the distant opposition, then outflank to grab the enemy pawn.

sl-eru.spoken: The rook slides across the third rank to the center, attacking the bishop. The defender tries to save it with knight and pawn moves, but those weaken the bishop's escape squares, and the piece gets trapped.

sl-es3.spoken: A quiet pawn move can be the whole tactic. It deflects the rook or pushes a pawn through. Once the pawn advances, the rook can no longer stop both pawns, and one of them promotes.

sl-esh.spoken: The king steps back to take the distant opposition, keeping the draw in hand. Opposition in its regular, diagonal, or distant form is the backbone of king and pawn endgames.

sl-esv.spoken: The king near the edge makes stalemate a constant threat. Checks can let the king slip out or end the game in a draw, so the queen controls squares while the king closes in.

sl-esc.spoken: The distant opposition keeps the draw alive. With an odd number of squares between the kings, the defender holds that exact distance and stops the opponent from breaking through.

sl-esq.spoken: The queen offers herself as bait for stalemate, but taking her is the trap. White sidesteps with the king, keeps the mating net tight, and the pawn keeps rolling toward promotion.

sl-ers.spoken: The rook slides to the third rank, freeing the pinned knight and aiming at either wing. That swing builds pressure on king or center, and if the back rank is loose, a rook drop to the last rank ends it.

sl-est.spoken: The king is cornered on the edge, and the knight races to the right square to control it. From there it keeps the king trapped and sets up mate on the adjacent square.

sl-esp.spoken: The pawn is the defender's last move. Taking it now may stalemate the king. Make a waiting move with your own king or pawn, force them to push, then capture.

sl-ery.spoken: The rook tour to the edge looks active, but it creates no real threats. Black simply takes a pawn on the other side, and White's pieces lack the coordination to back the plan.

sl-erv.spoken: The rook reroutes through the open file and swings across to capture on the center pawn, then slides to the side. With the queen and knight already poised on the kingside, the rook joins the attack and creates a decisive mating threat.

sl-es4.spoken: The bishop steps to the edge and hits the bishop while threatening promotion. If the opponent takes the piece, the pawn queens with checkmate. If the bishop retreats, the attacker repositions and still wins.

sl-es9.spoken: The king pushes the passed pawn, forcing the enemy king to block it. While the pawn holds the king in place, your own king steps in to win material—the threat is enough to end the game.

sl-esl.spoken: The rook can grab the hanging knight, but the win evaporates. Taking it can leave the opponent with no legal moves and force a stalemate, and retreating the rook lets them take your final pawn, ending in a theoretical draw.

sl-ese.spoken: The kings stand a full square apart, so ordinary opposition is off the table. Face them with an odd gap between, and the defender can reclaim the opposition the moment the attacker steps forward, holding the draw.

sl-esr.spoken: The bishop must refuse the take after check—capturing with it would allow stalemate. The rook recaptures instead. When the knight later falls, that capture helps, because it leaves Black with only one threat.

sl-esm.spoken: A queen down leaves little room for error, so the defender hunts for tactical tricks. A pawn offer on a critical square sets up fork traps if a minor piece takes, but if the queen accepts, the player must steer the game toward stalemate.

sl-es2.spoken: The rook sacrifices on the fifth rank, the king steps closer, and the recapture follows. When the defending king moves over, the pawn push forces a response, and the bishop slides to the diagonal behind the pawn line, breaking through and winning.

sl-esa.spoken: The defender stops the passed pawn at the earliest moment, then makes a passed pawn or a weakness on the far side as a decoy. That pulls the enemy king away and stalls all progress on the main front.

sl-esf.spoken: The king and pawn endgame is lost by one pawn, yet a draw still exists. Distant opposition keeps the black king out and holds the position.

sl-ess.spoken: In a queen endgame, the trapped king still has one resource: stalemate. Deliver mate while leaving the opponent a legal move.

sl-es7.spoken: The knight blocks the b-pawn's advance, and if it jumps forward it maintains the blockade. White has the extra pawn, so trading pieces favors White.

sl-eso.spoken: The check that permits stalemate must be avoided. Retreat the queen instead and keep pressing for mate.

sl-erm.spoken: The move order keeps several openings alive—Nimzo, Queen's Indian, QGD, or Benoni. When Black strikes at the center with the c-pawn, the Benoni appears and the center is under instant attack.

sl-ern.spoken: The light-squared bishop has no clear home because the knight blocks its natural diagonal. If White reroutes that knight, Black trades it off and pushes the center pawn, seizing a decisive initiative.

sl-ero.spoken: Black's early queenside pawn push grabs space and blocks White's flank expansion. White's central pawn advance strikes back at that pawn and ignites dynamic play.

sl-es5.spoken: The pawn push tries to lock the knight out of its best square, but it abandons the pawn beside it. The rook slides over, forces the trade, and Black walks into the endgame a pawn up.

sl-es1.spoken: The pawn push creates a double threat: rook checks on the open file, and the queen is lost for a rook. Sacrificing the rook first works too, since White's best reply is to take it, and the same tactic follows.

sl-erq.spoken: Restraining the queenside majority is the point of pushing that rook pawn. Skip it, and the opponent advances both pawns to launch the standard minority attack.

sl-esx.spoken: The attacking king must avoid cutting off the defender's last escape. That move can create stalemate when no pawn moves or captures remain.

sl-esu.spoken: The pawns sit on the third rank, the enemy king stands in front. Avoid the stalemate square; shuffle and push a pawn to drive the king off, then promote.

sl-et0.spoken: Keeping the pawn instead of capturing it avoids stalemate and keeps the win alive.

sl-etd.spoken: Keep the a-pawn and push the other. If both pawns go, a rook checkmate is all that is left; with the a-pawn alive, a second queen can follow the first.

sl-et9.spoken: When ahead in material, push a pawn toward promotion. Guard against perpetual check, which can turn your win into a draw.

sl-esy.spoken: The king is close and the pawn is near, so precision is critical. Careless play risks stalemate, so every quiet move must leave the enemy king a legal square.

sl-et2.spoken: The pawn is near promotion and the enemy king is cut off. Just march your king forward to escort it — the win plays itself.

sl-ett.spoken: The bishop takes the center, then a waiting move forces the king back to the square we want, keeping the mating net intact.

sl-etz.spoken: The bishop stands ready and passes the turn, keeping the zugzwang alive. If the knight tries to flee, the bishop steps forward and locks the position again.

sl-etu.spoken: The position is sound, but a waiting move is needed. Keep the setup intact, hand the move to the opponent, and force them onto a worse square.

sl-eu7.spoken: The defending king gets shuffled from one corner to the next, so the attacker stays patient. Waiting moves push the king to the edge, then toward the mating square.

sl-etq.spoken: The defense is stiffer, but the win still holds. Centralize the queen, push the b-pawn, and the pressure breaks through.

sl-ets.spoken: The knight's removal opens two entry squares for the king. Black can cover only one, so the penetration decides the game.

sl-etr.spoken: The knight sits on the strong square, chopping off the escape squares along the edge. Bishop and knight together fence the king in, covering every route out.

sl-et1.spoken: The king move decides the endgame. Stepping the wrong way lets the enemy king in, while the right square bars the door, keeps stalemate away, and lets the pawn promote.

sl-eta.spoken: The choice of pawn can depend on the enemy rook's activity. Pushing the f-pawn keeps that rook passive, but queening the e-pawn lets it seize the e-file with check.

sl-esz.spoken: The rook slides to the back rank, and if the knight captures, the king steps in. The knight is forced to a square where Black runs out of useful moves. Do not push pawns early—that hands Black stalemate.

sl-etc.spoken: The pawn is the win, not the mate. With the defender's pieces tied down, the path to queening stands open.

sl-eu9.spoken: The waiting move keeps every threat alive while handing Black the turn. With the knight pinned down and the pawn still under attack, Black must move the king, and White improves.

sl-eu6.spoken: The rook versus queen endgame is a win, but only with precision. A careless king advance lets the rook check forever, and a rushed move can allow stalemate or even a draw.

sl-eti.spoken: The rook sacrifice smashes the defense. When the knight recaptures, the pawn advances and forks the king and rook — promotion or material is unavoidable.

sl-et7.spoken: The stronger side pushes the pawn toward promotion while the defender blocks its path or seizes opposition. Whoever has the better-placed king decides the result.

sl-etb.spoken: The bishop is pinned to the long diagonal and cannot leave it. The advanced pawn is too far gone — even a check from the king cannot stop promotion.

sl-eu2.spoken: A material edge with no counterplay means you can shuffle and pass the move. Each waiting move forces the opponent to weaken something, and soon they blunder.

sl-etv.spoken: The defender must sometimes burn a move while holding off a passed pawn. The waiting move’s rank matters: placing too far up gives the opponent extra freedom and squanders energy.

sl-eu0.spoken: The king covers the key square, so the bishop must wait. A quiet bishop move puts the defender in zugzwang, and when the enemy bishop is forced to move, the path opens.

sl-et8.spoken: The pawn is the prize. The knight and king work together to drive the enemy king off the pawn's road, and the pawn marches through to promotion.

sl-etp.spoken: The king hides safely in the center while the queen stands centralized, cutting off checking squares. When the defender grabs the pawn, the queen turns the capture into checks and king attacks.

sl-eu8.spoken: The rook must hold the cut on the back rank. A careless step off it lets the king slip out, and the knight covers the escape square — the win dissolves into a draw.

sl-etj.spoken: The defender’s last resort is the rook sacrifice: once the enemy king steps off the pawn, the rook trades itself for it, and the remaining pawns build a fortress or keep perpetual threats alive.

sl-eu3.spoken: The knight wants to check the king and guard the pawn, but only one square does both. When the defender refuses to leave it, a waiting move forces the king out, and every escape leads to the same fight.

sl-etn.spoken: The king is driven to the edge, but the escape square must still be covered. A piece move that controls it also improves our position — one move does both.

sl-etg.spoken: In a rook endgame with the king cut off, the rook sacrifice clears the pawn's path to promotion. The defender's king cannot stop it, and the trade-down leaves a pawn endgame that wins despite the material deficit.

sl-etx.spoken: The king looks for an escape route. Place your pieces to control the critical squares—one piece seals the dark squares, another cuts the light ones—and the flight path disappears.

sl-et3.spoken: When pawns push deep into hostile lines and the defense collapses under the pressure, a swarm of them can dominate the board. The lesson: the quality of pieces matters more than their count.

sl-etk.spoken: The king cannot step in, so the side with the advantage pushes pawns instead, stripping the defender down to a single pawn. Then a quiet rook move forces the trade into a queen endgame where only one side gets a queen.

sl-ete.spoken: The passed pawn is on the seventh rank, and the enemy rook attacks it. Move the pawn forward first, not the king. Pushing forces the rook to react, while stepping the king toward the pawn first lets the rook get behind it or start counterplay.

sl-eu5.spoken: The king close to the pawn means a rush forward loses the win. A waiting bishop move hands Black the move, forcing a concession. Push early and the bishop gets deflected into a draw.

sl-eth.spoken: The king’s escape square is poisoned. Once the rook slides over to cut off the flight path, the black king has no shelter, and the rook falls with the pawn queening soon after. This differs from earlier lines, where giving up the rook bought a draw.

sl-ety.spoken: A waiting move keeps the structure intact while forcing the opponent to step, often into a worse setup. In endgames, that single tempo decides whether your coordination holds.

sl-eto.spoken: Centralizing the bishop forces the enemy king backward. From the center, its reach covers many squares and boxes the king in.

sl-et4.spoken: Passed pawns decide minor piece endings — checkmate is rare. If the pawns are locked, you must force a breakthrough to create one.

sl-etm.spoken: The rook sacrifice is not about material—it turns the direct advance into a mating net, where the passed pawn's counterplay dies with the king.

sl-etw.spoken: Waiting moves are powerful in the endgame. With few pieces left, the opponent often has nothing useful to do, so you pass and force them to wreck their own defense. This works for both sides.

sl-et5.spoken: A lone pawn against a rook rarely promotes. The pawn side can trade it for a better one or lean on connected passed pawns.

sl-eu1.spoken: The waiting move covers the critical square, forcing the defender's bishop off its best diagonal. When the defender shifts, it cannot get back in time.

sl-ev9.spoken: Do not rush the pawn. Pushing it early only grants the defender counterplay and makes the win slip away.

sl-eui.spoken: The bishop controls the key squares and pushes the pawns forward. It also defends the weak pawn while helping to capture more pawns.

sl-euy.spoken: The bishop drives enemy pieces onto passive squares, but the defender may still hold the draw.

sl-ev3.spoken: A lone king cannot be checkmated by a king and one minor piece alone. Bring in an extra pawn or piece to finish the job.

sl-ev2.spoken: The pawn wants to march, but the enemy king stands in its path and the enemy bishop patrols the long diagonal. Drive the king off that diagonal onto a shorter one, and the defense loses its flexibility.

sl-euf.spoken: The bishop's placement is everything in this endgame. Put it on the right square, and the enemy bishop can never reach its key defensive post, so your winning plan goes through.

sl-eue.spoken: The bishop stands guard, holding the enemy pawns in place. The attacking king probes for a way in, but the defender answers with exact king moves, shadowing the bishop and keeping the blockade intact.

sl-evd.spoken: The rook is poison — taking it invites a counter-capture. The win needs a knight sacrifice to set up a promotion threat that forces the win.

sl-evl.spoken: The queen must control the road to the corner. Cut off that path, and the defender's stalemate escape vanishes.

sl-eva.spoken: Rook endings appear in nearly every serious game, so the payoff for studying them outweighs every other endgame type.

sl-ev4.spoken: Rook endgames are the hardest to calculate because the rook can move so far, and fatigue makes the endgame even trickier.

sl-eub.spoken: A passed pawn must be met head-on. The bishop holds it only from the front; from the side or behind, the defense fails.

sl-eve.spoken: In a queen against rook pawn endgame, if the pawn sits on the seventh rank, the defender can hide the king in front of it. The attacker cannot approach without stalemate, so the game is drawn.

sl-eua.spoken: The king waits on the strong square, and the rook just marks time. Every black rook move lets the pawn fall, so the rook stays frozen, defending it, and Black makes no progress.

sl-eus.spoken: The bishop color matching the queening square does not guarantee a win. If the pawn runs too far ahead and the defender’s king already controls the critical squares, the fortress holds.

sl-euo.spoken: The bishop steps into the center and Black answers by attacking the king's bishop from the flank. White is forced to retreat, and Black uses that tempo to reposition the bishop and push the pawns forward.

sl-ev8.spoken: Endgame skill comes from study and practice, not rote memory. Knowing the principles underneath guides you when the position is new.

sl-euj.spoken: The defending bishop's square decides the outcome. Drive it onto a short diagonal, then deflect it at the promotion square to clear the queening path.

sl-ev5.spoken: Endgame study is preparation for a test you know is coming—every player will face these positions, so knowing them in advance is a practical edge.

sl-eut.spoken: The bishop guards the promotion square, so a direct push lets it sacrifice itself for the pawn. White must first deflect the bishop off the long diagonal, then the pawn promotes.

sl-ev1.spoken: The bishop sits on a long diagonal, and a pawn push loosens the blockade. That pawn break forces the defender to react, and the bishop trades or gains ground, cracking the defense apart.

sl-evk.spoken: The queen cannot stop a pawn one step from promotion by checking or blockading alone. The defending king just keeps threatening to queen, so the queen needs a special technique to force the win.

sl-euh.spoken: The pawn push offers a trade of all pawns, hoping to steer play into a bishop-only endgame where the extra bishop is worthless. The defender sidesteps that by keeping a bishop, and the winning chances stay alive.

sl-evc.spoken: The bishop checks and the king shuffles aim for one thing: a perpetual or a stalemate. White is up a piece but the passed pawn is too strong to win, so the task is to force the draw.

sl-evi.spoken: The queen must press close to the enemy king, cutting off its moves and forcing it to stand in front of its own pawn. A check from a square that covers the pawn's advance squares locks the position and wins.

sl-euz.spoken: The bishop endgame turns on king placement and the fight for the key diagonals. The attacker keeps the defender's king off its best square and aims at the weak pawns.

sl-euu.spoken: The bishop patrols the promotion square from a distance. Shuffling it back and forth along that diagonal changes nothing, because the defender simply mirrors the move and keeps the blockade.

sl-ev0.spoken: The bishop guards the long diagonal, but the defender has no ninth-rank escape. Force that bishop off its line, and the extra pawns march — promotion threats finish the game.

sl-evj.spoken: The result mirrors across the board. A pawn near one edge may win while its symmetric twin along the other edge draws, and that pattern repeats.

sl-evh.spoken: The queen alone often cannot stop an advanced pawn with the defending king nearby. She must rely on checks and pins to force the enemy king into awkward squares, buying time for her own king to approach and deliver the win.

sl-eul.spoken: The king must step precisely to cut off the bishop's path. If it does not, the bishop slides to the key square, chases the defending bishop off the long diagonal, and the queening becomes routine.

sl-eug.spoken: The extra pawn looks decisive, but the defender's bishop holds the queening square from its diagonal. The attacker must deflect or trade that bishop, yet the defender can shuttle between diagonals and keep control.

sl-ev6.spoken: Endgames repeat in your games like exam questions. Knowing the technique turns equal positions into wins. Rook endings appear most often, and the Philidor position is the drawing shield when you are a pawn down.

sl-euq.spoken: The extra pawn means nothing until it moves — with the rooks gone, it's a pure bishop endgame. Black's bishops work together to blockade the pawns, and the draw holds.

sl-eur.spoken: Fixing pawns on your opponent's bishop's color turns them into permanent targets for your own bishop—a lasting strategic weapon.

sl-eux.spoken: The bishop wants the long diagonal, but the defender's bishop controls it. Deflect that bishop from the diagonal, and the path opens to win.

sl-euv.spoken: The defending bishop must be squeezed onto few squares. With three or fewer legal moves, the attack usually wins; four or more, the hold may survive.

sl-euw.spoken: The bishop guards the promotion square from afar. Force it off that diagonal, and the pawn marches through.

sl-eun.spoken: Opposite-colored bishops turn endings upside down: the defender chooses whether to trade into one or keep bishops on. The call rests on pawn structure and king activity.

sl-euc.spoken: Bishop and pawn endgames hinge on one color question. When the bishop covers the promotion square, the win comes smoothly. When it does not, the defender's king can shelter in the corner and hold the draw.

sl-ewk.spoken: In a close endgame, losing a tempo with a waiting move can force the opponent into zugzwang and hand you the win.

sl-ewi.spoken: A piece shuffle is solid but slow. The opponent builds a sound defense, so you need a sharper, forcing idea.

sl-ewl.spoken: The direct push fails—the defender's waiting moves preserve the opposition and draw. Precise maneuvering loses a tempo, forcing the defender into zugzwang.

sl-evq.spoken: The pawn on the g-file leaves the defending king escape squares, so the queen can give checks while still attacking the pawn, and each check brings the king closer to the win.

sl-evu.spoken: The rook must choose its square with care. One extra step from the enemy king can decide whether the pawn promotes.

sl-ew7.spoken: The pawn one square back gives the defender a critical extra tempo. After promotion, the queen sacrifice arrives in time to dodge the stalemate and win.

sl-ewc.spoken: The defending king on the back rank is vulnerable when the enemy king advances, because the pawn can queen with check. A waiting move gains a tempo and forces the king into a worse square.

sl-ew1.spoken: The king must abandon the second rank, and every retreat costs a tempo. Once the rook is forced into the pawn's path, the pawn advances with tempo — a second tempo gained.

sl-ew4.spoken: A tempo check in the rook endgame forces the opponent to react, throwing their pawn-promotion plan off course.

sl-ewo.spoken: The king is boxed into two squares. Black must pick which pawn to push: the one that keeps a spare tempo, or the one that hands White a waiting move.

sl-evn.spoken: When the pawn is short of the seventh rank, checks drive the stronger king forward until the queen takes the pawn. If the defender clings to it, the queen blockades; on the seventh rank, mating threats appear.

sl-ew2.spoken: The bishop is chained to guarding the promotion square. Tempo moves push it onto a worse diagonal, then attacking that bishop buys a free move to redeploy your own.

sl-evz.spoken: The check looks tempting, but the king was already heading somewhere safe, so the tempo is an illusion. The real winning plan is simpler and was left on the board.

sl-eww.spoken: The bishop holds the key squares and keeps the enemy king caged. When it needs a move, it wastes a tempo. The king is forced from the pawn’s defense, the pawn falls, and promotion follows.

sl-ewx.spoken: The king seeks activity beyond the checks, but the pawn move that breaks the checking chain weakens the kingside and lets the opponent improve.

sl-evs.spoken: The rook pawn is the easy draw, but the bishop pawn is the trap. The defender hides in the corner, and the queen cannot take the pawn without giving up stalemate or perpetual check.

sl-ewr.spoken: The pawn races ahead, and the defender's king must scramble to catch it. One tempo short, the king arrives too late, and the rook check only draws from the wrong square.

sl-evy.spoken: The bishop's placement changes everything. From this square, it can be challenged by attacking the bishop directly, forcing a defensive move and gaining a crucial tempo to press forward.

sl-ewt.spoken: The rook must pry the king from the corner while the bishop tries to block along a key diagonal. Tempo moves deflect the bishop, then mating threats force the win.

sl-evv.spoken: The pawn race ends with both sides promoting, but king placement and move order decide the result. A quiet pawn push creates a threat against the queen, forcing a reply.

sl-evw.spoken: The pawn break must be timed with care. Push it too soon and you hand the opponent tempi or leave weaknesses behind. Arrange the supporting move first, and the balance holds — enough to secure the draw.

sl-evt.spoken: The promotion succeeds, and the queen versus pawn endgame is winning when she can force a trade or a mate. From the key square she covers both escape squares, so the enemy king cannot slip away. The queen either gets exchanged off or delivers checkmate.

sl-ewe.spoken: The king advances step by step while the knight can only shuttle, never making a real threat. Each time the check drives the king onward, it also attacks the knight—and every cycle wins a tempo, so the king's march gains speed.

sl-ewn.spoken: The pawn move looks passive but is the drawing idea. If the opponent pushes past, the capture creates a passed pawn and wins. If the opponent holds back, the other pawn advances and the position still holds.

sl-ewm.spoken: The bishop uses the tempo to slip behind the king, and the queen slides over to prepare a crossboard check. White must find the one exact king move first, then answer every queen check precisely — there is no time to spare.

sl-ew3.spoken: In a rook ending, gain a tempo before trading down to a pawn ending, so the opposition falls in your favor.

sl-ewa.spoken: The rook check burns a tempo and abandons the pressure on the f-pawn. This lets the enemy king advance and flips the evaluation.

sl-evo.spoken: The queen alone keeps the win alive, and the king must sit on the right square to dodge checks and escort the pawn home.

sl-ewv.spoken: A pawn push that looks helpful can hand the opponent a tempo or leave you with new weaknesses. In king and pawn endgames, every move of the pawn must be paid for in time.

sl-ew0.spoken: The king steps onto the critical square and forces the defender to waste moves repositioning. That extra tempo is what turns a winning position into a converted win.

sl-ew9.spoken: The pawn break is the whole game: on one side’s turn it wins, on the other’s it only draws. Opposition and king position matter, but the breakthrough decides.

sl-ew8.spoken: Lead with the quiet pawn move, not the aggressive one. If the king steps across, advance that same pawn again — the same position now, but with the opponent to move. He must give ground, and you win.

sl-ew5.spoken: The defender’s bishop is driven to a worse square, costing a tempo. That tempo buys time to swing the bishop across and renew the threat before the king can step over and stop it.

sl-ews.spoken: A spare pawn push like this is a stutter step: it hands the opponent the move and puts them in zugzwang. Each forward shove forces the king to step aside, and every repetition improves your position.

sl-ewj.spoken: The natural-looking rook move still loses the race. Black follows the same king-activation plan, and White falls a tempo behind. The winning idea is subtler—the king never needs to travel all the way to the corner.

sl-ewu.spoken: When the king needs to reach the far side quickly, a quiet pawn push opens the escape route without wasting tempo. Leaving the pawn behind is right—the enemy pawn is already stopped, and the king’s activity outweighs the material.

sl-ewd.spoken: A clean win was on the board, but the check still works. Failing to press with tempo lets the defender back into the game.

sl-ewq.spoken: The pawn’s position hands Black an extra tempo, so the king steps to the other side. That misstep costs Black a move, White keeps the opposition, and the win follows.

sl-evx.spoken: One careless push can turn a win into a draw when it lets the defender's rook reach the drawing setup. Rook behind the pawn leaves the attacker no easy way to dislodge it, and the defender holds.

sl-evp.spoken: The pawn sits on the seventh, on the rook's file. The defender's king is stalemated, the attacker's king too far, and the win evaporates.

sl-ex2.spoken: That small square the bishop stands on can turn a win into a draw. Forcing the defender's bishop onto a specific square earns a vital tempo.

sl-exk.spoken: In this queen endgame, one tempo tilts the balance between draw and win. The position looks fine for Black at first, but a precise check shows White wins by exactly that tempo.

sl-ex5.spoken: The bishop pawn endgame is a draw when white moves first—the king steps aside and stops black from reaching the key square. Black's checks run out, and the white king slips away.

sl-ex7.spoken: The first move is forced—any other move lets the opponent check and win. So White spends a tempo to keep the win alive.

sl-ex4.spoken: The winning method forces the enemy king onto the square directly in front of the pawn. Blocked by its own king, the pawn cannot promote, and the attacker gains a free tempo to bring their king closer.

sl-exw.spoken: The wedge pawn tempts you to sacrifice a strong pawn to restrict the opponent. Calculate the consequences first — the opponent may still have resources to defend.

sl-ey4.spoken: The rook reaches the seventh rank and becomes a monster—attacking pawns and boxing in Black's pieces. A rook on the seventh is the classic signature of a winning advantage.

sl-exv.spoken: Pawns are bargaining chips — giving one up hands the opponent extra defensive options. Keep the pawn and use it as a threat instead of sacrificing it early.

sl-exy.spoken: A famous Capablanca game shows the same shape: a pawn is given up to bring the king into play, and the advanced passed pawns then leave the opponent helpless.

sl-ey2.spoken: Ugly pawns, but the rook owns the seventh rank and creates constant headaches. Push that passed pawn and the structural damage stops mattering — practical chances outweigh the weakness.

sl-exf.spoken: The king's placement decides everything. If the defender reaches the key square in front of the pawn, the win slips toward a draw. A timely tempo move cuts that path off and preserves the win.

sl-exn.spoken: The king’s position decides the outcome. If the attacking king has crossed into the sixth rank, opposition is irrelevant and the win is routine. If the king lags behind, the defender shuffles the rook, keeps the king cut off, and holds the draw.

sl-exl.spoken: The defender chose the wrong king move, letting the black king advance up the board. That error loses, because the black king now joins the attack.

sl-exz.spoken: Accept the pawn. Refusing the sacrifice lets the opponent collect the positional gains without paying the cost.

sl-exe.spoken: The king is too far away to punish the flank advance. Pushing the pawn there holds, while pushing it one square short lets the queen slip around and take the pawn.

sl-ext.spoken: The rook must be forced back, not chased. One move drives it to a passive square while the pawn still threatens to promote.

sl-exu.spoken: The king's path decides the endgame. Choose the route that reaches the drawing square; the other roads lose.

sl-ey7.spoken: The queen trade is tempting, but the rook belongs on the seventh rank first. Activate it and attack the bishop before offering the exchange — that subtlety decides the game.

sl-ex1.spoken: A critical position may demand a winning tempo by redeploying the bishop to a stronger square. That single tempo separates victory from a draw.

sl-ex3.spoken: The king takes the long way around, not the direct path. The check arrives, the king steps past, and now the tempo flips — it is the opponent's move, and the position is zugzwang.

sl-ey9.spoken: Rooks on the seventh rank attack pawns and menace the king. The king is boxed in on the back rank, the minor pieces cover the escape squares, and the rooks shield each other.

sl-exj.spoken: In a pawn race, every tempo decides the game. The attacker must push the passed pawn instead of saving the bishop, because any delay lets the defender coordinate and hold the draw.

sl-exb.spoken: The king takes over the blockade, freeing the rook to make threats. The rook gains a tempo, holding the pawn in place while the king steps in to take over.

sl-exp.spoken: The rook side must pick the king's path with care. Step too far, and the pawn advances with check — the defending king gains time to close in. Keep the king near the action instead.

sl-exq.spoken: The defending king picks the square that offers the longest resistance. Staying closer to the queening square and blocking the enemy king's approach gives the best chance to hold the draw.

sl-ey8.spoken: The knight sits on a strong outpost, the rook owns the seventh rank, and the c-file is secure. The opponent must choose: swap queens into a hard endgame, or decline and hand over the c-file too.

sl-ex6.spoken: The defender misses a second drawing chance: rook to the key square, king beside it. The opponent then finds the winning cut-off, severing the rook from the play.

sl-ewy.spoken: A misplaced rook invites pawn attacks that gain tempi. Each thrust forces the rook back or lets the pawns roll forward, until they become unstoppable.

sl-ey5.spoken: The seventh-rank rook is a powerful asset, so an active developing move can outweigh keeping the material.

sl-ex8.spoken: A single supporting pawn can freeze the enemy rook and open the road for promotion. Miss that resource, and the queen arrives a tempo late, letting the defense coordinate and turn the endgame messy.

sl-exd.spoken: The pawn break opens a path for the king toward the enemy pawns. Without that escape route, the opposing king arrives first and promotes with check.

sl-exh.spoken: The bishop retreat is too slow. The knight seizes the entry square before the defender's pieces can cover the key light squares, and that invasion decides the endgame.

sl-exo.spoken: The defending king must stand close to the pawn to hold the draw. Far away, the rook alone can halt the pawn, but once the pawn advances too far, the rook cannot stop promotion without the king’s support.

sl-ey1.spoken: A rook on the seventh rank cuts the enemy king off and attacks the back rank. If the opponent ignores it, tactics follow fast — a discovered check or a forced queen promotion, sometimes checkmate.

sl-ex0.spoken: The immediate threat is to advance and promote with check. The opponent must spend a tempo to stop it, and that tempo decides the race.

sl-ewz.spoken: A blocked position rewards a tempo move: one forcing step that ties the opponent in a pin or breaks their coordination, and the game tilts toward a draw or a win.

sl-exg.spoken: The knight’s route matters: it hops from the edge toward the center, then to the outpost. The king’s exact square gives the knight the extra tempo it needs to arrive in time.

sl-exr.spoken: A worse king retreat leaves the win still in hand, but only with precise play. A careless check can stalemate the defender when the pawn is blocked and the king trapped.

sl-exm.spoken: The queen must close the distance, and the rook gets squeezed onto a square where it can no longer shield the pawn and dodge checks at the same time. The king’s placement and how far the pawn stands from promotion decide everything.

sl-ex9.spoken: In a queen endgame, a routine queen move lets the opponent force a trade into a drawn king and pawn ending. Instead, a king waiting move gains a vital tempo, since the opponent's queen is doomed regardless.

sl-exx.spoken: The pawn sacrifice trades material to deny the opponent a central break. Without that break, they get clamped. The new pawn chain is supported and shields the weak points.

sl-ey6.spoken: The doubled rooks on the open file make the penetration. Sacrifice a pawn for unclear compensation, then stack the rooks, drive out the knight, and land on the seventh rank to hit both weak pawns.

sl-ey3.spoken: The rook owns the seventh rank, and that alone is power, even when the pawns look ragged. From there it generates real threats, and the passed pawn turns into a constant headache for Black.

sl-exa.spoken: The king steps in to force the enemy king onto a worse square. That gained tempo decides the game, as it clears the way for an outside passed pawn.

sl-ey0.spoken: Accept the offered pawn. Taking is the only way to test if the sacrifice is sound; refusing forfeits any chance to punish it.

sl-ez1.spoken: A passive rook on a loose pawn is a long-term weakness, even when nothing attacks it right now.

sl-eya.spoken: The rook belongs on the seventh rank in an even rook endgame. From that outpost it attacks pawns and cages the enemy king.

sl-ezk.spoken: The bishop is tied to the three files beside its king. If it steps off, the rook attacks it and threatens mate at the same time.

sl-eyi.spoken: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, defend from the front. That keeps the blockade intact and holds the pawns.

sl-eyd.spoken: Passive defense — parking the rook to watch a pawn — lets the opponent improve freely. Active defense, even at pawn cost, creates counterplay and makes their task harder.

sl-eyc.spoken: The rook on the seventh rank menaces the exposed king with mate or material. The defender runs out of moves to meet both threats.

sl-ezj.spoken: The safer king comes from pawn moves that claim more space. When a bishop retreats to defend a pawn, it deactivates the piece — worse than simply losing that pawn.

sl-ez2.spoken: The king and rook take the lead once a pawn is beyond saving. The stranded pawn still distracts, but progress comes from activating the pieces and building threats.

sl-eym.spoken: Active defense is the only chance: trade pawns on the queenside to cut the material. Passive defense loses, because the attacking king will eventually infiltrate.

sl-eza.spoken: The rook tries to activate, but a knight maneuver supports the passed pawn and snuffs out the activity. With the rook neutralized, the extra pawns decide the game.

sl-eys.spoken: The passed pawn demands respect, and the queen stirs up threats around it. White must answer both, and that counterplay is enough to hold the draw.

sl-eyq.spoken: Set up the defense around active counterplay, not passive resistance, and the saving resource appears.

sl-eyb.spoken: The rook belongs on the seventh rank before the knight is taken. Grabbing material first lets the enemy king breathe; controlling the rank first restricts it and keeps the pressure alive.

sl-ezh.spoken: The knight sits strong on its outpost, but grabbing the pawn tempts a check that chases the king off — and the enemy king steps in front of the pawns to force a draw.

sl-eyu.spoken: The rook must act early or it gets buried. Passive moves hand the attacker time to build a win. Active play—checking or hitting pawns—is the only way to create counterplay.

sl-ez6.spoken: The knight is held in check by the bishop's placement alone. Move the bishop, and the knight rejoins the defense, so the piece must stay put to keep the bind.

sl-eyr.spoken: Passive defense lets the stronger side improve the position at leisure. Waiting moves hand over the initiative, and the defender never gets a chance to fight.

sl-eyg.spoken: The king stands badly and the pawns look beautiful, yet the win stays elusive. Active pieces and live counterplay let the defender find precise moves and hold the balance.

sl-ez5.spoken: The knight heads for the weak pawn and starts a slow squeeze. Steady pressure turns a balanced endgame into a win for the better technician.

sl-eyj.spoken: The rook's active counterattack is the best practical try. Passive defense lets White consolidate the weaknesses and then break through, so the defender must create counterplay instead.

sl-eyp.spoken: In a rook endgame a pawn down, the defender activates the rook for counterplay. A passive placement leaves it stuck forever and hands the attacker the initiative.

sl-eyh.spoken: The bishop must stay active, both defending and attacking along the same diagonal. That dual pressure holds the draw despite the two-pawn deficit, because the pawns cannot advance freely.

sl-eyk.spoken: The rook faces a fork in the road. Passive defense sinks into a lost position, while active play that drags the white king over is just as dangerous.

sl-ez0.spoken: The pawn push forces the defender to pick the most active setup. A rook lift or a king move creates instant counterplay or trades down to a draw.

sl-ezl.spoken: The rook and king are worth more than pawns in the endgame. A well-placed rook with an active king outweighs a few extra pawns stuck in bad spots.

sl-ez7.spoken: The knight grabs a pawn, then settles on the rim to block the queen from grabbing pawns back while keeping threats alive. The enemy king stays exposed, and the knight later hops to the f-file to renew the pressure.

sl-eyt.spoken: The defender must not retreat into passivity, since that only invites more pressure. Active resistance, like stepping the king forward, is required to meet the initiative head-on.

sl-eyo.spoken: With little material left, the defender's chances of survival rise sharply. The rook sits ideally to hold the passed pawn, and the king stands near enough to back real counterplay.

sl-eyf.spoken: The pawn can be defended laterally by the rook after it advances, freeing the king to escape to safety. Passive play lets the opponent invade; active defense saves the game.

sl-ezb.spoken: The bishop wants to reach the open diagonal, aiming at the king's weak pawn. Developing it there also blocks the opponent's bishop from its natural square, keeping your piece active and the pressure alive.

sl-ez3.spoken: The rook retreat shelters in place, doing nothing to disturb White's formation. White answers by lifting the rook and centralizing the king, building the breakthrough.

sl-ez8.spoken: The bishop moves to block the enemy bishop’s active square, then a second bishop lands to create a mate threat. White must answer that threat, and in the scramble Black takes a pawn.

sl-ez4.spoken: The king advances while the rook stays passive and the bishop is pinned to its defensive duty. Every black piece is tied down, so white strengthens the position and leaves no useful move.

sl-eyx.spoken: The rook endgame punishes a passive defender. Letting the weak pawn be guarded from afar lets the stronger side improve step by step, while active counterplay is the only way to create chances and escape the squeeze.

sl-eze.spoken: The capture looks tempting but frees the black king. The real target is the other pawn, so the knight goes hunting it instead. Removing that defender leaves the position far easier to win, and the other pawn stays put as a blocker.

sl-eyv.spoken: In a rook endgame, the best defense is to shed pawns. Trading one off reduces material and lifts the draw chances. A passive rook move just lets the attacker keep squeezing.

sl-ezf.spoken: The bishop sits on a diagonal ready to answer the knight's threats from both directions, and that wall keeps the king from forcing its way through.

sl-ezd.spoken: The bishop retreats to defend, but the knight already on the attack controls the key squares, so the defense collapses and the invasion goes through.

sl-eyw.spoken: Passive defense cannot hold when no fortress exists. The defender's pieces stay tied to weaknesses, and nothing can change that.

sl-ezc.spoken: The light-squared bishops stay because one covers the key square, keeping the enemy knight off it. The lone weak pawn stands defended, so the position holds.

sl-eyz.spoken: The defender's key resource is a knight strike at the pawn. That forces the opponent to guard it or lose it, and losing it simplifies the game to a clear draw. A quiet pawn move instead lets the opponent push the passed pawn and win.

sl-ezi.spoken: King activity and pawn weaknesses outweigh material equality in these endgames. Trading pieces can simplify the position, but choosing which piece to trade decides the outcome.

sl-eyl.spoken: The rook must stay active—on the first rank or the fifth—to block any breakthroughs. From there it harasses the pawns and gives checks while the king holds its strong position.

sl-ez9.spoken: The bishop slides out, holding off the pawn push for later. Its diagonal cramps the enemy knight's development, and the king cannot tuck into the corner because the bishop watches that diagonal and can pick off the pawns.

sl-eyn.spoken: Passive defense lets the stronger side grind forward. The defender must look for active counterplay, or the rook endgame slips away.

sl-eyy.spoken: Active counterplay beats passive defense. A rook that attacks weaknesses and creates threats forces the stronger side to respond instead of making progress.

sl-ezn.spoken: The extra piece outweighs the bad knight, and that piece decides the game.

sl-f0w.spoken: The king escorts the rook to take the pawn, then steps in front to shepherd the pawn home while the black king is locked out.

sl-f0h.spoken: The knight sits well but attacks nothing. Every piece needs a purpose. Fix the weaknesses first, then find a better square for it.

sl-f0b.spoken: The knight is exposed to the bishop's capture, and if it retreats to safety, the pawn falls instead.

sl-f0k.spoken: The king steps in only when the bishop leaves. Keeping that bishop on its diagonal holds the critical squares, so the capture is refused.

sl-ezz.spoken: A bishop drives the enemy rook onto a single safe square. Any other escape runs into a tactical refutation, a mate threat, or a skewer.

sl-f0o.spoken: The knight is buried on the edge, only babysitting pawns. Passive pieces offer no prospects, and without activity there is no plan.

sl-f08.spoken: White buys a passed queenside pawn by trading the a-pawns. Black's knight try only helps; with pawns on both flanks, defense gets harder.

sl-f0x.spoken: The rook shuffle is wasted time. White's rook slides behind the pawn, supports its advance, and leaves Black's rook stuck on defense, a tempo short of stopping it.

sl-f0t.spoken: The rook slides behind the separated passed pawns while your king locks out the enemy king—that is the whole win. Trading queens to grab a pawn is fine, but never let the enemy king come up to support them.

sl-f0p.spoken: The rook drops to the back rank and pins it, sharpening the rook's activity while Black is squeezed.
