sl-73v.spoken: The side check draws in rook endgames when the defender’s king is cut off.

sl-6kl.spoken: The rook on the open file faces the enemy queen and king on the same line. Sliding the rook there pins the queen or sets up back-rank mate threats.

sl-7fa.spoken: Connected passed pawns ram down the queenside after the trades. Even if one falls, the other stays dangerous, and threats from the rook or bishop can finish the game.

sl-7cl.spoken: The pawn capture is the critical test. Declining it leaves Black suffering all game, as White opens the file and seizes full control.

sl-7g6.spoken: The bishop sits on the pinning square, pressuring the knight. The standard setup follows: castle, place the queen on the central file, double rooks on the open lines, and enjoy the two bishops against a slightly shaky opponent.

sl-6i9.spoken: The pawn is frozen, pinned to the queen and unable to capture. White advances the f-pawn to pry open the d-file, squeezing the king while Black runs out of useful moves.

sl-6zv.spoken: The king takes the pawn, but the h-pawn advance is a trap. Push the passed pawns instead, and check with the knight to deflect the bishop that blocks the pawn's path.

sl-6xk.spoken: The passed pawn wins the endgame. Push it, then calculate two defenses. If the bishop slides to block, check, then swing the rook behind the pawn. If the king tucks in the corner, the rook drives the pawn home after favorable trades.

sl-6ju.spoken: The pin to the king strips a piece of all its attacking strength. It may seem to threaten something, but any move would expose the king, so the threat is an illusion.

sl-6m5.spoken: The fianchettoed bishop is the same idea on both sides, but Black arrives a half-tempo late and feels it in the center.

sl-7f6.spoken: The rook reaches the seventh after the trades, and Black strikes back with a pawn push. White's bishop hangs, but two connected passers on the sixth are overwhelming.

sl-6xu.spoken: The passed pawn decides the endgame because White cannot stop it. The knight is too far off, and the king is cut out of the action.

sl-799.spoken: The opponent aims for trades to force a draw, but that plan backfires—it hands the stronger side real winning chances. Opening with a draw in mind is a losing mentality.

sl-6oj.spoken: The exchange is a fair price once the king is bare. The moment White’s heavy pieces go hunting, the second rank and the kingside become the mating square.

sl-7gv.spoken: The queen has wandered while the queenside stays home. With the rook and bishop still on their starting squares, White plays with an extra piece, and the exposed king makes it worse.

sl-6se.spoken: The knight jumps to the center, hitting the bishop and a pawn. If the bishop flees, the knight grabs the outpost. If the queen defends, the center pawn falls, and then the weak pawn drops. Other ideas: a pawn push to pin a piece and open a discovery.

sl-7rz.spoken: The queen steps to that file to control the central square, backed by the knight. After the trade, the knight hops forward to bear down on the same target.

sl-8c1.spoken: A counterattack that matches or tops the threat is a solid defensive resource—this knight leap creates just such a distraction.

sl-8aw.spoken: Deep opening study pays off when you know your opponent. A grandmaster's book covering the French, the Caro-Kann, and the Philidor sharpens your score against all three.

sl-7uk.spoken: The knight jumps forward and hits the weak c-pawn. If the defender has not prepared against that jump, the knight lands with force, and the defender is pushed into awkward bishop moves that let the attacker chase the bishop forward and win the fight.

sl-7xm.spoken: The bishop sits on the pin, freezing the knight against the queen. Moving it away releases the pin and lets the opponent untangle. The pawn push the opponent tries is no threat—the reply simply advances a pawn to close the center.

sl-898.spoken: The knight is pinned and under attack. Black must answer with a move that breaks the pin and defends the knight at the same time.

sl-855.spoken: Passive waiting in your own territory hands the opponent time to build up and attack. Active play — preparing a central pawn break — beats mere reaction.

sl-8cn.spoken: The inaccurate capture hands White the initiative. Black's best response is piece activity, bringing bishop and queen to bear on the kingside, though White keeps the edge.

sl-8gz.spoken: The rook drives the breakthrough because the king is exposed and pieces hang. The king's escape fails to a bishop capture that opens the rook's invasion, so defense stays passive.

sl-8kd.spoken: The bishop is overloaded and pinned, so every capture wins. A rook takes the bishop with check, and if the bishop recaptures, the other rook takes on the same square and wins material.

sl-7py.spoken: The early pawn push weakens the square in front of the center pawn. With one bishop already eyeing that square, the push leaves it permanently vulnerable; with the other bishop, it additionally allows a pin on the knight.

sl-7qc.spoken: The bishop pins the knight, freezing that side of the board. White builds a pawn and queen support, then castles long to storm the kingside.

sl-8fn.spoken: Give up the rook trade, and the bishop offer lets White take the rook. White keeps pressure with queen and rook lined up, but Black still has counterplay on the queenside and a pawn move to stop the knight. The position is not lost yet.

sl-84h.spoken: The isolated pawn and the bishop pair are offset by one bad bishop. White stands somewhat better, but not by much.

sl-7ss.spoken: The intermezzo backfires: after the captures resolve, White sits a pawn down. The open file offers compensation, but the advanced pawn, defended three times, demands White prove it.

sl-88y.spoken: The bishop push challenges the fianchettoed bishop but ignores the center and leaves the knight pinned. The knight stays frozen, because moving it exposes the bishop or queen behind it.

sl-86i.spoken: The move order with the pawn and bishop steers the game into territory Black knows well, while White may not, like a kingside fianchetto setup.

sl-7yc.spoken: The bishop must find a home without blocking the rook's key attacking file. The natural square keeps that file free. But when the defender shields the bishop and trades rooks, the pressure dissolves.

sl-83z.spoken: The e-pawn sits in White's camp, nearly isolated—weakness and strength at once, a judgment call. White pushes the queenside, Black the kingside. Once a trade opens the a-file, only White's rook can enter; Black's cannot.

sl-86m.spoken: The bishop on the open diagonal pressures the center and clears the path to castle. If Black pushes the pawn, the bishop retreats to a safer square, keeping the central pawn break ready while dodging the pin.

sl-88k.spoken: The knight looks exposed and the pawn seems lost, yet the move invites it. If White takes, the knight strikes back, giving up the queen for a near-mating attack. White must retreat, and Black ends up a knight for a pawn.

sl-884.spoken: The battle centers on a key square. If Black advances that pawn, they equalize and their light-squared bishop outshines White's fianchettoed one. White's bishop move prevents the advance by threatening to pin the knight, making the push costly.

sl-9fw.spoken: The bishop slides to a diagonal that eyes the kingside, preparing the f-pawn's advance. That threat forces White to respond, and each reply spends a tempo until no waiting move remains.

sl-91z.spoken: The knight on the rim anticipates the fianchetto setup. Black aims to reroute it, castle by hand, and slide the bishop onto the long diagonal.

sl-8rj.spoken: The pawn advance loosens the king's shelter and leaves a dark square in front of the center pawn exposed. With the defending pawn no longer able to challenge that square, a white piece can settle there unchallenged.

sl-8pj.spoken: Opening the position with the pawn storm exposes your own king and hands the opponent's pieces more activity, while the breakthrough stays unclear. With the heavy pieces still on the board, king safety is everything.

sl-98p.spoken: Developing the bishop with tempo, the priority shifts to castling before any tactics begin. King safety rules the opening and early middlegame.

sl-9j4.spoken: The drift toward the edge is the real error, not the final blunder. The position becomes critical when only one move remains.

sl-95j.spoken: The push opens the bishop's diagonal and keeps the attack rolling. Black has played soundly and the position stands even, but White's pieces lack coordination and several hang by a thread.

sl-9lg.spoken: The pawns march to keep more space and start a storm, even if the king gets a bit airy. No immediate threat, so the push is justified.

sl-9le.spoken: The rook is the real target, not the immediate threat. Opening the rook's file matters more than pushing the adjacent pawn, and that pawn also feeds the attack forward.

sl-8y2.spoken: Black advances both flank pawns, securing the center pawn and preparing to challenge the bishop. White answers with two quiet pawn moves, building a flexible setup that lets the bishop drop back to safety if pressured.

sl-94k.spoken: When the attacker delays challenging the knight, the opponent strikes at the center at once. After the trades, that central pawn stays extra and the bishop pair comes along — enough for at least equality.

sl-93b.spoken: The knight on the queenside blocks the c-pawn. Moving the knight first frees the pawn, and the push gains space while challenging the bishop — a typical plan when Black seeks counterplay on that wing.

sl-8v6.spoken: The extra material and connected passers dictate the plan: defuse the attack, then push. The opponent must play faster and more efficiently to prove the sacrifice. Their thrust is a mistake, leaving your position strong.

sl-9gh.spoken: The bishop abandons its post on the critical diagonal, and the attacker immediately advances the kingside pawn to create a passed pawn. The defender's king cannot reach it, and with two passed pawns on opposite wings, they prove unstoppable.

sl-91n.spoken: In open Italian structures, the d-file pawn becomes a target for the knight, while the f-file offers control. Pushing the rook's pawn is precise—it stops the opponent's pawn from gaining space and keeps a key square ready for your pieces.

sl-91s.spoken: Black answers with a pawn thrust to hold back White's own advance. White has a few setups: pin the knight to fight for the key central square, fianchetto the bishop, or redeploy the knight. Black's natural reply develops the bishop.

sl-8s5.spoken: The c-pawn advance loosens control over the center square, yet it buys safety: any white knight hopping in gets traded off. It also opens the pocket for the king, sheltered behind the pawns and guarded by the bishop.

sl-92f.spoken: The rook overprotects the key square and keeps pressure on the pawn, while preparing the queen to reinforce. If the knight tries to reroute, the bishop still threatens, so the knight must retreat without gaining tempo, blocking its own plan.

sl-8zx.spoken: The pawn advance stops the knight from landing on that key square and sets up the next pawn push. It’s not a weakness when the sacrifices don’t work — it simply removes the knight’s outpost.

sl-9hb.spoken: The checking rook forces a king decision. Heading toward the edge traps the king, and the rook check drives it back, costing the pawn. The safer square keeps the king cut off but secure — with the rook alone, no win follows.

sl-93p.spoken: The knight was idle on its post, so it hops to the rim and eyes the squares the advanced pawn covers. If it is captured, the bishop gains a long diagonal and the f-pawn gets to march.

sl-96f.spoken: Sacrificing a pawn buys pressure and a queen trade. When a rook falls for a knight to kill those threats, the imbalance remains: up the exchange for one pawn, with a 3-on-1 queenside majority against a 4-on-3 kingside.

sl-8qn.spoken: The bishop takes and the pawn recaptures, leaving a weak square behind. Black can challenge that square with a flank pawn, while White still has a pawn to evict any piece that lands on the neighboring square. The camp is weakened, but the balance holds.

sl-9a9.spoken: The bishop sits passively, because the center push is met by trading pawns then knight, leaving the queen exposed to a double attack on bishop and pawn. The supporting bishop keeps the pressure on, and Black gets a strong position with a pawn break or capture.

sl-9o1.spoken: The pawn thrust provokes a central break, and if the opponent captures, the lines open for the attacker's pieces.

sl-9oj.spoken: The knight camps on the square that blocks the pawn's path and chokes our play. It outclasses our own piece, so the plan is to chop it off the board.

sl-asb.spoken: The bishop stares down the long diagonal but attacks nothing — the opponent has no opposite-colored bishop to contest it. The real diagonal is the one that feeds the passed pawn and fuels the attack.

sl-ach.spoken: The queen guards two pieces at once, so a rook takes the knight and the overloaded queen can't save it.

sl-9vf.spoken: Queen versus king: the heavy piece wins, but carelessness courts stalemate. Trap the king with no legal move and no check, and the win turns to a draw.

sl-9mm.spoken: The pawn advances to the sixth rank and keeps the initiative, while the enemy pawn that blocked the queen stays fixed. A pawn this deep restricts the opponent and sets up mating threats, especially while queens remain on the board.

sl-ap1.spoken: The uncastled king in a closed position is not a weakness but a flexibility asset. It enables pawn breaks and even a queen check to punish a premature advance.

sl-9ss.spoken: The protected passed pawn fixes Black’s pieces, while the knight stands active. When Black pushes to trade pawns and free the rooks, White answers by closing the file, leaving Black passive and the advantage intact.

sl-a3i.spoken: The queen is under attack, but stepping forward is the right call—it stops the enemy from taking that piece because the recapture would be lethal. Forced into defense, the opponent tries to swap rooks and build an impenetrable fortress.

sl-9r0.spoken: The bishop alone cannot push the pawn home. When the king is pinned to stopping the connected passed pawns, the bishop lacks support, and Black holds the draw by staying active and keeping the pawns shielded.

sl-a7d.spoken: Pins, forks, skewers, double attacks, discovered checks — each is a tool. Chain them in a forced sequence and they become a combination.

sl-9qu.spoken: The defending king must stay in front of the pawn while the rook cuts off the enemy king, and that fortress can hold a draw despite the extra pawn.

sl-a2k.spoken: The queen is pinned and attacked. Sliding it to a safe square unpins, keeps it active, and sets up threats like a queen-and-bishop mate on the edge.

sl-anj.spoken: In pawn races, lead with the pawn that steps onto the light square, since the enemy bishop controls those squares and the barrier is harder to break.

sl-a4z.spoken: Pushing the pawn here feels like a punishment, but it usually softens your own center and hands the opponent open lines. When you hold more space, trading pieces only helps them.

sl-af5.spoken: The pieces are tangled: bishop tied to knight, king boxed on the rim, knight pinned. Grabbing the pawn looks forcing, but after the recapture, opposite-colored bishops leave only a draw.

sl-9o4.spoken: Pawn pushes in the Dragon open lines toward the enemy king, but advancing your own pawns in front of your king can expose it, so timing decides whether they strike or backfire.

sl-a0e.spoken: The queen slides to a quiet square that guards every weakness, keeps every threat alive, and even invites an endgame if taken. Finding that calm move inside a tactical storm is the hardest part, especially in blitz.

sl-ain.spoken: The h-pawn sits on the wrong color for its own bishop, so it becomes a permanent target. The defender would rather have no pawn there at all, to free the bishop for a better diagonal.

sl-9zs.spoken: The early pawns and the knight's placement shift the line's punch—with no knight on the kingside, the pawn thrust loses its target. The setup mirrors a known structure, just with the knight on the queenside.

sl-blv.spoken: A stray piece cut off from the army is not just misplaced — it is a target.

sl-b94.spoken: The light-squared bishop takes command of the queenside after the exchange. It watches the key squares, pressures the kingside, and keeps working even when the pawns fall.

sl-bf0.spoken: The pawn is gone, but the position is not equal. The activity and the lasting attack are the compensation, and the pressure alone justifies the sacrifice — no need to rush and prove it.

sl-be8.spoken: The queen-for-bishop sacrifice is not a loss but a trade of material for initiative. After grabbing the queen, the opponent tries to consolidate and goes passive, and that passivity opens the door for counterplay.

sl-boh.spoken: The pawn will fall if pushed now, so the king sidesteps to guard it and make the push safe, while the knight locks the center. Castling instead lets the rooks double on the open file and take that pawn.

sl-bh3.spoken: The knight step is the main line. Black's central pawn push is the strong reply. White's pawn advance closes the center and fences in the bishop. Black then chooses a flank break or a queen retreat, with the knight and bishop completing development.

sl-b72.spoken: The bishop pair pays off over the long run, especially with open lines. When the pawn storm forces the bishop back, the space gained is real. Better to block the knight's outpost first, and the position stays balanced.

sl-azt.spoken: The rook that could take is left hanging on purpose. Black's rook is stuck, so White piles pressure on the bishop instead, forcing Black to waste moves shuffling that same rook again.

sl-b6w.spoken: In a closed game, the bishop pair pays off over the long run, especially when one bishop sits actively, guarding a central pawn while attacking an enemy pawn out on the flank.

sl-bbs.spoken: The opponent pushes a pawn to tempt your light-squared bishop into a trade. Refuse it — their bishop is bad, and keeping it on the board preserves your advantage.

sl-bpp.spoken: The other defensive plan pushes the pawn to break the grip, preparing to bring the king closer to the defense. White’s best try is offering the queen trade, but Black declines and marches the king into the fight.

sl-b0p.spoken: The pawn on that square is bait. Taking it lets the queen and bishop align on the long dark diagonal, and the threats against that pawn become worse than the gain.

sl-b9y.spoken: The knight offers the pawn back to strip away Black's active pieces and end Black's counterplay, leaving White's bishop pair against bishop and knight.

sl-bth.spoken: The exchange sacrifice is the cleaner path. It trades a rook for a piece, creates lasting pressure, and secures a pleasant advantage that remains solid even if the opponent regroups.

sl-cp1.spoken: Learning your own painful loss from the other side of the board reveals positional ideas and typical plans.

sl-cig.spoken: The centralized knight dominates the board. A well-timed check forces the king onto a worse square and unlocks tactical chances before any capture proceeds.

sl-ccu.spoken: The prepared player is not surprised. The deviation may look playable, but it leaves lasting weaknesses: doubled pawns and a bishop with no active role.

sl-c74.spoken: Black's pawn on the queenside locks the position, stopping White from gaining space or launching a minority attack. White keeps flexible pieces, but Black has stabilized the board.

sl-cll.spoken: Preparation is about options, not repetition. A repertoire with several ideas keeps you unpredictable and ready for anything your opponent plays, even a move you have never seen.

sl-c4m.spoken: The pawn moves prepare a quiet flank advance that also blocks White's own break on that side. Black is in no hurry, content to wait before pushing further forward.

sl-cgn.spoken: The queenside is sealed, so the attack must come on the kingside. Breaking with the f-pawn comes too slowly once the h-pawn has already loosened that flank.

sl-cke.spoken: The piece takes the pawn and wins material while keeping the initiative. If Black tries to recapture with the knight, the position collapses, so the capture is clearly correct.

sl-ct5.spoken: Pushing the kingside pawn to hold the center pawn forward weakens the king's shelter and locks in the bishop at home — the usual price of defending a pawn out front.

sl-c1o.spoken: The knight needs protection from the pin, so the pawn steps up to stop the bishop from pinning it to the queen. That is standard prophylaxis in this opening.

sl-cba.spoken: The immediate tactic is complicated and risky. Skip it—there is a clearer way to win.

sl-d0h.spoken: The game opened as an Exchange Slav, a line that usually looks completely level. White waits calmly for the opponent to loosen something, like a pawn push, and suddenly there are several targets and a winning position.

sl-bzj.spoken: Breaking pawn tension early hands White the open file. With doubled rooks aimed down it, threats pile up against Black's cramped pieces, and the pressure is too much to hold.

sl-cwb.spoken: Against the Nimzo-Indian, Black chooses between several plans. One advances the d-pawn, creating a Carlsbad structure and contesting a key diagonal. Another advances the c-pawn, keeping options open for a later f-pawn or d-pawn push.

sl-c79.spoken: The minority attack throws a pawn majority against a larger one. Pushing the b-pawn two squares forces the defender to capture, which opens a file for the rook, or to push past, which weakens the c-pawn and the square in front of it.

sl-cme.spoken: The pawn exchange keeps Black from taking the a-file pawn. The position stays flexible, leaving White several directions: pinning the knight, prodding the kingside, or centralizing the rook.

sl-cr0.spoken: The rook sits poorly on the closed file, and the bishop is misaligned. When Black offers the bishop trade, taking it eases the congestion that a cramped position suffers from.

sl-c45.spoken: In the King's Indian setup, Black's knight mirrors White's, but a rare bishop move stops the central pawn push cold—a grandmaster-approved alternative.

sl-c7h.spoken: The minority attack pushes the b-pawn against the opponent's queenside majority. If the pawn advance is stopped, a preparatory move on the a-file then re-launches it, and after the exchanges a backward c-pawn remains.

sl-c1z.spoken: The pawn is lost, but pushing the f-pawn to answer the frustration only punches a hole in the long diagonal and invites checks.

sl-bxb.spoken: The bishop drops back, and the pawn push invites a capture. If Black bites, the rook slides to the seventh, then swings over to aim at the bishop's diagonal. Black's rook defends, but White re-routes, doubles, and the king joins in to break through and win.

sl-c9m.spoken: The pawn steps forward, inviting capture. It looks like a weakness, but the file opens later for the rook. Yet this invitation is a gamble—the guest may turn and eat you.

sl-d7a.spoken: Two passed pawns against one is often worse than one against none. Pushing the extra pawn hands the opponent a passed pawn, leaving you with nothing.

sl-dc3.spoken: The pawn push sets up a French structure. White claims the center with the queen pawn, and Black answers in kind. The knight reroutes through the middle file to support the advance, shoring up the center pawn.

sl-d68.spoken: The bishop and knight coordinate to spring the Elephant Trap. When the trap resolves, Black nets a knight for a single pawn and walks away with a clear material edge.

sl-dck.spoken: The knight gets pushed back to the edge, heading for the kingside. A pawn gains a tempo on the bishop, forcing it to retreat. The center stays stable, so keeping the bishop supports a future pawn break instead of taking.

sl-dm2.spoken: The bishop steps into an active square, and the knight offers a trade to neutralize it. If the bishop takes, the queen recaptures and the knight that captured comes back off the board, leaving Black developed naturally and ready to push the c-pawn.

sl-dow.spoken: The center is the issue, not the knight on that square. Pushing the pawn there strikes back, gains a tempo, and opens a safe home for the knight.

sl-dk1.spoken: If Black tries Nb6 to defend, White takes the pawn with Nxe4 — the d5 pawn is pinned, and White wins the bishop on c6.

sl-djl.spoken: Checks first, then the biggest captures. With no check available, the knight is the first target, and taking it is the winning move — a piece down, material must be recovered.

sl-dk0.spoken: Black often faces a choice here: play Kh8 first, then e5. If e5 comes too early, White hits b7 and d5 at once with Qb3.

sl-dk8.spoken: Black’s knight on c6 risks becoming a target if White pushes it around. White may try to prove it’s offside, but Black stays calm — the knight can retreat or switch posts.

sl-dib.spoken: The knight steps back to defend the pawn while keeping the f-pawn free to advance and block the bishop's line. The feared pin is not a real problem, since doubled pawns are fine when the king is safe.

sl-dp6.spoken: The King's Indian Attack hands White an extra tempo from the same defense, adding a touch of space and initiative. When Black trades central pawns, the center opens and offers White targets—that choice carries risk.

sl-dkr.spoken: The center push lands with tempo because development is complete and the pawn advance is supported. When the knight flees, the bishop retreats along the same line, and the recapture with the queen gains tempo and opens the rook file.

sl-d7f.spoken: The pawn on the edge hangs, and the king must guard it while the bishop is pinned to its diagonal. By sacrificing one pawn, White creates two separated passed pawns with opposite bishops—a winning endgame.

sl-ds2.spoken: The bishop wants the open diagonal outside the pawn chain; locking it in with the pawn move is usually wrong. But that lock is fine when the opponent's pawn on the open file lets you later trade pawns and re-open the diagonal for the bishop.

sl-d4c.spoken: Sometimes giving up the rook is the only way to wake the pieces up and create perpetual checks or mating threats, even when it looks wrong.

sl-dwq.spoken: The knight steps into a powerful outpost and White holds the bind. A quiet pawn move keeps the bishop pressing down the long diagonal while Black's counterplay runs out of air.

sl-dk6.spoken: Black trades off pieces and comes out of the opening with open queenside lines and firm control of d4. White tries to stop the bishop trade with b3 and then c4, but Black still gets in Bb7 and Qb6, setting up the exchange.

sl-dj9.spoken: The bishop lands on that diagonal, and the opening is named. The pawn move on the flank is prophylaxis, stopping the pin and the knight attack before they happen.

sl-dam.spoken: The central square is the battleground. One side wants to push there for space and activity; the other must stop it or get overrun. The queen patrols the kingside from afar, stopping a freeing pawn break and keeping the enemy king stuck in the center.

sl-dc9.spoken: The knight comes to the center early, and the game takes on the shape of a Pirc Defense. But here the knight sits on the queen's side file instead of the rim, so the usual pawn break is not immediately on the table.

sl-dzp.spoken: The bishop cannot be taken, because capturing it opens a mating net. The attacking pieces work together to trap the king in the center while the defender's forces stay tied down.

sl-e0f.spoken: The rook tries to guard the back rank, but it fails. The queen is overloaded, so taking the rook opens the mate on the back rank.

sl-eap.spoken: The first move sets up a mating net, not a check. Every reply must be answered with mate, so the key is often a quiet move that creates multiple threats at once.

sl-euk.spoken: The bishop's long diagonal holds the draw by controlling the queening square. Force that defender onto a short diagonal, and the attacker drives it away to queen.

sl-els.spoken: The pawn move blocks the center and stops White from dissolving those doubled pawns. It builds a chain, and when the base comes under attack, the file opens for the dark-squared bishop.

sl-e4h.spoken: The knight sacrifice opens the discovered attack on the queen, but the defender's in-between move complicates the sequence — calculate every reply before committing.

sl-eup.spoken: The defender's king placement decides the result. If the bishop stays on the long diagonal, the draw is simple; if the king wanders, the attacker gains the distant opposition and the pawn falls.

sl-evm.spoken: The lone pawn on the seventh rank tempts stalemate when the defender's king hides in front of it. The queen's diagonal pressure drags that king into the open, then the pawn becomes the shield for mate.

sl-e1q.spoken: The bishop steps out early, and Black seizes the initiative by attacking the central pawn.

sl-eqp.spoken: When the opponent's pieces are still at home, that is the moment to open the position and strike. Lagging development justifies aggressive play.

sl-ec9.spoken: The a-pawn push looks like a waiting move, but it secretly prepares to relocate the bishop. If the bishop then moves and the opponent grabs the pawn, a knight hop traps the queen. The opponent sees this, leaves the pawn alone, and develops instead.

sl-ejp.spoken: Black chooses the Semi-Slav setup. White picks either the sharp bishop move or the quiet pawn move. If Black later plays the standard queen's bishop development and then pushes the c-pawn, that push is a tempo wasted because the c-pawn has already moved.

sl-e7h.spoken: In the English, black's fianchetto setup aims to prepare the central pawn break with the d-pawn, though that break can be hard to achieve.

sl-dz5.spoken: White's grip is so total that even a quiet waiting move keeps the dream alive. When Black tries to reroute a knight to challenge the bishop, White answers with an active queen move, and Black's position stays hopeless.

sl-fgo.spoken: The king reaches the pawn in time, so trading rooks offers no win. The black king cannot step toward the pawns without letting it promote, and the endgame stays level.

sl-fod.spoken: The open files and the target pawn give White a decisive pull. The pawn that blocks the bishop also becomes a target itself.

sl-fjc.spoken: The kings are tied down defending their pawns. Push the flank pawn to create a passed pawn, forcing the enemy king to abandon its post.

sl-fp1.spoken: After Qb3, Black can answer with Nb6, then d6, when the center comes under pressure. White's priority is fast development, not grabbing material—so bring the pieces out and coordinate the attack.

sl-fiq.spoken: The knight is the key. Plant it on a square where it attacks the enemy pawn, and that pawn falls. Even with the king guarding, the knight creates zugzwang—no useful moves for the opponent, and the pawn must be surrendered.

sl-flu.spoken: Against the king's pawn, White has three main setups: the bishop to a central diagonal, the bishop to the far wing, or an immediate central pawn thrust. Black's own pawn on the fifth rank holds the center and dares White to push forward.

sl-f5v.spoken: The light-squared bishops decide this structure. White must stop the trade, because if Black swaps them, the white king stays exposed in the center and Black gains real play. The knight guards the key square, so Black cannot challenge the bishop there.

sl-fo7.spoken: Opposite-side castling turns the open files into highways for the major pieces toward the enemy king. First breakthrough usually wins, so every move targets opening and using those files.

sl-fen.spoken: The natural knight move is solid, but the queen move is sharper—it hits targets at once, forcing a check that grabs material or pries open weaknesses.

sl-fd8.spoken: The backward pawn sits alone, with no friendly pawn beside or behind to push it forward. That makes it a fixed target for the rest of the game.

sl-fix.spoken: The king move to defend looks natural, but after trades the enemy king breaks in and takes over. Capture the pawn instead — it removes the attacker and leaves you with a passed pawn, worth the isolation.

sl-g95.spoken: White aims for e4 to secure that square, so Black's standard reply is d5, challenging the center and sparking a sharp fight.

sl-g4y.spoken: A capture or check here only fails, so look for a forcing move that makes a threat—attack the queen and force a response.

sl-g9z.spoken: The queen sacrifice drags the rook into a fatal capture, because the knight guards the queen. The king is sealed in by its own army, and the knight lands the final checkmate.

sl-g59.spoken: Forcing moves come first in calculation. Once the checks, captures, and threats run out, look one move deeper: a quiet move may set a new threat or hit an undefended piece.

sl-gjd.spoken: The knight leaps forward with a threat: a piece wants to plant itself on that key square, giving Black a decisive edge. White must answer that immediate danger.

sl-fwy.spoken: Down the exchange means a rook is traded for a minor piece. That imbalance often comes with positional or attacking compensation.

sl-gj2.spoken: The knight lands on the central outpost and takes hold of the center. Black rushes to trade it off before the grip becomes permanent.

sl-gbl.spoken: Trading off that pawn leaves Black recapturing into a central majority and a development lead for White. The tactical threat before Black castles often makes Black decline the capture and castle instead.

sl-gc5.spoken: The key square's defender is overloaded, so taking it with the rook fails to the queen. The opponent's best reply is to trade queens and remove the defender.

sl-fyh.spoken: The bishop slides in, answering the threat while holding the initiative — the trapped rook breathes again.

sl-fpy.spoken: Black can trade the solid setup for a sharper one: develop the knight to the c-file, where it hits the e-pawn. White must answer that threat, and the c-pawn stays safe.

sl-gbe.spoken: The bishop on the far diagonal is a target. A pawn thrust forces it to take the knight, because retreating leaves it trapped by the pawn it was eyeing.

sl-gep.spoken: The advanced pawn cramps the opponent's pieces and buys space. It also becomes a target. The knight adds pressure, so the defender must be willing to sacrifice material to keep the pawn and start counterplay.

sl-gnf.spoken: Sacrifice and attack, from the player who usually waits — while the usual aggressor defends. Roles can flip; the position dictates the style.

sl-gt5.spoken: The center and queenside decide the fight. Black posts the queen on the long diagonal and the bishop behind it, pressuring the b-pawn and creating counterplay.

sl-gsp.spoken: In this corresponding-squares endgame, one pawn shapes which side of the triangle works, so the attacker switches to the other side. Build a four-square matching system where every king square pairs with one unique reply.

sl-gul.spoken: The plan aims at the queenside: a pawn push creates a second target, and whether the opponent blocks it or not, a weakness remains to be exploited.

sl-gqa.spoken: The bishop threatens the h-pawn while the rook-pawn advance looms. Black’s queen steps to guard the key dark square, and that same move keeps watch over the central files.

sl-gw2.spoken: The pawn captures forward, and Black picks the response. Recapturing with the knight attacks the queen, forcing it to move. That tempo funds pushing the pawn to challenge the strong piece, then development follows, and the position turns comfortable.

sl-gz2.spoken: Black's plan to ease pressure with Nf6-g6 runs into a sacrifice on g6, blasting open the h-file. White's pieces sit ready to drive the attack down that file, where the black king stands poorly shielded.

sl-h00.spoken: Pushing the c-pawn here can transpose into Maroczy-like structures, where enemy pieces land awkwardly and a strong center becomes buildable.

sl-gu2.spoken: Pushing the a-pawn is risky: Black can sacrifice it to bring the king toward the center and the kingside, and that activity can turn the position winning.

sl-goj.spoken: Black needs complications, not quiet moves. Pushing the f-pawn opens files and stirs activity when the b-file is sealed. Passive play just lets White bring every piece in, and Black bleeds a pawn down.

sl-gyp.spoken: The pawn thrust gains space and gives the bishop a haven on its home diagonal. If the attacker pushes past, the knight steps back to cover the central break and shuts the pawn lever down.

sl-h35.spoken: The queen’s move both bolsters the center and answers the bishop’s pin by swinging over to hit two pawns. If the opponent defends with the queen, the knight hangs, so they must make a weakening pawn move instead.

sl-gqb.spoken: The attack succeeds even if the queens come off, because the rook and pawns stand better in the endgame. That trade is still favorable — the advantage is not only in the attack.

sl-h0u.spoken: Opening success is not a better position, but a middlegame you understand more deeply than your opponent.

sl-gwe.spoken: The bishop holds the kingside together, covering two critical squares. Pushing the f-pawn trades solidity for space and open lines, yet the bishop stays vital for defense.

sl-gzg.spoken: Black tries to take on c2 with the bishop, but White answers by swinging the rook to d7, generating threats and netting material. Black's pieces remain scattered while White's pawns advance.

sl-gq1.spoken: Black’s plan is to push the b-pawn and post the bishop on a square that provokes the e-pawn. If White advances that pawn, the queen's bishop falls and castling is ruined — so the bishop must come out first.

sl-hc3.spoken: The c-pawn holds the key central squares, and the king arrives in time. Black's extra pawn is not enough — the position is drawn.

sl-hdj.spoken: A passed-pawn race can end with both queens on the board. Whoever can force a queen trade wins the endgame; if not, perpetual check often holds a draw.

sl-hcy.spoken: A stop-move invites a sacrifice. Black gives up material to crack open the lines, and when White takes, the kingside blows wide open.

sl-hku.spoken: A single protected passed pawn rarely decides the endgame alone. You need a second weakness to exploit, a second front to attack, before the defense cracks.

sl-hir.spoken: White often posts the bishop on e3, daring Black to take it. If Black captures, White retakes with the f-pawn, welcoming doubled pawns for a stronger center and an open f-file.

sl-hai.spoken: The queen and king on one line invite a skewer or a discovered check that costs the queen. But if the pawn is undefended, the king just takes it.

sl-hj1.spoken: White plans Qd2, queenside castling, and f3: castle long and storm with the g- and h-pawns. The structure differs from the Sicilian — pawn on e4, not e7 — but the idea holds.

sl-hiw.spoken: Playing Bxc6 grabs the bishop pair, but Black recaptures and pushes e5. White gains a pawn yet struggles to develop, while Black gets easy pressure.

sl-hqi.spoken: A quiet move on the flank restrains the opponent's queenside expansion before it starts, accepting that the attacker's plan is not the only one and that slowing counterplay holds its own value.

sl-hcj.spoken: Black targets the e-pawn and prepares to crack open the c-file with a timely pawn advance.

sl-hrx.spoken: The f-pawn advance signals aggression. It claims control of the central square, denying the knight that outpost, and sets up the further push that rips open the light squares when the bishop joins the attack.

sl-huq.spoken: White may open the a-file or keep the tension. If the file opens, Black's c6 pawn becomes a lasting weakness, though Black gets activity in return.

sl-i5d.spoken: The pawn retakes instead of the queen, and that choice transforms it into a passed pawn. It also opens lines for the pieces, giving them room to work.

sl-hzc.spoken: The h-pawn push to the fifth square is risky where the sixth would be sound. It opens a hook on the kingside and leaves the c-pawn's pressure unanswered.

sl-i4g.spoken: Castling does not end the attack. One careless queen move lets the bishop and queen combine for a mating threat on the kingside, and the king falls still — castled is not safe.

sl-i5w.spoken: A flexible knight move keeps the bishop's diagonal open and readies a central pawn push. The white pawn needs defending, and when the defender arrives, the knight and bishop combine against that pawn, stalling White's usual regrouping.

sl-i6l.spoken: The bishop develops to pin the knight and pressure the center. Black readies the queenside push, but when White stops it, the knight reroutes to the c-file, where the rook, queen, and second rook all line up to trade on the outpost and squeeze the file.

sl-hu9.spoken: Playing cxb6 and then Na4 against the c6 pawn costs White the c5 pawn, letting Black's rook hit the b4 pawn—one weakness traded for another, so White won't go for it.

sl-i9o.spoken: Stalemate ends the game in a draw: no legal moves, no check. In checkers that position loses, but in chess it only draws, so when you are ahead, steer clear of it.

sl-i5q.spoken: The h-file is a target, but the fortress is sound. Pushing the kingside pawns opens a line for the rook, yet with no weakness to exploit, the plan likely yields nothing—the move is not an error, just a promise the position cannot keep.

sl-hyi.spoken: When Black has not played the pawn break that frees the queenside, White can comfortably move the queen off the center file. Black's knight to the natural square is unusual and blocks the freeing pawn push.

sl-i51.spoken: The bishop on the long diagonal is a major asset, not a casual trade. When the opponent challenges it, retreating to a safe square and then pushing the center pawn leaves their bishop with no counterpart, a lasting structural weakness.

sl-i16.spoken: Knights and bishops trade at equal value, but the pawn structure decides which one truly earns its keep. With many pawns on the board, the knight hops over them and thrives. With the board opened up, the bishop's long diagonals dominate.

sl-i02.spoken: The knight steps to the edge, and White faces a choice. Taking it invites rook exchange, which White refuses. The bishop belongs in the center, where it blocks the knight's reentry and props up the middle.

sl-i8j.spoken: The move that refutes the surprise is only playable here, not a move earlier, and that's the trap. The defender may reject it over the board after spotting a tactic, but an unseen in-between move rescues them.

sl-i3x.spoken: Black had a clean route to equality: trade knights, then push the d-pawn. Instead, the longer road leaves the king exposed, both central pawns weak, White's pieces active, and the defense much harder.

sl-i7g.spoken: Castling without queenside space lets Black push the pawns, gain ground, and kick the knight. The knight jumps to the center, but after trades Black recaptures and the bishop arrives with tempo on the queen — playable compensation.

sl-iut.spoken: The fancy promotion to a rook or bishop may not be enough to mate, so the win turns into a draw. The safe choice is always the queen.

sl-ic2.spoken: The outpost knight looks strong, but only if it gets support. Without a follow-up, it sits idle while the opponent challenges or ignores it, so its value depends entirely on what comes next.

sl-ijg.spoken: The rook bears down on the e-pawn, and White wants to push it forward. Black answers by hitting that pawn again and again, often sending a knight to harass it from the side.

sl-iof.spoken: The patient defense fails once the pawn is taken and the bishop recaptures. The queen then awakens with a double attack, and the scattered pieces have no good answer.

sl-ifp.spoken: The king joins the pawn race from the front while the opponent's king is locked out. The pawns advance, and the knight stops the passed pawn from afar — that distance is its strength.

sl-idc.spoken: The queen's bishop is often the problem piece here. Black aims to bring it out actively, to the long diagonal, ready to bear down on the center.

sl-ivv.spoken: The knight lands with a mate threat on the king, but the queen's strike fails because the escape square stays open. The bishop that once covered it has already left, so the king slips free.

sl-ion.spoken: The pawn push creates the threat of pinning the knight against the queen. When the rook slides out to dodge the pin, the bishop still lands on its target—Black's only active piece. If Black trades it off, White's remaining plans gain real strength.

sl-idd.spoken: The pawn has been pushed twice, and that costs time. Find one move that serves two purposes: give the bishop a better diagonal and take the knight’s key square away—then the pawn is defended.

sl-ixd.spoken: The queen provokes a pawn push that opens the diagonal for her. When the knight is traded, the pawn advance gains space and builds a chain. If the opponent blocks that advance, the tempo lost lets the queen settle in, and the bishop has no easy square.

sl-imu.spoken: The first move is no pawn push and no check. That alone trims the candidate list sharply.

sl-id8.spoken: The pawn push is a mistake: it lets Black break out with either the knight or the pawn. Keep the bishop on the long diagonal; when Black answers on the flank, that is second-best.

sl-isv.spoken: The bishop develops to the long diagonal and White castles kingside. Black sets up the knight, bishop, and queen on their squares and castles queenside. Opposite wings and opposite majorities—White's passed pawn on the kingside, Black's on the queenside.

sl-ijj.spoken: The bishop gives itself up, but the capture walks into a queen strike. Black must refuse the bait and make a quiet move, so the bishop retreats and renews the threats. The defense is forced, and Black comes out a pawn up in chaos.

sl-ij5.spoken: The resulting pawn structure gives White extra central space, but Black owns more room on the queenside. Black expands with pawns, then pushes the c-pawn to open a route for the knight.

sl-ixf.spoken: Knight captures the pawn, and the b-pawn recaptures. Pushing the center pawn grabs space and builds a strong pawn center, opening easy development. Black castles, and the bishop slides to the diagonal aiming at the king's fortress.

sl-iwy.spoken: The bishop move is safe now, because the knight guards the queen's tactic. White strikes the center with the pawn. If black takes, the bishop recaptures and keeps developing. If black holds the center, the knight comes out and stops the pin with tempo.

sl-izd.spoken: In rook endgames, the king's activity is a huge asset. Even with equal material, the side whose king is more active often holds or wins. Exposed pawn weaknesses become serious liabilities late in the game.

sl-j0v.spoken: The queen steps out early because Black's development is almost finished, and she backs the bishop's coming move to g4. She also sets up instant mating threats on h2.

sl-izg.spoken: In a bishop endgame, when one side has two connected passed pawns, the defender's king must camp on the squares of his own bishop's color. That keeps the king on the right squares to back up the bishop's defense and steer clear of defeat.

sl-j39.spoken: A rook on the seventh rank pins the enemy king and locks down their pieces, forcing them into total passivity.

sl-j24.spoken: After a4 Bb7, White must not play c3 — it lets Black play d5 and equalize comfortably. In this setup, c3 is simply inaccurate.

sl-j1z.spoken: Trading on d5 is fine here, even though White gives up a bishop for a knight. The rook is already on e3, so retreating would waste a tempo.

sl-j31.spoken: The rook drops to the seventh rank—a classic winning pattern. The passed pawn marches, the defense is frozen, and the material gain decides it.

sl-iy4.spoken: White offers the queen trade, which Black accepts, and the game quiets down into a purely positional struggle. Both sides simply activate their pieces.

sl-j2z.spoken: The open file, the bishop pair, the extra pawns — White holds every lever in the position. Black is worse, but still breathing, and one defensive resource must be respected.

sl-j05.spoken: The natural defensive move is a trap. Sacrifice on that square; any recapture opens the door for the recapture and the rooks roll in — the attack turns monstrous. Extreme caution required.

sl-j47.spoken: The pieces lack harmony, so the advantage endures, with a spare pawn on the kingside. A queen step to the center earns engine approval at low depth and echoes a legendary player's choice, proving human instinct can match or beat early machine analysis.

sl-j0x.spoken: Black plays g3, then Re5. If White takes, Black recaptures and follows with Rae8, piling on the e-pawn. That rook lift is automatic in this structure.

sl-j15.spoken: Rook to e8 is Black’s standard attacking lift, setting up double rooks or a swing to e6. Since it poses no immediate threat, White’s best reply is Nd2, catching up in development.

sl-iy0.spoken: Black’s kingside light squares are the target — g4 is a sacrifice. If Black takes, White strikes with knight takes e6 and the queen joins. But Black can ignore it with knight c6, and White only wins the h-pawn. The pawn on h7 shields the king.

sl-jjp.spoken: The bishop faces a choice once the knight and pawn chase it away. Trading it off wins a pawn but hands over the bishop pair and hands Black active play.

sl-jev.spoken: The bishop's threat is real, but Black ignores it and strikes the center. Even hanging pawns are acceptable when the plan demands it. Trust the preparation and follow the idea, not the opponent's pressure.

sl-jnh.spoken: The king is barred from its escape square by the threat of a knight fork, while the loose pawn sits as a second target. One setup piles check, fork, and a hanging piece into a single web of threats.

sl-jdu.spoken: The queen must split the enemy king from the defending rook. Driving the king to the edge and bringing your own king up to support the queen creates threats that force the rook to fall.

sl-jqw.spoken: The knight gravitates to that weak square in front of the doubled pawns, a magnet for white pieces. Black trades the queenside pawn structure for the dark-squared bishop and kingside attacking chances, especially along the half-open g-file.

sl-jeu.spoken: The bishop steps out to a sharper square, and Black answers with a pawn push and a rook on the open file. A knight hops in to hit the h-pawn, which is defended twice but attacked three times, and the resulting checks create chaos.

sl-jmu.spoken: The king recaptures on the bishop, and suddenly white has no good passes. Black must dodge the tempting pawn push that lets white escape, and instead push the rook pawn first — it blocks white's counterpush, frees the bishop, and sets up a winning plan.

sl-jbt.spoken: The rook cannot shield the king at once—the enemy king attacks it. So the rook steps to a safe square first, often the fourth rank, to set up the bridge.

sl-jl6.spoken: The defending king races to the corner in front of the pawn. If he gets there, the bishop's pawn endgame often ends in a draw through stalemate tricks, and the same mechanism works from either side.

sl-jo3.spoken: Recapturing restores material but leaves the pawn weak and unguarded, so White is still effectively down in the center. Best development posts the bishop to prepare castling, the rook to challenge the pawn, and both pieces to eye that weak square.

sl-jqe.spoken: The bishop slides out to a familiar square, clearing the way for a knight fork. Both captures in the center fail: queen recapture lets the knight jump, and knight recapture lets the bishop fork the queen and the kingside pawn, then the knight leaps anyway.

sl-jo8.spoken: The pawn push claims the center while the king is exposed. If the queen grabs the flank pawn, the rook slides to the open file and the attack continues. When the knight comes out, the bishop retreats to a safe diagonal to keep the pressure.

sl-jrp.spoken: The bishop pins the knight against the queen, and a pawn strikes the knight. The defender harasses the bishop with a pawn push, forcing it to choose a square.

sl-jkt.spoken: The king must find the one square that holds the draw. That move lets the pawn be taken, and after the recapture the king stands ready to stop the last pawn. Every other step loses—one allows a pawn push that mates or strips all the pawns.

sl-jox.spoken: The pawn move stops the knight and bishop from landing on the enemy side. The bishop then develops to a square where it holds the center, and the knight heads for the hole to strike it. If the knight arrives, the bishop steps back and keeps control.

sl-jzq.spoken: Space is counted by the pieces that attack squares in the opponent's half. Tallying those attacks gives a rough measure of who owns more space.

sl-kcm.spoken: The king is in range, so the skewer forces the defending king off the queening square. Then the queen centralizes to escort her own king forward and shepherd the pawn home.

sl-kdy.spoken: The trades cost the bishop pair, but the queenside majority and a passed pawn on the d-file are the payoff. Black’s position folds, and the a-pawn runs through.

sl-k9c.spoken: The center and both wings hold firm while space is conceded. The opponent's threats never break the structure, and the game turns sharp the moment they commit too deeply.

sl-ksj.spoken: The bind needs quiet preparation before the attack begins. When the knight threatens to strike the bishop, pawn moves must first secure the center and guard the base before the bishop can step out.

sl-kij.spoken: The rook drives the king to the edge, and the king holds opposition. When the pattern is set, one waiting move passes the turn without check and without changing the structure, forcing the enemy king to a worse square.

sl-k40.spoken: The trades simplify the game into a rook endgame. White’s three-on-two majority on the kingside gives real chances, while Black’s queenside offers no progress.

sl-ko9.spoken: The rook lands on the central file and the knight is hanging. If it retreats, the bishop follows and the d-pawn collapses. White's activity, safer king, and Black's complete lack of counterplay make the position strategically lost.

sl-ky0.spoken: The knight sits on a light square, eyeing a dark one. From there it forks the king and rook, and the rook’s active-looking move is exactly what lets it in.

sl-k9q.spoken: The fortress holds despite White having a bishop and a pawn, because the bishop cannot control the queening square. Correct play makes it a draw.

sl-kc9.spoken: The queen cannot force mate alone; the king must advance to join the attack and cover the escape squares.

sl-kei.spoken: The bishop recaptures to develop, and the queen eyes the f-pawn. But this plan strands a backward pawn on the central file, and that weakness outweighs the play.

sl-kol.spoken: The knight lands on its natural square, but the pawn chain blocks its best jumps. Rerouting it through the other route aims it at the center hole and readies the pawn break.

sl-kog.spoken: The bishop sits well, but a knight would sit better. Push the bishop into a forcing capture that hits the enemy knight. If the king takes back, the knight steps in to attack the queen, and once the queen flees, a fork wins the rook.

sl-kjl.spoken: In corresponding squares, a triangle of three squares—two diagonal, one central—gives the strictest correspondence. Each side has only one path between the diagonal squares, so the defender's options shrink and the mapping becomes unambiguous.

sl-k5t.spoken: The knight develops to the edge, not the center. From there it can return to press the backward pawn, or swing to the other side to keep both options alive.

sl-kxp.spoken: The knight steps in, and the pawn lunges to chase it off. White can capture with check, or take with the knight, forking queen and rook, and the fork wins material.

sl-kkd.spoken: The move that loosens the king's shelter is often a target, yet sometimes it is the right choice. It can fight for the center or stop the opponent's pawn from advancing, especially when their bishop cannot punish the weakened diagonal.

sl-k8v.spoken: White protects the knight with a second knight, so when Black captures it, White recaptures with that knight and avoids doubled pawns.

sl-jzi.spoken: Development wins. When your opponent falls behind in it, strike—open lines with a pawn break or sacrifice to break through.

sl-kqu.spoken: The pawn is bait. When the queen pressures it, the bishop trades itself for the knight instead of pushing a pawn, and the queen guards the target while the threat on the center remains.

sl-knq.spoken: The knight settles on a home square behind the pawns, forming a solid wall. Do not capture the center pawn early; first bring the rook to support the pawn push that claims the center.

sl-k0y.spoken: The bishop forks both rooks, winning material and ending the fight. The defense is to grab the passed pawn first, then get the rook behind it and push — stepping to the side instead lets the fork in.

sl-lt0.spoken: Play Bc4 and Qe2, then push e5 and e6 to build a powerful center. That setup invites sharp play: White may give up the queen for three pieces, though the center pawns fall.

sl-lqa.spoken: The center pawns stake their claim, but Black's path is not yet fixed — several healthy moves still lead to different openings.

sl-lko.spoken: The attack is over, the king is safe but doing nothing, and with the initiative gone, the structure may be the next thing to crack.

sl-l4f.spoken: The knight on the outpost is the key piece. Black wants to trade it off with the bishop, but first must spend a move to stop the knight from jumping in. Once the knight is gone, the center break and queenside play open up.

sl-l63.spoken: The bishop steps out to make room for the queen. She defends the pawn and aims at the enemy base. The knight develops to guard that outpost, and the other knight comes out to block the annoying jump.

sl-ljz.spoken: The bishop sacrifice on the kingside only works when the enemy queen cannot rush to defend the back rank.

sl-lfm.spoken: The bishop stops the pawn from on high, but that long diagonal gives it too much ground to guard. Drive it onto a shorter one, and the king steps in to finish the job.

sl-l70.spoken: The pawn looks free, but taking it walks into the attack. White keeps pushing with pieces aimed at the g-file while the knight jumps to the strong square.

sl-loq.spoken: The knight holds critical squares and backs the bishop trade, steering play into a strong knight versus bad bishop ending. The queen loops around to the other wing, aiming at the weak pawn.

sl-l1f.spoken: The kingside pawn break is the lever. It opens lines and leaves the king exposed, while the backward pawn and the loose center square demand constant care. With no clear way to activate the pieces, Black's side plays itself.

sl-ltc.spoken: e5 is a powerful move for White: it blocks the bishop's diagonal, grabs space, and sets a trap for the queen. Black has to answer precisely or the queen gets caught.

sl-ld3.spoken: The position may whittle down to rook and pawn endgame, which demands technical precision. Confidence is fine, yet the path is anything but simple.

sl-lkc.spoken: The knight lands on the central square, and White must choose the recapture. The queen takes back, keeping the king safe and the pawns intact; the pawn take exposes the king and ruins the structure.

sl-llv.spoken: The pawn duo stands strong when the knight stays. Capturing it lets the bishop recapture and seize the bishop pair with a central pawn mass. Pin the knight to the king instead, and then the enemy knight jumps forward, supported by pawns.

sl-l7e.spoken: A passed pawn is a criminal that should be kept under lock and key. If it’s blockaded, it is harmless; if it’s free, it runs.

sl-l24.spoken: The bishop move tempts to break open the center, but it fails because the kingside pawn is loose. The opponent first probes with a pawn push to force the queen to declare a square, yet that square still leaves the weak pawn hanging, so the break never works.

sl-luv.spoken: The bishop takes the knight, but the queen recaptures with venom. If castling instead, the knight jumps forward, attacking the pawn. Meet it with the knight to the center, then swing it wide, eyeing the queen and shielding the pawn.

sl-m83.spoken: The knight is for harrying pawns; the king is for stopping them. Put the right piece on the right job, especially against a rook pawn.

sl-md6.spoken: The dark-squared bishop is your strongest piece in this setup. Trading it for a knight to win a pawn is tempting, but it lets White's threats grow too strong, so the trade fails.

sl-mgm.spoken: The bishop recaptures, then the rook slides to the seventh rank, hitting the queen. Every escape square fails: one flight loses her to a rook check, the other lets a knight trap her. The rook reaches that rank and the extra material decides.

sl-m9t.spoken: Retreating the bishop keeps the pressure; capturing would hand the queen a tempo and let the bishop fix its gaze on the kingside.

sl-m1d.spoken: The queen takes the piece, but that gift comes with a price. The enemy strikes at exposed pawns and the king, while the bishop sits idle and must be roused to guard the monarch and fuel the assault.

sl-m0l.spoken: Castling kingside is safe here when your pieces are developed and you control the center—even with that pawn pushed forward. King safety comes from activity and central control, not pawn structure alone.

sl-m0i.spoken: Rooks on the same line can shut each other out, so side-by-side placement wastes their power. Put them on separate lines to seal off the king's exits.

sl-mj6.spoken: The Hedgehog offers several pawn breaks, each aimed at a different part of the opponent's structure. One famous idea involves a rook on the g-file supporting a pawn push there, a plan taken from a classic game.

sl-m1w.spoken: Once Black pushes the pawn, the position sharpens. The long-term risk is the knight: if White consolidates, it retreats to a passive square.

sl-mgn.spoken: The knight is ready to leap in and trap the queen. They find one saving resource, but it can be undone. Take the bishop anyway, and the recapture comes with check, forcing the queens off, but they keep four extra pawns, one passed.

sl-lx8.spoken: The queen steps out with a threat: if Black castles, the bishop takes the knight, then swings over to pressure the queen and force a pawn weakness. That opens the door to a serious attack, and if Black falters, it can end in mate.

sl-m18.spoken: The queen takes the bishop, inviting the rook to recapture. After rook takes rook with check, the queen answers back, and the result is two connected passed pawns with a safe king — a technical win.

sl-meg.spoken: The rook outnumbers the knight, but a hasty win slips away. The defender holds by trading rook for knight at the right moment, turning the game into a pawn ending where king opposition decides the outcome.

sl-m9s.spoken: The pawn push attacks the bishop, which steps back along the diagonal. Capturing on the knight would hand Black a tempo against the queen, and taking the pawn is not forcing because Black's queen reply carries threats.

sl-mcr.spoken: The knight is heading for the outpost. The pawn push that would stop it is impossible while the bishop hangs on the long diagonal, so the queen must first defend, and only then can the pawn advance.

sl-lx5.spoken: The knight's retreat invites the pawn break. Pushing the f-pawn traps the bishop, so avoid it. The other pawn advance harasses the knight and then opens the center, or it comes at once with wild play against the king.

sl-msd.spoken: Black's center grip and kingside pressure make this an upgraded Benoni for him. The extra queenside pawns are hard to mobilize and one can become a target.

sl-mmg.spoken: In this F3 Nimzo, White’s plan is to open lines toward the black king. The knight goes to g5, stopping e7-e4, which would shut the bishop’s diagonal.

sl-mnw.spoken: Black often aims for b6 and Ba6, trading off White's light-squared bishop — that's the key defensive plan. If Black instead plays Nc6, that chance is gone, and White's bishop stays strong.

sl-mrm.spoken: The f-pawn advance loosens the kingside and hands White new targets, unsettling the position. Black stands solid and gains nothing from complications.

sl-mmx.spoken: Black's queen sits active on a5, but White's coordination is stronger. If Black takes the bishop, White's king recaptures with tempo, gaining time and leaving White the better structure.

sl-mq0.spoken: En passant answers the pawn push. After the recapture, the rook attacks the knight. If the bishop is taken, the rook strikes and the queen and bishop join in. If the pawn blocks, the bishop captures, and the recapture allows a fork.

sl-mqm.spoken: The unique solution forces every white move. Any deviation stretches the mate longer. When alternatives match in length, the record-setting position has none.

sl-mmj.spoken: White’s down a piece but the attack is strong. Bring more force in with Rf3—a queen check just hands Black time to rally.

sl-mp6.spoken: The rook pawn reaches the sixth rank, and the defender runs to the far corner to hold the draw. A careless pawn offer or king step lets the bishop build a wall and shut the win down.

sl-n8c.spoken: In a race of passed pawns, the king's activity and rook placement decide everything. Cutting off the enemy king turns the sprint into a stroll.

sl-na2.spoken: The rooks belong on the open file. Any side move wastes time, so commit them there and let them do the work.

sl-n76.spoken: The pawn wedges into the king's fortress, guarding the squares that keep the net closed. The queen slides through the dark squares it weakens, and mate or resignation follows.

sl-mxq.spoken: The doubled f-pawns are a price, not a sentence. Black can refuse them by pushing the d-pawn first; when the bishop pins the knight, the knight steps aside, the queen slips to her best square, and castling stays intact.

sl-msl.spoken: The kings drift one square farther off, and the win evaporates. Black's plan is the pawn break, then the other pawn one step sooner. With both pawns advanced, neither side can force a thing, and the position is dead drawn.

sl-n05.spoken: White castles, and Black's d5-pawn finds itself attacked three times but defended only twice. Passivity like Be6 lets White lock the center with e3 and follow with Nb5, securing a positional edge.

sl-myy.spoken: The knight and pawn duo, with a pawn on the adjacent central file, keeps every option alive and answers nearly any white setup, from the London to the double-fianchetto systems.

sl-mxr.spoken: The king is still in the middle, so long castling shifts the fight to the center files. The backward pawn on the open file becomes a target, and the offside bishop leaves the kingside underdefended, while the rook on the other wing does nothing.

sl-mt8.spoken: Castling queenside tucks the king away and brings the rook to the center, delaying the pawn recapture. The knight presses the d-pawn, but the bishop aims at the king's field, threatening the weakness where the h-pawn never moved.

sl-mzc.spoken: Trading pieces after Nxd5 Be6 looks natural, but it's not best. Black gets easy play.

sl-n0d.spoken: White’s f-pawn leaves the king exposed, and Black’s king is safe, so despite the pawn structure, Black stands better with more active play.

sl-mup.spoken: Against the doubled fianchetto setup, White's central push gains space and reshapes the game into a Benoni-style structure with a pleasant edge.

sl-mz5.spoken: In the Tarrasch French, Black hits the center with c5 and White pushes back with c4, keeping the tension. The position stays about even, with White holding only the edge of moving first.

sl-mv1.spoken: The b-pawn is a counter-sacrifice to pull the bishop off its diagonal. With that piece deflected, central pawns advance to strike, and the fianchettoed bishop adds pressure on the center.

sl-n04.spoken: In this Tarrasch line, White looks to clamp down on the queenside, with ideas of Qc2 and Na4 hitting the bishop on b6 and the d5 pawn. Black needs active play here, or he faces a slow positional squeeze.

sl-n2x.spoken: The pawn push drives the black pieces back, and then white collects the center pawn. From there, the play offers a trade of both rooks for the queen, or a bishop move that wins the exchange.

sl-n0c.spoken: White's pawn on d3 is a target, and only f4 can remove the knight on d4 to eliminate it. But f4 weakens the kingside and leaves e3 vulnerable.

sl-mzq.spoken: If White plays Nxc6, Black reinforces the center, but White avoids the isolated pawn. Black’s active play gives compensation.

sl-n67.spoken: After the central break, Black's king move walks into a winning tactic — checks and captures net the queen.

sl-n38.spoken: The Najdorf offers White many sound plans: sharp main lines, classical setups, the flank pawn push, or a fianchetto. The English Attack, with its early king-pawn advance, brings club players the same fierce attacking play as the Yugoslav against the Dragon.

sl-o1i.spoken: The weak push opens lines toward the king and leaves the kingside exposed, so the side with the initiative strikes immediately.

sl-nnv.spoken: The opening mix-up leaves White with the bishop pair and pawns on both flanks, while Black's pawn weakness on the dark squares means a lifetime of passive defense.

sl-ns3.spoken: The Mar del Plata setup keeps options open on the queenside. An early pawn push gains space there, and a quieter one shows the flexibility of the whole formation.

sl-nn7.spoken: White dodges the complications with Rc7, and Black answers Bc5. A tactical clash follows: a knight lands on e6, queens come off, and Black ends up winning the b-pawn.

sl-o1p.spoken: The b-pawn advance is a recurring theme, but urgency matters. The rook and queen support it, yet the real priority may be striking the center pawn or pressuring the knight before pushing.

sl-ne9.spoken: Playing the pawn first secures the Semi-Slav and dodges the exchange line. That move order keeps the center tense, so White can't simplify with the pawn trade.

sl-o2u.spoken: Winning demands the most precise continuation, one that leaves the opponent zero chances. In a team tournament, risk avoidance is paramount, so keep that diagonal open and bring the king into play.

sl-nzy.spoken: A move to the side can provoke and prepare at once: it asks the opponent to declare their plan while setting up a pawn thrust at the knight. Play it only when no immediate threat or central clash demands an answer.

sl-nea.spoken: The triangle setup hands White three paths. The quiet pawn move shuts in the light-squared bishop. The knight move invites the sharp line where Black wins a pawn and White scrambles to reclaim it. The aggressive pawn push starts the Marshall Gambit proper.

sl-o23.spoken: In pure knight endgames, material alone doesn't decide. Piece activity, coordination, and the king's role matter greatly. A missed pawn break let the opponent's defensive setup stand, and with it gone, progress becomes possible.

sl-o1c.spoken: Once the defender's king is cut off, the pawn cannot be stopped. The rook builds a bridge to escort it forward and promote.

sl-nna.spoken: In the Ruy Lopez, White sometimes chooses Qe2, but here a different plan appears: Bb1, intending b3 to guard the queenside light squares instead of a3. This line is seen as a more flexible setup.

sl-nie.spoken: The bishop stays home on purpose. Holding it back keeps White's f-pawn advance toothless, and leaves the way open to swing it to the long diagonal.

sl-nw2.spoken: The bishop pins the knight, a setup many dislike, yet it fits the plan. White shields the pawn, fianchettoes, and keeps queens on for pressure. Black provokes queenside weaknesses; White gains the open file and the bishop pair.

sl-o6c.spoken: White keeps developing and connects the rooks, building pressure against the isolated pawn and the enemy king.

sl-o6g.spoken: The queen alone cannot force the win here; the rooks stay on to threaten mate, because trading them down opens no path through the fortress.

sl-of8.spoken: After Black pushes d4, e4 turns into a weak square that White's knight can later occupy. The knight on f1 is also free to redeploy and back up the attack.

sl-ofc.spoken: Black’s knight hits g5 to stop the bishop from going there, but White plays Bg5 anyway. Black must take, and White recaptures with the bishop, keeping that knight active and dangerous.

sl-o9j.spoken: The knight leaps forward and cramps the queen's choices. If she grabs the pawn, the rook slides beside her and she is trapped. She picks her escape square, but the bishop's discovery springs, and now the queen has no safe path home.

sl-om2.spoken: The pinned piece cannot legally step off the line to the king, so it cannot grab the checking unit. Spotting the pin decides which checks and captures actually work.

sl-okc.spoken: Castling queenside keeps the king safe. Refusing it leaves the king exposed, and every attempt to hold the knight opens another check.

sl-ogp.spoken: The king is chased to the edge. The queen pins the bishop along the diagonal, then a second bishop steps in to pin the queen herself. The doubled pressure wins material.

sl-odz.spoken: The queen, bishop, and knight all aim at the square in front of the enemy king. Pieces that don't join the attack, like a passive knight or a rook far away, are irrelevant and safe to ignore.

sl-o9x.spoken: Staking the queen on a losing attack shows the mindset is still set to attack when the position calls for consolidating or taking the draw. The move does not lose on the spot, but it steers the game toward defeat.

sl-o70.spoken: The knight lands on the strong square, and every white defender is already covering the central pawn. Black's pawn push is playable but weakens the kingside: the knight now eyes two outposts, and while black struggles to win the pawn, white opens lines.

sl-ocb.spoken: The bishop is rushing to the far dark squares, forcing Black to spend tempi to stop it. When Black pushes the pawn and White recaptures, the right recapture keeps the queen active where she also restrains the opponent's pawn push.

sl-ou3.spoken: The knight move chokes the queen and bishop, so it’s rarely worth it. Black answers with a central pawn push, reaching a flexible, solid setup.

sl-opn.spoken: Black's early c4 shuts the center and blocks White's bishop from the b1-h7 diagonal. It's a deliberate plan to restrict White's pieces and set up a queenside push.

sl-oqv.spoken: Black's h6 hits the knight on g5. White can capture on h6 and pry open the h-file, but that costs White's own pawn structure, so the attack must be weighed against the damage.

sl-ov7.spoken: The rook choice looks small but carries real weight. Keeping that rook on the d-file holds the center and answers the pawn break before it lands; sliding the other rook forward is the lazy option that lets Black's plan breathe.

sl-oqn.spoken: The knight on the edge isn’t trapped, since taking it lets the queen give check. Pushing the pawn gives the knight a way out and creates luft, so the back rank stays safe.

sl-opy.spoken: Black's knight move targets White's dark-squared bishop, and trading it off is key. If that bishop survives, it dominates the open board, especially since Black's b4 push leaves the dark squares weak.

sl-ot7.spoken: The h-pawn strips the king's cover, forcing the rook to babysit the king. That rook never joins the attack.

sl-oso.spoken: Queenside castling is rare in closed queen-pawn openings. It usually creates a double-edged game where both sides storm opposite wings.

sl-oyc.spoken: The rook's true endgame edge over a bishop or knight is not mobility—both cover equal ground on their lines—but that the rook can always offer itself in exchange, while the minor piece can never force that trade.

sl-oxe.spoken: The backward pawns sit easier to defend in this structure. Black contests both central squares, White contests the other two, so the pawn cannot advance, but the knight can settle on that forward square.

sl-opl.spoken: White’s e4 push creates tactical chances; if black captures, Rxb4 or Qg5 strike with multiple threats. White’s center attack proves decisive, while black’s queenside play lags too far behind.

sl-oqa.spoken: White's h3 is not urgent, since the pin on the knight poses no real threat—Black can simply hold onto the light-squared bishop. Space and the bishop pair are White's main trumps, but Black stands firm.

sl-ox6.spoken: Castling is still blocked, so one move must guard the center and prepare the king’s escape. Trading bishops gives up the pair, and stepping the king loses the d-pawn. The right move defends the queen, so the rook can recapture and open the way to castle.

sl-or1.spoken: Black opens the position willingly, and that is suspect, because White's army is better poised for open lines. Swapping rooks on the f-file suits White, but if White starts that exchange, Black's queen emerges with threats.

sl-oug.spoken: White’s queenside pawns are cracked, Black’s bishop on d7 sits idle, and White’s bishop on d2 has no scope. With opposite-colored bishops, the attacker gets the edge in the middlegame.

sl-or8.spoken: Black's queen attacks the king, but White ignores it. The mating pattern follows, and White has a forced mate, with a perpetual check as an alternative.

sl-oya.spoken: The pawn chain leans queenside, and the hole in front of it is a permanent outpost. The center looks solid, but that weakness lets Black chip away at it.

sl-ou2.spoken: Trading knights is the cleanest answer, and when Black recaptures with the pawn, the central push arrives unopposed. Black has survived the opening without problems—not better, but comfortable.

sl-oys.spoken: The extra tempo in the reversed Benoni funds a knight jump that trades a set of minor pieces. That trade is the standard principle here, and it dulls Black's activity while giving White room to breathe.

sl-p15.spoken: Black pushes the pawn to invite support for a queenside expansion. The rook steps to the open file, a developing move that also answers the pawn's threat.

sl-p27.spoken: White fianchettoes on the kingside with g3 and Bg2, keeps the center flexible with d3, and faces a well-analyzed Sicilian line where the main continuations often end in near-draws at top level.

sl-p5b.spoken: White takes on d5, and if Black recaptures with the knight, White grabs the b5 pawn. Swinging the bishop to a8 after that gives up less grip on the a2-g8 diagonal than taking d5 earlier would.

sl-p68.spoken: Black has given up two pawns to get active pieces. The light-squared bishop is gone, leaving White’s king on g1 exposed and the light squares near it weak. Black’s whole army is in the fight, but White’s queenside pieces have not developed.

sl-p2u.spoken: The pawn sits undefended, and the diagonal lies open. Pushing the g-pawn exposes both, nearly losing. The bishop belongs on the long diagonal, where it guards the pawn and seals that line.
